Srinagar, Sep 15: After a gap of more than two years, the Mutahida Majlis-e-Ulema (MMU) Jammu & Kashmir on Tuesday held a major Ulema meet and Seerat Conference in Srinagar, with more than 70 Ulema and Mashaikh participating in deliberations on pressing social, moral and religious issues.
The one-day conference, held under the chairmanship of Mirwaiz Umar Farooq after authorities granted permission for the gathering, saw participation from religious scholars from different parts of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
Ulema from Kashmir districts, as well as Jammu, Poonch, Rajouri, Kargil and Doda, attended the conference, which emphasised greater coordination and interaction among religious scholars, mosques and madrasas across the region.
The conference adopted two broad resolutions, one focusing on contemporary social challenges and the role of Ulema and religious institutions, while the other stressed unity within the Muslim Ummah, sectarian harmony and mutual respect despite differences of Maslak.
The first resolution expressed concern over drug and substance abuse, suicides and self-harm, mental and emotional distress among youth, irresponsible use of social media, weakening family bonds and the disconnect between young people and religious and community institutions.
The participants stressed that Ulema, Imams, mosques and madrasas could play an important preventive and supportive role in addressing these challenges by creating safe spaces where young people and families can discuss emotional distress, loneliness, anxiety and family pressures without fear of stigma.
The conference called for greater awareness among Imams and Ulema about signs of emotional distress and urged them to encourage families to respond with compassion and guide those in need towards professional counselling and mental-health support.
As part of the proposed outreach, the MMU resolved that designated Friday sermons would focus on a common social issue across participating mosques, enabling Ulema across Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh to collectively raise awareness about issues requiring urgent societal attention.
The MMU also decided to endeavour to hold regular, preferably monthly, meetings in different districts and areas, involving local Ulema, Imams, mosques and madrasas to identify local concerns and develop practical responses.
The conference further stressed that mosques and madrasas should increasingly function as centres of guidance, youth engagement, family support and community welfare alongside their religious and educational responsibilities.
On drug addiction, the Ulema called for a consistent approach to tackling substance abuse and expressed concern over the simultaneous expansion and normalisation of alcohol.
The conference said efforts against drug addiction could be undermined if new liquor licences are issued and alcohol availability is expanded in the name of tourism. It called upon the government to reconsider such an approach and stop further promotion and expansion of alcohol availability.
Environmental responsibility also figured prominently in the deliberations. The conference recommended using Friday sermons and mosque-based programmes to create awareness about reducing plastic and polythene use, preventing littering and dumping of waste in water bodies, and protecting wetlands.
The participants expressed concern over the condition and encroachments affecting Dal Lake, Wular Lake, Nigeen Lake, wetlands and other water bodies, stressing that conservation of nature and protection of shared natural resources constituted a moral and religious responsibility.
The second resolution focused on unity within the Muslim Ummah and urged Ulema to maintain mutual respect despite differences in schools of thought and interpretation.
The conference acknowledged that differences of Maslak have historically existed within the Ummah, but stressed that such differences should not become a source of hatred, hostility or division.
The participants emphasised that the mosque's Mimbar is an Amanah, or sacred trust, and should not be used to promote sectarianism, ridicule another Maslak, spread hatred or deepen divisions.
The conference called upon Ulema from different schools of thought to promote mutual respect, dialogue and brotherhood and to focus religious discourse on shared moral, spiritual and social responsibilities.
It also stressed the need for greater interaction among Ulema from different regions and schools of thought. The proposed district-level meetings are expected to provide a platform for strengthening communication, mutual understanding and cooperation among religious scholars and religious institutions.
The participants said the role of Ulema and religious institutions should extend beyond ritual matters and remain closely connected with people's everyday concerns, particularly the anxieties and aspirations of the younger generation.
The MMU said the conference was intended to mark the beginning of a sustained process of grassroots engagement rather than end with the adoption of resolutions. The proposed initiatives include coordinated Friday sermons, district-level meetings, counselling and community awareness programmes.
More than 70 Ulema and Mashaikh participated in the event. Among those present were Moulana Rehmat-ullah Mir Qasmi, Mufti Azam Nasir ul Islam Farooqi, Mufti Nazir Ahmad Qasmi, Mufti Mohammad Yaqoob Baba Madani, Moulana Masroor Abbas Ansari, Moulana Showkat Hussain Keng, Mufti Enayat Ullah Jammu, Sheikh Mehboob Ali Wajdani, Mufti Abdul Rashid Miftahi, Pir Rehmatullah Sahib, Moulana Syed Tayyub, Mufti Syed Sharief Ul Haq Bukhari, Mufti Ajaz ul Hassan Banday, Mufti Zia ul Haq Nazmi, Mufti Pirzada Reyaz Ahmad, Moulana Adnan Nadwi, Sibt Mohammad Shabir Qumi, Moulana Ghulam Rasool Noori, Moulana Ali Akbar, Moulana Syed Shah Waris Shah Bukhari and Pir Iftikhar Ahmad Kamli, among others.

Actor Tatyana Ali is advocating for Black and Indigenous maternal health
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Actor and singer Tatyana Ali has become an important voice in a growing movement to improve maternity health outcomes for Black and Indigenous mothers and babies by addressing systemic racism and inequity in maternity care. Ali has been calling for reproductive justice since experiencing what she calls "obstetric violence" during the delivery of her first-born son Aszi in 2016.
Ali, 47, says being a mother is the most important role of her life, as she embarks on the latest chapter of her Hollywood career. She will compete on the new season of Dancing with the Stars on ABC, starting Tuesday, September 15. Ali is perhaps best known for her role as the lovable Ashley Banks on the NBC sitcom The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air in the 1990s. Since then, she has acted in TV and digital series, movies and released an album.
Ali and her husband Vaughn Rasberry are raising two sons, Alejandro and Aszi. In an interview with NPR, she said it was the birth of her oldest, Aszi, that eventually made her want to speak out for Black and Indigenous mothers.
Ali described having a normal pregnancy with Aszi and the days of waiting for his birth as filled with joy.
"So excited and just waiting, waiting, waiting, waiting, waiting. My mother's song when she was waiting for me was 'cuando, cuando, cuando – when when, when? When are you coming?' I sang that song. I thought we were prepared," she said.
But during the delivery at the hospital, Ali says her birth plan was immediately ignored. And she was physically restrained.
"It went from a small group of people in the room to many people in the room screaming, yelling at me," she said. "I was held down by about four people."
Ali described chaos and aggressive and dismissive behavior by the doctor and nurses.
"Faces, screaming, terror, panic. I needed somebody to help me," she said.
Ali says her hospital records detail the doctor using a high-risk emergency procedure that is rarely used. The Zavanelli maneuver is a last-resort procedure performed when a baby is stuck inside the birth canal. Ali says in her case, her son was already crowning when the doctor pushed him back inside of her. "After they pushed him inside me, and I remember roaring. I convulsed after that. Like my body – I can hear the bed just go buh-buh-buh-buh," she said, describing the sound of the bed shaking. "And I was out."
The doctor then performed an emergency c-section to deliver her son.
Aszi became strong enough to go home after several days in the neonatal intensive care unit. Ali says at the time, the hospital's head urologist told her the infant was in shock from his traumatic birth. Ali says it took some time for her to realize she had experienced "obstetric violence." She blames systemic racism in healthcare, after hearing similar stories from other women of color.
"It wasn't just me. I was just one tiny drop in a very, very large bucket that has been overflowing for a very, very long time," she said.
Black maternal health in America
The United States is arguably the most dangerous country in the developed world to give birth to a baby, with a much higher rate of maternal deaths compared to other wealthy nations. 649 women in the U.S. died of maternal causes in 2024, according to federal data.
But there is a huge disparity in the numbers: Black mothers were more than three times as likely to lose their lives from pregnancy-related causes than white women.
Many in the maternity care field are concerned by stories like Ali's and the statistics. Dr. Tamika Auguste is chair of women's and infants' services at MedStar Washington Hospital Center.
"I can't tell you how many Black women have said to me: 'Hey Doc, don't let me die,'" she said in an interview. "The poor rates in outcomes of Black maternity patients is something that rocked us to our core."
Auguste says important work has been done in the maternal healthcare field to improve protocols and guidelines to address conditions like cardiac issues, hemorrhaging and hypertension, which are more prevalent among Black women. But she says there's still the problem of bias.
Auguste points to the dangerous misconception among some in medicine that Black patients have a higher threshold for pain. She believes it's key for medical teams to acknowledge that disparities exist and communicate intentionally about bias to prevent it from affecting patient care.
"We are very purposeful in looking at outcomes with a lens of demographics of different racial breakdown of different types of data," said Auguste.
She says those discussions are moving the needle slightly. Her hospital in Washington, D.C., employs about a dozen midwives.
"Physician, midwife, doula, nurse, anesthesiologist, working together as a team. That is critical," said Auguste.
But access to maternity care is a barrier. Dr. Auguste's own hospital recently closed one of two postpartum units, citing financial pressure. More than 500 hospitals closed maternity wards between 2010 and 2022, according to a study published in the medical research journal JAMA.
Nationwide, more than half of counties don't have hospital-based labor and delivery services, according to the non-profit organization March of Dimes. The group calls these maternity care deserts.
In the South, Black and Indigenous women are more likely to live in areas without adequate access to maternity care providers, according to KFF Health News. People of color are also more likely to be uninsured.
Healing journey
Ali says, through her own healing, she has found beautiful relationships and support in the Black and Indigenous maternal health community. She travels the country speaking at conferences and other events, sharing her personal story and talking about solutions.
Ali founded a business called Baby Yams to fund grants to Black and Indigenous birth workers and students. Her team makes heritage baby quilts in vivid ankara and batik fabrics. Each quilt has a special name and represents protection and strength.
"They're this storytelling machine of the possibility, the hope," explained Ali.
Baby Yams donates part of the proceeds to the Birth Future Foundation, which provides grants to midwives, doulas and student birth workers.
"There are solutions. The solutions exist now," Ali said. "There are birth centers, there are midwives educating themselves, doulas going into practice."
A midwife in Alabama is one of many birth workers who has benefited from Ali's financial support. Nadia Gramby says she completed her licensing requirements to advance from a doula to a midwife thanks to a Birth Future Foundation scholarship funded by Ali.
Gramby, 41, says her work helping families across Alabama is especially important because nearly 40% of counties in the South are maternity care deserts, according to March of Dimes. Gramby says her practice is an important option, especially for Black families that may not otherwise have immediate access to care.
"It is an amazing joy to see families who feel safe and know that they're seen, and they made decisions to make sure that their children are born in safe environments, where they feel comfortable, and they feel cared for and they have been educated and they are empowered," she told NPR.
Black midwives and doulas have had a rich history in African American life and communities for centuries.
Midwives are medically trained to perform many of the same functions and procedures as doctors when women are having babies in low-risk situations. They deliver in hospitals alongside physicians, birth centers and in homes. They also frequently collaborate with doulas, who provide non-medical support. Research shows midwife births lead to lower rates of complications.
A report released this year by March of Dimes finds midwives are critical and part of the solution to expanding access to maternity care, especially in rural and under-resourced communities. The group is calling for policies to remove requirements for physician supervision and increase reimbursement rates from Medicaid and private insurance.
But some physicians and policymakers worry about the safety of giving birth outside of hospitals, especially when there's an emergency. Midwives can't perform surgery for example, so that can mean delays to getting emergency treatment. Some states have laws making it harder for midwives to practice.
When Ali became pregnant with her second child, she and her husband searched carefully for the right midwife and found one. She says that time around, her birth plan and desires were acknowledged.
"We deserve to be cared for. We deserve to have choices. We deserve to have control over our own bodies," she said. "We are beautiful. We are deserving of loving hands."

Spaceflight is a risky business. Keeping astronauts healthy, especially their hearts, has driven Benjamin Levine’s career as a top consulting cardiologist to NASA. Now that a Mars mission is on the horizon, his most recent research continues to test how well exercise maintains the heart’s structure and function during prolonged spaceflight.
In their paper published Tuesday in Circulation, an international team reports results from 13 astronauts who performed onboard echocardiograms during their six months in space. That imaging showed mild but transient changes in the heart when moving from Earth gravity to microgravity, revealing how long-duration spaceflight affects cardiac size and function, and what happens when landing on Earth and in simulations of Martian gravity.
Their conclusion: Initial changes in the astronauts’ heart structure and function stabilized over six months in space, and then returned to normal after they got back to Earth. The authors credit exercise regimens for protecting the astronauts’ hearts from prolonged time in space and in a simulation of Mars-like low gravity.
Microgravity changes how fluids flow to and from the heart. Heart chamber walls change their shape, altering how the heart pumps blood. That’s where exercise and strength training can come in.
“The single most novel thing that we showed was that after six months in space, when you come back down to Earth and then are exposed to three-eighths gravity, which is the gravitational gradient that we will experience on Mars, that nobody, not a single astronaut, had a cardiovascular response that was more stressed than the upright posture on Earth before they went,” Levine, director of the Institute for Exercise and Environmental Medicine at Texas Health Presbyterian Dallas, said. “That was really reassuring to me.”
A mission to Mars, at the moment planned for 2035, requires two six-month journeys in microgravity sandwiched around 18 months on the red planet. Weightlessness is well known to weaken bones and muscles. Beyond the temporary dizziness astronauts can experience after returning to land, there were concerns about how their health and performance might be affected when they first stepped onto Mars to begin their work there.
Beyond that concern, Levine reminded his audience in a 2024 Grand Rounds lecture that while deaths in the U.S. space program have come only from equipment failure, there’s always the possibility of a medical emergency. An example: the medical evacuation in January, a first for NASA. Because astronauts are typically middle-aged men and women, Levine said, the most likely cause of a catastrophic medical problem would be a cardiovascular event.
Previous research in the field had used blood pressure and heart rate to infer how well hearts were functioning. For the new study in Circulation, the researchers went beyond those markers of heart health, teaching astronauts how to use echocardiograms, ultrasound tests that create moving images of the heart, during space flight to better see physical changes and the potential impacts of countermeasures, meaning exercise.
Levine spoke with STAT about these latest findings. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
Tell me what’s different about your research.
This study is really the first time that the full expression of the cardiovascular adaptation to spaceflight has been described across a prolonged exposure to space relative to the typical gravitational gradients that we experience every day on Earth.
Are there caveats about what you learned?
These are astronauts who were able to do their countermeasures. When they got down to Earth, they had a lot of medical support, and some of them got IV infusions. But what would happen, for example, if an astronaut got injured and couldn’t exercise? That might be a problem, and they might be more compromised when they land.
Before we go any further, how did the astronauts perform their own echocardiograms?
You can’t fly a sonographer into space, so the whole concept of remote guidance really evolved from NASA. With a little bit of training, I can have a sonographer on the ground talking to the astronauts and with some diagrams saying, OK, put your probe here on the side of the sternum. Now rotate it 10 degrees counterclockwise. Tip the tail down towards the left hip. Breath in, breath out, hold it, push the green button, capture, and boom, we can get research-quality echoes that way.
Are astronauts healthier than regular folks?
I love the crew and the astronauts; they’re wonderful people, but they’re not particularly remarkable physical specimens.
What do you recommend for in-spaceflight fitness?
In the context of the space program providing transportation to Mars, they’re going to have to have exercise devices and tools to preserve the entire spectrum of human adaptation to physical activity. So it’s not just the heart, of course. It’s the skeletal muscle, it’s the bones, it’s the brain, it’s the mental status.
What kind of exercise can be done on a spacecraft?
You saw how important just this flywheel device that they had in Artemis II was to the crew. I mean, they just loved getting on it and practicing with it and using it, but going to Mars, it’s not going to be as big as the space station. The space station has a treadmill and a bike and a weight system.
What in the way of equipment might be on a vehicle headed to Mars?
That’s what the NASA exercise scientists are working on right now — it’s not really for me to determine. For the engineers, it’s always a balance of mass and volume. How big is something? How much room does it take up? How much power does it require? And can we integrate that into a vehicle that can take astronauts all the way to Mars?
How did you arrive at exercise as a possible solution?
We’ve done a lot of studies using bed rest, ground-based models showing that if you just decondition, if you go to bed, if you eliminate a hydrostatic gradient from the head to the foot, the heart shrinks and atrophies and gets functionally stiffer. And if you exercise while you’re in bed, that is completely eliminated.
You say in your new paper that the heart is remarkably plastic, as in nearly 75% of the left ventricular muscle mass is responsive to changes in physical activity.
The amount of blood the heart pumps per beat falls by 50% between the supine and the upright posture. That’s why some people faint when they stand up.
That sounds like POTS, or postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome.
POTS is a very good model. The reason I take care of patients with POTS is because they fundamentally have a gravity disease. The approach that I use for patients has been informed by the studies we do in spaceflight.
What should those of us on Earth keep in mind?
What captures the attention of the American public and provides the support for what is a quite extraordinary engineering and scientific expense to explore the universe is the human in the loop. We sent lots of rockets into space around the moon, but it wasn’t until the astronauts of Artemis II went on TV and went around the moon to the backside that people said, “Oh, my God, this is just incredible.” And so, as we think about all these engineering challenges, what may be the single most important limitation and important connection is the health and safety and well-being of the astronauts.

'The crowd shouted that we'd stolen someone's genitals' - deadly rumours spread on social media
- Published
More than 80 people were killed between October 2025 and July this year following false accusations about what is termed "genital theft", the BBC Global Disinformation Unit has found after gathering data from police forces across six African countries.
The killings are linked to rumours that a simple tap on the shoulder can cause a man's genitals to shrink or disappear. They are being fuelled by widespread misinformation on social media.
"They were shouting that we had stolen someone's genitals and we didn't have any way to escape because there was a huge crowd," Tanzanian mechanic Boniface Mgala told the BBC about his ordeal in April when he was badly beaten by those convinced he was a genital thief.
His experience was similar to those in videos seen by the BBC: men claim that their genital organs - penis and testicles - have vanished or shrivelled after coming into contact with strangers and a mob then demands that alleged perpetrators return what they have supposedly stolen.
Such claims are rooted in longstanding fears and superstitions - and are not new on the continent, particularly in communities where belief in witchcraft remains widespread. Social media has amplified these fears.
The recent wave of rumours appears to have started last year in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where similar claims had surfaced in 2008.
They progressively spread across the region to Burundi, Zambia and Tanzania as well as Mozambique, Angola, Malawi and Kenya.
In Zambia, the hearsay about disappearing genitals first gained traction in March when a woman was lynched, going on to spread panic across the border in Tanzania.
At his home in Mpemba near Tunduma, a busy trading town in Tanzania by the border with Zambia, Mgala traces his fingers along the sickle-shaped scar that runs down the right side of his head as he reflects on his traumatic experience.
"If I had known how close I would have come to death on that day, I wouldn't have gone into that restaurant to eat. Only we don't know how close death is," the mechanic says.
He and his friend had gone into Tunduma on 1 April to meet a client about a car sale and decided to eat lunch beforehand. They had not long sat down in the restaurant when they were dragged outside by a mob.
Two smaller scars on his chin and a missing tooth are other visible marks of his ordeal.
Amid the beating, he lost consciousness. Mgala regained awareness in hospital two days later to news that his friend had been killed.
Back at his house where he lives with his wife and their four children, he now walks with a limp and says he also suffers from constant headaches.
He has not been able to return to work at his mechanic shop but says neighbours and friends have helped cover the cost of some of the medicine he needs.
On the same day that Mgala and his friend were attacked, commercial photographer and businessman Michael Silavwe says he witnessed another similar assault in Tunduma, where he says anxiety had been building after videos about stolen genitalia had begun circulating on TikTok.
Outside his shop he saw people running and says he learned that a man had been accused nearby and was being beaten - and later set on fire.
"After they set him on fire, the police arrived at the scene and everyone scattered and ran away," the 23-year-old told the BBC.
In a video of the attack verified by the BBC Global Disinformation Unit and viewed more than 100,000 times across TikTok and Facebook, a group is seen beating a man while demanding he return the victim's allegedly stolen genitals.
"Those incidents kept escalating and people kept getting beaten," Silavwe said, adding that at the time young people like him did feel scared, but he understands now there is no truth to the rumours.
I came to realise it was not true"
Asha Steven Mwakilasa, a 50-year-old tailor and fashion designer in Tunduma, which is in Momba district, agrees: "I came to realise it was not true."
This does not stop her anxiety - especially if her husband or sons are out, but she says she is grateful that the police are now mounting patrols.
Momba district commissioner Elias Daniel Mwandobo told the BBC local investigations suggested there was deliberate criminal intent behind some of the incidents: "Individuals conspired to commit a crime and incite public panic for their own benefits."
Another video recorded in Tanzania's main city of Dar es Salaam shows a crowd marching a man down a dusty market street, pushing, grabbing and striking him and insisting he returns the genitalia, as the man pleads his innocence.
The BBC Disinformation Unit verified similar videos of attacks in Mozambique and Kenya.
Dozens of these recordings of mob violence, alleged first-person accounts, warnings about alleged incidents, commentary and videos framed as reports of events in particular areas are circulating across TikTok and Facebook.
Many of those analysed by the BBC, including some showing mob violence, remain online.
"We are reviewing the content shared with us and will take action on those that are found to violate our policies," a Meta spokesperson told the BBC.
TikTok has yet to respond to a BBC request for comment.
With some social media creators, who warn viewers to be vigilant, it is often unclear whether they believe the claims or are primarily seeking engagement.
Alongside these posts, some users promote so-called charms said to protect against genital theft, while comedians have parodied the claims through comedy skits.
Smartphones and social media make rumours spread faster, reach larger audiences and become more difficult to control once they begin circulating, says author Julien Bonhomme.
His book, The Sex Thieves: The Anthropology of a Rumor, examines how hearsay about "sex thieves" spread and why people believe them.
People are not simply hearing claims that someone has lost his genitals - they are seeing distressed men say it has happened to them, or watching crowds respond to accusations, he says.
Videos shared on social media can make unverified claims appear more believable, he says, because of their immediacy, describing this as "one of the most significant differences" between the current digital environment and earlier outbreaks.
The worst-hit country has been Mozambique, where the police said in May that 55 people had been killed in six weeks, including a police officer, health workers and civil servants.
Mozambique's President Daniel Chapo publicly condemned widespread rumours and deaths, saying the claims were false and the government had found no medical evidence to suggest anyone had lost a part of their body.
The two healthcare workers were attacked at their home and workplace in April in Cabo Delgado province - a region that borders Tanzania which has been affected by an Islamist insurgency for nearly a decade.
The health facilities in the areas of the attacks had to close for weeks while the authorities launched public awareness campaigns to counter the claims.
As part of the health campaign, the government said some of the fears could be linked to Koro syndrome, a mental illness otherwise known as missing or genital retraction hysteria.
The most recent incidents of violence have occurred in Kenya, where five people were killed by mobs in the coastal counties of Kwale and Mombasa.
After the first incidents were reported in July, Mombasa County Commissioner Mohamed Noor blamed some content creators for spreading the claims to boost engagement "simply to attract views and attention".
"Such misinformation can easily lead to loss of life," Noor told the BBC.
He said police had since contained the violence and made several arrests, including a father and son who were sentenced to a year in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a woman they accused of causing men's genitals to disappear.
Similar claims also fuelled mob attacks in Malawi, leaving eight people dead.
Back in Tunduma, in neighbouring Tanzania, even as mechanic Mgala recovers from the physical impact of the assault, the emotional pain is still raw.
"It still hurts me deeply when I think back to the senseless manner my friend died because I still don't know what was going on," he said.
"To suddenly find yourself being pelted with stones for no reason, and then end up losing your life?"

Meta adds new subscription tiers for businesses, creators and 'AI power users'
The company's Meta One plans range from $2.99/month to $499/month.
A few months after rolling out subscription-based features for Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, Meta is adding a new lineup of subscriptions to its paid offerings. The company introduced a new batch of "Meta One" plans aimed at creators, businesses and "AI power users."
The new subscription tiers combine exclusive features with expanded access to Meta's growing slate of AI tools. In a blog post, the company writes that its main apps and Meta AI will "stay free," but there will be additional benefits for those willing to pay a little (or a lot) extra.
Exactly how much extra depends on how you use Meta's apps and what features you want. The company is still offering "single product plans," which include Facebook Plus ($3.99/month), Instagram Plus ($3.99/month) and WhatsApp Plus ($2.99/month). But it's now adding "bundle" options that combine all those benefits with additional Meta AI usage for tasks like AI image and video generation. These include a new "Core" plan ($7.99/month) and a "Premium" tier ($19.99/month).
There are four additional tiers aimed specifically at creators and business owners. The Meta One "Essential" plan ($14.99/month) combines some of the benefits of Meta Verified subscriptions with its newest AI offerings, including the company's business agent.
Meanwhile, the higher-end plans include some features that businesses and creators have long hoped for. For example, the "Advanced" business plan for Instagram ($49.99/month) includes the ability to schedule Stories posts and the option to embed four clickable URLs into post captions and Reels each month. The company began testing the latter feature earlier this year as part of Meta Verified. Both the "Advanced" and "Expert" ($149/month) tiers also come with the ability to delegate account access to additional people without the need to hand over a password. Other perks include notifications when another account reposts your original content and more visibility in Instagram's in-app search.
Finally, the most expensive Meta One "Max" plan ($499/month) combines all of the benefits of the plans detailed above, along with the highest-capacity access to Meta's business agents. It also offers a benefit that's proved particularly elusive to Instagram creators: an "unlimited" ability to request support from an actual human, as well as the option to request an actual phone call with "a real person" who works for the company.
The new subscriptions are a significant expansion for Meta, which has been testing Meta One plans alongside some of its more resource-intensive AI offerings, like image and video generation. And while it's not clear if Meta's AI features alone are a big draw for users, the company says its early plans have already gained some traction with more than 15 million sign-ups for subscriptions and trial subscriptions.
Meta is also planning to expand the subscriptions to cover more than just its core apps. The company says subscription-based features will eventually arrive for its video-editing app, Edits, as well as its AI glasses.

Nato fighter jets shot down a drone over Lithuania after an alert was issued in the capital, Vilnius, and surrounding region, while Poland scrambled fighter jets less than a day after retrieving a suspected Russian drone adrift in its waters.
The Lithuania drone was shot down near the central-southern village of Pratkunai outside the city of Kaunas, said emergency authorities early on Tuesday. The drone came from neighbouring Belarus and was heading west, according to information from Lithuania’s crisis management centre that was reported by national radio LRT.
Gitanas Nauseda, the Lithuanian president, posted in the early hours of Tuesday: “A drone that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed by Nato fighter jets. With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region.”
Poland meanwhile activated its air force as a preventive measure amid Russian drone attacks on Ukraine. On Monday, the Polish military recovered a suspected Russian drone from the sea on the Baltic coast in northern Poland.
On Tuesday morning, the Lithuanian foreign minister, Kestutis Budrys, thanked allies “whose presence helps protect our skies and strengthens our security”.
“This is best example of allied unity and resolve in action – sending a clear message that Nato stands vigilant, committed, and ready.”
Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – all Nato members on the Russian border – have repeatedly had drone incursions into their territories since Moscow began its war against Ukraine.
A Nato fighter shot down a Ukrainian drone over Estonia in May, the first interception of a foreign drone in the airspace of a Baltic state by Nato air police since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In Poland, the defence minister, Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, said on Monday: “The military has located and recovered a drone from the Baltic Sea near the beach in Rusinowo, close to Jaroslawiec.
“Preliminary inspection indicates that it is a Russian military drone.”
A Polish armed forces spokesperson said the drone appeared to be a Gerbera – a cheap long-range aerial drone made of materials like plywood and foam. They are often used as decoys but can also carry explosives. It was recovered by a hydrographic vessel off the coast of the village of Rusinowo.
The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, has repeatedly warned that Nato countries should expect an increase in provocations from Moscow.
A Russian drone hit a passenger train on Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday, shortly after former the British prime minister, Boris Johnson, and other foreign diplomats had used the same line.

Mark Carney said Canada will pursue a “unique security and economic alliance” with Europe as he positions his country as a base to build in the “new global economic order”.
Speaking to investors, company executives and government ministers at the inaugural Canada Investment Summit on Tuesday, the prime minister pitched Canada as a “safe harbour” and lucrative home for foreign capital as his government looks to reduce its reliance on trade with the United States.
Over the last 18 months, the relationship with the US has fractured, leaving Canada searching for ways to avert economic devastation.
“The world is becoming more divided and dangerous. Sovereignty and openness are now in tension. Economic integration is being weaponised. Tariffs are used as leverage,” Carney said – a nod to the Donald Trump’s penchant for trade levies.
“Canada recognised the rupture earlier than most. Our response reflects the two lessons we have taken from it: First, we must take care of ourselves, and second, we must take care of each other. Taking care of ourselves means building our strength at home and diversifying our partnerships abroad.”
While Carney has referred to the trade spat as a “war”, there was a duelling sense of optimism at the summit among senior Canadian officials that the country’s more global perspective could usher in hundreds of billions in fresh investment into the country.
That shift has been exemplified in recent weeks by Carney’s effort to strengthen Canada’s economic and political ties to the EU. Noting in his remarks at the summit that Canada is the only non-European member of Europe’s defence procurement initiative, the prime minister said his government will pursue a “unique” relationship with the bloc. He mused about the range of possibilities, including the prospect of visa-free travel and work between the two that has been raised in recent days, but said Canada and the EU were in early stage of talks.
Carney will be the guest of honour at the European parliament’s plenary meeting in Strasbourg this week. He will attend European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s annual state of the union speech on Wednesday, where she is expected to sketch out new areas for EU-Canada cooperation. On Thursday, Carney will address MEPs in von der Leyen’s presence. The commission president hastily changed her plans to stay in Strasbourg, after being criticised over her initial “unacceptable” decision to skip Carney’s speech and return to Brussels.
European officials are seeking to bring Canada as close as possible to the EU short of membership. But it will not be called associate membership, as the EU seeks to maintain a clear distinction between members and nonmembers. The long experience of Brexit negotiations cemented the EU’s preference not to split the four freedoms of its single market – free movement of people, services, goods and capital – so any deepening of the Canada relationship will be built around this red line. More immediately, the EU hopes to improve ties on raw materials and energy.
Javier Moreno Sánchez, a Spanish socialist MEP, who leads the European parliament’s Canada delegation, said he wanted to hear “concrete steps” from von der Leyen on how to improve the EU-Canada relationship, calling for greater mobility for professionals, more student exchanges, joint work on defence and artificial intelligence.
“Canadians are the most European people outside Europe and that is the key point for the development of our relationship,” he said. “Due to the difficult geopolitical geoeconomic situation in the world and the difficult relationship we have, both Canada and the European Union, with our traditional partner, the United States, I think it is the moment to have a closer relationship with Canada.”
The EU and Canada already have a wide-ranging relationship, including a free-trade agreement and separate deals on digital cooperation, raw materials, research and a shared green alliance. Earlier this year, Canada became the first non-European country to join the EU’s €150bn defence loans scheme, meaning greater opportunities for Canadian defence firms to supply Europe.
But irritants persist. Ten EU member states, including France, Italy and Poland, have not ratified the landmark EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) nearly a decade after it was signed, meaning parts of the deal are yet to enter into force.
French lawmaker Valérie Hayer, Emmanuel Macron’s ally in the European parliament, acknowledged the problem. “In the French parliament this agreement has yet to be ratified, notwithstanding the [trade] figures which are extremely good. That is why I call on political leaders [in France] to do their bit to act responsibly as elsewhere to make sure that we [the EU] can count for more in world affairs.”
Hayer’s centrist Renew group, only the fifth-largest in the European parliament, is calling on EU member states and the commission to speed up Ceta ratification and launch an awareness-raising drive so European and Canadian companies have better knowledge of the trade opportunities. But ahead of a year of big elections – in France, Italy and Poland – progress on ratifying the 10-year-old agreement looks uncertain.
EU-Canada’s trade in goods and services hit €130bn in 2025, an 80% increase since 2016 when Ceta was signed. But this pales in comparison to trade with the US, which is worth nearly US$880bn.
Despite a deliberate push to increase global trade, Carney acknowledged the geographic realities of Canada’s proximity to its southern neighbour, and the reality, which most economists concede, that the US will remain Canada’s largest trading partner.
“We will always be neighbours, and Canada will continue to be the US’s most important partner in many key areas,” he said. These arrangements work when we engage as true partners that respect each other’s traditions and sovereignty.”
In recent weeks, Trump has both threatened Canada’s economy and mused about a North America under the umbrella of an expanded US.
Event host Erik Schatzker told attendees that Canada was neither a “bystander nor a victim” in the dramatic geopolitical shifts that have defined the Trump era. “Canada is a protagonist. Canada has agency. Canada is defining its own future.”
Carney said foreign investment has dramatically increased and the federal government was on track to balance the operating budget one year ahead of schedule, an announcement that received applause from the crowd. He announced a corporate tax “mega-deduction” that would help compete with similar incentives in the US allowing companies to immediately deduct 100% of the cost of new investment across more assets than previously permitted.
Carney also confirmed Canada would open four of its major airports to foreign investment in order to “unlock their true value”. The prime minister also said his government would “apply [the] lessons” of instances in which allowing partial private investment had failed.
But that theme – soliciting hundreds of billions in foreign investment while also reshoring domestic capability – has frustrated some.
Ahead of the summit, thousands gathered in downtown Toronto for the Many vs the Money counter protest. Organisers said public money should not be used to reduce the risks of private investment while communities are left to shoulder the social and environmental costs of these projects.
“Mark Carney’s here selling Canada to the international community,” said Stephen Hill, a lone protester standing outside the hotel as key figures arrived to the prime minister’s speech. “I’m Canadian. We’re an Aboriginal-led investment coalition. We want in. But you can’t get a returned email. You can’t get a returned phone call. You can’t get through to his ministers. So I’m here from British Columbia to try and get his attention and to tell him to think of Canadians first.”
Ahead of Tuesday’s summit, the prime minister’s office announced nearly C$500bn in new domestic investment.
“Canada has what the world wants,” Carney said during media availability late Tuesday morning. “The difference, this week, is that we didn’t cross an ocean to make our case. The world came to us … but what matters most is what we do for ourselves.”

DA announces death penalty decision in Nick Reiner murder trial
The decision was announced a day after an emotional tribute to Rob Reiner at the Emmys
Nick Reiner will not face the death penalty if he’s convicted of killing his parents, Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said Tuesday.
Hochman announced the decision ahead of a Tuesday court hearing for the 33-year-old son of famed filmmaker Rob Reiner and photographer Michele Reiner.
A grand jury indictment was unsealed last month charging Nick Reiner with two counts of murder with special circumstances. He is accused of using a knife to kill his 78-year-old father and 70-year-old mother.
Prosecutors allege the killings involved lying in wait, extreme violence, and "a high degree of cruelty, viciousness, or callousness" against particularly vulnerable victims. The indictment bypasses a preliminary hearing and moves the case straight to trial.
"In deciding whether or not the DA's office was going to seek the death penalty, we have gone through a rigorous review, where we look at the aggravating factors as well as the mitigating factors," Hochman told reporters outside the courthouse ahead of the hearing.
"We have spoken to the victims' family. We have spoken to prosecutors and law enforcement and have worked with the most senior people in the district attorney's office. After a careful and thorough review of all these factors, the district attorney's office will not be seeking the death penalty in this case. That means the maximum sentence that Mr. Reiner will be looking at is life without the possibility of parole."
Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Sam Ohta had previously conditionally sealed the grand jury transcripts following defense motions aimed at preserving trial fairness. Prosecutors noted that the victims' surviving children, Jake and Romy Reiner, requested the transcripts remain private to avoid additional trauma.
Autopsy records show the couple died from "multiple sharp force injuries." LAPD officers arrested Nick Reiner near USC less than six hours after his sister discovered the bloody scene on Dec. 14. He remains held without bail.
Meanwhile, a bitter legal fight brews over Nick Reiner's access to a $1.5 million trust fund his parents established in 1993. Defense attorneys argue the mandatory inheritance is needed to retain private counsel after prominent lawyer Alan Jackson left the case for nonpayment. However, access to the funds faces hurdles under California’s "slayer statute," which bars killers from profiting from their victims' estates.
Reports reveal tension boiled over the night before the murders at a holiday party hosted by Conan O'Brien, where Rob Reiner reportedly argued with his son over erratic behavior. Sources indicate Nick Reiner, who has a documented history of severe drug addiction, homeless spells, and a schizophrenia diagnosis, checked into a Santa Monica hotel hours later, where police subsequently discovered blood.
Rob Reiner, the iconic star of All in the Family and legendary director of The Princess Bride and When Harry Met Sally, married Michele Singer in 1989. The double homicide has devastated Hollywood and left the surviving family pleading for privacy.

Jadavpur University (JU) saw night-long rampage and vandalism on August 20, when a mob, armed with sticks and rods, allegedly stormed the campus.
The violence followed a heated altercation late on August 19 between activists from the Akhil Bharaitya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) from the university’s engineering department and members of the Left-wing student outfit, Democratic Students’ Federation (DSF), and other student organizations. The ABVP alleged that its members were assaulted and that several workers required hospitalisation. Students from the engineering faculty disputed the claim and offered a counter-account of the incident.
By midnight, an armed mob allegedly entered the campus, apparently seeking to avenge the earlier altercation. The attackers tore down and set fire to placards, festoons and flags belonging to various student organisations active on the campus. The mob also surrounded Aurobindo Bhavan, the university’s administrative building, trapping students inside.
The violence was captured by CCTV cameras installed across the university campus. Students and journalists also recorded several videos of the incident. Alt News accessed multiple such recordings and analysed them to establish the identities of those involved in the ruckus.
What happened at JU: A Blow-by-Blow Account
Around 9:30–10:30 pm on August 19, the DSF-run Faculty of Engineering & Technology Students’ Union (FETSU) held a general body meeting on the campus. The meeting had been announced through the union’s social media account.
ABVP and the allied Right-wing student outfit, Nationalist Students’ Front (NSF), opposed the meeting, citing a Calcutta high court ruling that no activities could be undertaken from student union offices until fresh student union elections were held. According to students present, ABVP and NSF members were outnumbered and were forced to leave the spot. A few DSF members were also injured in the ensuing scuffle.
Ayantik Pal, a third-year B Tech student who attended the meeting, said the GB meeting had been convened to elect signatories for the union’s email ID, Facebook account and bank account. Since the last FETSU election was held in 2020, he said, the meeting was intended to allow the union to continue its functioning.
According to Pal, ABVP activists at the meeting repeatedly objected that it was illegal. He said they nevertheless participated when names for the signatories were being proposed, before becoming agitated as the meeting progressed. They allegedly abused some students, calling them “Naxals” and “Maoists”, following which a scuffle broke out.
Accounts diverge over what happened immediately afterwards.
According to students, Nikhil Das, an ABVP research scholar and president of the organisation’s JU unit, attempted to enter the undergraduate and postgraduate students’ GB meeting and allegedly tried to provoke a confrontation. Students said they intervened to stop him, escalating the situation. They alleged that three DSF workers were injured in the assault by ABVP activists and that one was taken away towards the Sulekha Crossing. ABVP denied these allegations.
ABVP, meanwhile, claimed that Das was assaulted during the GB meeting and subsequently had to be hospitalised at KPC Medical College and Hospital. BJP MLA from Jadavpur Sarbari Mukherjee visited him at the hospital. Students alleged that during the visit, she threatened that ABVP and BJP workers would retaliate if those accused in the assault did not surrender. She later repeated this on camera.
Around midnight, a crowd of approximately 50–60 people gathered outside Gate 4 of the university, which is the only entrance that remains open at night. By around 12:30 am, the group entered the campus.
Pramita Basu, an undergraduate Philosophy student, said that after 7 pm, everyone entering the campus is required to show an ID card, including hostel residents. However, according to her, the crowd entered without being stopped by the guards stationed at the gate.
The group moved from Gate 4 towards the Science-Arts crossing, where some wall graffiti was allegedly damaged, before turning towards Aurobindo Bhavan, the university’s administrative building. Videos from the night accessed by Alt News show some members of the group carrying saffron flags.
Meanwhile, students who had remained on campus after the earlier confrontation gathered inside Aurobindo Bhavan. According to them, they had decided to stay back until morning because they had heard that ABVP activists were looking for them outside the university.
Pal said an all-faculty GB meeting was also convened that night, with students from the arts, science and engineering faculties discussing what to do next. Around 12:30 am, he said, a university staff member alerted them that a mob had entered the campus and advised them to protect themselves.
“Within minutes, we saw a stream of mobile flashlights coming towards Aurobindo Bhavan from the side of the green zone. A few students present at the green zone were thrashed by this mob,” Pal said.
The students then woke the guards at Aurobindo Bhavan, obtained the keys and locked themselves inside, according to Pal.
The crowd that reached the building tried to break through its collapsible gates but failed. It then tore down red flags, festoons and posters belonging to student organisations and set them on fire outside the administrative building. Students trapped inside alleged that members of the crowd abused them verbally, threw stones and eggs at the building, and attempted to throw burning flags inside. Footage of the episode was broadcast live on television and recorded by students and journalists.
The violence continued until around 2 am. Around the same time, another group gathered outside Jadavpur police station and allegedly attempted to breach the entrance to the university’s main hostel, located next to the police station.
At the protest, ABVP West Bengal leaders were reportedly heard telling the media that the organisation was “putting the last nail in the coffin” of the “Dimagi Naxals” and would carry out “surgical strikes” at Jadavpur University to suppress them.
By around 2:30 am, the crowd had dispersed. The students who had taken shelter inside Aurobindo Bhavan began leaving the campus at around 5 am.
Alt News procured a third CCTV footage from University sources, where several persons of interest can be spotted as present on the campus on the night of August 20.
The confrontation did not end with the dispersal of the mob.
Around noon the following day, the Student Federation of India (SFI) and other Left student organisations held a protest near the Lenin statue at Jadavpur 8B bus stand. Kolkata Police barricaded the area and stopped the protesters from proceeding towards the university. Around 2 pm, an ABVP rally that began from Golpark reached Gate 4 of the university. Students inside the campus also gathered in response. As Gate 4 was kept locked to prevent outsiders from entering, a face-off between the two groups on either side of the gate ensued.
During the confrontation, members of the ABVP crowd were seen standing on the historic university emblem designed by artist Nandalal Bose as they attempted to cross the closed gate and enter the campus.
Visuals of Rajyeshwar Sinha, a professor of Bengali at JU, holding the partially damaged University emblem went viral.

ABVP Denial
Directly denying any role of ABVP, the outfit’s central working committee (CWC) member Subhabrata Adhikary said on a talk show on ABP Ananda, that ABVP had no connection with the rampage at Jadavpur University on August 20. When pointed out by the anchor that people in the mob were holding ABVP flags, Adhikary said, “It doesn’t prove anything. SFI workers have done the vandalism while holding ABVP flags”. When asked if ABVP was condemning the night-long violence, he again said, “It is clear that ABVP has no connection with the incident.”
Talking to The Times of India, south Bengal ABVP secretary Neelkantha Bhattacharya, too, denied his presence during the campus violence. However, he then said, some of ABVP boys entered the campus “out of over-enthusiasm. The gate was open. We just pushed inside. I went at most 10 steps inside the university to get them out”.
Adhikary, on the other hand, contradicted his own statement on ABP Ananda, and told TOI, “I was standing right by the gate. I have no connection with the mob. After hearing about the situation, I went there to ensure that no untoward incident happened. ABVP has no involvement in any vandalism.”
CCTV and Video Footage Disprove ABVP Claims
Alt News examined CCTV footage from the intervening night of August 19-20 and identified several prominent ABVP faces and BJP-linked political figures on the campus.
1. Subhabarta Adhikary
Visible in JU CCTV footage-1 (Captured by a camera fixed on the external wall of PG Arts building)
As the gate opens at 12.38.17 am, Adhikary is one of the first persons to enter the campus, followed by a crowd. When the group nears a large white SFI banner, he is seen saying something in an animated manner. Within seconds, others in the crowd tear down the banner. It is not clear whether he instructs them to do it or tries to dissuade them.
2. Neelkantha Bhattacharya
Visible in JU CCTV footage-2 (Captured by a camera installed on a pole at the science-arts crossing).
Around 12:40 am, Neelkantha Bhattacharya is seen carrying a rod or a stick while instructing a group. In the same footage, at the 12:39:22 am mark, Subhabrata Adhikary is seen next to him. They are in front of the PG science building. At 12:40:28, the two once again can be seen together. This time Bhattacharya is carrying sticks in both hands.
It is worth noting that Bhattacharyya first told TOI that he was not present on the campus. Then, he claimed, he had barely taken 10 steps inside the gate. The distance from Gate 4 to PG Science building, according to Google Maps, is over 360 feet, i.e., about 110 meters.
3. Somsurya Banerjee
Visible in JU CCTV footage-3 (Captured by a camera on the outer wall of security guards’ room at Gate-4)
Banerjee, an NSF activist, is spotted on the campus around 1.14 am on August 20. Banerjee had earlier courted controversy by claiming that cows were slaughtered within the University during Iftar.
4. Aditya Mondal
Visible in footage captured by Mrittika TV, a local media outlet.
The portal captured the exact moment when the crowd entered the campus, in a livestream. Although the video was later deleted from the page, Alt News accessed the footage. In that video, (embedded in the story above) Aditya Mondal, the ABVP candidate for the recently held election to internal complaint committee (ICC) of the Arts Faculty, was spotted near the PG science building. The wall had an SFI graffiti, where a person was seen urinating on the Nazi Hakenkreuz. The writing next to it said, ‘Break Fascism with Red’. Mondal was seen with a group that tried to rub the symbol off. Mondal can be heard saying, “The left-naxals had insulted the symbol of India, Swastik. We are correcting it.”
5. Partha Chakraborty
Visible in the footage captured by students stuck inside Aurobindo Bhavan, during the rampage.
Partha Chakraborty, a Bharatiya Janata Yuva Morcha (BJYM) worker from the Dhakuria area, was also present at the scene. In videos captured by the students stranded inside Aurobindo Bhavan, he was seen burning flags of SFI and other Left organizations in front of the collapsible gate of the building, and throwing the burning flags inside. Three days later, on August 23, he was seen with BJP’s losing candidate from Kasba assembly Sandeep Banerjee and South Kolkata Yuva Morcha leader Shatadru Ghoshal.
6. Abhijeet Roy (Raja)
Visible in JU CCTV footage-3 (Captured by a camera on the outer wall of security guards’ room at Gate-4)
Another prominent face identified in the footage from that night is Abhijeet Roy alias Raja, the election agent of Jadavpur MLA Sarbari Mukherjee. In a video posted on social media, Roy was seen standing with a group outside Gate-4, with one member holding an ABVP flag. ABVP leader Neelkantha Bhattacharya is part of the group. Roy’s entry into the campus was also captured on CCTV footage. He is seen interacting with a group of men with former VC Buddhadeb Sau standing at an arm’s length.
7. Buddhadeb Sau
Visible in JU CCTV footage-1 and JU CCTV footage-3.
The most talked about entry on that eventful night was perhaps that of Buddhadeb Sau, professor of mathematics and ex-VC of the university. Sau’s presence raised eyebrows not only for the fact that it is unusual for an academic of his stature to be on the campus past midnight, but also because of his Sangh connections. He is associated with the RSS-backed Akhil Bhartiya Rashtriya Shaikshik Mahasangh (ABRSM), and represented the organisation at a joint press meet held by Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh JU unit, ABVP JU unit and ABRSM JU unit, held after the campus violence.
Sau can be spotted in JU CCTV footage-1 and JU CCTV footage-3. In the JU CCTV footage-1 feed, he is seen entering the campus through a side gate at 12:39:44 am, and exiting through the same gate at 12:44:35 am. For the entire duration, he stood in front of the security guards’ room, occasionally speaking to others. From 12:44:09 till his exit 26 seconds later, he is seen watching others tearing down what appears to be political flags put up on Gate-4.
Sau is seen once again in JU CCTV footage-3. This time he was captured by the camera installed on the outer wall of security guards’ room at Gate-4, at 1:06:33 am. This time also, he is seen standing in front of guards’ room.
Asked about his presence during the rampage, Sau told TOI, “I went to the spot as soon as I received news of the disturbance. No one from the authorities was present there. I was concerned. I told the police to get additional cops to manage any potential flare-up. Once the group retreated and the situation was brought under I returned to my quarters. I went and tried to protect the students; is that my crime?”

Apple's latest iPhone and iPad software—iOS 27 and iPadOS 27—is here. While this release won’t make as big of a splash as Apple’s big Liquid Glass redesign in the prior version, there's still plenty here that could change how you use your device.
iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 focus largely on stability improvements that you’ll notice in your everyday use. There are several quality-of-life improvements, like how Shortcuts are significantly easier to set up, but the big highlight is the Siri AI upgrade. Here's everything you need to know.
Updated September 14, 2026: We've refreshed this story to reflect the latest updates and that iOS and iPadOS 27 are rolling out today.
Is Your iPhone or iPad Compatible?
Apple sometimes drops a few older devices from the support list with new versions of its operating systems, supposedly because the aging hardware can’t run the latest screen behaviors without feeling sluggish. (Apple typically supports iPhones and iPads for six to seven years.) But there's good news this year. iPhones from 2019 and newer—the iPhone 11 and up, including the iPhone SE (2nd Gen)—will support iOS 27.
That means any iPhone that received iOS 26 is still compatible with iOS 27. If you're unsure of your iPhone model, go to Settings > General > About and look at the model name.
iPads aren't as straightforward, as they have a unique naming structure. Apple retired the “generations” moniker and is now using the chipset to denote the iPad model. You can check your iPad model using Apple’s support documentation. A few iPads are cut off from the iPadOS 27 update, including the 8th-gen iPad from 2020 and the 5th-gen iPad Mini.
- iPad: 9th gen and later, including A16
- iPad Mini: 6th gen and later, including A17 Pro
- iPad Air 11-inch: 4th gen and later, including M2, M3, and M4
- iPad Air 13-inch: M2 and later
- iPad Pro 11-inch: 2nd gen and later
- iPad Pro 12.9-inch: 4th gen and later
- iPad Pro: M4 and later
How to Install iOS 27 or iPadOS 27
The final versions of iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 are here. Before installing, it’s very important that you back up your devices. Head to Settings, tap your name at the top, and select iCloud. Then tap iCloud Backup, and tap Back Up Now. Read our How to Back Up Your iPhone or iPad guide for other methods and more details.
Then, head to Settings > General > Software Update and choose iOS 27 or iPadOS 27 when you see the option. Installation will take several minutes, and your iPhone or iPad will restart, so set aside several minutes for the whole process.
Siri AI, the new assistant, will ask to index your phone or iPad to learn more about you, your apps, and your data so it can be more helpful. This indexing takes a while—anywhere from a few hours to a couple of days—so be prepared to wait a bit.
Apple Intelligence Only Works on Select iPhones
Remember—even if older iPhones and iPads receive the iOS 27 or iPadOS 27 update, that doesn't mean all of the new features will be available. Apple Intelligence is still only compatible with the iPhone 15 Pro and newer and select iPads, meaning that several artificial intelligence features are unavailable on older devices.
Top New iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 Features
Here's a top-line view of some of the biggest changes coming to iOS and iPadOS 27. The updates are largely the same across both operating systems.
Siri is finally becoming “a more capable assistant,” or so Apple claims. The company says this is largely thanks to its third-generation foundation models, developed from the ground up with Google's Gemini models. However, Apple says it isn't using Google's infrastructure to power Siri interactions and that no user data from Siri actions gets shared with Google.
Siri AI has an all-new look when you activate the assistant. It now resembles a glass orb. You can type or talk naturally to Siri, and there's even a dedicated Siri app where you can revisit previous conversations or pick up where you left off on a different device. Siri is also now in the camera app, giving you a more direct way to start a visual search, much like Google Lens. You can even point the camera at a restaurant bill, and Siri can split the tab between you and your friends.
The assistant understands your personal context, so it can comb through your emails, messages, and photos to find relevant information based on your query. It can then take action on your behalf, whether that's drafting an email in a specific tone or getting wine recommendations for a particular dish. Siri's voice is more expressive, but you can also customize the assistant's voice, its expressiveness, and its pace.
We've collated all the new things you can do with Siri AI if you want to try the revamped assistant.
Apple has focused on making iOS run faster in this update. The company says app launches are up to 30 percent faster, newly captured photos in your Photo Library load up to 70 percent faster, and AirDrop transfers are up to 80 percent faster. The iPhone will do a better job switching between Wi-Fi and cellular, so you hopefully won't have that awkward minute with no service while you wait for your device to switch networks as you leave the house. Many of these upgrades will affect older iPhone models, like the iPhone 11, thanks to a better-optimized CPU Scheduler.
Hate Liquid Glass? Love Liquid Glass? You have some options to make it work for your tastes in iOS 27. Apple says it has generally updated the design language to improve readability and contrast. App icons are sharper, for example. But you now finally have a slider in the Settings menu that lets you adjust the intensity of the Liquid Glass look, from super clear to more opaque. You can customize this in Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass.
Apple spent a lot of time in the WWDC keynote talking up child safety features in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27. A new Setup Assistant lets parents choose system apps and other essential apps for the child when first setting up an Apple device. An Ask to Browse feature means any new websites the kids encounter in Safari get sent to a parent for approval, and a feature called Communication Safety prevents children from seeing nudity or violence in the Messages or FaceTime apps; those are blurred by default.
Also new are Time Allowances and Schedules. Time Allowances let parents set an allotted amount of time kids can enjoy specific app categories (like Entertainment)—Apple has guidance on how much time makes sense based on the child's age. Schedules let parents choose what apps are available during different times of the week. All of this is also easier to view in a redesigned parental dashboard.
The Photos app is getting a small infusion of Apple Intelligence AI features, though remember that these features only work on iPhones that support Apple Intelligence (iPhone 15 Pro and newer).
The existing “Clean Up" feature—which lets you select objects in photos to remove (like a trash bag or people in the background)—now performs better thanks to Apple's upgraded foundation models. If the object you want to remove is larger, it will likely run through Apple's Private Cloud Compute servers for processing, but for smaller jobs, it will still handle the task on-device.
Extend is a new feature in the Photos app. This lets you expand a photo to add a little more to the edges—maybe you accidentally snapped a pic too close to a subject and want to give them some visual breathing room. It will generate what it thinks should be there based on the photo's context. (This feature works with Apple's diffusion model in the cloud.)
Finally, there's Spatial Reframing. This lets you alter a photo's perspective. Maybe you shot a little too high up and want to reframe the photo to make it look like you were crouching down further. The software will use generative AI to fill in the gaps after you change the perspective in the image (though Apple preserves faces and pets as much as possible to avoid altering them with fake pixels). You can read more about these features here.
Tap the Edit button on a photo and go to Tools to access the features in the Photos app. They're free features, but Apple sets usage limits, so you'll have to pay up for a higher-tier iCloud subscription if you want to use them more regularly.
Want to create AI slop? Apple has a more powerful image-generation model for its Image Playground app, meaning you can create higher-quality AI images in virtually any style—even photorealistic. The new version of Image Playground defaults to that photorealistic style if you don't specify a style in your prompt. These features have daily usage limits based on your iCloud subscription.
Similar to Google's Magic Cue on its Pixel phones, Apple is adding one-tap actions to Messages and Mail apps. If someone messages you about grabbing milk on the way home, you'll see a button to add it as a reminder. Or if someone asks about hanging out on a specific date, you'll see a Calendar button to create an event with one tap. These features were removed from the final version of iOS 27 but will be added in a future update.
Similarly, the Phone app now has a feature called Call Context. If you're on a call with Delta, for example, you'll see relevant flight information on the dialer screen, so you don't have to hunt in your email for a confirmation number during the call.
If you've ever tried to make a shortcut in Apple's Shortcuts app, you'll know it can be a little complicated. Now it’s getting easier. Instead of plugging in various rules and triggers, you can type what you want, and the Shortcuts app will understand your intent and set up an automated task for you. So you can naturally say, “Text my wife my ETA when I leave work,” and the Shortcuts app will set up an action that uses location services, Maps, traffic data, and Messages to automate a text message that fires off when you’re headed home.
Got a lot of tabs? Safari will now organize your many tabs into topics. Safari can also “notify” you when a web page changes, like a price drop or a restock.
Then there's Custom Extensions. This lets you describe a feature you want in Safari, and it will generate an extension. (It will first suggest existing third-party extensions that may be similar to what you're looking for.) For example, you can say, “When I hit the toolbar button on a recipe website, give me a button to save the recipe, add a star rating, and let me make comments; make the interface look nice.” Safari will generate the extension, and that's it. Extensions you make on one platform, like your iPhone, will carry over to your other devices, like your Mac.
You can read more about these Safari features here.
- Better search in Apple Mail: Apple says a new ranking system will filter more relevant emails to the top of your search.
- Easier Calendar event creation: You can use natural language to create a calendar event instead of filling out a bunch of fields. Type at the top, “Every Friday, make an event to water the plants,” and it'll make the event in a jiffy.
- Dual Capture in FaceTime: You can now share video from your front and rear cameras at the same time during one-on-one calls.
- Accessibility improvements: Apple’s VoiceOver accessibility mode has richer image descriptions, and there’s a new captioning feature that generates subtitles for any video you watch (kind of like Google's Live Transcribe), even translating them into other languages.
- Maps upgrades: Flyover mode in Apple Maps lets you view a 3D map. Now, in iOS 27, Apple is combining aerial imagery with its Visual Intelligence models to render 3D models with far more detail. That means more detailed 3D buildings and trees.
- Custom EQ with AirPods: AirPods are finally getting a custom equalizer, letting you customize the mids, lows, and highs in the AirPods settings menu.
- Better iCloud Shared Albums: Android and Windows users can now more easily join iCloud Shared Albums and contribute their own photos. These albums also now support full-resolution images. You can now also create slideshows in the Photos app, save a video frame as a photo, and add star ratings to photos and videos to filter them.
- Apple Health updates: The Health app now supports perimenopause and menopause, meaning the cycle-tracking feature can notify you when patterns suggest perimenopause.
- Home app updates: If you have security cameras in your Apple Home app, you'll now receive smarter notifications that better describe what is happening around your home, much like Google and Amazon's richer notifications on their respective smart-home platforms.
- Password fixes: If the Passwords app warns you about weak or compromised passwords, it can now automatically fix them for you.
- Message syncing improvements: Apple says notifications for missed messages and unread count sync more quickly when you return to your iPad after some time.
