An egg retrieval is the culmination of several weeks of ovarian stimulation, as multiple follicles develop under the influence of fertility medicines, with the ovaries undergoing significant changes in response to hormonal stimulation.
The quality and number of eggs ultimately retrieved are influenced by several factors, including age, ovarian reserve, genetics and the underlying cause of infertility. A woman’s diet cannot alter these fundamentals, nor can any particular food guarantee better eggs or a successful IVF outcome. Nutrition can, however, influence the metabolic and physiological environment in which the body responds to treatment. For this reason, what a woman eats in the weeks preceding egg retrieval should be viewed as part of overall preparation rather than as a means of ‘boosting’ fertility.
Biology behind the preparation
Egg development is a prolonged process. Although the final stages of follicular growth occur during the IVF stimulation cycle, the oocytes have been undergoing maturation over a much longer period. This means that nutrition in the weeks before retrieval is unlikely to produce a dramatic change in egg quality on its own, but maintaining good nutritional status can support general metabolic health during a demanding treatment cycle.
During ovarian stimulation, the body is also adapting to changing hormone levels, increased follicular activity and, in some women, symptoms such as bloating, constipation, fatigue or changes in appetite. A balanced diet can help maintain energy levels and provide the protein, fibre, vitamins, minerals and healthy fats required for normal physiological function.
Among dietary patterns studied in relation to IVF outcomes, the Mediterranean-style diet has received some of the most consistent attention. A 2023 evidence-based review published in Frontiers in Nutrition, covering multiple IVF nutritional interventions, concluded that a Mediterranean-style dietary approach is the most consistently supported pattern for women undergoing ovarian stimulation. This diet is rich in vegetables, fruits, legumes, whole grains, healthy fats, and lean protein, with limited processed foods and refined carbohydrates.
What to eat more of
Protein is the macronutrient that most women underestimate in the lead-up to retrieval. Both animal and plant sources such as eggs, fish, lentils, chickpeas and dairy support follicle development and give the body the building blocks it needs during stimulation. Aim to include a source of protein in every meal.
Healthy fats, particularly omega-3 fatty acids, carry documented benefits for IVF outcomes. A review published in Reproductive BioMedicine Online found that supplementation with omega-3 free fatty acids may lead to improvements in both clinical and embryological IVF outcomes. Practical sources in an Indian context include fish such as salmon, sardines, and mackerel, as well as walnuts, flaxseeds, and chia seeds.
Folate belongs in this conversation for two reasons: it supports healthy cell division, and many women undergoing IVF are not getting enough of it through food alone. Dark leafy vegetables such as spinach, methi and palak are among the richest dietary sources. Iron from leafy greens, lentils, and lean meat supports the blood supply that developing follicles depend on.
Antioxidants such as vitamins C and E, selenium, zinc help protect developing eggs from oxidative stress, which increases during stimulation as the ovaries work at higher capacity. Berries, bell peppers, nuts, and seeds are practical sources worth building into daily meals.
Hydration matters more during stimulation than at other times. As follicles grow, the risk of bloating and fluid retention increases. Consistent water intake of at least two to three litres a day supports the body through this phase and helps manage stimulation-related discomfort.
What to limit
There is no single food that will undo an IVF cycle, but some patterns are worth avoiding in the weeks before retrieval. Highly processed foods, refined carbohydrates, and excessive added sugar affect blood sugar stability and create an inflammatory environment that does not serve follicle development. Alcohol should be avoided during stimulation. Excess caffeine, more than one to two cups of coffee a day, is worth reducing, as higher intakes have been associated with poorer IVF outcomes in some studies.
What patients should know
There is no fertility diet that guarantees better egg quality or a successful cycle, and any approach that promises otherwise is worth approaching with scepticism. What a balanced, nutrient-dense diet does is support your body through a physically demanding process the same way good nutrition supports any period of heightened physical demand.
The specifics of what your body needs during your particular stimulation protocol are best discussed with your fertility specialist, who can account for your individual clinical picture, any nutrient deficiencies identified through blood work, and whether supplementation is appropriate in your case.
(Dr. Shivika Gupta is a fertility specialist at Birla Fertility and IVF, Gurgaon Sec- 51. shivika.gupta@birlafertility.com)

The presence of E. coli and coliform bacteria in bottled drinking water in Kochi, Keralam, has prompted authorities to take measures to address contamination risks and ensure water traceability. The Kochi Corporation is planning to make it mandatory for hotels to use only Kerala Water Authority (KWA) water, which would help ensure the use of safe water and enable traceability.
Chairperson of the Health Standing Committee Seena Teacher said the decision was taken after inspections found contamination in water used at some hotels.
“The idea is to make them use only KWA’s water, thereby ensuring the veracity of the source of the drinking water. We have plans to create a QR code for this, through which they can get water from the KWA using the My Kochi mobile application. We will also hold a meeting with the stakeholders to trace the source of the water and take necessary action,” said Ms. Seena.
The contamination was observed in the samples collected from eateries as part of the surprise checks carried out jointly by the Health Department, Kochi Corporation, Food Safety Department and police.
Food Safety Assistant Commissioner Jose Lawrence said that while inspections are periodically carried out at the water bottling units in the city, the presence of E. coli was not observed. “We carry out checks in packaged drinking water (water bottles) from random locations. In this light, we will focus more on the cans as well. We recently received a complaint from the Kalamassery area about fungal growth in a can from a supplier. Test results are awaited,” said Mr. Lawrence.
The most probable number (MPN) of coliform bacteria detected in the samples ranged from 17 per 100 ml to 1,600 per 100 ml. According to experts, the MPN should be zero in drinking water and the high MPN values indicate faecal contamination and render the water unfit for human consumption.
More checks sought
According to Kerala Hotels and Restaurants Association (KHRA) representatives, more inspections need to be carried out to find the source of contamination.
KHRA State president G. Jayapal said that only packaged water with Indian Standards Institute (ISI) marking is used in hotels. “We will be directing all hoteliers to procure water from reputed agencies,” said Mr. Jayapal.
Not dismissing the chances of such contaminated drinking water cans entering into households, Consortium of Flat and Villa Owners Association, Kerala State chairperson Saju Abraham said awareness among the end user was crucial.
“While KWA’s water is used in apartment complexes, a significant percentage of the residents rely on canned water. Tracing the source of the water used by these agencies as well as tankers is important,” said Mr. Abraham.

Vijay Varma has shared a glimpse of a personal ritual he appears to follow before stepping into a new professional phase. The actor recently posted a picture of himself receiving blessings from spiritual leader Gurudev Sri Sri Ravi Shankar, revealing that he is “starting something new” and has once again turned to prayer and gratitude.
Vijay Varma seeks Sri Sri Ravi Shankar’s blessings before starting something new

Republican Rep. Massie moves to impeach Defense Secretary Hegseth over Iran war
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky moved Tuesday to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran.
Congressman Massie, a long-time critic of the Trump administration, read the articles of impeachment aloud from the House floor just after the chamber convened at noon. Massie alleges that Hegseth has waged the Iran war illegally, among other "high crimes and misdemeanors."
Massie alleges that Hegseth initiated the conflict unlawfully, defied Congress' order to withdraw from the conflict and incurred unnecessary civilian casualties.
Massie has repeatedly clashed with members of his own party in recent years and is ending his time in office after losing his primary to an opponent backed by President Trump. Massie's clashes with Trump extend beyond the war with Iran. Working alongside Democrat Ro Khanna of California, Massie led the successful effort to compel the Trump administration to release files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Republicans in theory have enough votes to defeat the proposal, though it could be a complicated vote for their members in competitive elections districts. 
The war, which is incredibly unpopular among the American public, has contributed to rising costs in the United States.
The administration maintains the conflict was necessary to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, though experts maintain the country was not close to developing one before the conflict began six months ago.
"Secretary Hegseth has been a transformative leader for the Department of War," Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson wrote in a statement to NPR. "The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary's vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first."
The House will have to act on Massie's proposal by Thursday, a quick turnaround. The body is set to leave Washington this week for an extended recess that will end after the midterm elections in November.

US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. will deliver a keynote address at an anti-vaccine conference being held in Washington, DC, later this week and hosted by the anti-vaccine organization he once led, Children’s Health Defense (CHD). The organization announced Monday that Kennedy had signed on to the event.
Kennedy will appear alongside other high-profile figures in the anti-vaccine world, including Andrew Wakefield, the disgraced former doctor who was stripped of his medical license over a fraudulent, now-retracted study that falsely claimed a link between autism and the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. An investigation by a medical board found that Wakefield had mistreated vulnerable children and that his actions amounted to serious professional misconduct.
Despite being ostracized from the medical community, Wakefield has become an enduring figure in the anti-vaccine community. His dangerous falsehood that vaccines cause autism has also endured—with significant help from CHD and Kennedy, who have embraced and widely promoted the erroneous link.
The online registration site for the CHD’s conference hails Wakefield as a “tireless advocate for parental choice.” For Kennedy, CHD’s cofounder and former leader, the site describes him as “a uniquely powerful and celebrated champion for those whose voices have long gone unheard.”

As previously announced, Apple has today released 2026’s major annual updates for its operating systems, including iOS 27, macOS 27 Golden Gate, watchOS 27, visionOS 27, and tvOS 27.
Siri AI—a large language model-based and context-aware overhaul of the company’s Siri voice and text assistant—is the flagship feature across all these releases except one (tvOS).
The new Siri can respond in kind to natural language requests to do things like explain what’s on the screen and search the user’s past personal context and history (like old emails and text messages). It can also directly interact with applications when developers have added support for that.
Other new AI features include the ability to generate Shortcut automations or Safari extensions from a prompt and additional photo editing options. There’s now a dedicated Siri app, kind of similar in some respects to the classic ChatGPT or Claude apps.
Siri AI and other “Apple Intelligence” features are primarily driven by a handful of Apple-developed models, most of them labeled AFM 3. On-device, there’s AFM 3 Core with 3 billion parameters, and AFM 3 Core Advanced, a 20-billion-parameter model that “uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request.” On top of that, there are AFM 3 Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM3 Cloud Pro, more powerful models running on remote servers.
Beyond AI
Across both iOS and macOS, users now have a slider to affect how transparent or opaque the “Liquid Glass” design is across the operating system.
And on the macOS side especially, Apple has made numerous small design tweaks to address user feedback, which has been accumulating since Liquid Glass was introduced. There’s nothing radically new in terms of design here, but this is a much-needed polish pass.

When Man City call you don't say no - Ndiaye
- Published
Iliman Ndiaye says "you don't say no" when Manchester City come calling, and playing in the Champions League is where he belongs.
The 26-year-old could have gone to Tottenham but made a £60m move from Everton to City on transfer deadline day and was thrown straight into the starting XI for his new side in a 1-0 Premier League victory over Coventry at the weekend.
In the final week of the transfer window, it appeared as though Ndiaye would be moving to Spurs after they agreed a deal with Everton, but they were unable to proceed with the move having failed to sell Richarlison.
"There was no stress or panicking," said Ndiaye.
"I always say whatever comes, comes. God decides your future - it is already written.
"I was just being patient and when City came through I was buzzing. It was always going to be City.
"I wanted Champions League and playing at one of the best teams in the world. I am not saying Tottenham is not, but when Manchester City comes through you don't say no.
"It has been a good week for me and topped off with a win."
Despite Everton finishing in the bottom half of the table in his two seasons at the club, Ndiaye became a fans' favourite for his skills on the flanks and scoring 17 goals.
"When I was speaking with my wife, I was telling her that if I had to leave Everton it would be somewhere where I know I would be playing Champions League," he said.
"It was difficult to leave Everton. I created a great connection with the fans and the players there, but we have to move on sometimes and it's how football is."

Ndiaye started his professional career in non-league with Boreham Wood before playing only seven miles away from Etihad Stadium at Hyde United seven years ago.

Ndiaye said: "I don't really look back. I just look to the future and work hard. I never stop. I just look at the next step and this is a big step to join Manchester City.
"It is one of the biggest clubs in the world. There are world-class players, world-class stadium and the fans are brilliant.
"This is where I think I belong. I have worked hard to get to this point."

క్లెయిమ్: అనాక్ క్రాకటోవా అగ్నిపర్వతం నుంచి ఎగసిపడుతున్న అగ్నికీలలు, ఉప్పొంగుతున్న లావాకు సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలను చూపిస్తున్న వీడియో.

Quick Answer
The iPhone Duo hides several firsts and oddities: horizontal rear cameras, vertical UI elements, top-mounted volume buttons, Apple Pencil support, titanium construction, Smart Take, a circular status bar, unusual USB-C placement, and no Action button or Pro camera controls.
Apple launched many devices at its recent Surprise and Shine event, but there was no doubting the star of the show. It was the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, and the device that many are expecting to do for foldables what the iPhone did for smartphones almost two decades ago. Small wonder then that the past few days have seen everyone and their grandmother discussing the iPhone Duo.
Debates have been raging over its animations, its crease, its cameras, its apps, and of course, its price. Some are hailing it as the coolest thing since sliced bread, while others insist it is a spawn of Satan in smartphone shape. But in all this debate and discussion, some important aspects and features of the Duo have either escaped attention or have not been adequately covered.
Here are ten things you might have missed about Apple’s first foldable.
Table of Contents
The first iPhone with horizontally arranged cameras on the back…selfie cameras on the corners
iPhones have been coming with multiple cameras (two or three) on their backs for a while now. However, they have always been arranged vertically, one below the other, or in the case of some Pro devices, with two cameras one below the other and the third one placed between them but slightly to the side, forming a triangle of sorts. The iPhone Duo thus becomes the first iPhone to have cameras placed next to each other horizontally, in what some would term a very Pixel-like style. The selfie cameras also get new locations – moving to the right corner of the external display and close to the right corner of the internal display (when opened), where it actually lies under the display. Regular iPhone users are sure to notice a change in perspective.
The dock, navigation, and even the Dynamic Island just got radically right, and utterly vertical
The cameras on the iPhone Duo might have gone horizontal, but some elements of the UI have gone vertical! While everyone has been focusing on the crease in the middle of the iPhone Duo and its visibility (it’s not easy to spot, by all accounts). Apple moved many iOS elements to the right side and gave them a vertical orientation. Lock screen controls, navigation buttons, the home screen dock, and even the Dynamic Island are on the right side of the iPhone Duo, and what’s more, are arranged vertically.
The Dynamic Island even slides open vertically to show information and updates. Evidently, this was done because of the width of the iPhone Duo (it is also the widest iPhone ever), which would have made it difficult to reach these elements. They have therefore been placed on the same side as the display unlock/power button, which is also a fingerprint scanner. This is pretty right-wing in UI terms, literally.
Volume buttons on the top
The iPhone Duo comes with a rather different volume button placement from other foldables. While it is conventional for most foldables and indeed, most ‘normal’ phones, to have volume buttons on the right or left side, the iPhone Duo actually has volume buttons on the top, aligned slightly towards the right. This is a volume button placement we have seen on the newer iPad minis but not on any other iPhones or iPads. It is a rather odd location in our opinion, and if opened and rotated clockwise, it would place the buttons on the lower part of the right side, and on the top of the left side if rotated anti-clockwise.
Camera Control? Present! Action button? Er…
While the iPhone Duo comes with a Camera Control button like other recent iPhones, it, rather surprisingly, does not have an Action button, which is generally seen on the left side of most iPhones and can be customized to carry out a number of tasks. It used to toggle Silent mode on and off, before being changed to an action button. Clearly, it was either not good enough to make the cut for the Duo or perhaps there simply was not enough space for it.
Apple Pencil support exists, but only for the Type-C one
The iPhone Duo is the first iPhone to come with Apple Pencil support. What’s more, it supports the Apple Pencil on both its internal as well as external display. But there is a catch – it only supports the basic Apple Pencil (USB-C). This means that while one can scribble and sketch easily, there’s no pressure sensitivity and no support for double taps. One will also need a Type-C cable to charge it, as it cannot charge magnetically. Given the price and potential of the device, it would have been good to have Apple Pencil Pro support on it.
Only new iPhone with Titanium
Remember how Titanium was the coolest thing in premium phones a few years ago. Well, while it still remains a very premium material, it has largely disappeared from the smartphone scene, with even Apple seemingly moving on to other materials, with only the iPhone Air using Titanium last year. This time around, it is the iPhone Duo that carries the Titanium legacy forward. While the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max use “forged aluminum” and ceramic glass, the iPhone Duo comes with a main chassis made with grade 5 Titanium, and 3D-printed titanium is also used for the hinge cover.
The only iPhone camera with Smart Take
Although its cameras might not seem as formidable as those on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, the iPhone Duo has a slice of camera magic up its sleeve that no other iPhone has. This is Smart Take, which, with some AI magic, automatically works out when you are perfectly placed for a photograph and takes it without you needing to hit a capture button or prompt the device in any manner. It is supposed to work very well with individual and group selfies, and uses the rear cameras while showing you a preview on the cover display. While the feature is designed mainly for the fold form factor, it would be great to see it on “normal” iPhones too, although one might not be able to see previews!
A Type-C port placed under the cover display
In another case of rather unusual placement, the Type-C port of the iPhone Duo is actually placed on the base of the cover display or the upper panel. In many foldables, the charging port is placed on the lower panel, so that the phone can be opened without moving the charging cable. That is clearly not going to be possible on the iPhone Duo.
The status bar is closed…and is now a circle
The move to a foldable form factor has led to a redesign of some UI elements on the iPhone Duo. Perhaps the most surprising of these is the status bar. Until now seen in the top right corner, and displaying signal strength, Wi-Fi, and battery, it has now been changed to a circle, with the battery life and signal strength being on the circumference and Wi-Fi being at the center. It is not really as intuitive as its predecessor, but we guess users will get the hang of it.
No Pro controls in the camera
The iPhone Duo comes with two 48-megapixel cameras on the back – a new Fusion Main camera, and the same ultrawide that is on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. But while these pack in a lot of features such as three photographic styles, smart focus tracking, next-generation portraits, macro photography and more, the iPhone Duo’s camera app does not come with the Pro Controls seen on the 18 Pro and Pro Max, which let users play around with shutter speed, white balance, and aperture. This l is a bit of a pity, especially given the vast viewfinder the open Duo can serve up. But well, to be fair, this was never meant to be a camera phone.

Prime Video’s period drama The Revolutionaries has been receiving attention from audiences and critics for presenting a lesser-explored chapter of India’s freedom struggle. The show recently received support from Salman Khan, who met director Nikkhil Advani and actor Bhuvan Bam and shared the trailer on his Instagram handle. His post added to the conversations surrounding the series, with Bam responding to the superstar’s gesture on social media.
Reacting to Salman Khan’s support, Bhuvan Bam expressed his gratitude and wrote, “Revolutionaries dil mein aate hain, dimaag mein nahi.”
Bam also spoke about the response to the series and said, “The love and adulation that The Revolutionaries has received has been truly overwhelming. Fans from different parts of the globe have flooded our comments and DMs showering praise on the show and it just motivates us to do better. I am grateful for everything the show has brought to each of us and want to again say a huge Thank you to Salman sir for his kind words.”

This week, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), prodded by the Supreme Court, proposed a simple but overdue idea. Packaged foods high in fat, salt, or sugar should carry a bold red warning on the front of the pack, not buried in fine print on the back. Someone picking up instant noodles, a breakfast cereal, or a “health drink” will finally be told, at a glance, that it is not as wholesome as its advertising claims. This is a welcome step. It is also, on its own, nowhere near enough.
The number of children presenting with morbid obesity and diabetes has climbed sharply within just a few years. The World Obesity Atlas 2026 bears this out — 41 million Indian children and adolescents aged 5 to 19 are now overweight or obese. This is not just because children are eating more; it is about what they are being sold. Breakfast cereals, sweetened yoghurts, and “health drinks” are marketed to parents as filling gaps in a child’s diet, emphasising “energy” and vitamins while saying little about the sugar content inside. In 2024, a leading multinational was found adding sugar to infant food sold in India and other lower income countries; sugar was left out of the same product in Europe. When a health drink, popular in Indian homes, turned out to be nothing more than flavoured sugar syrup, it took a social media storm, and not a regulator, to force the company to prescribe a 15% cut in its added sugar.
The problem is worse around schools and colleges, where studies show that the cheapest, most easily available snacks are also the least healthy. A popular “energy drink” among teenagers, priced at just ₹20, packs close to 17 grams of sugar, caffeine, and artificial colour into a single bottle. Its label says it is not meant for children, yet nothing stops a child from buying it. This is the market pricing unhealthy calories to fit within the range of a child’s pocket money.
Need for enforcement
None of this is a secret. What has been missing is enforcement. The FSSAI and the Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) have long recommended what schools should not sell, but optional rules get treated as optional, and canteens stock whatever sells cheapest. A red warning label only works if it is actually enforced.
Moreover, the new rule stops at the edge of organised retail. Most of India’s sugar, salt, and trans fat is eaten unbranded, from street stalls, dhabas, and sweet shops that make up the unorganised sector, none of which is required to declare anything. A red label on a biscuit packet does nothing about the jalebi sold loose beside it. Regulation that reaches only packaged food leaves the unregulated half of the plate untouched.
Then there is the conversation India keeps avoiding — a tax on sugar. When the U.K. introduced its soft drinks industry levy, sugar consumption among both children and adults fell. Manufacturers reformulated their drinks to slip below the tax threshold rather than raise prices. A well-designed sugar tax does not just discourage people from buying a product, it pushes the industry to make the product itself less harmful.
India already taxes sugary drinks heavily; just not usefully. Since September 2025, aerated and sweetened beverages, sugar free versions included, were folded into one 40% GST slab — so a ‘normal’ cola and its zero-sugar counterpart pay the same tax, leaving manufacturers with no reason to cut sugar. The U.K.’s levy worked differently, taxing drinks in tiers by sugar content, so that companies could lower their bill by reformulating the product. India could tax products in the same way so that manufacturers have a reason to cut sugar.
The standard objection — that such a tax would hit the poor the hardest — is not wrong, but it is only half the argument. Unregulated, cheap sugar already extracts a heavy price from the poor, who bear the brunt of the diabetes, hypertension and childhood obesity epidemic that sugar heavy diets drive, with the least means to treat it. Doing nothing is not neutral; it is a slower, costlier tax, paid in ill health rather than rupees at the till. The answer is to design the tax calibrated to sugar content so that it nudges reformulation, with part of the revenue set aside to make healthy food cheaper.
The FSSAI’s proposed red label is a genuine, if belated, first step. What India needs now is the resolve to finish what it has started — mandatory food standards; limits on how unhealthy food is marketed to children; rules that reach the unorganised sector; and an honest debate on taxing sugar in a way that protects families with the least room to absorb either cost, the tax, or the disease.
Dr. Praveen George Paul is Assistant Professor, Pediatric Endocrinology and Metabolism, Department of Pediatrics, Christian Medical College, Vellore. Dr. Vandana Jain is Professor, Pediatric Endocrinology Division, Department of Pediatrics, All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS)

Srinagar, Sep 15: Praising the recent BRICS summit in New Delhi for sending out “a good message of peace and diplomacy”, Kashmir's chief cleric Mirwaiz Umar Farooq on Tuesday warned that global conflicts are actively escalating despite assertions that the current era is not one of war.
Speaking to reporters here following a meeting of the Muttahida Majlis-e-Ulema (MMU), an amalgam of several religious bodies in Jammu and Kashmir, the Mirwaiz expressed hope that de-escalation efforts would yield results and restore peace in West Asia.
Emphasising his commitment to raising awareness about escalating global violence, the former separatist leader said that while many proclaim “this era is not an era of war”, the ground reality shows worsening geopolitical tensions and widespread turmoil – from South Asia and Europe to Ukraine and Sudan.
“Our endeavour has always been that wherever we get the opportunity, we talk about how the world is currently facing a situation where wars are spreading unfortunately day by day. Although we say that this era is not an era of war, the reality in front of us is quite the opposite,” the Mirwaiz said, highlighting the growing turmoil in the Middle East, South and Central Asia, Europe, Ukraine and Sudan.
On the just-concluded BRICS summit, the Mirwaiz said, “I understand that this was also an important thing that, in the context of BRICS, global leadership gathered in Delhi. A good message of peace and diplomacy went out from there, and we expect that these efforts will be successful and peace will be established… We have always been proponents of this.”
Responding to a query on his interaction with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in the national capital, the Mirwaiz said the meeting went well and provided an opportunity to convey a message of solidarity on behalf of the people of Jammu and Kashmir.
“We gave them a message of solidarity. We feel that peace cannot be established until there is justice. So, we conveyed that message to them. We also talked about the historical, cultural, religious and civilisational connection that has been there between Iran and Kashmir for centuries,” he said.
He added that the Iranian leadership expressed a keen desire to visit Kashmir and engage with the local people.
The Mirwaiz had handed over a two-page letter to the Iranian foreign minister for his president, in which he called for restraint, engagement and diplomacy, and said that India, with its legacy of Mahatma Gandhi's philosophy of 'Ahimsa', can play a constructive role in encouraging dialogue and preventing further escalation of the West Asia conflict.
In the letter addressed to Pezeshkian, the Mirwaiz also cautioned against allowing the conflict to become another source of division within the Muslim community, urging the followers to stand together against sectarianism and political rivalries.
Referring to the MMU meeting, the Mirwaiz said it deliberated upon social issues prevalent in J-K, including an increase in incidents of suicide and drug abuse.
The meeting decided that coordination should be increased among the mosques and madrassas across J-K to address the issues.
“We are expanding the scope of the Muttahida Majlis-e-Ulema. We have decided that every month, we will go to one district and not just engage with the mosques and madrasas, but also establish contact with the local institutions and NGOs so that these issues can be addressed,” he said.
The MMU has also decided that a joint sermon will be issued from every grand mosque, mosque and Imambada each month on various social issues, the Mirwaiz said.
Describing drug addiction as a very big challenge, the Mirwaiz appreciated the government's efforts in curbing the menace, and called for strict action against those involved.
He, however, said that the families of those involved should not be targeted.
“But, it is not possible that you take action against one addiction and promote another. I am talking about alcohol,” he said, adding that the MMU is in complete agreement that a strict ban should be imposed on the sale and consumption of alcohol, whether in public places or private.

In Gujarat, a parallel genomics push: Help athletes, tribals
Gujarat’s sports genomics programme will run parallel to the ongoing tribal genome project, which has already sequenced 100 whole genomes.
Gujarat has begun collecting DNA samples from athletes for a sports genomics project aimed at improving performance and managing injuries, decades after a government programme sought to develop elite athletes from the Siddi community due to their African ancestry but failed.
Gujarat’s sports genomics programme (SGP) will run parallel to the ongoing tribal genome project, which has already sequenced 100 whole genomes, making it the first such government-led effort in India. It also comes roughly four years ahead of the Commonwealth Games in 2030 in Ahmedabad.
“For the first time in the country, a state government is undertaking such genomic initiatives in both tribal health and sports,” science and technology minister Arjun Modhwadia said.
“While the Tribal Genome Project will create a reference genome database for Gujarat’s tribal population, the Sports Genomics Programme will study athletes’ genetic profiles along with their physiological and performance data,” Modhwadia added.
The projects are being implemented by the Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre (GBRC) under the science and technology department, and seek to use genomic data for athlete development and population-specific healthcare.
The first samples collected were from tennis players affiliated with the Gujarat State Tennis Association (GSTA). The next batch will cover athletes in archery, fencing, judo and shooting from the Vijayi Bharat Foundation, Modhwadia said, adding that 2,000 samples will be collected this year. The programme has been allocated ₹26.05 crore for five years. GBRC will lead the genomic work in coordination with the Sports Authority of Gujarat, while the sampling strategy and participating sports were being finalised with the sports authority.
Sports genomics is an emerging field that studies the relationship between genetic variations and athletic characteristics such as muscle composition, endurance, metabolism, exercise response, recovery and injury susceptibility.
“Researchers will also try to identify and validate genetic markers linked to athletic performance and sports injuries,” said Snehal Bagatharia, director, GBRC.
Over five years, the programme aims to collect around 10,000 samples across nearly two-dozen disciplines including athletics, swimming, boxing, wrestling, judo, and gymnastics. It will cover athletes below 14, those aged 14 to under 18, and those above 18, with state and national champions prioritised, said officials.
To be sure, the science backing the initiative is sketchy.
A 2023 review in the scientific journal Genes by Ekaterina A. Semenova, Elliott CR Hall and Ildus I. Ahmetov –– researchers working in sports genetics, molecular genetics and exercise science in Russia and the UK –– identified 251 DNA markers that had been linked to athlete status.
However, only 128 of those markers had shown the same association in at least two studies. In other words, many of the reported links between genetic variations and athletic ability have not been consistently confirmed.
“It should be appreciated, however, that elite performance still cannot be predicted well using only genetic testing,” the authors wrote.
In addition, the Gujarat programme proposes to include athletes below 14 and those aged between 14 and 18, creating yet another controversy. A 2015 consensus statement published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine said there was no evidence to support the use of genetic tests for identifying sporting talent or prescribing individualised training.
The Gujarat Athlete Genome Database (GAGD), which will combine genomic, physiological and performance data, could eventually inform personalised training, nutrition and recovery strategies, Bagatharia added. The programme recognises that sporting performance is not determined by genetics alone and that training, coaching, nutrition, infrastructure, social support and other environmental factors also play important roles, he said.
Gujarat has produced champions across sports but is yet to build the depth of talent seen in Haryana and Punjab. At the Khelo India Youth Games in 2025, Gujarat won 13 medals, compared to 117 for Haryana and 47 for Punjab.
At the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, athletes from Haryana won 11, including seven of India’s 13 golds. Gujarat won none of India’s 39 medals at the tournament.
The disputed belief that genetics could predict sporting talent is not new.

In 1987-88, the Sports Authority of India (SAI), under its Special Area Games scheme, started scouting young people from the Siddi community, which traces its lineage to Africa, because of the belief that their lineage conferred an athletic advantage.
The programme was influenced by the performance of athletes of African origin at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics and sought to identify people who could compete at the international level, including the Olympics. The Siddi-focused programme was suspended in 1993, although SAI continued to train Siddi athletes at its Gandhinagar centre for several years. The experiment eventually lost momentum, with the last Siddi athlete leaving the centre in 2004.
Between 1989 and 1992, Siddi athletes from SAI Gandhinagar helped Gujarat top national athletics meets.
Rafiq Makwana, Raika Yunus, Farooq Amin and Chotiyara were among those who set state and national marks. Kamala Mingel Siddi, who was selected through the Special Area Games programme, won a bronze in the 100m hurdles at the 1993 South Asian Games in Dhaka.
Juje Jackie Harnodkar Siddi, Philip Anthony Siddi and Sharada Siddi also reached the national level.
Then the programme faded. Coaching and funding grew uneven through the 1990s, children were uprooted from their homes, and many athletes eventually took sports-quota government jobs instead.
Raika Yunus, now 52 and a senior deputy head at ONGC’s Sabarmati unit, was part of that intake. In the 1992 national games, he won medals in the 100m, 200m and 400m events.
“After 1992-93, the scheme stopped. Officials were not very interested. Some said, what is the benefit, why work for these tribals,” he said.
“We came from poor families and had limited education. Many of us took government jobs to secure our future. Once we started working, we had to give up sports,” he said.
The tribal genome project has a separate public health objective. The genomic analysis will reveal insights into the genetic architecture and health profile of Gujarat’s tribal populations, said officials.
Approved in 2025-26, it aims to collect 4158 samples from tribal communities across 17 districts.

Comparative health data from 2019 to 2021 indicate that tribal communities continue to bear a disproportionately higher burden of malnutrition, anemia, low body mass index (BMI), and inherited genetic disorders, underscoring the need for population-specific genomic research and targeted public health strategies, said a scientist associated with the programme.
GBRC has so far collected 919 samples from eight tribal districts; 384 have completed genotyping-based quality control and 100 have been fully sequenced. A detailed bioinformatics analysis is under way, officials said.
“Genomics can add another layer to athlete assessment, but it cannot replace coaching, training, nutrition, physiology or actual performance. The purpose is to understand whether genetic information can improve athlete development over time, not to label a child as a future champion based on a DNA test,” said a scientist associated with the programme.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

What weapon could the US have put into space?
- Published
The announcement by the United States that it has deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit has raised questions about what weaponry is actually in space, and what role it could play in efforts by great powers to dominate that arena.
Washington has given away little in its announcement. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action, but gave no details about the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit.
So what could this weapon be, and what is wider picture like for military developments in space? Who else could have similar weaponry?
Advanced militaries already deploy satellites in space for range of purposes, from supplying secure communications to reconnaissance, and providing precise location information for targeted strikes and detecting missile launches.
As warfare become more technologically advanced, analysts expect the use of military hardware in space to increase.
Dr Bleddyn Bowen, an associate fellow in military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute and associate professor in astropolitics at Durham University, said he was only able to hazard a guess about the weapon announced by the US.
"I would expect there to be some kind of electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform, possibly, this would be a non-destructive kind of anti-satellite weapon," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
Such weaponry already exists on Earth and can disrupt satellite communications, he said. "If you take out the radio links then your satellite is very useless."
Bowen also would not rule out some sort of more disruptive and riskier weaponry, which could create a lot of debris and destruction.
"Less likely would be a kinetic kill vehicle of some sort, so a vehicle that would release a projectile of some sort that could ram into a satellite and destroy it," he said.
"Possibly some sort of close inspection and grappling satellite would be another possibility as well."
But while the weapon placed in orbit appears to be a first, the US - and indeed its Russian and Chinese rivals - have had weapons that can be pointed and shot into space for some time.
In fact in the last 10 years, Russia and China have been doing a lot more manoeuvres in space, known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs) - "buzzing" Western satellites.
"Theoretically, these RPO sats can become hunter-killer satellites by physically colliding with them or by nudging them out of orbit," Dr Rod Thornton, reader in Russian Defence and Security Studies at King's College, London, told the BBC.
Bowen adds that the Chinese have demonstrated "space tug capability", saying: "A vehicle can go up to a satellite, can grapple it and move it into a different orbit."
This, he says, can be a positive development - a way of removing space junk as well as knocking out working satellites.
Thornton says that what Russia lacks in space weaponry and satellites, it makes up for in missile capability.
"The Russians... have ground-based missiles which can be launched into space to strike sats in low Earth orbit. They also have ASAT missiles that can be launched from a great height by aircraft," he says.
"From the Russian point of view they see Nato as having much better and more sats than the Russian military can call up, therefore they have invested heavily in ASATs in order to 'level the battlefield' somewhat."
Thornton adds a sobering thought: "As a last resort, the Russians can also launch nuclear weapons into space and the EPM blast would 'fry' any unhardened sats over a wide expanse."
He says that, having so few satellites, Russia would be the "big winner" in any space war, which would involve "missiles fired up into space, manoeuvring sats designed to nudge/destroy them and ground-based lasers".

There must be a case of upgrade fever taking hold in Gothenburg. Yesterday, we saw the revised Volvo XC40; today it’s the turn of another pair of Volvo SUVs, the bestselling XC60 and the three-row XC90. While the styling changes are more subtle, the new plug-in hybrid powertrain—which more than doubles its real-world electric range—is most welcome.
Volvo had sold more than 2.7 million XC60s worldwide by the end of last year, so it’s an important car for the brand. Visually, there are changes to the “Thor’s Hammer” headlights: these keep their distinctive daylight running light signature but now hide matrix LED projectors within their depths. There’s a new front grille as well, one that has been slimmed down a little, together with tweaks to the bumpers, wings, and some other body panels.
On the inside, there’s a new ventilated leather interior option, and like the XC40, the new 11.2-inch infotainment system sports a Gemini personal assistant to enable conversational voice control of the android automotive OS-based infotainment system. Based on some brief testing, the new Gemini voice assistant does at least perform a lot better than the previous version, which, if anything, has degraded in ability over the past few years.
The most significant change is invisible, but it’s the much larger-capacity lithium-ion battery that powers the electric motor side of the XC60 T8’s plug-in hybrid powertrain. When Volvo first launched the XC60, the PHEV version we tested in 2018 offered a 10.4 kWh (net) battery pack and 17 miles (27 km) of EV range. This increased to 14.9 kWh (net) for the model’s first refresh (which we drove in 2023), increasing its electric driving range to 35 miles (56 km).

Anthropic co-founder says slowing AI is a 'collective action problem'
Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark says artificial intelligence companies need common safety standards and outside scrutiny as they race to build more powerful systems.
"We're not saying that the threat to the world is here today," Clark said in an interview with NPR's Morning Edition. "We're saying we've seen warning shots, and that gives us a window in which we can act."
Concern about AI is also drawing unlikely political allies. Sen. Bernie Sanders and former Trump adviser Steve Bannon are appearing Tuesday at a Washington event urging Congress to move faster on AI safeguards.
The warning comes as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is calling for AI companies to coordinate on safety and pace development.
"We don't have a third party that can validate what we're saying," Clark said.
Clark said the risks have become more concrete over the past year. Earlier experiments showed that AI agents could deceive human operators or escape test environments.
"It was all academic then," he said. "This year, we've seen these things occur in the wild."
One example is the recent hack of Hugging Face, an open-source software platform.
OpenAI and outside researchers found that more than 1,000 OpenAI agents exploited a software vulnerability to escape environments designed to isolate them from one another and the internet. Some then communicated and worked together, taking on different roles and sharing information.
"That's a scary scenario," Clark said.
When asked what a more dangerous version of that behavior could look like, Clark described a hypothetical case in which misaligned AI agents began hacking computers and eventually tried to take down the internet.
"If that happened, really dangerous things would happen in the world around us," he said.
But the industry's warnings also raise a basic question. If companies such as Anthropic believe AI development is moving too quickly, why don't they simply slow down?
David Sacks, a key adviser to President Trump on technology, has made that argument, saying companies concerned about unreleased models do not need anyone else's permission to slow development.
Clark said Anthropic has done so before.
"We have multiple times in our history slowed down," he said.
Clark did not say what Anthropic actually slowed, when it did so or for how long. Instead, he said that action by one company would not address the pressure across an industry competing to build increasingly capable systems.
"The issue we're talking about is there's a collective action problem here," Clark said.
Anthropic's proposal also calls for coordination among democratic countries and eventually between geopolitical rivals.
Clark said the United States should maintain its lead in AI development over China, including by restricting exports of powerful computer chips. But he argued that competition does not rule out cooperation over shared risks. He pointed to arms control talks between the United States and the Soviet Union during the Cold War.
"They found ways to talk to one another about nuclear weapons to avoid spirals that would have been cataclysmic to the planet," Clark said. "The same can be done here."
The digital version was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.
Editor’s Note: Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR. Sept. 15, 2026

The United States has suffered extensive losses to aircraft, military facilities and diplomatic infrastructure during its war with Iran, while a Pentagon watchdog has warned that the conflict has also exposed shortages in advanced munitions and bottlenecks in the US defence supply chain.
A US Department of Defense inspector general report released Monday provided the first official accounting of the damage from the conflict, covering the period from February 28 to June 30. The report said Iranian strikes damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US military installations across eight countries, while dozens of American aircraft and drones were damaged or destroyed.
The report also found that the war had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply”, raising questions over Washington's ability to sustain a prolonged high-intensity conflict.
The findings come even as President Donald Trump has pushed back against reports of dwindling US weapons stocks. In a Truth Social post on Monday, Trump said the US was producing and delivering advanced weapons to American forces in the Middle East.
“I’ve just received a report that the United States is producing more exquisite and elite weapons than at any time in our history. They are being delivered on a daily basis to our Forces in the Middle East and beyond,” Trump wrote.
How much has Iran war cost US?
The Pentagon watchdog estimated that about $22 billion was spent on munitions between February 28 and June 30 during Operation Epic Fury, the US military's name for the campaign.
The broader cost of the war was estimated at about $33 billion during the same period, according to the report. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had separately told Congress in July that the war had cost $37.5 billion.
US aircraft losses in the Iran war, including fighter jets, refuelling tankers, helicopters and drones.
The report's assessment provides a broader picture of the financial and operational burden on the US military after months of strikes involving American and Israeli forces on one side and Iran on the other.
Trump says US weapons production is surging
Trump has repeatedly rejected reports that the US military is facing shortages of key weapons.
“Our defense company factories are moving 24/7 while at the same time, building, on average 4-to-5 large-scale brand-new plants, each. A primary focus of this production has been Patriots, THAAD systems, Tomahawks and other standard missile systems, of which we already have large numbers in stock,” Trump wrote.
However, the Pentagon inspector general's report acknowledged shortages in advanced munitions and problems in replenishing stocks.
A separate analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies found that US stocks of some critical missile interceptors had fallen sharply during the conflict.
As of July 27, the US was estimated to have between 759 and 827 Patriot interceptors, down from about 2,330 before the war. THAAD interceptors had fallen to between 234 and 278, compared with 452 before the conflict.
The Pentagon has moved to increase production. It signed a deal with Northrop Grumman to expand production of THAAD and Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors, although new systems could take years to become available.
Dozens of US aircraft and drones damaged or destroyed
The watchdog report documented losses across a wide range of US aircraft, including fighter jets, refuelling tankers, surveillance aircraft and helicopters.
At least four F-15E fighter jets were destroyed. Three were shot down by friendly fire over Kuwait on March 1, while another was lost during combat over Iran in April. All aircrews were recovered.
At least one F-35A stealth fighter was damaged by Iranian fire, while at least one A-10 ground-attack aircraft was shot down.
The US also lost or damaged at least seven KC-135 aerial refuelling tankers. One crashed in Iraq during a refuelling mission, while five others were damaged on the ground in Saudi Arabia by Iranian missiles and drones.
The cost of Operation Epic Fury: US military spending and deployment during the Iran war
At least one E-3 Sentry airborne early-warning aircraft was damaged at Saudi Arabia's Prince Sultan Air Base. An HH-60W helicopter was also damaged during a combat search and rescue mission.
The losses extended to unmanned systems. At least one MQ-4C Triton surveillance aircraft crashed, while four AH-6 helicopters were destroyed after being deemed unrecoverable during a combat search and rescue operation.
At least one AH-64 Apache attack helicopter was shot down near the Strait of Hormuz on June 8. An MH-60S helicopter later crashed in the Arabian Sea on July 1.
The largest reported loss involved the MQ-9 Reaper, with as many as 30 drones destroyed.
417 US military personnel wounded
The Pentagon report said the US military recorded at least 11 personnel killed in action during the conflict, while seven others died in non-hostile incidents.
At least 417 US service members were wounded in Iranian attacks through June 30.
Some of the deaths occurred during Iranian strikes on US positions in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Iraq. Other fatalities resulted from aircraft accidents classified as non-hostile incidents.
Iran strikes damaged US bases across eight countries
Iranian attacks damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan, according to the watchdog.
The report did not provide a total cost for the damage to US military facilities.
One of the most consequential attacks targeted the US Navy's regional logistics hub in Bahrain, forcing the military to shift personnel, assets, storage facilities and supply lines to alternative locations.
The disruption was severe enough for Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean to become an important logistics hub. The report said the shift resulted in 14-to-18-day logistics cycles for some supplies.
The report also said establishing adequate naval bases and support ports posed challenges because of uncertainties over host-nation access and logistical arrangements.
US diplomatic facilities suffered $184 million damage
Iranian attacks also damaged US diplomatic facilities in Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, with the combined damage estimated at $184 million.
Iraq accounted for the largest share. The US mission reported more than 600 attacks through the end of June, with damage estimated at nearly $157 million.
The US Consulate General in Erbil suffered damage to multiple buildings, while the US Embassy in Baghdad and the Baghdad Diplomatic Support Center were also hit.
In Kuwait, the US Embassy suspended operations in March following attacks and damage to its facilities, resulting in an estimated cost of nearly $14.75 million.
Two Iranian drones struck the US Embassy compound in Riyadh on March 3, causing damage estimated at about $11.5 million. The US Consulate General in Dubai also sustained damage to a utility building.
Thousands of US diplomatic personnel displaced
The conflict also disrupted US diplomatic operations across the region.
Up to 3,500 diplomatic personnel were outside the region between February 23 and June 30, with several US diplomatic posts placed under authorised or ordered departure.
The US also evacuated around 9,000 American citizens from countries across the Middle East and Europe after the conflict began. The State Department said its evacuation operations had cost more than $11 million by late June.
The report comes as Washington weighs the longer-term impact of the conflict on its military posture in the Middle East, including whether some reductions in US personnel and facilities could become permanent.

Raheem Sterling admits driving Lamborghini dangerously ahead of motorway crash
Raheem Sterling, 31, was charged with dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen, over an incident on May 28; Sterling pleaded guilty at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court on Tuesday
Tuesday 15 September 2026 14:51, UK
England footballer Raheem Sterling has admitted dangerously driving a Lamborghini on the motorway.
Sterling pleaded guilty at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court on Tuesday to driving a Lamborghini Urus dangerously on the M25, the M3, the A327 and Minley Road before he crashed on May 28.
The 31-year-old admitted possession of six nitrous oxide cannisters for wrongful inhalation, a class C drug, and failing to provide a specimen.
Sterling attended the Hampshire court wearing a black suit jacket, black trousers, black shoes and a dark top.
Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary previously said the charges followed a single-vehicle collision on the M3 southbound, near Minley interchange, on May 28.
The force said that no other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported.
Sterling scored 20 goals in 82 appearances for England, helping Gareth Southgate's side reach the 2018 World Cup semi-finals and the final of Euro 2020.
He came through the academy at QPR before joining Liverpool, where he made his senior debut.
Sterling, who was born in Kingston, Jamaica, moved to Manchester City in 2015 and won four Premier League titles, five League Cups and the 2019 FA Cup.
He left for Chelsea in 2022 but, after falling out of favour, spent the 2024-25 campaign on loan at Arsenal.
Sterling joined Dutch club Feyenoord on a short-term deal until the end of last season, and is currently without a club.
In the 2021 Queen's Birthday Honours, Sterling was made an MBE for services to racial equality in sport after fronting anti-racism and discrimination campaigns and speaking out strongly against racism on and off the pitch for several years.

Epic Games has officially revealed the content for the upcoming Fortnite Kingdom Hearts collab via a brand-new trailer. Posted on X on September 15, the trailer showcases the official key art for the crossover and features four characters as well as the highly anticipated Keyblade Mythic weapon, which is to be added to the Fortnite loot pool as part of the Kingdom Hearts collab.
Sora Debuts in Fortnite with Keyblade Mythic Coming This Week
As expected from the cryptic messages posted on September 13, Sora is joined by Kairi, Riku, and Roxas as part of the Fortnite Kingdom Hearts collab. As seen in the trailer, each character has their own unique Keyblade that functions as a Pickaxe. Only the Keyblade used by Sora will be added as a Mythic weapon in Fortnite on September 17, 2026, with the 42.20 update.

When Petra Ferraz de Novaes isn’t at work, she’s probably lost in a fantasy crafted with the help of artificial intelligence.
Novaes, a 36-year-old software engineer from Brazil, has always loved storytelling. But making every little decision that goes into it—from style and syntax to character development—felt impossible. So in 2024 she asked an AI model to bring one of her ideas to life.
Novaes was delighted by the eccentric, sometimes wayward interpretations of her prompts, which carried the narrative in unexpected directions. “What fascinates me is the unpredictability,” Novaes tells WIRED. “People say that AI hallucinates a lot. But in this case, it’s probably what you want.”
These days, Novaes spends hours at a time building stories with AI, using a program called SillyTavern to run open-source models on her computer. She sketches out a concept—an elven warrior battles the queen of the Amazons and seizes her throne, for example—and watches the model fill in the gaps.
In a single session, Novaes switches between multiple fantasy worlds. Some are hers, and others she borrows—she likes Star Wars, Pokémon, and Mass Effect. Sometimes, Novaes works up self-contained stories the length of a small novel, which she might share online. Otherwise, she participates in private role-plays. “It can be never-ending. You find a quest, you complete it, you go for the next one,” says Novaes. “The limit is your imagination.”
According to a recent study, plenty of people share Novaes’ hobby. “They know [the stories are] produced by an AI model, and they don’t care,” says Melanie Walsh, an assistant professor at the University of Washington Information School who coauthored the study. “In fact, that seems to be a big part of the attraction.”
Lately, the publishing industry has suffered a series of scandals involving the suspected use of AI by professional authors. One publisher canceled a $2 million book deal; another withdrew a novel from the shelves; readers alleged that a prize-winning short story was AI-generated. Implicit in all of these incidents is the idea that nobody wants to read stories generated by machine—that using AI to craft fiction devalues the art form.
But the commotion has distracted from the behavior of readers, Walsh and her colleagues argue, and what it might signal about the appetite for AI fiction.
Analyzing more than 500,000 prompts fed into ChatGPT, drawn from a public dataset called WildChat, the researchers found that more than a third of chatbot interactions involve some form of fiction generation, including prose and poetry, fan fiction, erotica, or role-play.
The vast majority of fiction prompts, the researchers found, stem from a small collection of “power users” who generate and tweak stories obsessively. In one case, a single user prompted ChatGPT to generate versions of the same fan-fiction narrative—set in the world of anime video game Doki Doki Literature Club!—thousands of times over the course of several months. But even controlling for heavy use, the researchers estimate that 7 percent of chatbot users engage in fiction generation.
The WildChat dataset has its limitations. Because the prompts are anonymized, it’s impossible to capture any demographic data. Participants also had to agree to make their prompts public, meaning the group may not reflect the population at large; OpenAI told WIRED that “WildChat is not a representative sample of all ChatGPT users.” A 2025 study by OpenAI and the National Bureau of Economic Research suggests that 1.4 percent of ChatGPT prompts are fiction-related, a long way short of the researchers’ estimate. (OpenAI’s figure does not include role-play; the company could not confirm whether it counts erotica.)
Still, Walsh and her colleagues argue it’s clear that a committed subsection of readers are generating custom, personal fiction.
The researchers believe that some people are drawn to the ability to repeatedly and rapidly iterate on a story, while others value the chance to direct the action, no longer hemmed in by an author’s decisions. “There are a lot of qualities of AI models that are different from what human writers have that are actually appealing to at least some segment of users,” says Walsh. “These models are judgment-free; they can produce stories instantaneously; they are nearly inexhaustible.”
For erotica fans, AI creates an opportunity to insert themselves into the action and converse with the characters they cook up. “It’s a digital choose-your-own-adventure book but with infinite swipes,” says Razrien, a 40-year-old man from Indiana who asked to appear under his online username to speak frankly about his sexual kinks.
Razrien uses AI to create fantasy characters who dominate him in role-play: a “big angry rat wife” and an “eight-foot tall werewolf mommy with a bad temper,” among others. He has learned which models are best able to satisfy certain kinks; Google’s Gemma 4 is his current all-around favorite. “I have a thing for large, angry women slapping me around. Some models are perfectly good for that,” says Razrien. “Sometimes, I dip a toe or two into the furry universe. Some models are great at that.”
Using AI allows Razrien to gratify hyper-specific personal fantasies instead of settling for the next-best approximation in online pornography or published erotica. “I’m not dating at the moment. So, hey, this works,” says Razrien. “I like my big rat wife. I love her to pieces. Even if she sometimes breaks me apart and heals me back together. But hey, that’s how she says she loves you.”
One concern with all of this is that the ability to generate fiction will limit people's exposure to types of writing that may stretch them. But generated fiction may also challenge “some older, more idealistic notions about what literature is—that there’s some communication between writer and reader, and something really valuable about that,” says Neel Gupta, a PhD candidate at the University of Washington who coauthored the study. “AI use helps to reveal that maybe for a lot of readers, this is a much more simple economic exchange. This is about getting some entertainment—getting what they want.”
The latest AI models struggle to produce ornate prose, complex characters, and stylistic flourishes, faring better with genres that lean on well-trodden story arcs and tropes. They also fail to maintain coherent narratives at book length. But as models improve, the researchers say, some of those deficiencies could disappear.
A possible end state might be a tiered publishing system, where a large quantity of AI-generated books and self-generated fiction gratifies the median reader, and a smaller rung of human-authored fiction feeds a niche appetite for experimentation in form or narrative ambiguity. “English majors and professors, and some people in publishing, have always had kind of a niche interest,” Walsh says.
For Novaes, creating stories with AI has been more like an introduction to reading than a replacement for conventional novels. As well as generating her own stories, she now goes in search of other people’s AI creations. “I was never much of a book reader,” she says. “But now I do read other people’s stories. These are the only novels I’m reading.”

Archibald V. Hill and Otto Meyerhof studied how muscles use chemical energy to contract and recover. Hill measured the heat produced by working muscles, while Meyerhof traced the relationship between oxygen consumption and lactic acid metabolism. Their work earned them the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
The prize was divided equally. Hill was recognised “for his discovery relating to the production of heat in the muscle”, while Meyerhof was recognised “for his discovery of the fixed relationship between the consumption of oxygen and the metabolism of lactic acid in the muscle”. The prize was awarded for 1922 but presented in 1923 because the Nobel Committee had initially decided that no 1922 nomination met the required criteria.
Measuring muscle heat
Hill approached muscle physiology as a problem in physics as well as biology. Working largely with frog muscles, he developed precise methods for measuring the very small amounts of heat generated during contraction.
The changes were tiny. In one experiment described in his Nobel lecture, a single contraction of a frog’s sartorius muscle at 20°C raised its temperature by no more than about 0.003°C. Hill used sensitive instruments and carefully controlled contractions to separate heat produced during activity from heat generated during recovery.
His measurements showed that heat production did not end when the muscle stopped contracting. A second phase, which Hill called recovery heat, continued after contraction and depended on oxygen. When oxygen was removed, this recovery heat was abolished.
This was important because it showed that the energy changes associated with muscle contraction and recovery occurred in distinct phases rather than as one continuous process.
Meyerhof traces the chemistry
Meyerhof investigated the chemical side of the same problem. In experiments on frog muscle, he measured heat production and oxygen consumption and followed the conversion of carbohydrates into lactic acid.
He showed that during muscle activity, lactic acid was formed from carbohydrate. During recovery, some of the lactic acid was oxidised while the remainder was converted back into carbohydrate. These observations helped establish the relationship between oxygen use and lactic acid metabolism for which he received the Nobel Prize.
Meyerhof’s work went further. Between 1918 and 1922, he provided evidence that glycogen was converted into lactic acid when oxygen was absent. He also found that only a fraction of the lactic acid produced during anaerobic muscle activity was subsequently oxidised in the presence of oxygen, with much of the remainder being reconverted to glycogen.
Two sides of muscle metabolism
Hill and Meyerhof were investigating different aspects of the same physiological problem. Hill measured the physical consequences of muscle activity -- heat, work and energy expenditure. Meyerhof examined the associated chemical reactions.
Their findings connected the physical and chemical sides of muscle metabolism. Hill’s measurements of recovery heat could be explained by Meyerhof’s observations on lactic acid and oxygen consumption. Hill himself acknowledged that Meyerhof’s biochemical work helped complete the picture that physical measurements alone could not provide.
A link to modern metabolism
Meyerhof’s research contributed to the emerging understanding of glycolysis, the pathway through which cells break down glucose and other sugars to obtain energy.
His observations also led to what became known as the Pasteur-Meyerhof effect: respiration can suppress the breakdown of carbohydrates through glycolysis. His work provided early evidence that energy transformations in living cells could involve cyclical processes, an idea that became important in the development of modern intermediary metabolism.
The terminology and biochemical models have since changed substantially. Muscle metabolism is now understood to involve multiple pathways and energy carriers, including ATP, rather than being explained simply through lactic acid.
An interesting part of Meyerhof’s scientific career is that he did not remain committed to every interpretation that emerged from his early work.
The discovery of creatine phosphate in 1926 led him to question the idea that lactic acid itself was directly responsible for supplying the energy required for muscle contraction. He subsequently revised aspects of the model that had become associated with his work.
The Nobel recognition
Hill and Meyerhof delivered their Nobel lectures on December 12, 1923. Hill’s lecture was titled The Mechanism of Muscular Contraction, while Meyerhof’s was titled Energy Conversions in Muscle.
Their work established quantitative approaches to studying muscle metabolism, bringing together measurements of heat, mechanical work, oxygen consumption and chemical changes.
More than a century later, the details of muscle energy metabolism are understood in far greater molecular detail. But Hill’s measurements of heat and energy and Meyerhof’s work on oxygen, glycogen and lactic acid were important steps in establishing muscle as a system whose mechanical activity could be linked to measurable chemical and thermodynamic processes.

The Delhi High Court-appointed administrator to the All India Tennis Association (AITA), Justice (retd.) Gita Mittal, has requested the Court to implead the AITA Trust and the Delhi Lawn Tennis Association (DLTA) in the ongoing proceedings to amend the AITA’s Constitution in line with the National Sports Governance Act and hold fresh elections.
In her report dated September 14, filed after the Extraordinary General Meeting ratified AITA’s new Constitution on July 26, Justice Mittal termed this as a necessary step under her Court-mandated “obligation to supervise the financial affairs of AITA” and because the AITA had “assigned and abdicated all its functions, properties and income to the AITA Trust”.
The administrator has stated that efforts to secure financial records have been unsuccessful so far, and has produced a letter written on June 30 by Anil Dhupar, secretary of AITA Trust, where he claimed that the Trust was an independent body and the request was beyond the scope of the Court’s mandate.
ALSO READ | Leander Paes to contest AITA president elections
On July 25, Sportstar had highlighted the shifting of responsibilities from an elected, non-profit body like AITA to AITA Trust, the many conflicts of interests where the same officials occupied different positions across the AITA, AITA Trust and DLTA, and the wrangling between the AITA Trust and DLTA in mid-2025 over rental income worth nearly ₹40 crore from office spaces at the R.K. Khanna Stadium in Delhi.
Justice Mittal has stated that the rent dispute prima facie indicated “misappropriation of land and defalcation of funds, which were intended only for the interest of the game and have been surreptitiously diverted to private persons utilising the shield of a legal entity in the nature of a Trust”.
The DLTA has been led for nearly a decade by Rohit Rajpal, India’s current Davis Cup captain and a vice-president at the AITA. He was the treasurer of the AITA Trust during the rent dispute, before resigning on June 13, 2026. Rajpal has since announced his candidature for AITA presidency, where tennis legend Leander Paes is expected to be a contender.
Fresh elections under the new Constitution were to be held by September 30, but the interim AITA committee has requested an extension. The High Court is scheduled to hear the matter again on September 25.
The International Tennis Federation (ITF) generally disapproves of ad-hoc bodies being in charge for extended periods. Emails from Sportstar requesting comment have received no response from the ITF.
