For over a month and a half, residents of Chitpur Jyotinagar Colony in Cossipore, North Kolkata, have been without regular water supply after five public taps serving the colony ran dry following pipeline work in the area. Home to around 5,000 people, the 200-metre-long stretch is largely inhabited by people belonging to the Muslim community, and from lower-income backgrounds.
Residents, whose daily lives and livelihoods have been disrupted, alleged that water supply has been deliberately cut off by the state’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government to target them on the basis of their identities and force them out of the slum.
It is worth noting days after the election results were declared, local BJP MLA Ritesh Tiwari had pledged not to do anything for Muslims in his constituency. “Today, in front of Baba Bholenath, I swear, I will not do one job for them (Muslims) in the next five years. Will not issue any certificate for them. I am saying this live. I do not care about what anyone else says or thinks,” he had said.
Residents of Jyotinagar this colony, around 95% of them Muslims, depend on informal jobs for their sustenance. While women manage household chores in the morning before working at nearby factories in the afternoon, where they clean glass bottles and break glass panels into shards, most men work as daily wage labourers, masons, drivers, rickshaw pullers, or at factories.
How Did Water Supply Stop?
Alt News visited the water-deprived area, located a few meters from the over 200-years-old Cossipore Gun and Shell factory. The colony has five taps, which used to supply water from 5 am to 11 pm daily. Since July 29, after water supply was cut off, all five taps have been dry, locals said.
Locals said that water supply was perfectly normal and no complaints from the neighbourhood was made to the local civic body or any authorities, and yet, pipeline work was carried out in the area by the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) from July 26-28.
“Pipeline work was happening, they had dug two pits, one at the beginning of the slum and another at the end, marking the slum. On July 28, the water supply stopped around 11 pm. The next morning, we were waiting for the water supply to return. It has not been restored since,” said a resident, Mohinudeen Sheikh.
Sheikh, along with other residents, alleged that the pipelines were shut during the night while the roads were being repaired. “They used the cover of midnight to close the pipelines and mend the streets. We had no water from the early morning onwards,” he claimed.
‘They Also Took Away Electricity’
Residents said the water crisis was accompanied by a disruption in electricity supply as well. “They took away both water and electricity,” one youth said.
“They thought we were drawing electricity illegally from the main line, so they stopped the supply,” said a resident, Pinki Bibi. “All our houses have separate electricity connections and we receive separate bills. Then how can they say we are drawing electricity illegally?”
Residents claimed that electricity was restored after more than a week, following an incident during the Kanwar Yatra when poor visibility allegedly led some Kanwariyas to fall into the pothole-ridden lane. Alamgir Biswas, secretary of the Jyotinagar Colony, said that the supply was restored 10-15 days after the Basti Unnayan Samiti protested against the disruption.
Locals alleged that Calcutta Electric Supply Corporation (CESC) said the main-road connection had been shut to verify whether allegations of illegal electricity tapping were true. However, electricity supply remained available in the lanes branching off the main road. After seven days, CESC was able to verify that no illegal tapping was taking place and restored the connection, they added.
‘They are Trying to Evict Us’
Residents alleged that the disruption of these essential services was a part of a concerted attempt to evict the slum dwellers. Alamgir alleged: “The plan was to cut off the basic needs of water and electricity so that we leave the area. In this area, there is absolute communal harmony. Hindus and Muslims live harmoniously together. However, this government is trying to create a rift between us.”
Morjina Begum, who works at the glass factory, also alleged, “They are trying to evict us from this colony and therefore employing these tricks of cutting off the water supply. We are not new to this place. I was born here. My grandfather had settled here years ago,” while asserting, “We are not going to leave this place so easily. We will fight.”
Begum said residents had also approached the local councillor, Suman Singh, but has received no meaningful assistance as of yet. Alt News tried to speak to Singh, but he did not answer our calls till press time.
Saraswati Biswas, a 60-year-old Hindu resident, alleged that Tiwari, the newly elected MLA, had referred to the residents as “Bangladeshis and encroachers”. “He is calling us Bangladeshis and encroachers. How am I a Bangladeshi? My forefathers used to live here. I have proper documents proving that I am an Indian. I voted this year,” she said.
Legal Entanglement With Kolkata Port
While investigating the possible reason behind the elongated water supply disruption, Alt News found an intricate legal entanglement between the residents of the colony and the authorities of the Kolkata port.
As per legal records, the entire colony is built on a parcel of land measuring approximately 3478 square metres officially belonging to the Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata. On February 23, the estate officer of the port issued an eviction order for the colony.
Alt News accessed the order, and found that it was issued based on the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. The notice terms the residents of Jyotinagar Colony as ‘unauthorised occupants and/or trespasser to the port property’. The estate officer ordered the residents to vacate the land within 15 days of date of publication of this notice. Before the eviction order was passed, a hearing took place, wherein, port authorities submitted that ‘there is potential threat to communal unrest’ due to the existence of the colony.
According to legal documents accessed by Alt News, the residents of the colony came to know about the existence of this eviction order on June 9. The residents alleged that after the change of government in West Bengal, local BJP supporters started to campaign for the demolition of the slum. The locals claimed that they began deeming the colony as “a den of illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators”.
In order to seek legal protection from the eviction drive, residents appealed before the chief judge of the city civil court, Calcutta, however, on August 18, the court declined to grant any immunity from eviction to them.
The Port authorities in their submission before the city civil court had mentioned that ‘unlawful activities’ were ongoing in the colony. They described the premises as congested and unsafe for human habitation, citing the presence of inflammable materials and several uninsulated electrical wires that could potentially cause a fire. They also lodged two police complaints at the North Port police station on September 9, 2020 and July 25, 2022.
On August 19, the residents appeared before the Calcutta high court, seeking protection from eviction. The court granted an interim stay order on the eviction process till September 18. In the meantime, the water and electricity disruptions happened, which residents believe was done to purposely disrupt their lives to expedite the eviction.
Nine residents of the colony: Alamgir Biswas, Pinki Bibi, Mafajel Gazi, Sk Mainuddin, Rahima Bibi, Saraswati Biswas, Anita Prasad, Lima Bibi and Bonani Bibi appeared as petitioners before the high court. In their appeal, the residents had informed the HC that although the proceedings recorded before the estate officer of Kolkata Port mentioned two persons: Hafizul and Tarcina Bibi as respondents from the colony, the order does not record that any notice for eviction, under section 4 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, was issued publicly.
It was also submitted before the HC that the order issued by the Kolkata Port does not record that the petitioners were called upon to show cause against the proposed eviction, were afforded an opportunity to produce evidence or were given an opportunity of personal hearing.
According to Section 4 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, all concerned persons, that is all persons who are in occupation of the public premises, have to be given the opportunity to show cause why they wouldn’t be evicted.
Section 4(3) of the Act clearly mentions: The estate officer shall cause the notice to be served by having it affixed on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the public premises, and in such other manner as may be prescribed, whereupon the notice shall be deemed to have been duly given to all persons concerned. However, the order issued by the estate officer makes no mention of any such notice being issued or served. This issue was also raised in the petition before the high court.
A team of lawyers including Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya, Samim Ahammed, Md Nasirul Hoque and Ivi Banerjee represented the residents legally. Speaking to Alt News, Ahammed said, “The Port authorities are claiming that the land in question is their property. But in reality, it is public property. Therefore, a government body like the Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata, must ensure the fundamental rights of the public, in this case, their right to shelter.”
The State has the power to regulate and make sure people follow the law and cannot occupy public property illegally. They are exercising this power through the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. But while doing this, the State cannot treat people unfairly or take away someone’s home and leave them without shelter. Having a place to live and being able to live with dignity are part of a person’s inalienable rights protected by the Constitution, he explained.
Simultaneously with the HC appeal, another appeal was submitted by the residents before the chief judge of the city civil court seeking the restoration of water connection. This prayer, however, is still pending.
According to the port authorities, the total damage incurred due to the existence of the colony, starting from 1990, has reached approximately over Rs 61 crore. As per the legal records, the estimated monthly damage amount is calculated to be more than Rs 19 lakh rupees, and the port is losing more than Rs 2 crore annually in terms of revenue due to the colony.
Questions Of ‘Communal Targeting’
The geographical location of the water disruption has become a point of contention for residents, who have alleged that this is a form of communal targeting.
When one walks along Khagendra Chatterjee Lane towards the Ganges, with the Gun and Shell Factory on the right, the road turns left towards the river after two temples, and becomes Chitpur Strand Road. The Cossipore Jetty is on the right, followed by Jyotinagar Colony.
Residents showed Alt News the two points where pipeline work had been carried out. They said the entire stretch between the two points had remained without water. They also alleged that the points where the road was dug up correspond to the boundaries of Jyotinagar Colony, which has a predominantly Muslim population. According to the residents, taps immediately before and after this stretch, located in predominantly Hindu residential areas, continue to receive water.
Alt News checked the taps inside the colony and found them dry. Taps located immediately before and after the stretch where the pipeline work had been carried out, however, had water supply. We found that the tap directly opposite a temple, just before the first point where the road had allegedly been dug up, had water supply. The tap at the other end, near the second point where digging had taken place, also had water. In between, however, an approximately 150-metre stretch, had no water supply.
‘A Basic Need’
For residents, the suspension of water has led to tremendous daily struggle. “Water is a basic need. There are so many people in our colony, and there is no water. People have to stand in queues to fetch water from the taps that are present in the nearby areas. Though people are sharing their taps, they prioritise their own needs. This affects our work,” a resident said.
A woman in her mid-twenties, while cleaning utensils, showed buckets filled with water fetched from the river. “Look at the condition of the water we are using to clean. It is so muddy and filthy. At this point, all we can hope is we don’t fall ill,” she said.
The monsoon season has made it more difficult. “The water level is very high in Ganga now, so it becomes dangerous to bathe in the river or fetch water. The river water is muddy and unfit for consumption. But we are left with no option,” an elderly woman said. “We are scared that our children will develop skin infections. There are already a few cases,” said a woman in her thirties, while standing in queue to bathe her children.
Residents have to walk some distance from their colony to a functioning tap to fill water, which they then transport back on vans.
Locals Allege Administrative Apathy
Alamgir elaborated that after water and electricity supply was cut off on July 29, the following day, locals reached the corporation office and complained. “They took my number and told us that they would look into the matter. But nothing happened. On the following day, we submitted a written complaint at the main corporation office in Hatibagan. They also told us they would try to look into it. However, as everyone can see, nothing has changed as of yet,” he said.
Several residents had approached the local police station, the councillor, and MLA Tiwari, seeking their intervention, but no official visited the colony to inspect the reality so far, they lamented. Residents also said that when a group of women approached Tiwari, he dismissed them stating he was not responsible for the disruption of water supply and refused to restore it.
Further, Pinki Bibi alleged that Tiwari had used communal slurs and threatened the locals with eviction. “While talking to the people, he threatened them, ‘If I want, I could demolish the mosque that was built in the colony. And evict the entire colony with it,’” she said.
Morjina Begum told Alt News that residents believe they are being purposely treated this way because of their Muslim identities. Asked why they felt this was the case, she referred to speeches by chief minister Suvendu Adhikari and the local MLA following their election victories, in which they said they would not work for Muslims because Muslims had not voted for them. “Where are we supposed to go? There are so many of us?” she asked.
Also Read: I swear I won’t do anything for Muslims, says Bengal BJP MLA Ritesh Tiwari
Burdened by the uncertainties of their future in the colony, an elderly woman in her 70s, sitting on the threshold of her house, said, “I pray that in my next life I am not born as a Muslim in this country.”
On September 9, Minakshi Mukherjee, CPI(M)’s central committee member, visited the locality along with other workers and leaders, and expressed her solidarity with the residents and protested against the eviction drive. At the initiative of the party, a water tanker visits the colony every two to three days to provide residents with an alternative source of water.
MLA Ritesh Tiwari Responds
When Alt News asked Tiwari about the predicament of people in his constituency, he distanced himself from the issue, saying, “The plot belongs to the Port. The people have a feud with the Port. The Port had ordered them to vacate. Later, the high court ordered them to refrain from taking temporary coercive action. The water supply is provided by the KMC. So, what role do I play here? What can I say here? The matter is sub judice, and it is better for political leaders to refrain from making any comments.”
When asked whether he could stand by the people of his constituency and help restore their water supply, he said, “This is not my job…they [residents] have sought the assistance of established political leaders… so they should keep faith in the people they have called. Should they lose that faith so quickly?”
Upon being further prodded on why he was not helping people in his own constituency, the MLA replied (in Bengali), “Why don’t you do my part of the job!” (“Amar bhaag er kaaj ta apni kore deben”)
All photos by Ankita Mahalanobish.

The Himalayas are melting faster - and India's economy is 'at risk'
- Published
The Himalayas are approaching a dangerous threshold as glaciers melt faster, glacial lakes grow more unstable and the mountains face a widening gap in monitoring, according to new research.
The findings come in the aftermath of devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet, which killed more than 1,300 people and caused widespread destruction, highlighting the growing risks from a rapidly changing Himalayan environment.
Himalayan glaciers are now losing mass 65% faster than they were a decade ago, the report by global consultancy Systemiq, produced with the Integrated Mountain Initiative and with technical contributions from the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) and GB Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment, says.
Yet only about 21 of the estimated 40,000 glaciers across the Himalaya-Karakoram region are being monitored in detail and on a sustained basis, according to the report.
That monitoring gap matters because the physical landscape is changing rapidly.
As glaciers retreat, they can leave behind expanding lakes held back by unstable deposits of rock and ice. At the same time, warming is destabilising permafrost - permanently frozen ground that can thaw as temperatures rise - and high mountain slopes, increasing the possibility of cascading hazards, the report says.
India already has evidence of the scale of the risk.
Some 18% of Indian land is Himalayan, yet the region accounts for about 35% of disasters, according to the report.
The government told parliament in July that 56 glacial lakes had been classified as "very high risk", external following a 2025 scientific assessment of 189 high-risk lakes in the Indian Himalayan region. The Central Water Commission is monitoring 2,485 glacial lakes larger than 10 hectares across India's Himalayan river basins, the government said.
The Himalayas have already seen devastating examples of what can happen when glacial lakes burst their natural dams.
In 2023, a glacial lake outburst flood in Sikkim killed at least 70 people and caused widespread damage to roads, bridges and hydropower projects. In 2021, a similar disaster in Uttarakhand killed more than 200 people after a massive flood swept through the Rishiganga and Dhauliganga valleys.
But the danger is not confined to spectacular floods.
The Himalayas are a vast natural water system feeding rivers that sustain hundreds of millions of people across South Asia. ICIMOD says "peak water", external is expected around mid-century in most Hindu Kush Himalayan river basins - the point at which glacier runoff reaches its maximum before declining as glaciers lose mass.
The new research puts an unusually large economic number on that dependency.
It estimates that Himalayan water underpins roughly 20% of India's GDP, sustaining wheat, rice, tea, hydropower and pilgrimage economies. Yet the mountain states capture only about 5% of that value, it says.
"The Himalayas are the Third Pole," said economist Lord Nicholas Stern, chair of the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at the London School of Economics. "Unlike the Arctic or Antarctic, this pole has hundreds of millions of people living beneath it."
"This is national and international infrastructure," he said, warning that the ecological system underpinning it is "approaching a tipping point".
Not all the forces driving glacier loss are beyond the region's control.
The Systemiq research estimates that roughly a third of Himalayan glacier melt is driven by black carbon, much of it originating from brick kilns in the plains. Soot deposited on snow and ice absorbs more sunlight and accelerates melting.
Unlike global greenhouse-gas emissions, black-carbon pollution is a lever that India and its neighbours can act on directly, the report argues.
"The Himalayas are approaching a tipping point, with millions of lives and livelihoods hanging in the balance," said Arushi Chopra, Systemiq's senior director and lead author. "Glaciers are melting faster than they were a decade ago."
The report proposes 10 priority transitions, ranging from reducing black-carbon emissions and expanding glacier monitoring to improving disaster early-warning systems and changing the way tourism is developed in the mountains.
One priority is to strengthen disaster preparedness, with governments agreeing in advance what action to take when hazards emerge - from evacuation to protecting vulnerable infrastructure.
Another is to rethink tourism. The Indian Himalayan region receives roughly 400 million tourist visits a year, according to the report, and researchers argue that the objective should shift from maximising visitor numbers towards generating value that is retained and reinvested locally.
Pema Gyamtsho, director general of ICIMOD, said the risks were becoming increasingly complex.
"Glaciers are retreating, permafrost and high-mountain slopes are becoming increasingly unstable, and communities and infrastructure downstream face growing risks from complex and cascading hazards," he said.
And those risks do not stop at the borders drawn across the Himalayas. Such hazards, Gyamtsho said, "do not respect national borders, and no single country can address them alone".
That makes cross-border monitoring, shared risk information and early-warning systems, and joint investment in resilience increasingly urgent - not just to save lives, but to protect the livelihoods and economies of hundreds of millions of people who depend on the mountains.

In the latest addition to the bulging category of streaming bundles, Amazon Prime Video is launching a package including AMC+, BritBox, MGM+, PBS Masterpiece and Starz.
The $29.99-a-month U.S. offering is priced 39% below the cost of each of the five individual services.
In recent years, dozens of combinations of streaming have hit the market, creating a crowded marketplace. As streaming pay-TV provider YouTube TV has evolved into the No. 1 distributor, it has sliced and diced its offerings into a range of packages and price points. Rival operators Charter, Comcast and DirecTV have followed suit.
While it continues to support its own original titles, Prime Video is also increasingly looking to serve as a one-stop streaming shop for consumers disoriented by choice. Similar to rival Roku, the Amazon platform offers dozens of streaming services as add-ons for Prime subscribers, including a number of bundled offerings. The consumer proposition, along with creating a centralized hub where they can access streaming, is also to simplify payments. With individual services, a pain point for subscribers comes in with turning services on and off, changing tiers or updating credit cards across multiple providers.
Watch on Deadline
The new bundle is the first Prime Video has offered encompassing five services. That number is not unprecedented in the market overall, however, as Comcast recently expanded its StreamSaver package to encompass six different streamers.
“Our subscriptions and bundles business continues to see incredible growth because we stay focused on delivering unmatched selection, value and convenience,” said Ryan Pirozzi, Head of Prime Video Channels, U.S.

Hilsa tide turns as India sends 500MT fish to Bangladesh over 2 months: 'Usually the other way round'
Another 150 MT could be shipped in the coming weeks, as Gujarat’s rising Hilsa production drives the unusual cross-border trade.
In a first, India has exported around 500 metric tonnes of roe-filled Hilsas from Gujarat to Bangladesh in the last two months and another 150 MT of the fish is likely to be exported in the coming weeks, people aware of the developments said.
“Usually, it is the other way round. Hilsa from Bangladesh, which is considered the best for its taste, is imported around the Durga Puja time. But this is for the first time that Hilsa is being exported to Bangladesh. It is primarily the roe-filled Hilsa from Gujarat,” said SA Maqsood, secretary of the Fish Importers’ Association in West Bengal.
Also read: Hilsa spotted in Ganga near Ghazipur in UP, decades after barrage cut off migration route
Bangladeshi Hilsa prized for taste and demand
Hilsa is often tagged as the “Queen of Fish” for its taste . The Bangladeshi-hilsa found in the Padma River, is considered to be tastier than its Indian counterpart, which is found in the Hooghly River in West Bengal. Outside West Bengal, the Bangladeshi Hilsa is in great demand in Assam and Tripura.
“The prime reason behind the export is the huge production of jilsa in Gujarat. Only the roe-filled fishes are being exported. In Bangladesh the fish-eggs would be processed separately and exported to other countries, while the fish would be dried for future consumption as dried fish in Cox Bazar, Chittagong, Sylhet and other areas,” said Maqsood.
Also read: India gets continued market access for agri, marine products to EU beyond Sept
Hilsa breeds in Gujarat’s reservoirs and rivers
“In Gujarat, while a residential population of the hilsa is found in the Ukai reservoir, shoals of the fish migrate from the Arabian Sea to river Narmada and Tapi for spawning,” Basanta Kumar Das, director of Central Inland Fisheries Research Institute, said.
Fish traders in West Bengal said that as the consumption of the fish is very little in Gujarat, most of the catch is sent to West Bengal. The consignments reach Howrah and Kolkata from where they are sent to other parts of the state including north Bengal.
Meanwhile, with the festive season round the corner and Durga Puja scheduled in mid-October, fish importers in West Bengal have already approached the Bangladesh authorities like every year requesting to allow export of the silver delicacy to West Bengal, where it is in high demand.
Also read: CMFRI drafts national guidelines for marine ecolabelling to boost seafood exports
Bangladesh resumed limited Hilsa exports to India in 2019
While the former Sheikh Hasina-government imposed a ban on the export of hilsa in 2012, every year since 2019 a few thousand metric tonnes of the fish were allowed to be exported to India during this time of the year. It was considered as a Durga Puja gift.
In 2024 the Bangladesh government allowed around 49 companies to export 2420 MT of the fish to India through the Petrapole border.
“This year we have already written to the Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and other ministers and officials,” said Maqsood.
In 2025, West Bengal procured around 5000 MT of Hilsa from Gujarat, ten times more that what is usually procured annually.

'These are not isolated incidents,' EU's von der Leyen warns
The European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen condemned “reckless and dangerous Russian behaviour.”
She saidthe events in Denmark and Lithuania were “not isolated incidents,” but “part of a broader pattern of Russian aggression and provocation against Europe, testing our readiness and our resolve.”
“Russia will find our resolve only growing stronger. We are reinforcing our collective deterrence and defence, together with Nato. And we are stepping up the pressure on Russia,” she said.
Italy has decided to extend for another 15 days the suspension of the European Union’s Schengenborder-free arrangement with Spain, Reuters reports Rome’s interior ministry said on Tuesday.
Italy names Russia as probable source of drone shot down over Lithuania
The Italian defence minister Guido Crosetto has said that the drone shot down by an Italian Nato fighter over Lithuania “most probably” came from Russia.
The downed drone fell in a rural area near Lake Kaunas, in the centre of the country. Lithuania’s defence minister, Kęstutis Budrys, said Nato allies had been informed about the incident and discussions were under way. A presidential security adviser, Deividas Matulionis, said the drone may have strayed off course.
Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – all of which are Nato members and share a border with Russia – have regularly reported drone incursions since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. A Nato fighter shot down a Ukrainian drone over Estonia in May.
German chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Tuesday there was no viable parliamentary majority in Germany outside his coalition with the Social Democrats (SPD).
Dismissing the prospect of a minority government, Reuters reports Merz said “I was elected for four years and want to use this time to solve problems,” adding that he hoped to agree on further reforms with the SPD after upcoming state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
After the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt, observers are closely watching those elections for more signs of faltering public support in Merz’s policies.
A Ukrainian army unit has launched a counteroffensive against Russian forces near Lyman, an embattled town in Ukraine’s east, AFP reports the unit’s commander said Tuesday.
The area has been the site of intense battles throughout the four-and-a-half-year war.
“The 3rd Army Corps has launched an offensive operation called Vivaldi in this sector,” the commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps, Andriy Biletsky, said in a video on Telegram.
It was reported that Ukrainian troops had made a small pocket of gains north of the town, whose capture could pave the way for Moscow’s forces to sweep south and threaten the Ukrainian-held Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.
Dutch railway tracks disrupted by sabotage in 30 locations, operator says, as King opens new parliament session
Let’s catch up on the situation in the Netherlands (10:03, 11:40).
In the latest update, the track operator Pro Rail has said that various pipes and other items were found at 30 locations across the country.
All trains in the vicinity of the track blockages were halted, while there were also serious disruptions elsewhere, including to international services to Germany, Reuters reported.
In some cases, there were also cases of new blockages re-appearing in the same places after they were cleared, NOS reported.
The incident comes on Prinsjesdag, or the Prince’s Day, when King Willem-Alexander formally opens a new session of parliament and sets out the government’s plans for the 2027 budget.
Lithuania to send a note to Belarus about drone incursion as investigation continues, minister says
Meanwhile, Lithuanian foreign minister Kęstutis Budrys said that Lithuania will deliver a note to Belarus to set out what it knows about the overnight drone incursion into its airspace.
He added that the work to determine the type and ownership of the drone was underway. “We will take other actions based on that,” he said in comments quoted by Lithuanian broadcaster LRT.
Budrys added that Nato’s eastern flank “must be strengthened and its resilience increased” amid growing tensions with Russia.
Helicopter incident between Russia and Denmark reflects rising tensions, expert says
Miranda Bryant
Nordic correspondent
Experts said that Monday’s incident on the Danish straits reflects increasing tensions between Denmark and Russia that is slowly moving towards Cold War levels.
Ebsen Salling Larsen, a military analyst at the Center for Joint Operations at the Danish Defence Academy, said it is normal for Danish ships, helicopters or planes to go out to monitor Russian state-owned ships and warships. Sometimes this prompts Russian crew to point weapons at them or use a tracking radar.
But Monday’s incident, during which Russian flares were fired at a Danish helicopter, was unusual and marked a “change in pattern”.
“There’s an ongoing tension and the incident yesterday talks to that increased tension somewhat,” said Salling Larsen. “If you go back to the cold war you have more incidents of ships bumping into each other and so forth. We are slowly reaching that level again.”
The show of force, he said, was a reaction to Danish support for Ukraine and the Baltic states.
It is unlikely that Denmark would close the Danish straits, he said, because Copenhagen wants to follow international law and has its own vested interests in being able to move freely.
“That would be a Pandora’s box we would rather not open,” he said. “We are a small state with a large merchant fleet so we have some interests there as well.”
Russian frigate issued no warning or attempted radio contact before firing flares at Danish helicopter, minister says
Meanwhile, Denmark’s defence minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters that no warning or radio contact was made before a Russian frigate fired flares towards a Danish military helicopter.
He also said the flare from the frigate passed “within a matter of meters” from the Danish helicopter.
Bruus said it showed Russia’s increased willingness to take risks in its aggressive behaviour.
Russia's ambassador blames Denmark for helicopter incident
After speaking to the Russian media (12:25), Moscow’s ambassador to Copenhagen Vladimir Barbin was somewhat more incendiary in his comments to the Danish media.
He told Danish broadcaster DR that essentially it was the Danish helicopter that provoked the Russian ship, branding it a “reckless” behaviour.
He also accused Denmark of showing “no interest … in preventing the situation from escalating.”

Ukraine-Russia war latest: Poland scrambles jets as Putin attacks Kyiv with jet-powered drones
Major Russian attack comes as Nato fighter jet shot down a drone in Lithuania shortly after midnight
Poland scrambled fighter jets in the early hours of Tuesday as it responded to Russia's latest attack on Ukraine involving jet-powered drones.
Ukraine’s Air Force issued several warnings to Ukrainians, asking them to seek shelter as Russian forces fired jet-powered drones across all of Ukraine.
It remains unclear how many drones were fired but at least some of them likely travelled beyond Ukraine's borders, with a Nato fighter jet shooting down a drone in Lithuania shortly after midnight on Tuesday.
Lithuanian officials said the drone likely entered from Belarus and was shot down near Pratkunai village in southern Lithuania, near Kaunas.
A drone alert was issued earlier in the capital Vilnius and surrounding region.
Military drones straying into the airspace of Russia's neighbours have stoked concerns that Russia's war in Ukraine is spilling over Nato's borders.
This comes as Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv was ready to support a US-led proposal for a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire protecting energy sites – but only if Washington could ensure Moscow was genuinely ready to comply.
EU struggles to agree extension of Russia sanctions
The EU has pushed back the expiry of Russia sanctions listings by seven days until 22 September, a spokesperson for the EU's Irish presidency said on Monday, after failing to agree on a six-month renewal.
At issue is whether to de-list Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov. France has joined Slovakia in a call to remove him, citing national security concerns, EU diplomats said.
"France is one of the countries most committed to increasing pressure by all means on the Russian war machine, as well as to supporting Ukraine," a French diplomatic source said.
“We face a specific national security issue and wish to respond positively to international partners who have approached us regarding Mr Usmanov."
EU sanctions require unanimous approval from all 27 member states and must be renewed every six months.
Putin's close aide funds Trump Jr's wedding celebrations
Donald Trump Jr's new wife, Bettina, has confirmed that their May wedding weekend celebration was partially funded by a man with close ties to Russian president Vladimir Putin.
In a post on her Instagram page on Monday morning signed by the couple, Bettina Trump wrote that the man, Umar Kremlev, was a “dear friend,” who “very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding.”
“It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful,” it went on.
ProPublica reported that Kremlev “footed the bill for hundreds of thousands of dollars of wedding expenses,” including paying to rent out one of two private islands where the three-day party was held and a fireworks show.
Kremlev was recently honoured with the Order of Friendship by Putin, according to the International Boxing Association, and accompanied Putin to China as part of a Russian delegation, according to the Chinese state media cited by the outlet.
US imposes Iran-related sanctions on Russia's VTB
The United States imposed further sanctions on Russia's VTB Bank, accusing it of involvement in Iranian sanctions evasion.
The action builds on sanctions imposed against VTB, Russia's second-largest lender, in 2022, when the bank was targeted following Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The US said VTB had opened offices in Iran, established banking relationships with sanctioned Iranian lenders and helped build financial channels designed to facilitate trade and financial coordination between Moscow and Tehran.
“Under Operation Economic Outcast, Treasury will continue to target and disrupt those who provide material, technological, or financial support that allows the Iranian regime to sustain its terrorist enterprise,” treasury secretary Scott Bessent said in the statement.
“Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran’s enablers,” he said.
Bessent warned last week that president Donald Trump's administration would sanction a large bank as it continues to apply economic pressure on Tehran to end a more than six-month US conflict with Iran.
Watch: Zelensky says Ukraine will support energy ceasefire as 'first step' to end war
North Korea's Kim vows to expand ties with Russia
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un said he would "expand and deepen" joint work with Russia in a message to Russian president Vladimir Putin, state media KCNA reported this morning.
In a reply sent on Monday to Putin's congratulations for North Korea's 78th founding anniversary, Kim said Pyongyang's government had a firm will to broaden cooperation with Russia "in a comprehensive way" based on friendship, mutual assistance, and what he described as the countries' alliance relations.
Kim also said he was convinced of Russia's victory in the current "sacred war for defending the security interests of the country and international justice", language that appeared to refer to Russia's war in Ukraine.
He pledged his "invariable support" for Putin and the Russian people.
The remarks come as Moscow and Pyongyang have drawn markedly closer, with North Korea sending troops to fight alongside Russian forces in Ukraine in 2024 and deepening military cooperation under a mutual defence pact.
Animal rescuers severely injured in Russian drone attack while saving dogs in Ukraine
A Ukrainian animal rescuer has said he is “grateful to be alive” after his car was struck by a Russian drone while rescuing a group of stranded dogs from near the frontline.
Ruslan Horbal, a volunteer for Animal Rescue Kharkiv (ARK), was on a rescue mission in Ukraine’s war-torn eastern city of Kramatorsk, when a Russian drone hit the vehicle, killing one of the rescued dogs. He had only just gathered the animals into the back of the car when the attack took place.
“It happened very fast. There was an explosion, smoke and glass everywhere,” recalls Mr Horbal, who was hospitalised after the attack, in an interview with The Independent. “At first, I was confused. It took me a moment to understand what had happened. Then I started checking if everyone was alive and if the animals were OK. That’s when I realised I was badly injured too. There was a lot of blood.”
Animal rescuers severely injured in Russian drone attack while saving dogs in Ukraine
Russia hits petrol station and warehouse facilities in Kyiv, mayor says
A drone hit a petrol station in Ukraine's capital of Kyiv in the early hours today, mayor Vitali Klitschko said on the Telegram messaging app,
There was also a strike on warehouse facilities in another part of the city. A Reuters witness heard an explosion in Kyiv.
The attack comes after US president Donald Trump said on Monday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to hit each other's energy targets.
Russia has recently started hitting petrol stations in Kyiv, expanding the range of target facilities. In recent months, Russia hit some 300 petrol stations, mainly in or near Ukraine's frontline regions.
Zelensky says Ukraine will support energy ceasefire as 'first step' to end war
Volodymyr Zelensky has said Kyiv was ready to support a US-led proposal for a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire protecting energy sites – but only if Washington could ensure Moscow was genuinely ready to end its war.
Zelensky made his comments in his nightly video address after US president Donald Trump said that Ukraine and Russia had both agreed not to hit each other's energy targets.
“If this can become the first de-escalatory step, a step towards ending Russian strikes against our critical infrastructure and our strikes in response, Ukraine is ready to support de-escalation,” Zelensky said.
"So far, no one has seen any genuine willingness on Russia's part to bring the war to an end. But if our American partners can secure Russia's genuine readiness to end the war aimed at destroying lives, and to do so honestly and on a long-term basis, Ukraine will take its own de-escalatory steps,” Zelensky said.
Drone attack damages industrial facility in Russia's Samara region
A drone attack has damaged an industrial facility in the Russian Samara region on the Volga River, governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said on Telegram, without naming the facility.
The region is home to a number of large oil refineries.
Missile attack damages Ozon warehouse in Russia's Taganrog
A missile attack has damaged a warehouse of Russian e-commerce company Ozon in the port city of Taganrog in Russia's south, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said on Telegram.
He added that a gas pipe and a few residential buildings were also hit.

Eyeing a curved monitor? Here are the pros and cons to consider
They're great for gaming, but not as good for other use cases.
Curved monitors have come a long way since the first slanted screen in the form of the Samsung SE790C launched back in 2015. Heck, we now live in a world where Dell is launching 52-inch 6K ultrawide curved monitors. Not that you need to buy a giant screen to get the benefits of that curvature (though larger curved screens are definitely more immersive).
If you're currently reading this on a flat panel but have always been intrigued about the curved alternative, we're here to break down the upsides and occasional disadvantages of owning this type of monitor. Are curved monitors worth the premium you often have to pay over their flat cousins? Do they really make playing PC games more immersive? And just why are so many ultrawide monitors curved? We'll touch on all that as we weigh the pros and cons of embracing the bend.
Are curved monitors really worth it?
As someone who has owned curved monitors for years, I'm obviously going to be a bit biased. For me, curved monitors are most definitely worth it, though I'd throw in a couple of caveats (which I'll touch on shortly). The biggest advantage of using a curved monitor? This type of display can provide addictively immersive gaming experiences. If you're a hardcore Steam player who spends dozens of hours a week playing the best PC games, a curved panel can be a great option.
I regularly play my favorite PC titles on my 49-inch Samsung Odyssey G9 OLED. It's a spectacular screen for gaming. So many larger curved monitors are either ultrawide or super ultrawide. When a PC port gets the sort of loving attention it deserves, the addition of proper support for 21:9 and 32:9 aspect ratios can be game-changing.
I've been playing a lot of Death Stranding 2: On the Beach lately, and watching Hideo Kojima's elaborately directed cutscenes in 32:9 feels incredibly cinematic. The flipside is that, unfortunately, many modern story-driven games still only support 16:9 cutscenes, leading to huge black bars on curved ultrawide monitors. Still, if you own a large curved display (that's likely to be 21:9), the increased field of view in racing games and first-person shooters can be transformative.
Curved monitors can also be great for productivity, especially when dealing with ultrawide models. My aforementioned 49-inch curved behemoth (that's 5120 x 1440 pixels) gives me the same screen real estate as working across two 27-inch 1440p screens. On a curved ultra or super ultrawide, it's easier to multitask thanks to those wider dimensions, making it a doddle to accommodate multiple browser windows alongside, say, Photoshop. On larger monitors, the curvature of the screen also makes it more comfortable to look at the edges. That's because they're physically closer to the center of the panel than they would be on a flat monitor, meaning you don't need to turn your head as much.
What are the disadvantages of curved monitors?
There are definitely instances where picking up a curved monitor over a traditional flat panel doesn't make much sense. Price is one of the biggest factors. Because so many curved screens are 34 inches or larger, they're naturally more expensive than many flat monitors (they're also trickier to manufacture). Staying on the topic of size, a curved monitor is often going to take up more desk space than the flat panel alternative.
There are other scenarios where the dimensions of a curved monitor can potentially make life awkward. As the sides of a curved display obviously jut out more than the center, these types of panels aren't ideally suited for mounting because they won't sit flush against a wall. They're also not a great fit for a multi-monitor setup. Trying to line up a curved display next to a flat screen just isn't going to provide a seamless experience. Oh, and if you work in an office and regularly view content with colleagues on the same monitor, that's going to be awkward, as curved monitors are designed to be viewed at central angles.
If you're a prosumer art editor or graphic designer who regularly edits work in Photoshop, buying a curved monitor probably isn't a wise investment either. Though curved displays can be brilliant for gaming, image editing on such a screen isn't always ideal, as the curvature can create distortion around the edges. Doing precision work that requires perfectly straight lines/grids in Photoshop? You'd be better off with a flat monitor.
Why are ultrawide monitors normally curved?
Though flat ultrawides do exist, when you get into the 34-inch and above range, 21:9 displays are more commonly curved. Why is this? It's partially down to manufacturers wanting to give gamers more immersive experiences. Many curved ultrawide monitors are packed with gaming features, like Nvidia G-Sync and VRR, and there's no denying curvature can provide a sort of wrap-around vision effect when your face is pressed to a screen. Sitting at close proximity to a curved monitor is essential to get that real sense of immersion. That's probably why curved TVs failed, but curved gaming monitors thrived.
There are slightly more boring practical reasons why so many ultrawide monitors are curved. Working with a 21:9 aspect ratio is going to make you turn your head more often than viewing a 16:9 display. To lessen the amount your eyes have to dart back and forth, an ultrawide with curved edges makes it slightly easier to view the whole screen.

At Apple’s recent hardware event, the software powering its foldable iPhone Duo stood out, with translucent Liquid Glass effects and vertically stacked icons. But you don’t need to snatch a folding smartphone to reap the benefits of Apple’s iOS 27 updates.
When iOS 27 leaves beta on Monday, Siri AI’s standalone app and smartphone search integration will likely be the most immediately obvious change for many iPhone users. But it’s worth digging even deeper to uncover helpful additions to key apps, like Apple’s Safari browser, as well as revamps to underutilized apps, like Shortcuts.
The version of Safari available in iOS 27 looks fairly similar to the last iteration, with a few key updates tucked away in the settings. These Safari features are powered by Apple Intelligence, which requires an iPhone 15 Pro or newer (they're also available on iPadOS 27 and macOS 27).
Notify Me
If you’re shopping online and want a quick price-drop notification, you can use the “Notify Me” feature to scan a webpage on a certain cadence and look for changes. First, head to the page you want to track and tap the three-lined hamburger menu icon in the top right corner of Safari. About halfway down, you’ll see this option listed.
“Safari can let you know when a website updates the content you’re interested in,” reads the feature’s description. Here you’ll find an open text box where you can describe what change in content you want Safari to scan for, as well as how often you want it to check.
For example, my couch is broken, so I’ve been eyeing a few different replacement options. I have two final contenders from CB2, but both are out of my price range. So, I set up a “Notify Me” for Safari to scan the pages each day for a significant discount. Whichever one goes on sale first will likely be what I decide to get, and now I don’t have to refresh the pages manually every day.
While many other browsers have similar shopping features, like the price-tracking bell in Google Chrome, I appreciate how this feature stretches beyond just buying stuff. You can also use Safari to scan for ticket drops, privacy policy changes, and other content updates.
Describe an Extension
If you’ve experimented already with the “Describe a Shortcut” feature for iPhone automation, then “Describe an Extension” for Safari will seem familiar. It's located under the same settings menu as the “Notify Me” tool, just a little further down.
The feature asks you to type what you want the extension to do, then generates a custom option. Some of the suggested prompts in Safari revolve around boosting productivity, like “display a reading time estimate as a badge on the extension,” maintaining better focus, like “make the web page grayscale,” and more random ideas, like “show a colorful and explosive firework every time I tap.”
It took only a few seconds for each of those three examples to generate. Safari also suggests pre-made extensions during the process that could fit what you’re looking to do. As I scrolled through the internet with all three of the new extensions activated, everything worked as expected. While I’ll likely only keep the grayscale one to help me focus while reading online articles, the fireworks felt whimsical in small doses.
Organize Tabs
I am a glutton for mobile tabs, especially on Safari. I’m rarely ever exiting out of anything and always just pop open something new, which leaves me with hundreds upon hundreds of loosely connected, completely unorganized tabs—until now.
This feature is in the wider browser tab view accessible by tapping the two overlapping squares at the bottom-right corner of your screen. Swipe to a tab group brimming with websites and look for the three-lined button in the top-left. Here’s where you can choose to allow Safari to “automatically create topics” based on those tabs.
It takes a few seconds to organize everything after you activate this feature, but it did a great job of finding helpful trends in those 500+ tabs. For example, it grouped all the WIRED articles I had open and created a tab topic for upcoming San Francisco event pages and comedy clubs I was considering checking out.

Americans loathe how Trump is handling AI and the numbers keep getting worse
‘The American people despise President Trump when it comes to his handling of artificial intelligence,’ CNN’s data guru Harry Enten said Monday
A new poll has shown just how much Americans loathe the way President Donald Trump is handling artificial intelligence.
Just 23 percent of Americans believe Trump has handled artificial intelligence well, while 57 percent say he’s handled the issue poorly, according to a survey from the University of Massachusetts Amherst published Monday.
“The American people despise President Trump when it comes to his handling of artificial intelligence,” CNN’s Chief Data Analyst Harry Enten told viewers Monday.
“Trump’s net approval rating of AI. That’s approval minus disapproval. Look at this overall — he’s 34 points underwater! My goodness gracious! And somehow, that’s become worse over the course of the year because back in March, he was closer to around 25 points underwater,” Enten said, noting that Trump was 61 points underwater with independents on the issue.
The president —known for his own rampant use of AI-generated images and videos on social media, including a photo depicting himself as Jesus and a video depicting the Obamas as apes — has pushed for fewer regulations on the technology as the biggest AI companies called for a slowdown in development in the name of safety.
“You would have to combine [French ocean explorer] Jacques Cousteau with The Little Mermaid to get as far underwater as Donald Trump is with independents on AI,” Enten said on CNN Monday.
“As I said, the American people, and independents especially, absolutely despise President Trump when it comes to this issue that is becoming even more key as we lead up to the midterm elections.”
AI has taken over the stock market, with chipmaker Nvidia being valued at more than $5 trillion, and it has woven into the lives of everyday Americans as they ask their chatbots how to use the ingredients in their fridge to make dinner or how to let their date know that there won’t be a second one.
But behind the AI buzz emerged a fear of what the technology is actually capable of, with former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon warning amid his resignation last week, “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Trump has brushed off serious concerns about the safety of AI amid reports of the technology hacking into external systems and being used to answer questions about how to make biological weapons.
“We’ve seen a lot of concerning reports about AI. Should the AI industry slow down or be more regulated?” a reporter asked Trump at the Irish Open Sunday.
“We’re leading China in AI,” Trump replied. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world. And frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”
The president said the U.S. “could put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up. And they’re bringing up things that won’t happen.”
Trump then went on a social media posting spree, calling concerns about AI a “hoax.”
“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China,” he wrote on Truth Social Monday.
Aside from concerns about the potentially dangerous capabilities of AI, many Americans are worried about the construction of data centers that power the technology, citing negative impacts on the environment and their quality of life.
“[Trump] looks at the polling. He looks at what people are saying,” a senior White House official told Politico earlier this month. “Polling isn’t necessarily great on data centers, but it’s incumbent upon us to explain our position. I think that’s part of what he was trying to do.”
In Trump-fashion, the president blamed members of the Democratic Party for a surge in concerns about AI, writing in one of his Truth Social posts Monday, “These are all Radical Left Dumocrats, who never give up, but seldom win. Hopefully, the Voters have seen the light!”

Kids want a bar of chocolate, but parents want a healthier snacking option. For years, this has been one of the toughest equations for nutrition-conscious parents, who often found themselves negotiating tantrums in the kids’ food aisle of every supermarket. A new crop of Indian D2C brands believes it has found a way around that tug-of-war. Their proposition is simple: don’t ask children to eat differently but make the food they already love better. One example is Little Joys. It is betting that adding protein to a ‘roti’ is easier than getting a child to try a new food. The health and wellness platform launched a protein mix to add into the dough and batter for rotis, dosas and pancakes. That’s one example of how healthy snacking and kids-centric food is getting a revamp. Jaipur-based Gladful puts sprouted lentils and millets into familiar breakfast mixes, while The Whole Truth’s Next Gen range includes milk mixes, snack bars and protein blocks. For the urban millennial parents these brands are targeting, paying a premium can be easier than finding the time to prepare everything from scratch. But the purchase still has to satisfy two people: the child who eats the product and the parent who pays for it. Little Joys’ founder Revant Bhate told us, “The hard thing in building a kids brand is building for two customers. A 10-year-old wants great taste, while a parent wants proof that the product is good and effective. And the bar for winning both over keeps getting higher.” Meanwhile, parents aren’t the only ones scrutinising what these brands are promising. In June, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) flagged 15 brands, including Storia, Two Brothers Organic Farms, PLAN B, The Health Factory, Troovy and Emami’s Healthy & Tasty, over allegedly misleading branding and claims. Expressions such as “healthy”, “organic”, “zero maida” and “vegan” came under scrutiny. This leaves us with a question: can these brands convince parents that better ingredients and better formulations are worth paying for? The Fine Print Behind ‘Healthy’ The market is crowded with both legacy and new-age brands offering products positioned as healthier options for children. But what are these brands bringing to the table? According to Gladful cofounder Parul Sharma, brands are trying to balance nutrition, taste and trust with information on actual formulation, laboratory analysis and compliance with FSSAI requirements. Serving sizes and nutritional values should also be relevant to the age group being addressed. She also pointed to the ICMR’s recommended dietary allowances for children aged seven to nine. The ICMR’s nutrient requirements framework distinguishes between average requirements, recommended allowances and upper limits. Sharma also said finding the right balance is a challenge for many brands. For instance, reducing sugar or changing conventional ingredients can affect taste and texture. Similarly, using higher-quality or more recognisable ingredients can increase formulation and ingredient costs. Talking about clean labels, Mansi Baranwal, the cofounder of Troovy cofounder, said most brands highlight healthier ingredients such as pulses, millets and jaggery on their labels, but often list “spices and condiments” at the end. “These spices and condiments may contain silicon dioxide, disodium inosinate, disodium guanylate and tertiary butylhydroquinone, or TBHQ, alongside artificial colours and flavours, emulsifiers, firming agents and gelling agents. My concern is how far brands are willing to go in reworking these parts of the recipe to keep their ingredient promises,” she added. Baranwal said leaving out these ingredients means the seasoning would not stick evenly, leading to repeated failed batches and lakhs spent on innovation. Troovy now spends approximately ₹10-12 Lakh a month on laboratory testing, covering raw materials and finished products. Baranwal’s concern is that brands should not stop at asking whether an additive is allowed today. They should also keep looking at the evidence behind its use. At the same time, an unfamiliar ingredient name does not automatically mean it is unsafe. Surviving The Cost Sheet A young brand needs suppliers willing to work with small orders, unfamiliar formulations, and repeated trials. Baranwal of Troovy said that combination can make manufacturers reluctant. The volumes may not justify the effort, and the innovation adds risk. This also leaves founders doing work that a larger food company can spread across specialist teams. “In a startup a small team is managing everything -R&D, procurement, production, quality, manufacturer relationships. And they also have to handle testing and compliance with the same level of diligence as the giants,” she added. Then comes the next- ingredient bill. Prices of better oils, protein ingredients, alternate sweeteners, and nuts are high. And have risen further in recent months. Most brands, so far, have absorbed some of that increase through lower gross margins rather than passing the entire cost on to consumers. So where can the savings come from? Sharma pointed to procurement, manufacturing scale, packaging, production yields and distribution. She argues that brands need to make the entire operation more efficient instead of simply cutting ingredients. Shelf life is another part of the equation. It has to work not just at the manufacturing stage, but through distribution and the time a product spends in a household. Sunitha Vishwanathan, partner at Kae Capital, believes brands concentrating only on D2C and quick commerce risk building on too narrow a base. Established food companies already have the retail reach that challengers are trying to build, and moving into those stores requires rethinking what each pack earns. “The pack sizes, price points, and margin structures that work on Blinkit don't automatically translate to a kirana shelf or a supermarket aisle.” That means a recipe that works in production still needs a pack size and selling price that works wherever the parent buys it. Otherwise, wider distribution can bring more orders without resolving the margin problem. Winning A Place In The Next Grocery Basket Farmley’s 2026 snacking survey, which covered more than 6,000 respondents across cities and age groups, found that nearly 60% of the parents surveyed were willing to pay a premium for healthier snacks for their children. This is an encouraging signal, but willingness to pay is only the first step. Vishwanathan believes that with so many brands claiming to offer healthier snacks, the real edge will come from specific, demonstrable nutritional benefits rather than another list of ingredients that a product does not contain. She pointed to areas such as protein for active children, gut health and cognitive support as propositions companies are exploring. But these are still claims that need evidence. For Sharma, the clearest commercial evidence comes from watching what households do after the trial. Are they buying again? How long does the next order take? Does the product still sell once the introductory offer ends? She also looks at revenue from returning customers, retention over time and whether families use the products across everyday eating occasions. “Ultimately, the strongest signal is whether consumers stop thinking of the product as something they "try because it is healthier" and start buying it because it has become part of their regular household food routine,” Sharma added. For now, these brands have found parents willing to listen. As they grow, the harder decisions will come when an ingredient gets costlier, or a retailer asks for a bigger margin. What they choose to protect then will tell us how much their promise is worth. SPOTLIGHT| Inside Poco Mico’s Premium Kidswear Play Founded in 2024, Poco Mico is a kidswear D2C brand that offers premium and durable clothing for children, alongside home care products such as crib mattresses, cushion covers and mats. It is designed for children up to 10 years old. The brand caters to different age groups and occasions, with its portfolio spanning casual wear, party wear and wedding wear for children. Its D2C-first model allows it to target parents looking for premium everyday and occasion-led kidswear. Poco Mico claims to use certified cotton with its soft-skin-touch technology, designed to provide comfort while retaining the fabric’s size and colour and reducing shrinkage. The brand only sells products via its own website. The Deep Dive Ecommerce Buzz AppsForBharat Data Dispute: A Bengaluru court has restrained Veda Mandir parent Way2News from using AppsForBharat’s confidential data and IP after allegations of proprietary data sharing by a former employee. AppsForBharat is seeking ₹1 Cr in damages. Zomato’s COD Tantrum: The foodtech giant has started levying a separate fee on some cash-on-delivery orders, ranging from ₹5 to ₹13, with some users reporting charges as high as ₹21. The payment-linked fee comes as Zomato looks to boost monetisation and encourage online payments. Triptii Dimri’s Beauty Bet: The actor has joined eye-focused D2C beauty startup Peep Beauty as an investor and co-creator. Founded by former Keventers cofounder Aman Arora, the startup has raised ₹12 Cr and is building around coloured contact lenses and eye makeup. The Operator Question What are the biggest challenges in building a kids’ nutrition brand for children aged 6-14 in India, and what does it take to get the product, parental trust and repeat purchases right at an early stage? We reached out to Astha Jain, the cofounder of kids’ ayurvedic wellness brand Ayuvya, to understand the playbook here. Here’s what she divulged: Tailored Customer Experience: A new buyer and a returning one have completely different questions. New customers need education around how to use the product, what to expect and when they can realistically see results, while returning customers need continuity through dosage reminders and the next steps in their regimen. In Ayurveda, where results depend on consistent use over weeks, getting the first-timer journey right is critical to driving the second order. Use Check-Ins To Prevent Silent Churn: Instead of reaching out only when it is time to sell again, Ayuvya uses structured check-ins after purchase. Day 7 helps identify usage mistakes before customers give up, while Day 14 checks for early signs of progress. This allows the brand to address issues during the usage journey and makes the eventual reorder part of an ongoing conversation rather than a cold sales pitch. Rope In Doctors To Build Trust And Improve Outcomes: Ayuvya offers free consultations with its Ayurvedic doctors to help customers choose and use the right products. Jain believes personalised guidance improves adherence and outcomes while addressing a larger trust problem in the category, where customers have often encountered exaggerated or fake Ayurvedic claims. A conversation with a practitioner can build more trust than marketing communication alone, she added.

'People are still afraid of those three letters': Fighting the stigma of HIV
RIO DE JANEIRO -- "People are still afraid of those three letters," says Gareth Thomas, a former Welsh rugby star.
He's talking about HIV. Thomas became a global champion for people living with HIV when he announced that he was HIV positive in 2019.
Since then, he has been a strong advocate for sharing knowledge about the virus –- and what it's like to live with it.
This summer, he came to Rio de Janeiro to participate in the International AIDS Conference and to spread his message as part of the Tackle HIV campaign.
"I thought I was gonna die"
That message resonates with another advocate: Welton Gabriel, a 36-year-old event organizer from Sao Paolo.
Sitting in a bar overlooking the world-famous Ipanema beach, Welton Gabriel recalled the night 12 years earlier when he learned he had tested positive for HIV.
"I thought I was gonna die," he remembers.
For a while, his life did hang in the balance. Gabriel had contracted a treatment-resistant strain of HIV — he believes that the sexual partner who infected him had been taking medication but decided to stop, allowing the virus to mutate. It took seven months before doctors were able to get the infection under control.
"The amount of virus in my body was really high," he says. "I was initially started on a medicine that gave me a lot of problems with my liver, and my eyes became yellow. But then I was changed to the treatment that I am still on, which is working."
Despite the trauma he'd endured, and the fact that his condition was under control, when Gabriel chose to tell close friends that he was HIV positive, many cut contact. "They did not want to talk with me," recalls Gabriel, who lives in São Paulo.
Such discrimination remains one of the biggest hurdles to ending AIDS as a public-health threat in Brazil, a country of about 214 million which has the greatest number of people living with HIV in Latin America — nearly 1.1 million.
While Brazil's public healthcare system provides free access to medications that can suppress HIV and prevent transmission, allowing people to live normally, many still face a lifetime of stigma. Research from UNAIDS Brazil, a nonprofit that works closely with government agencies in the country, suggests that more than half of all HIV positive individuals in the country have experienced some form of discrimination. Gabriel lost friends, and others have been excluded by their own family or denied opportunities at work after disclosing their HIV status.
Today, Gabriel works as an activist with Barong, an organization that supports vulnerable communities across Brazil by offering mobile testing, education and information about HIV protection. He has come to realize that much of the discrimination stems from a place of fear.
Despite advances in HIV science — highlighted at this summer's AIDS 2026 conference in Rio, where researchers discussed developments from a monthly pill that can block HIV transmission to new strategies aimed at long-term remission — Gabriel says perceptions of HIV in Brazil have changed little since 1990, when the iconic Brazilian singer Cazuza died of AIDS at age 32.
Charismatic and talented, Cazuza went from school dropout to wealthy superstar during the 1980s and captivated the Brazilian public. His struggle with the debilitating effects of AIDS turned HIV into a household discussion topic within the country. However, Gabriel says that many people are unaware of the extent to which medical science has changed the prognosis of HIV over the past three and a half decades. As a result, he says that HIV is still commonly viewed as a death sentence.
"For a lot of Brazilians of that generation, that's still the symbol of HIV," says Gabriel. "When I learned I was HIV positive, I looked on Google, and the first thing I saw was the story of Cazuza."
'You can live a normal, happy, healthy life"
Gabriel had come to Ipanema Beach to speak with teenagers from disadvantaged communities as part of a Tackle HIV event organized in partnership with Thomas, Viiv Healthcare and AIDS-related charities. The effort aims to shift public attitudes by bringing accurate information to young people who are often left out of mainstream health outreach.
Speaking at the event, Thomas suggested that people still ostracize those living with HIV because of a lack of knowledge about the virus. He says it's common for people to be unaware of the modern medications that can prevent and control HIV.
""Many people don't know that you can live a normal, happy, healthy life if you start medication straight away, and so people avoid getting tested, avoid the result or avoid the medicine taking," says Thomas.
The consequence is preventable deaths. In Brazil, national health data shows that 27% of HIV positive people are only diagnosed and treated once their condition has progressed to a late stage, known as advanced AIDS. By that point, their immune system is severely weakened, leaving them highly vulnerable to life-threatening infections. In 2024, the most recent year for which data is available, more than 9,000 people in Brazil died from AIDS.
"We're losing ground every year"
Beatriz Grinsztejn, a Brazilian infectious-diseases specialist and former president of the International AIDS Society, describes this as tragic, given the availability of free tests and treatments. "People don't access what is available, and this is really painful," she says.
Even when timely diagnoses are made, convincing people to keep taking their medication is another challenge, even if that treatment is keeping them alive. Government figures show that 82% of HIV-positive individuals in Brazil are taking HIV-suppressing antiretroviral drugs — a seemingly impressive number yet well short of the U.N.'s target of 95%.
Gustavo Passos, equality and rights officer at UNAIDS Brazil, says this gap undermines the country's push to eliminate AIDS as a public-health threat. "On the treatment part, we're losing ground each year," he says. "The data we have implies that it's related to how people connect with health services."
Passos says that many people living with HIV feel stigmatized even by healthcare professionals, fearing that their status will be illegally disclosed without their consent, which causes them to lose trust in the system meant to support them.
Gabriel sees this dynamic play out in daily life. "It's about being judged if you're seen taking your treatment each day, and the pressure that puts on people," he says. "If someone feels judged, a lot of times they will stop the treatment."
"A lot of homophobia and transphobia"
While Brazil is commonly depicted to outsiders as a place of uninhibited sexuality — on social media, it's popularly described as one of the most promiscuous countries in the world — the reality is quite different.
Since 2014, lawmakers at federal, state and municipal levels in Brazil have proposed more than 200 pieces of legislation to ban all discussions of sex and gender education in schools. The legislative trend has continued to surface elsewhere: Two years ago, protests broke out in major cities over a proposal to equate abortion with homicide.
As Grinsztejn points out, Brazil has very high rates of violence against sexual minorities, citing Rio as a notable example. "The best gay destination in the country has a lot of homophobia and transphobia," she says. "The number of murders of trans people is one of the worst on the planet." Most victims are young: While general life expectancy in Brazil is 76, the transgender population's life expectancy is 30-35, which Grinsztejn says has been attributed to high rates of violence.
She says that this feeds into wider perceptions of HIV as a disease of immorality and deviance, driving discrimination.
Her fiancé never spoke to her again
Fabiana de Oliveira, a 57-year-old activist with the National Network of Women Living with HIV, an organization formed by women living with HIV and AIDS, says HIV discrimination in Brazil is also heavily gender-skewed.
She recalled her own experience of being diagnosed with HIV at 26. Her fiancé and partner of eight years, whom she suspected of giving her the virus, never spoke to her again. "I never saw him after that day," she says. "His family came to the hospital to check if I had HIV, and told me that I was no longer welcome in their house."
Living in Catanduva, a municipality in the state of Sao Paulo with just 100,000 people, she grew accustomed to feeling the judgment of others and even herself. "Women in Brazil are never the ones who are being cared for," says de Oliveira. "We are expected to take care of everything, the husband, the children, so it's hard to equate HIV as being part of your identity. You end up asking yourself, 'Was this my responsibility?' and it places a lot of burden on your mental and emotional health. Many women living with HIV in Brazil end up isolating themselves."
When it comes to the persistently damaging effects of stigma, the irony is that Brazil has also played a major role in innovations which have the potential to ultimately end the HIV epidemic. Lenacapavir, a twice-yearly injectable drug which can block HIV with virtually 100% effectiveness, was recently approved by regulators after reviewing global clinical trial data, including research carried out in Brazil. The country is now leading a large real-world study of lenacapavir across multiple cities to understand how the drug can be effectively implemented in public-health settings.
But de Oliveira is skeptical about whether such innovations can have the necessary impact without wider education campaigns and more openness in discussing HIV.
"People are more afraid of how society is going to perceive them than they are of the virus," she says.
Yet Gabriel has also seen firsthand how mindsets can change when people learn more about HIV. In the months and years after he disclosed his status, he was able to explain to his family and friends that he wasn't going to die, and correct misconceptions about how the virus could be transmitted.
"When I was able to explain more, some of my friends did eventually come back," he says. "Even if I originally felt discriminated against, it later allowed everyone to be more present and more aware."
