A cancer survivor hoped to work — then she lost her Medicaid disability coverage
Taya Hailstone has been in remission from childhood Hodgkin lymphoma for five years. But the cancer's lasting damage to her organs and nerves can make basic tasks, like loading a dishwasher, hard.
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Still, Montana's health department decided last year that Hailstone is no longer eligible for low-cost disability health coverage through Medicaid. The department switched her coverage to the state's Children's Health Insurance Program, another Medicaid program — three months before she aged out.
Before making the decision, the state didn't seek records from the medical team treating Hailstone, according to letters from those doctors reviewed by KFF Health News. Rather, the administrative ruling came after state officials learned the now-19-year-old had stopped receiving Social Security disability payments. She said she did that because she hoped to get healthy enough to work and save some money — beyond what's allowed under the strict income caps tethered to those payments. But her health changes day to day, and she said for now she's still too sick to consistently work.
Hailstone, who lives with her mom, has been able to keep Medicaid coverage while they appeal the case. She said that without Medicaid she can't afford the treatment to manage the aftermath of her cancer.
"It feels like this process was made to make you give up," Hailstone said.
Patients with disabilities have long struggled with administrative hoops, blunders and confusion when trying to qualify for federally subsidized health coverage because of their illness. Now, new federal Medicaid work requirements mean states face the additional task of deciding who qualifies for a medical exemption. That means reviewing medical cases for an even larger swath of Medicaid enrollees.
Attorneys, researchers and advocates who specialize in public aid said disability cases like Hailstone's — though separate from the incoming work requirements — are an indication that states aren't ready to decide who should be exempt from those requirements. As a result, they said, more people will be denied coverage in an opaque process.
"This will be the story of millions of people," said Anthony Wright, who heads Families USA, a national nonprofit that advocates for ways to make healthcare more accessible.
Jon Ebelt, a spokesperson with the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services, said the state doesn't comment on individual Medicaid cases.
An estimated 18.5 million people will have to meet the new federal requirements, by proving they're working, going to school, or volunteering to keep their Medicaid coverage, according to the Congressional Budget Office. More than 40% of those enrollees live with a chronic health condition, according to KFF.
Some will be excused from those rules if they can prove they're too sick to work.
More than 5 million people are expected to lose Medicaid coverage by 2034 because of the work requirements, according to the CBO.
Work requirements become law
Many Republican policymakers and the Trump administration have touted Medicaid work requirements to preserve coverage for the neediest. Congress made that national policy through last year's One Big Beautiful Bill Act and gave states until January 2027 to implement work-for-coverage rules.
Some states are starting those checks early. Montana began in July. Nebraska initiated work requirements in May.
In the federal law creating the work requirements, Congress allowed states to exempt people who have an illness that qualifies them as "medically frail." Many states created plans for those judgment calls, only to be surprised when federal officials released rules for the requirements that went beyond what Congress outlined, by also requiring enrollees to prove their illness makes it too hard to work.
Families USA and other organizations have argued the new rules force states to set up a patchwork of systems that, together, would be larger and more complicated than the Social Security Administration's own disability review system. Last year, that federal program cost more than $5 billion to administer to roughly 7 million people nationally. For comparison, Wright said, the federal law provided $200 million for states to share as they implement the work requirements. States are paying contractors millions of dollars to prepare often already flawed public aid systems to meet the new standards.
In June, 25 states sued the Trump administration over the medical frailty rules, arguing they're too hard for patients to meet and for states to assess. That case is ongoing.
Hailstone was diagnosed with blood cancer at age 10. Her intestines tore, which led to their partial removal. As a result, her body struggles to process food and she can face severe dehydration. She said lingering side effects from her cancer treatment can leave her mind foggy and cause her hands and feet to swell enough that it's hard to grip a fork or walk across a room.
Cancer dominated nearly half her life. It left mental scars, too.
"Some days you feel fine and then you suddenly crash," Hailstone said.
Hailstone and her mom live in Roundup, a central Montana town of roughly 2,000 people. They regularly make the nearly two-hour round-trip drive to Billings for specialized care. She typically has three medical appointments a week to see her physical and occupational therapists and a mental health counselor.
Hailstone said she's lucky she has her mother's help navigating Medicaid. Her mom, Kyla Hailstone, said that the state hasn't clearly defined how it determined her daughter's disability status and that its appeal process has been slow and dysfunctional.
Taya Hailstone would qualify for Medicaid based on her income if she can't prove her eligibility for disability coverage. But that would mean proving she's too sick to meet the work requirement — putting her in the same position of having to rely on a state review of her illness.
"If I lose this, this is life-changing," Hailstone said.
"Things fall through the cracks"
Hailstone qualified as disabled through the federal government as recently as 2024, about a year before the state said it was dropping her coverage. State officials can do their own medical review to determine whether someone meets the federal definition of a disability to access Medicaid.
"Whether that happens is always a bit of a crapshoot just based on state capacity," said Megan Dishong, deputy director of the Montana Legal Services Association, which helps low-income people navigate public programs. "Things fall through the cracks."
Ebelt said the state health department accepts disability decisions from the Social Security Administration. The state agency can conduct an internal disability determination if a person doesn't have one from the SSA, but Ebelt said it doesn't have to if a person qualifies for coverage another way.
"We are committed to treating every client with respect and helping those who are eligible receive appropriate Medicaid coverage," Ebelt said.
Montana instituted a three-month grace period for the work requirements. State officials won't begin disenrolling people for noncompliance until October.
Pamela Herd, a University of Michigan social policy professor who has studied bureaucratic obstacles to public benefits, said convoluted disability cases are common enough for attorneys to specialize in accessing aid.
"When we've designed public programs in ways that people can't figure out whether they're eligible without consulting lawyers, we've done something wrong," Herd said. "That has huge, huge implications for what's to come."
Montana officials have said they'll automatically review medical records that could help patients qualify for an exemption. Even so, the federal guidelines released in June mean patients will probably still face additional steps to guarantee an exemption.
Meanwhile, already overstretched doctors worry they'll face the burden of judging whether someone's illness qualifies them for a work exemption.
Dishong said that between now and October, Montana officials could offer more clarity on how the process will work. She said she's worried the state will end up "with a slow-roll mess" instead.
"This is a problem that's just starting," Dishong said.
As for Hailstone, she's now reapplying for Social Security disability payments. That aid would limit how much she can work. But it would also guarantee access to Medicaid.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

Even before she jumped, Ancy Sojan was hard to overlook. Standing at the top of her mark on the synthetic runway at Bhubaneswar’s Kalinga Stadium during the Inter-State Athletics Championships a few weeks ago, she cut a striking figure — electric blue acrylic nails, bold eye shadow and lipstick, neon yellow spikes, a stark white headband, large hoop earrings, layered gold chains and jangling bracelets. She really is one of the most distinctive figures in Indian track and field.
And that’s precisely how Ancy likes it. She considers herself more than just a long jumper.
“I want people to notice me. I feel like I’m a performer as much as an athlete. Like a magician,” she tells Sportstar. “I want to get the audience excited. I love every moment I’m on the field. I want the spectators to be amazed by what I’m doing. I love their eyes on me when they’re clapping and cheering. I want them to say, ‘That’s insane. It’s better than watching it on video!’”
Her appearance, however, is only part of what makes her stand out. The 25-year-old heads to the Asian Games as one of India’s leading medal prospects in athletics. At Bhubaneswar, Ancy smashed one of the longest-standing records in Indian sport, leaping 6.88m to erase Anju Bobby George’s 6.83m mark, which had stood since the 2004 Athens Olympics. Her jump is the best in Asia this year, 12cm clear of the next-best mark, and the second-best by an Asian jumper in the last 33 years.
When she steps onto the field at the Paloma Mizuho Stadium in Nagoya, expect Ancy to be blinged out.
The nails, earrings, chains, hair and makeup are not merely accessories. They are part of how Sojan prepares herself to compete. Even her spikes come with their own rules. At Bhubaneswar, she had a new pair.
“I have one set that I keep just for competitions. I never take them to the training area,” she says. “I wanted that new feeling, an extra something for this competition.”
The nails too were chosen to match her blue competition kit. “They’re very attractive and you can see them from far away. They make me feel more confident.”
On competition mornings, the transformation takes about an hour.
“Doing my makeup on the morning of a competition is like getting ready for me. I feel very cool and relaxed when I do it. I like playing energetic songs that get me hyped up. I’m having fun. I watch long jump videos. I get my hair braided, then I apply eyeliner and lipstick. Finally, I glue on my nails.
“I want to look as beautiful as possible. I want to be someone who can be seen from anywhere.”
After her events, she likes to go back and watch herself.
“I’m obsessed with how I look. I’m obsessed with my body and muscles. I love the intensity with which I run down the runway and then take off. I look at my eyes and how focused they are. There’s this madness and aggression, and I love seeing that.”
There is no embarrassment in that ambition.
Ancy has heard people say she is showing off. She knows there are those who believe an athlete should simply compete and let the performance speak for itself. But she sees no contradiction between looking good and wanting to be taken seriously. Ancy herself admits to being a fan of long jumper Malaika Mihambo’s hoop earrings and sprinter Sha’Carri Richardson’s colourful braids. But she is also clear that she is neither adapting nor inventing a persona.
“This is who I am.”
Ancy grew up in Nattika, a fishing village on the Arabian Sea in Kerala’s Thrissur district. She is the daughter of an autorickshaw driver. Her first coach, too, drove rickshaws. Hers is as modest a background as they come. Yet, there were signs of the personality that would eventually become one of her trademarks.
“I think I’ve always been this way. When I was a kid, I was a dancer. I was always in school plays and skits.”
During one play, she was supposed to be pushing another girl on a swing. Instead, she spotted a cameraman.
“I was just posing for the camera! So I’ve always been like that since childhood. I’ve always loved the camera. They say, ‘The moment the cameraman arrives, she starts posing!’”
There was even a brief possibility that the camera might have taken her away from athletics.
When she was young, Ancy had long hair that fell below her waist. Filmmakers looking for a young girl with long hair heard about her and approached her mother about an audition.
But by then, she had started athletics. Her coach told her she needed to cut her hair if she wanted to train properly.
“So when they came for the audition, my mother told them they were a week late! I’d already gone into sports.”
She occasionally wonders what might have happened had she gone to that audition.
“When I first heard I wasn’t going to go for that film audition, I was really unhappy. But now I think I’ve done okay. I’m still getting in front of a camera. It’s just a different way. I’m still travelling around the world and people still want to see me.”
Athletics gave her another stage. And as far as she can remember, she has always liked to perform.
“I remember I used to put bangles on my hands and run in sub-district competitions because I liked the sound they made when I ran down the runway. That’s the kind of person I am.”
She laughs when she remembers how people reacted.
“A lot of people judged me for it. They would ask, ‘Why is this young girl wearing so many chains?’ But I never bothered. It’s my life. I love wearing jewellery and make-up. What is it to you? It makes me feel confident and I think it’s cool.
“And it’s not as if I don’t perform. I know how hard I’ve worked to get to where I am now.”
Away from the spotlight
For someone with such an obvious inclination for the limelight, Ancy admits that she did not enjoy waiting in the wings. Despite her accomplishments — by 2023, she was already an Asian Games silver medallist at Hangzhou — there was a time when she felt she was living in the shadow of other athletes.
One of them was compatriot Shaili Singh, herself a junior world silver medallist who was considered the heir apparent to Anju Bobby George. Anju herself thought as much. After Shaili jumped 6.76m to move to second on the Indian all-time list, Anju told Sportstar she expected Shaili to break her national record one day.
Ancy admits she noticed this.
“I know a lot of the attention was on other jumpers. At that time, it felt a little strange. I was wondering what I needed to do to make people notice me as well.”
Few can doubt Ancy’s willingness to back up her self-belief. For all the attention she pays to her appearance, there is little frivolity in the way she approaches her sport.
In 2025, Ancy was diagnosed with PCOS, a hormonal condition that caused her to gain weight rapidly. The extra kilos weighed her down and her form dipped unexpectedly. After tests finally identified the cause, Ancy underwent an intense training and diet regimen to get into the shape she wanted.
“I love rice and biryani, but I completely cut everything like that out of my diet. I knew that if I wanted to be a world-class jumper, I had to make sacrifices.”
At the start of the 2026 season, the change has been dramatic. Ancy lost eight kilos, dropping from 63kg to 55kg, while her body-fat percentage has fallen from 26 to 13.
As she got into the best shape of her career, Ancy soared, capping it with the stunning performance in Bhubaneswar.
“I wanted to make a statement. This is a record; now they have to consider me too. I am also special. Before, there were people saying, ‘She’s showing off so much and she’s only the third-best Indian jumper.’ But now I’m the best. So what are you going to say now?”
The reaction to her jump was overwhelming.
“I saw that my coach was happy. People were blowing whistles. When I looked at my phone, there were so many messages — be it on WhatsApp or Instagram. Everywhere I looked, I could see my photo.”
But what stayed with her was not the attention itself.
“The thing I felt was that the national record is in my name. 6.88m! It’s such a big number.”
Bigger dreams
The number is big enough to raise the question of whether Ancy has peaked too early, at a domestic meet rather than an international competition. Those who know her say that is unlikely.
“I’ve seen Ancy for a long time. She’s someone who doesn’t change her intensity. She’s the same everywhere. She could jump a national record in a district meet or at the World Championships. If she’s feeling good, she’s going to jump big,” says State-mate and one of India’s top men’s long jumpers Murali Sreeshankar.
What better place to make another big jump than Nagoya? And while India will be hoping for her to win gold, Ancy is already thinking beyond it.
“I’m looking at the Asian Games not just as a competition in itself, but because the qualification period for the next World Championships will begin after that. I need to repeat my jump over there. The qualification standard for that competition is 6.86m. I want to do these kinds of jumps.
“Because I’ve passed 6.88m, it won’t feel like something difficult to do at the Asian Games either. I’ve already done it, so I’m confident.”
Her confidence is not confined to Asia. The 6.88m has taken her into the world’s top 10.
“There was a time when I was 80th in the world. But I’m also getting confident that I can compete with them and show that India’s not that far behind.”
Ancy knows others are already taking notice of her. At the Asian Indoor Championships earlier this year, she says the Chinese audience loved what they saw.
“I even gifted some of my ornaments to one of the Chinese players, Shiqi Xiong [who won the gold medal and who is expected to be Ancy’s biggest challenge in Nagoya]. I gave her some of the rings and chains I was wearing. She likes that stuff a lot.”
In India, too, her personality has admirers.
“I know there are a lot of young athletes who look up to me. They’re willing to let their personalities come out more as well. And now that I have the national record, no one can say that the two can’t go together.”
And there is something even bigger on her mind.
When she closes her eyes, Ancy sees it clearly: 7 metres.
When she first arrived at the National Camp, she told coach Anoop Joseph that she wanted to jump that distance. “He was thinking, ‘Who is this little girl who thinks she’s going to jump 7m?’”
Even with the national record to her name, Ancy wants that 7m mark.
“6.88 is a number, but 7m is a brand. It’s a magical mark. It’s like being the first person in space. I want to be the first Indian to do it.
“I want to, of course, do well in the big tournaments, but I really want to jump 7 metres. When people think of who got to that mark, I want them to look at me and say, ‘It’s the one and only Ancy Sojan.’”

India’s AI story is moving beyond models, and the next quest is about how AI is being deployed, integrated into workflows, governed and navigated to deliver measurable value. Last month, Inc42 reported that enterprise LLM adoption in India is taking a vertical turn, with companies such as Razorpay, Fractal, BharatGen and Tech Mahindra building models for payments, healthcare, agriculture and education rather than general-purpose chat. A fortnight ago, we reported that enterprise AI deployment was getting a reality check, with organisations imposing budget caps, approval gates and unit-economics scrutiny on AI features well before they reach production. This suggests that value is shifting towards the layer where AI is deployed, governed and measured, and away from the layer where it is merely demonstrated. The ecosystem data agrees. The Bharat AI Startups Report 2026, published by Inc42 with Google, put India's AI market at $126 Bn by 2030, led by enterprise AI growing from $11 Bn to $71 Bn, and noted that 47% of enterprises are already moving pilots into production. Capital is following the same logic. Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn across 57 deals in H1 2026, nearly four times the $162 Mn raised in the same period last year, according to Inc42's Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, H1 2026, even as overall startup funding slipped 9%. But the more telling signal is not how much capital is flowing into AI. It is which problems capital is being asked to solve. Against this backdrop, Inc42 returns with its monthly AI Startups To Watch series. The twelfth edition highlights five emerging startups building across AI operations, education, sovereign compute, financial services deployment and enterprise execution. These are not simply startups using AI as a feature. They are trying to build businesses at the point where AI stops being a demo and starts carrying consequences. With that said, here are the five emerging AI startups that caught our attention in September. Editor's Note: This is not a ranking. The startups featured here are a curated selection by the Inc42 editorial team and are listed alphabetically. Oppex AI | Helping Engineers Detect, Investigate, Resolve Production Incidents Faster Every time a company ships new code, something can break in production. Engineers get paged, often at night, then lose hours finding what went wrong. Clues sit scattered across logs, dashboards, customer complaints, and old fix notes, and alerts pile up faster than a small team can clear them. Oppex AI is trying to automate that work. Founded in 2025 by Prasun Kumar and Pranit Kumar, the Bengaluru startup has built an AI system that reads across a company’s monitoring tools, support tickets, cloud systems and internal notes, then points to the likely bug. The platform groups alerts describing the same issue into one incident, learns a company's setup so its answers improve over time, and remembers earlier fixes so nothing is lost when the on-duty engineer changes. Oppex says its agents resolve issues five times faster with half the on-call engineers. Within eight months of writing its first line of code, it deployed its platform across enterprises in India, the UK, the EU, and the US, targeting the global AIOps market, projected to reach $41.6 Bn by 2030 at a 30.3% CAGR. ProLearn | AI-Native Learning Companion Personal tutoring works. It has simply never scaled. Most Indian students preparing for board exams or entrance tests still learn from recorded lectures and static test papers, with little feedback on where exactly their understanding breaks down. ProLearn is trying to put that attention inside a phone. The Bengaluru startup was founded in April 2026 by Ravneet Singh, a former Vedantu executive. He is building an AI-native learning companion for K-12 students and aspirants preparing for JEE, NEET, UPSC and CAT. The companion is built for conversation rather than content delivery. It listens to how a student explains a problem, asks questions back, adapts to their pace and walks them through a solution step by step, the way a tutor would. ProLearn raised ₹30 Cr in a pre-seed round led by BEENEXT to build its AI and reasoning infrastructure and curriculum-aligned content ahead of a public launch. It is targeting India's AI tutors market projected to reach $1.2 Bn by 2031. Quantum Tiger | Sovereign AI Systems For Architectural Autonomy Most enterprises running serious AI workloads still do it on someone else’s infrastructure, sending sensitive data across borders to models and cloud services they do not control. For banks, hospitals, defence contractors and government institutions, that is becoming unacceptable, commercially and legally. Quantum Tiger wants to make the alternative smaller. The Kolkata-based startup was founded in 2025 by Rana Dutta and Manas Paul, and is building full-stack sovereign AI infrastructure that lets organisations train and run AI workloads within their own trusted boundaries, without depending on public cloud infrastructure. Its stack pairs an AI operating layer with purpose-built compute hardware designed to run large language models locally at predictable latency, doing training and inference on the same system so enterprises are not billed for every external call. The company says the system is engineered for data locality and continuous model adaptation across heterogeneous workloads. Quantum Tiger is targeting the sovereign AI infrastructure market, estimated at $15 Bn in 2025 and projected to reach $177.09 Bn by 2035. Vecton AI | Production-Ready AI For BFSI Financial services is where AI promises the most and delivers the least. Banks and insurers sit on decades of structured data and repetitive, high-volume processes, yet most AI pilots inside them never leave the sandbox, held back by regulatory requirements, legacy architecture and the cost of reworking core systems. Vecton AI is built to solve just that. Founded in 2025 by Himanshu Goyal and Gaurav Mandlecha, the Bengaluru startup positions itself as an AI transformation partner for banks, financial services and insurance companies. It works across AI consulting and strategy, process automation, custom-trained models and autonomous agent development, with a delivery model built on forward-deployed engineers who stay with the client through implementation. It ships production-ready, compliant agent systems and machine learning workflows aligned with BFSI regulatory standards, focussed on sales acceleration, customer engagement, document processing, and intelligent copilots. Vecton is targeting India's AI in BFSI market, estimated at $1,069 Mn in 2025 and projected to reach $9,425.2 Mn by 2034. Zenalyst | AI Workforce For Enterprises Every CIO says the same thing: dashboards everywhere, answers nowhere. Enterprise decisions still depend on numbers scattered across ERP, CRM, banking and document systems, stitched together by hand. By the time a finance team spots a variance, the quarter it belonged to is closed. Zenalyst is building agents that do the work rather than describe it. The Bengaluru-based startup was founded in May 2025 by Nagendra Singh, Sanketh Krishnappa and Vijay Jha, and its ZenForce platform connects to more than 150 enterprise systems across ERP, CRM and banking to run finance, procurement and legal workflows. Zenalyst is targeting the autonomous finance market, projected to reach $112.84 Bn by 2031. Its agents include ZenBank for treasury and money operations, ZenProcure for procurement and ZenCollect for order-to-cash and contract intelligence. Zenalyst positions ZenForce as deterministic rather than probabilistic: reasoning is gated through verification steps, queries are grounded in the customer's own schema, and customer data is never used to train external models. Elon Musk is seemingly done attacking Apple over its decision to integrate ChatGPT into iPhone features.
Back in 2024, when the partnership was first announced, Musk slammed the integration as an agreement from Apple to let OpenAI install “creepy spyware” on users’ devices. The next year, he sued, claiming the partnership gave the firms a “monopoly” on Apple users’ AI prompts, which allegedly harmed competition in both smartphone and chatbot markets.
For Musk, the fight with Apple seemingly escalated after he believed that his chatbot, Grok, was perhaps being illegally blocked from topping Apple’s App Store rankings. Everyone knows that when you’re at Olive Garden, you’re family.
But in the 44 years since the casual Italian-American restaurant chain was founded, few have embraced it with the ardor that Braden Sinclair has. In fact, way back in his Little League days, a coach named him “Breadsticks.”
“I had to go to Olive Garden for my birthday, ate too much, missed an entire game,” Sinclair tells WIRED. “One of my coaches decided that because of my initials being B.S., and my number being 11—which he said looked like breadsticks—and then that story, that I had to be called ‘Breadsticks’ for the rest of the season.”
He maintained that close relationship with the chain for many years, until, in 2019, he was rewarded with an almost unfathomable distinction: Sinclair is one of just 50 human beings on the planet to ever secure an Olive Garden Lifetime Pasta Pass.
Unlike the thousands of 13-week Never Ending Pasta Passes that the chain has offered at various intervals since 2014—this summer, a batch of 10,000, priced at $100 apiece, sold out within seconds—Sinclair’s heavy gold card bears no expiration date. It entitles him to as much pasta, toppings, breadsticks, and soup or salad as he cares to eat, for as long as the chain endures and he remains a loyal customer. (No delivery, though, to be clear. A pasta bowl so bottomless demands that one take a seat of honor for the dine-in experience.)
How exactly does Sinclair wield his kingly rights at Olive Garden? All is revealed on his new website, Lifetimepastapass.com, where he crunches the many numbers—both financial and dietary—on his many meals there. And, with a continually updated poll that decides what he should order the next time he drops in, it’s easily the closest you’ll ever get to having the lifetime pass yourself.
Sinclair nabbed his license to feast during a special promotion, when Olive Garden announced that the first 50 people to buy a temporary pasta pass would have the opportunity to upgrade it to the lifetime pass for an extra $400. To this day, Sinclair wonders if his timing was really that good or if the company deliberately selected him to receive the ultimate prize.
“I had sort of a joking relationship with their Instagram for years, just like chatting back and forth,” he explains, adding that it felt a little “weird” and something like “divine intervention” that he won given his coziness with the brand. An Olive Garden vice president of marketing FaceTimed him with the good news, he recalls.
Reactions to the card from Olive Garden employees range from awe to confusion. “They always take it back to the kitchen, show it to people,” Sinclair says. “Managers will come out and ask questions. The other end of the spectrum has been having to kind of prove it's real, which is rare, and I totally understand. Like, if I managed a restaurant and someone came in with a gold card that said I don't need to pay, I would also have questions.”
Now a 33-year-old father of two young kids, Sinclair doesn’t gorge on heaping plates of carbohydrates the way he used to (and, since frequenting Olive Garden makes him more conscientious about the rest of his diet, he’s avoided packing on the pounds). But he says the Lifetime Pasta Pass somewhat justifies his continued fixation on the restaurant, which was a familiar comfort when his family temporarily relocated from Maine to Wisconsin during his childhood. In 2016, he paid homage to the place with a tattoo of its famous rotary cheese grater; the caption reads “SAY WHEN.” He also began collecting vintage T-shirts that the chain had released in the 1980s and 1990s.
This year, Sinclair unveiled the project that brought all of his Olive Garden experiences together in one place. Lifetimepastapass.com documents his “infinite tour of Italy” by showcasing not only his backstory and extensive merch collection but all the data you could ever want about how he has used his rare privilege: number of restaurant visits since 2019 (112), bowls of pasta eaten (152), calories consumed (154,817), meal value ($1,878.87) and total tips ($607.00).
You can also keep tabs on a map of which locations Sinclair has tried—while the South Portland, Maine, restaurant is his home base, he has ventured up and down the Eastern Seaboard. Other charts show his most favored pasta type (rigatoni), sauce (alfredo), and topping (crispy chicken fritta), as well as the monthly frequency of his Olive Garden visits; he dined there nine times in August, the most since he set a personal record of 20 visits in October 2019, shortly after winning the pass.
With a decade of experience in data analytics and visualization, Sinclair saw all this as a fun application of his talents. But he also wanted people to have “skin in the game,” as he puts it—so he built a dashboard where anyone can vote on the combination of ingredients that make up his next pasta order.
“I thought it was just gonna be a joke among my friends,” Sinclair says. “You know, share it on Instagram, so maybe 10 of my friends would go in and vote, and then the next day five, and then the third day no one would care, and it would be over.” Instead, after he shared the project on a couple of subreddits, he was stunned to tally over 700 votes on his next meal. He wound up eating angel hair with spicy alfredo (a new sauce offering) and crispy shrimp fritta.
“A big reason why I wanted to do this is I just kept getting rigatoni with alfredo, five-cheese marinara, and crispy chicken, like on repeat,” Sinclair says. “I was like, ‘I need to branch out.’” His best discovery so far? “I realized that alfredo and meatballs is an insane combination,” he says. “It's so good.”
In some ways, Lifetimepastapass.com is a reflection of Sinclair’s belief that the card comes with great responsibility. Besides tipping diligently, he also skips the refills, aiming to be a “respectful” and “low-impact” diner who doesn’t flaunt his status or make a shift harder for staff. “I see some pictures of people with the [regular] pasta passes who go crazy,” he says. “Bowls full of grated Parmesan just because they can.” Meticulously tracking his own Olive Garden journey toward various virtual “trophies” earned by hitting benchmarks in categories such as “lifetime breadsticks eaten” (he’ll reach the bronze level at 100, gold at 1,000) and “longest streaks of consecutive weeks with at least one visit” seems, by comparison, a kind of reverence for the institution.
If there’s an unexpected downside to the Lifetime Pasta Pass, it may be a certain loneliness at the top. Because Covid-19 hit shortly after people claimed the cards, the promotion has been largely memory-holed, and whatever plans Olive Garden could have had to celebrate or connect the winners were never realized. Sinclair has stumbled upon only a couple of other passholders via social media and has no idea how often others may go to the restaurant these days.
Meanwhile, it’s not always easy to convince your pals to meet up at a restaurant just because you eat there for free. “There's only so many times I can go sit at the Olive Garden by myself,” Sinclair says. “I have some friends who are nice enough to go with me, but oftentimes they’ll just kind of sit there and eat some breadsticks.” And though Sinclair’s wife is an admitted fan of the chain—she’s eaten there with him since their high school days and promised in her wedding vows to go whenever he wants—he finds it “wisest” to seek alternatives whenever they manage a kids-free date night.
The good news is that Sinclair’s 4-year-old is a likely Olive Garden devotee in the making. “I'll probably start bringing my oldest son a little more just because he's obsessed with pasta,” he says. “I think he'll genuinely enjoy it.”
Just not before a Little League game, of course.

Between surviving an illness and returning to regular life, lies a journey of a thousand small victories. Physiotherapy helps people take those victories, one step at a time.
There is a moment after a heart attack or stroke that very few people talk about. It is not the moment the ambulance arrives. It is not the moment the doctors say the patient is out of danger. It is the moment when the hospital doors close behind you, you return home, and everyone expects life to slowly return to normal.
But what does ‘normal’ mean?
For someone who has had a stroke, it may mean learning to walk again, using an arm that suddenly feels unfamiliar, finding their balance, or simply getting out of bed without someone holding their hand. For someone who has survived a heart attack, it may mean taking that first walk outside without constantly wondering whether their heart can handle it.
And sometimes, the hardest part is not the physical limitation. It is the fear. “What if it happens again?” That question can stay with a person long after they have left the hospital. This is where physiotherapy becomes much more than a set of exercises.
What rehabilitation entails
We often imagine rehabilitation as someone working hard in a gym, lifting weights or walking on a treadmill. The reality can be much quieter.
For a stroke survivor, the first goal may simply be to sit upright without support. Then to stand. Then to take a few steps. For the family watching, it may seem like very little. For the person doing it, it may feel like climbing a mountain.
A physiotherapist is there for these moments. Not just to count repetitions or measure strength, but to help someone understand that progress does not always have to be dramatic. Sometimes, progress is one extra step. Sometimes, it is standing for ten seconds longer. Sometimes, it is being able to walk to the bathroom without asking for help. And sometimes, it is simply finding the confidence to try.
What patients go through
Imagine being someone who used to walk to work, play with their children, exercise regularly or climb four flights of stairs without giving it a second thought. Then you have a heart attack. Suddenly, your heartbeat becomes something you constantly notice. You begin questioning every sensation. Is this normal? Am I too tired? Is my heart rate too high? Should I stop?
That fear can lead people to become overly cautious and inactive. Cardiac rehabilitation can help break that cycle. With appropriate medical assessment and supervision, patients can gradually return to physical activity, improve their exercise capacity and learn how to manage their cardiovascular health with greater confidence. The physiotherapist’s role is not simply to say, “Push harder.” It is to say: “Let us understand what your body can safely do today—and build from there.”
Not only for the elderly
A stroke or heart attack is often imagined as something that happens late in life, after the age of 60 or so. But when it happens to a younger person, the shock can be enormous. Someone in their 30s or 40s may suddenly find themselves worrying about things they never expected to question. Will I be able to go back to work? Can I take care of my children? Can I travel? Can I exercise again? Can I return to the sport I love?
They may look perfectly healthy from the outside. But inside, they may be dealing with fatigue, weakness, uncertainty and fear about what comes next. That is why rehabilitation cannot simply be based on a person’s age or diagnosis. A younger patient may need to return to a physically demanding job. A sportsperson may want to return to competition. A parent may simply want enough energy to play with their children. Rehabilitation has to fit the life that person wants to return to.
The patient is not a diagnosis. This may be one of the most important things a physiotherapist learns. A medical report might say stroke. It might say heart attack. It might list numbers, test results and medications. But none of those words explain who the patient is. They do not tell you that the patient loves taking their morning walk. They do not tell you that someone has a child waiting at home. They do not tell you that being able to climb the stairs independently means more to that person than almost anything else. Good rehabilitation starts with a simple question: “What do you want to get back to?” The answer may be different for every person. And that answer becomes an important part of the treatment.
Preventive goals
Physiotherapy is also about preventing the next story. Rehabilitation should not only begin after a crisis. Physiotherapists also have an important role in helping people become more physically active, develop healthier movement habits and reduce preventable health risks. Physical activity is an important part of cardiovascular health, but exercise is not a prescription that can simply be copied from one person to another.
The right type, intensity and amount of activity depend on the individual. For someone recovering from a cardiac event, exercise may require appropriate medical guidance and monitoring of symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure and exercise tolerance. For someone recovering from a stroke, rehabilitation may involve improving balance, strength, coordination, walking and everyday functional activities.
The goal is not to push everyone to do more. The goal is to help each person do what is right for them—safely and consistently. The greatest thing a physiotherapist restores is not movement. It is the part of someone’s life they thought was gone forever.
We often say that physiotherapists help people move. But perhaps that does not quite capture the whole story. Physiotherapists help people return to the things that make life feel like life.
(Shanthi Dass is a sports physiotherapist and managing director of Synergy The Clinic, Chennai. synergytheclinic@gmail.com)

Across Southeast Asia, artists and cultural rights defenders are increasingly being cast as threats — to public morality, political order and dominant narratives about gender, sexuality, identity and belonging.
This is especially true for queer and trans artists, whose bodies, stories and performances often challenge the boundaries that states, religious authorities and conservative movements seek to impose. When they are surveilled, attacked or their work is censored, the consequences touch the foundations of civic space: the right to speak, gather, remember, imagine and contest power.
ArtsEquator’s Southeast Asia Artistic Freedom RADAR Database documents this reality across Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam. In its 2025 report, RADAR recorded 159 challenges to artistic freedom across the seven countries. The findings closely mirror those of the CIVICUS Monitor, which rated Myanmar and Vietnam as “Closed,” Cambodia, Thailand and the Philippines as “Repressed,” and Malaysia and Indonesia as “Obstructed.”

The US war against Iran has cost the Department of Defense more than $38 billion through August 1, with the conflict potentially adding another $2 billion to $3 billion or more each month, depending on the intensity of fighting, the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office said on Tuesday (September 15).
“As of August 1, 2026, the armed conflict with Iran has cost (the Department of Defense) approximately $38 billion,” the CBO said in an assessment, referring to the war that began after US-Israeli strikes targeting Iran on February 28.
The agency warned that the monthly cost could increase further if the conflict escalates.
“These expenses could be higher still if the violence escalated further,” the CBO said.
The CBO said the estimate largely reflects the cost of replacing munitions expended during the conflict and equipment lost in battle, along with higher fuel costs for the US military and other expenses.
The estimate does not include costs related to US military personnel killed or injured in the conflict, or longer-term veterans' healthcare and disability compensation.
The analysis was prepared following a request from Rep. Brendan Boyle, the top Democrat on the House Budget Committee, along with other Democratic lawmakers.
The estimate broadly aligns with an earlier assessment by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who told the Senate in July that the Iran war had cost the Pentagon about $37.5 billion.
The CBO said the conflict's broader economic impact is being felt through higher inflation, primarily because of disruptions to oil and natural gas shipments.
Iran's retaliation included blocking the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for global energy transit. The disruption, along with shipping problems in the Red Sea, has reduced energy flows and pushed up costs.
The CBO estimates that inflation in the first quarter of 2027 will be about 0.5 percentage points higher than it had projected in February, based on the personal consumption expenditures price index.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, is also expected to be 0.3 percentage points higher than previously forecast.
Higher inflation could, in turn, push up interest rates on US Treasury securities, adding to the government's borrowing costs.
The findings come as the Iran conflict enters its seventh month, with the war and elevated prices emerging as major issues ahead of the US midterm elections.
The White House requested $87.6 billion in supplemental funding in June, largely to support the war effort. Congress has not yet approved the request.
The CBO noted that its estimates are subject to considerable uncertainty because the Defense Department declined to provide information requested for the assessment. The budget office instead relied on government databases and publicly available reports.
The cost of replacing weapons and equipment is also raising concerns about US military stockpiles.
A Pentagon inspector general report released on Monday said the war had resulted in “strategic inventory shortfalls.”
“This nonpartisan CBO report makes clear that the war has also cost American taxpayers tens of billions of dollars and counting, while continuing to drive up costs,” Boyle said.
He also criticised President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans over the spending, arguing that the administration was willing to spend tens of billions of dollars on the conflict while warning about the cost of domestic programmes.
(With AFP, AP inputs)

raw_text: Investment firm Novastar Partners has made its maiden India bet by investing an undisclosed sum in Aviral Bhatnagar-led venture capital fund A Junior VC (AJVC), becoming a limited partner (LP) for the firm. Founded in 2024 by Bhatnagar, AJVC is a pre-seed focused investment firm that closed its maiden fund at ₹200 Cr last year. It has made 32 investments to date, backing early-stage startups like Iztri, Handy Panda, Mindcase, among others. Backing startups at the pre-seed or idea stage, AJVC typically invests ₹1.5 Cr for 9% equity. The firm then works closely with founders to build out the business by helping refine product, optimising hiring and people strategy, assisting in sales and marketing, while also aiding in finance, legal and compliance operations. Investment firm Novastar, which is building a private equity fund-of-funds, intends to support AJVC and its portfolio companies by facilitating follow-on funding rounds and providing networking opportunities as well as direct operational assistance. AJVC’s investment strategy, its tech-led sourcing infrastructure, and Bhatnagar’s network in the early-stage investment ecosystem were the key reasons driving Novastar’s decision to back the firm, Novastar’s managing partner Dhruv Jhunjhunwala shared with Inc42. “We believe a programmatic approach, like the one that AJVC is pursuing, where you build a sufficiently broad portfolio of a number of companies while maintaining discipline around selection, can be one of the most effective ways of investing at the pre-seed stage,” he added. Founded by Jhunjhunwala in 2025, Novastar operates a SEBI-registered category II alternative investment fund (AIF) that aims to back leading venture capital funds as a LP, as well as making direct startup investments. The fund focuses on sectors like AI, consumer tech, financial services, healthcare, and deep tech. It also aims to diversify its bets across the startup life cycle with plans to allocate around 15% of its capital to early stage strategies, the majority towards growth stage strategies, and a small share towards late stage strategies including secondaries and continuation funds. Jhunjhunwala declined to share details around how much capital Novastar has raised till now or the capital it plans to deploy. “In the medium term, we would love to announce our next set of investments that would be across funds and companies. But right now, our focus is on continuing to build the right portfolio and partnering with the right set of fund managers,” he said.

One of the Pentagon’s largest costs has been the US$21.7 billion spent replacing munitions used in the conflict.

In July, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth estimated the Iran war had cost US$37.5 billion.

The higher inflation will also boost interest rates on Treasury securities, the report said.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to another working week. We hope the weekend respite was relaxing and invigorating. Now, though, that oh-too-familiar routine of meetings, deadlines, and the like has returned with a vengeance. You knew this would happen, yes? To cope, we are relying, as always, on a cuppa stimulation. Our choice today is blueberry hibiscus. Feel free to join us. Remember, no prescription or prior authorization is required. AstraZeneca disclosed that a breast cancer pill failed in a pivotal trial testing it as a first-line therapy in advanced tumors, a result that could limit the use of the medicine, STAT notes. The drug, camizestrant, in combination with another medicine did not outperform standard treatment on a measure of how long patients went before their cancer progressed. The drug earlier this month won accelerated approval in the U.S. as a treatment for patients who develop a mutation in their tumors that’s a sign of emerging drug resistance. Had the trial been successful, it could have opened up a much larger market for the drug.
Scholar Rock received U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval for the first-ever therapy that targets the loss of muscle in spinal muscle atrophy, raising hopes that patients with the rare neurological disorder might have a better chance of moving and walking independently, STAT writes. The FDA approved the drug, Isembyld, for use in adults and children 2 years and older who are currently receiving SMA therapies that target SMN2, a key gene for neurons that control movement. The approval marks another step forward for patients with spinal muscular atrophy, a rare and progressive disease that destroys nerve cells that control speaking, breathing, and walking. Babies who go untreated usually die by the age of 2.

As calls for artificial intelligence regulation intensify, US President Donald Trump’s team have made it clear that if lab leaders want to implement an industry-wide slowdown, they’re going to have to do it themselves.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called on the US government to regulate AI companies within a wider effort to slow the pace of the technology’s development in an essay published Saturday. The essay received rare endorsement from both OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who owns chatbot Grok, following a week of intense debate about the technology’s threats to human safety. Microsoft chief executive officer Satya Nadella also called for pacing development.
Calls for AI slowdown and regulation have intensified after a number of researchers voiced major concerns in the last week about the speed of the technology’s advance. “AI progress is increasing,” former DeepMind researcher Rishub Jain told WIRED. “And as AI becomes more capable, it poses more risks.”
But David Sacks, co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, wrote on X, “If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible. But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission. Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel … Most of all, stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic.”
Amodei had requested the government enable competing AI companies to work together on standards without breaching antitrust law, either by participating in discussions or issuing a waiver for the companies involved. He also called for government assistance in establishing international coordination, including with the Chinese Communist Party, though critics wondered how effective this would be. “China is very unlikely to join a global agreement, as you know,” Sacks wrote.
Concerns about the US ceding its lead in the technology to China have caused the US government to mostly push back against the notion of slowing the pace of its development. “You have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” Trump said during a visit to Ireland. “We’re leading China on AI,” he added, “and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."
The US largely views China’s AI ecosystem as an economic and national security threat, and has previously been caught short by the country’s advances in the technology. “If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, and that is a threat to every single American,” House Speaker Mike Johnson told CNN on Sunday. “So, we’ve got to have balance. We’ve got to have steady hands at the wheel.”
In the meantime, companies say they are going to start taking voluntary steps to reestablish public trust that they are acting responsibly. On Sunday night, OpenAI’s Altman committed to a proposal by Amodei to give embedded third party evaluators employee-level access to their firms to check practices and products were safe, and report incidents. While these measures will have “significant costs,” he wrote on X: “Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness.”

I cannot overstate the importance of having an air purifier that not only has enough power to actually purify a room's air but also caters to your home's particular needs. Pollutants like wildfire smoke, pollen, unventilated gas stoves, pet allergens, and even litter box odors can be potentially harmful additions to the air you breathe in your home.
Air purifiers from Coway have been a consistent top pick in our guide to the Best Air Purifiers for years, including the Coway Airmega Mighty2, which was released in March this year. Its predecessor, the Coway Airmega Mighty, had been our reigning “Best Affordable Air Purifier” for many years as well. I was excited to test the newest mid-size option built for medium to large rooms in Coway's Airmega line, where it sits between the compact Airmega 50 or 100 and the higher-capacity 350 or 450 models.
Released at the end of August, Coway’s Airmega Halo is an affordable, lightweight air purifier that aims to deliver whole-room air purification at an accessible price point. Plus, its focus is on promoting a healthier night's sleep with smart sleep features and quiet noise levels when in sleep mode.
Overall, it delivers on most of its promises, but I ran into some problems during field-testing that made me question its sensor, and I wish it had more transparency with pollutant levels.
Simple Design That’s Maybe Too Simple
The Halo is only 9.7 pounds, making it lightweight and portable as far as air purifiers go, but it doesn't have accessibility features like a top handle or wheels for easier moving. It has a small cutout in the back to grip, but because I have an upper-limb disability, moving it was awkward—I essentially had to hug the purifier to maneuver it, since I don't have large hands that can easily grip the inlet.
The purifier's cylindrical design with a 360-degree air-intake structure draws in polluted air from all sides, making for fewer spatial constraints and more options for placement around the home. The inside of the machine uses Coway's HyperVortex filtration system, which is an aerodynamic fan and duct design that Coway states is “inspired by eagle wings and golf ball dimples.” It uses wing blades to stabilize airflow, along with aerodynamic blades for powerful airflow for the generator fan and dimples to reduce air resistance for smoother air intake.
Setup was extremely easy—I just needed to unscrew the bottom, remove the filter from the plastic protective covering, screw the bottom back on, and plug it in. There's no need for a Wi-Fi connection, no app, and no remote. I started testing air purifiers earlier this year, and I've found I actually like having a connected remote, or better yet, an app that allows me to monitor air quality and adjust settings from afar. This model had neither. I also appreciate getting transparent numbers of pollutant levels directly from the machine rather than relying on colored lights, but this machine had the latter.

Gender disparity in organ transplantation is a global problem affecting each step of the transplantation process, from organ donation, recipient listing, waiting times and access, to post-transplant outcomes. This inequality is most visibly expressed in the overrepresentation of women as living donors, while men continue to be the majority of transplant recipients.
What the data reveals
India’s case is a particularly striking example of this gender imbalance. Women constitute the majority of living organ donors, but men get the majority of transplants. As per recent data from the National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organization (NOTTO), between 2019 and 2023, 63.8% of living organ donors were women and 69.8% of transplant recipients were men.
This is not a new divide. In 2019 and 2020, roughly two-thirds of living donors were women, but only about a quarter of recipients were women. A 2025 analysis found that women accounted for 36,038 of the 56,509 living donations over the five-year period studied, also highlighting the scale of the imbalance. Of these, however, only 17,041 were transplanted into women, as against 39,447 transplanted into men.
This gendered pattern raises a fundamental question: why are women expected to give and men positioned to receive in disproportionate numbers? The answer goes far beyond biology.
Behind the donations
Women’s decisions to donate organs are shaped by a complicated interaction between sociocultural expectations, economic conditions and family structures. In many Indian homes, women, particularly wives and mothers, are still expected to put the needs of their families before their own. The expectation can be particularly sharp in the case of a life-saving transplant for a close family member.
Studies have noted the role of women in familial organ donation. Mothers are, on average, 73% of all parental donations, and wives are 91% of donations between married couples. These figures are suggestive of a long-standing social tendency to assign the bulk of care work to women, and perhaps even to the final act of bodily sacrifice.
Psychological and experiential reasons may also play a role in women’s higher willingness to donate. Past experiences with the health care system, such as pregnancy and delivery, may increase familiarity with medical settings and trust in health care providers. But these explanations have to be discussed in the light of the strong influence of social conditioning. What seems like a personal choice can sometimes be influenced by expectations, emotional duties or an unspoken belief that a woman should make sacrifices for her family.
Patriarchal attitudes can also be a disincentive for men to become donors. Men are generally considered the primary breadwinner and economic provider for their families. Thus, the prospect of a man needing major surgery, a long recovery period or a temporary loss of income might be seen as an unacceptable financial risk. Such pressure can transfer the burden of donation to women.
This dynamic is particularly problematic when financial dependency is a factor. The costs of evaluation, surgery, recovery and the potential loss of household income may make male donation seem less feasible. In such cases, women may be subtly, and in more troubling cases, explicitly encouraged to donate, because they are seen as more expendable in the family’s economic structure. Thus, the line between voluntary altruism and coercion can become perilously blurred.
It is, therefore, the duty of healthcare providers to fully discuss these issues at every stage of the process, explain the ramifications of a donation and t ensure that they are indeed personal choices of women, and not influenced by other factors.
What needs to change
This has implications for more than just transplant statistics. Essentially, it’s a question of equity, autonomy and justice in healthcare. An organ donation system cannot be truly equitable when it is based on social and familial pressures about who is supposed to donate, and on socioeconomic or structural barriers about who gets the transplant.
Interventions are required at several levels to address this gap. Awareness must be the starting point, but awareness is not enough. Transplant services and community-based initiatives should be extended to rural, underserved and marginalised regions and not be confined to major urban centres. In particular, women should have equal access to information, evaluation and transplantation services.
Equally important is strengthening psychosocial assessment of potential living donors. Pre-transplant evaluation should not only include medical suitability and financial considerations, but also explore the wider social environment in which the donation decision is being made. Healthcare professionals should be trained to recognise warning signs of coercion, domestic abuse, threats, violence, manipulation and financial dependence. Donors must be provided with real opportunities to make informed and voluntary decisions, including the opportunity to withdraw without fear of repercussions.
Better and more comprehensive data collection is also needed in India. Good, disaggregated data on donors and recipients – disaggregated by gender, age, socioeconomic status, geography, relationship to recipient and other relevant factors, would enable policymakers to better identify disparities and design evidence-based interventions. Grassroots research is important because national averages can hide significant inequalities at the regional and community level.
The challenge is to move beyond the financial transaction of organ donation, and to acknowledge the quieter pressures that can exist within families. Sometimes coercion doesn’t take the form of an explicit threat. It could be the expectations of a wife, the responsibilities of a mother or the assumption that a woman should sacrifice herself for the family’s survival.
The bigger message is hard to miss: gender inequality does not stop at the hospital door. It can influence who gives, who gets, who waits and ultimately who gets a chance to live.
(Dr Shivakumar S. Patil is consultant, renal transplant surgery, Manipal Hospital, Hebbal. shivakumar.patil@manipalhospitals.com)

In early September 2026, people shared an alleged screenshot of an X post from the platform's Twitter era purportedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump posting on his @realDonaldTrump account, "Don't let Obama buy the election by handing out unlimited free money to states."
Users shared the image after Trump's pledge to give $5,000 to every U.S. adult should the Republican Party win the 2026 midterm elections. The president announced the pledge during the GOP midterm convention in Dallas on Sept. 10, calling the payments a "Trump dividend."
The screenshot of the alleged tweet spread on Bluesky, Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X and other platforms.
(Thomas Mohr accessed via Bluesky)
Some users drew direct comparisons between Trump's alleged remark in 2012 and the news of his $5,000 pledge. Others referred to the "dividend" as bribery and socialism.
(@mandyarthur accessed via X)
In sum, the 2012 Trump post is real. He tweeted (archived) it on Oct. 30 of that year, one week before the Nov. 6 elections.
Don't let Obama buy the election by handing out unlimited free money to states.
— Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) October 30, 2012
Snopes emailed the White House for its response to users comparing the 2012 post to the "Trump dividend." We will update this article if we receive further information.
The 2012 elections concluded with former President Barack Obama winning a second term. The Democratic Party picked up two seats to continue maintaining a majority in the Senate. Republicans lost eight House seats but continued their control of the legislative chamber.
For further reading, we previously published a collection of 24 things Trump actually posted on Truth Social, including, for example, an Easter Sunday post threatening Iran to open the Strait of Hormuz or be "living in hell," as well as a Memorial Day message addressing "scum" that spent years "trying to destroy our country."

Pennsylvania says an unvaccinated woman has died from measles-related complications
An official in Pennsylvania has confirmed the measles-related death of a 40-year-old woman. Jefferson County Coroner Greg Furlong told NPR that the woman, who died on Saturday, was unvaccinated.
"This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease," a statement from the coroner's office said.
Officials have not released the woman's identity, but said she was a resident of Jefferson County. This is the third death that Pennsylvania state officials have linked to measles this year. No other states have announced measles deaths in 2026.
On Friday, the Pennsylvania Department of Health reported 676 measles cases so far this year. It also reported 52 new positive cases from Wednesday to Friday.
Pennsylvania officials and the federal government have clashed over the number of measles-associated deaths in the state in recent weeks, as the U.S. faces a nationwide resurgence of the illness. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention declared that the highly contagious virus had been eradicated from the U.S. in 2000.
Last week, the CDC reported more than 3,200 confirmed measles cases in the country.
The agency said it was reviewing whether to count two measles-related deaths involving infants in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania. After Gov. Josh Shapiro announced the state's first two deaths, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. said on X the announcement appeared to have been "premature" and "may even have been altogether fabricated by one of the Governor's hopeful staffers."
This clash is notable, as NPR's Rob Stein has reported. "The CDC usually defers to the state's determination" of cause of death in this kind of outbreak, "so the agency can alert the public, doctors and health officials around the country."
The CDC lists the number of measles cases reported in each state for 2026, as well as the number of hospitalizations. The agency has not listed the number of deaths for this year. Instead of giving a figure, there is an asterisk that explains: "The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause."
Kennedy has said on X that NCHS "will update as it receives and reviews submitted records."
The Jefferson County Coroner's Office also emphasized measles can lead to severe complications at any age.
"While cases of severe illness remain uncommon, this tragedy highlights that measles should not be taken lightly," said Chief Deputy Coroner and Public Relations Officer Jason Stiver in a statement. "Public health measures, early recognition of symptoms, and consultation with healthcare providers are important tools in protecting our community."
The county coroner's office is working with the Pennsylvania Department of Health on the case. Pennsylvania and South Carolina have the highest numbers of confirmed measles cases in the U.S., according to federal data.

Defense agencies of Mexico and the US have announced they are implementing a new collaborative strategy to combat drones used by criminal organizations. The operation, dubbed High Eagle, or Águila Alta, builds on recent tests of anti-drone technologies carried out along the border between the two countries.
The first phase of the strategy took place between August 31 and September 2 along the border between San Diego and Tijuana, Mexico. Initially, both military forces—simultaneously on the ground from their respective territories—tracked commercial drones used by criminal entities. In the second phase, the agencies neutralized the unmanned aerial vehicles, with support from fixed and mobile anti-drone systems. These activities began on September 7 and will continue through September 21.
The information released by Mexico’s Secretariat of National Defense, known as SEDENA, does not specify the kind of technology involved in the mission. However, US Northern Command has suggested that the operation might employ high-energy lasers. These extremely concentrated beams of light can—in various phases—detect, track, illuminate, damage, or destroy drones from a distance.
The US Army has invested in a particular laser system known as the Locust platform, which is designed for mounting on military vehicles. Authorities have had this technology at their disposal since September of last year, when the company that produces the system, AeroVironment, delivered the first two functional prototypes to the Armed Forces.
So far, it has not been confirmed that these systems are being used in Operation High Eagle, though the Mexican authorities have increased access to these state-of-the-art weapons. Last month, SEDENA and the US Department of Defense signed an agreement allowing the Mexican military to access the US Army’s digital marketplace for acquiring anti-drone systems at competitive prices.
Representatives from both countries have stated that the aim of this new operation and recent agreements is to strengthen efforts against organized crime, especially human and drug trafficking. Earlier this month, the US Northern Command announced it had disabled or destroyed approximately 300 drones linked to criminal activity this year, a third of which were taken down in August. Within recent weeks, 11 of the targets were involved with cartels.
The operation stems from the US-Mexico Bilateral Implementation Group. According to SEDENA, it aims to ensure security on both sides of the border, while respecting the national sovereignty of both nations and “prioritizing the interests of the Mexican State at all times.”
The US ambassador to Mexico, Ronald Johnson, stated that the agreement would strengthen both countries’ ability to combat cartels and address bilateral security challenges.

The Eiffel Tower has reopened after a one-day strike was called in response to the landmark’s management ordering female staff to keep out of sight at the request of a visiting religious group.
City Hall, which operates the Paris landmark, has apologised for breaching France’s republican principle of equality and ordered a full inquiry.
Workers at the tower walked out on Monday, closing the landmark to visitors, after female colleagues were sidelined and replaced during a visit organised by a Hindu religious group at the weekend.
In a statement, staff said they objected to “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit.
“Some were asked to leave their posts and wait in separate rooms. In some posts, women were replaced by men. All female employees were instructed not to pass through or enter certain areas while the [Hindu] delegation was present,” they said in a statement.
Employees said they were shocked to find themselves in a situation that was “deeply contrary to the values of equality and nondiscrimination”.
“The Eiffel Tower is the symbol of France. We believe it must also be exemplary in the values it promotes and the way it treats staff,” the statement said.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement, whose members made the request in advance of a visit on Saturday, apologised.
“To our knowledge, nobody was refused access to the Eiffel Tower at any moment. Nevertheless, We offer our sincere apologies to anyone who may have been hurt or offended by this situation,” it wrote in a statement.
BAPS is close to India’s ruling Hindu nationalist party, Bharatiya Janata, and was in France to consecrate its first major temple in the country on Sunday.
The public-owned Eiffel Tower operating company (SETE) acknowledged that BAPS had requested that “interactions with women” be limited, and said it should not have accepted these conditions. “They are not in keeping with SETE’s values or the principles of equality between women and men and the neutrality that must guide the organisation of visits to the monument,” it said.
Emmanuel Grégoire, the mayor of Paris, has promised an investigation to “get to the bottom of this as soon as possible”.
He said moving female staff out of sight was unacceptable.
“These are not my values nor those the Eiffel Tower must represent,” he wrote on X.
Ariel Weil, mayor of the Paris Centre district and president of SETE, said he was unaware of the “shocking and unacceptable” conditions afforded the visiting group.
“I confirm again the Eiffel Tower’s commitment to republican values and gender equality,” he said.

Ed Sheeran says it was 'not my decision' to drop Macklemore from tour
- Published
Ed Sheeran has posted a long statement on Instagram, saying it was not his decision to drop Macklemore from his current US tour.
The US rapper - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - was ejected from the line-up after making pro-Palestinian statements at two dates in New Jersey.
His comments drew criticism from Jewish groups, after which some venues put pressure on the tour promoters to have him removed from the line-up.
In his statement, external, Sheeran said he had spoken with the venues "at length all week to try and build a bridge" - but the promoters, Messina Touring Group, had ultimately decided to remove Macklemore from the bill.
"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," he wrote. "Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me.
"I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."
The star also attempted to explain his decision not to become embroiled in political issues.
"I am not complicit," he wrote. "I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care.
"Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own, personal way."
He continued: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds.
"Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes.
"However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: Peace.
"I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed. If we only focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change."
Hind's Hall performance
The controversy began on 4 September, when Macklemore performed at Ed Sheeran's concert at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.
He told the audience: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."
He then performed his song Hind's Hall, which is dedicated to pro-Palestinian protestors at Columbia University and condemns Israel's military action in Gaza, while video footage of the devastation in Gaza was shown on the big screen.
Some of the audience cheered - but there was almost immediate criticism online.
The Israeli American Council launched a petition demanding his removal from the tour; while the campaign group StopAntisemitism said the musician had ambushed fans with propaganda - a claim that was amplified by the pop star Pink, who reposted it on Instagram.
The next night, Macklemore returned to the same stage and directly addressed his "Jewish brothers and sisters" in the audience.
"Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way a criticism of you," he said, adding that he wanted people in Gaza and the West Bank to know they had not been forgotten.
Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.
The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.
During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
'Most successful tour'
After days of press coverage, Macklemore announced on Monday that he had been dropped from the line-up.
In a statement on Instagram, he said the boycott had been organised by Robert Kraft - the billionaire owner of the Gilette Stadium in Massachusetts.
Kraft - who once hired Ed Sheeran to play at his wedding - confirmed he'd made the decision to bar Macklemore, saying his venue would not "provide a platform for hate speech," accusing the rapper of "a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric".
"I agree with Macklemore, too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft said.
However, he did not address the claim that he'd asked other venues to put pressure on the tour.
Tour promoter, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone magazine that it had been told by venues that they would not allow Macklemore to perform, "which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans."
In his statement, Macklemore said he empathised with the difficult position Sheeran had been put in, but criticised the English singer for not taking a stance.
"Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I've lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed," he wrote.
He also emphasised that, although he was only able to complete two shows on the tour, if his words succeeded in "turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I've ever been on."
