Content warning: This piece includes descriptions of nonconsensual sex and intimate image abuse.
On the afternoon of Sunday, November 2, 2025, Maddie Kowalski stopped by a house in Gainesville to drop off a present. The University of Florida sophomore had traveled to Japan that summer, where she’d picked up an action figure from the manga One Piece as a gift.
Students referred to this building near the main campus, which has long been associated with the UF chapter of the frat Phi Delta Theta, as “Fort.” A brick multifamily colonial-style house, it was a typical frat-boy residence with worn hardwood floors, exposed cables, and “THIS IS FORT” spray-painted in UF’s orange and blue colors on the fence lining the perimeter. Phi Delta Theta didn’t have a great reputation on campus; at the time, they were being investigated for accusations of hazing. But the boys who lived there were Kowalski’s best friends: “It was a safe space, I thought.”
A few hours later, Kowalski, then 19, was at an apartment drinking when a friend told her something that would alter the trajectory of her life: Did she know that a nude image of her was circulating at FSU, a university a few hours away?
Kowalski would later learn that the image was making the rounds on Snapchat, and people were talking about it on the anonymous campus social network YikYak. When she opened the app, “that’s when I started crashing out,” she says. As Kowalski scrolled, she saw what appeared to be hundreds of messages about a “DZ” girl. (She was in the sorority Delta Zeta.) They were now referring to not just an image, but a video. Some were joking about masturbating to it.
The situation was about to get worse. Around 6 that night, an anonymous account on X with the handle @SteveCumfull posted the video, saying: “Meet Maddie Kowalski, queen of Delta Zeta.” Kowalski had no idea who the poster was, but she immediately identified the setting in one shot as Fort. In the video, the floor is dirty, with debris strewn everywhere. She’s lying on the ground naked, her eyes half-closed, touching herself while flanked by a group of men in shorts. While their faces weren’t visible, they appeared to be some of the same guys she’d been hanging out with just a few hours prior, she realized with a sinking feeling in her gut. In another shot, from a different night and at a different location, she is being penetrated by two men.
The video that ended up going viral on X was a compilation of three different clips: one, mentioned above, that was taken at Fort earlier that fall, and two that were recorded during a separate sexual encounter with two strangers. Kowalski says she met the latter in October, not long before the video went viral, when she was walking home after a night out drinking. She was heavily intoxicated and only remembers “parts of” what happened: “I didn’t recognize myself at all.” She says she did not consent to being filmed, let alone have that content shared publicly.
What had been a piece of salacious on-campus gossip, transmitted via anonymous social media and group texts, was now a national story. X removed the post containing the video, but late the following day, @SteveCumfull posted it again. Then they posted a screenshot of a cryptocurrency token they’d bought with Kowalski’s name on it, with a market cap of $11,400. “Put your children’s college savings into this,” they tweeted. @SteveCumfull could have been anyone: a close friend, a neighbor, a mutual with an axe to grind. Whoever they were, they now appeared to be profiting from the worst moment of Kowalski’s life.
Over the next 24 hours, Kowalski sat paralyzed on her couch as anonymous people on the internet endlessly harassed her; they posted her old photos, her dad’s LinkedIn, and even his golf handicap. They called and texted her parents all through the night, saying things like, “I gave your daughter drugs and fucked her”; one anonymous man told Kowalski’s father he’d had sex with her and had since tested positive for HIV while playing the call live on Spaces, X’s live chat feature. Another posted on X placing bets on whether, by the end of the coming week, she’d start an OnlyFans or kill herself.
Kowalski called her best friend, Lexie Blake, who was then a sophomore at the University of Mississippi. She “wasn’t even really saying words,” Blake recounts. “She was just sobbing, hysterical.” When Kowalski’s father showed up at her apartment, she was too humiliated to face him. She tried to jump out of her fifth-floor window.
By Monday afternoon, #Maddiekowalski was trending on X nationwide, with more than 1,200 posts using the hashtag. Content about her—much of it showing her incapacitated, naked, and engaging in sex acts—had been viewed more than 8.5 million times.
Kowalski had heard about this happening to other college girls before; one of them, a University of Mississippi (Ole Miss) student named Mary Kate Cornett, had been doxed in the same way nine months prior. These campaigns were the work of the burnerverse (or “beev,” or “BV”), a loosely connected network of anonymous “burner” accounts on X, mostly operated by students and alumni, with the primary purpose of discussing college sports.
But Kowalski was learning in real time that, outside of talking shit about athletes and posting photos of crushed red Solo cups, this faceless corner of the internet has another mission: destroying the lives of young women.
Kowalski is tall and slender, with blue eyes and natural red roots that peek out of her dyed hair, which is sometimes brown and sometimes blonde—her “Neapolitan thing.” Like most 20-year-olds, she’s effortlessly deadpan, gushing about the TV show Dance Moms and skewering Miami club culture (“nobody there has a job … and it’s like, I’m not willing to talk to old men for a Birkin.”)
But in many ways, she seems younger than 20 when I visit her family’s house, located in a Florida suburb where preternaturally tanned kids drive golf carts on the sidewalks. She sits on the couch next to her family’s 12-year-old dog Bailey, her knees drawn up to her chest under a pink Lilly Pulitzer blanket. Often, she deflects when the conversation veers toward what happened last November, scrolling through her phone or abruptly commenting on her false lashes, or her spray tan, or her dog’s farts.
“If I’m fidgeting or looking at my phone, it’s because this whole thing obviously makes me uncomfortable to talk about,” she says, speaking to a mainstream news outlet for the first time. “There’s a lot of emotions underneath the surface. But I am trying not to be upset.”
Her hesitation is understandable: The women targeted by the burnerverse were private citizens before their names, rumors, explicit images, or videos went viral. WIRED has identified 10 women who have been doxed by the burnerverse, most of whom were between the ages of 18 and 21. The virality follows a specific pattern: salacious gossip about a college girl’s sex life, or nude photos and videos of her, make their way to YikYak or Snapchat before being disseminated by burner accounts on public social media platforms. Sometimes, the content has even made national news, with aggregation websites like TheSportsGrail or Barstool Sports employees amplifying the victim’s humiliation.
Communities of burner accounts crop up around most large schools with prominent sports teams. Networks of a Big 10 university, like Michigan State or the University of Maryland, will have a slightly different flavor than that of an LSU or an Ole Miss, which are part of the Southeastern Conference. Kowalski’s video went viral within the SEC burnerverse before spreading nationally.
Like most online communities, the SEC burnerverse has its own vernacular, consisting of allusions to frat boy culture. The men’s designer Peter Millar, known for his preppy collared shirts and chinos, is often referenced; as are Zyn, various SEC football coaches, “bouse” and “touse” (shorthand for a “top” or “bottom”), and “bag” (cocaine). Some take advantage of their anonymity to post racist, homophobic, and antisemitic comments.
The ecosystem is sprawling and diverse. Many, if not most, sports burner accounts are fairly innocuous, congregating in X Spaces or group DMs to post memes about new recruits or competing teams. Some will even try to rein in the unrulier factions by denouncing them, arguing that they’re a poor representation of the team’s fandom, says Owen McCarthy, a recent graduate of Michigan State University who reported on MSU’s burnerverse. “To a certain extent there’s an awareness that it might behoove them to create a positive online environment” for the school, he says.
Like most online communities, burners adhere to a hierarchy, with some accounts amassing more clout based on their follower count or a particularly viral tweet. The men’s ages range widely. One burner fan account for an East Coast university team tells WIRED that in his group DM of around 200 people, there are members as young as 15 and as old as their mid-forties. There’s also some level of engagement between the burners and college athletics departments: Users often tag coaches or athletes to try to get their attention, and sometimes the more influential accounts will instruct people to “comment on potential recruits’ online stuff and tell them how great [the school] is,” the burner says.
There’s also evidence that some college sports athletics departments are aware of the burners and even maintain cordial, semi-symbiotic relationships with them, akin to the dynamic between a brand and an influencer account. According to McCarthy’s piece, one prominent MSU burner account alleged that the school invited burners to an event unveiling the football team’s new alternate uniforms. Athletics staffers would even send him photos of meetings with potential recruits: “It was like, ‘Wink, wink, nod, nod, if you want to post these pictures, feel free to do so,’” they said in the report. (A top official at MSU told McCarthy that this was not “part of athletic department strategies.”)
Many burners are run by school alumni or casual fans, but a non-negligible number of them are associated with fraternities, as evidenced by the photos of Greek events they post or the affiliation in their bios. Blake, who is involved in Greek life at Ole Miss, says it’s an open secret on campus that potential new members are strongly encouraged to create burner accounts in order to pledge. (Ole Miss did not respond to a request for comment.) These are “guys who would buy you a drink, who’d take you out on a date, who are your little brothers or your best friend or your boyfriend,” she says. “It could literally be anybody. It’s not mean or troubled guys doing it, or guys who need validation. It’s guys with wealthy families and support systems and college educations.”
For many of these accounts, the ultimate objective is going viral, through whatever means necessary. “They want to see something go viral that they created, and they say things like, ‘The burnerverse has made it big time,’” one person with a burner account, who asked not to be identified, tells WIRED. “They take pride in that in a twisted way. Getting their stuff on Barstool and ESPN is the goal.”
Sometimes, this involves scouring their school’s incoming students’ Instagrams and posting photos of young women for the purpose of mocking or humiliating them. But the most surefire way to go viral is to dox stereotypically attractive young women like Kowalski—even better if they’ve transgressed sexual norms in some way. There’s a sense that the health and vibrancy of the community is contingent on the sexual humiliation of women. “Feels like the beev is slowly dying,” one tweet from this past May reads. “We need another college girl to get exposed for a revival.” Another: “Feels like a national holiday every time a new whore gets exposed on the BV.”
The most well-known case is Mary Kate Cornett, a then 18-year-old University of Mississippi student who went viral in February 2025, after an X user with the handle @thekendallroy tweeted, “Anyone else hearing rumblings of this Ole Miss girl banging her boyfriend’s Dad?” The rumor was false, but @thekendallroy’s post exploded, racking up 313,000 views in just under two days. It didn’t take long for other burners to post her full name.
Prior to being doxed, Cornett tells WIRED she was largely unaware of the burnerverse. “It’s like they have this blueprint for what to do every time they decide to destroy a girl’s life,” she says. “That excites them, for some odd reason.” Cornett became a top trending topic on X, thanks to the story being boosted by former NFL player Antonio Brown and the prominent ESPN talking head Pat McAfee, a former Barstool personality. McAfee repeated the rumor on a special taping of his talk show—without naming Cornett, though he did name her sorority—and then posted that clip to his YouTube channel, which has nearly 3 million followers.
Four months after spreading the false rumor on his show, McAfee apologized and deleted a tweet featuring the clip of him talking about it; the video itself, however, is still up on his YouTube channel. (Neither Barstool nor McAfee responded to a request for comment, and ESPN declined.) But the damage had been done: Cornett was barraged by thousands of harassing texts, calls, and voicemails; a SWAT team was even sent to her mother’s house the day after McAfee’s show. She has spent the past year and a half working with lawyers and forensic experts to identify burner accounts. “There’s very little accountability,” says Cornett’s mother, Leslie. “You can lie online and do whatever you want. Then your life moves on, and [the girls’ lives] stop.”
The BV “whoreverse,” as some burner accounts call it, started to coalesce in June 2024, when an account named Arthur Cacciatore posted the name of an undergrad at a large Southern state school, who was falsely rumored to have slept “with like 35% of the SEC.” The girl’s name became a trending topic on X, with Barstool Sports writer Jack Mac amplifying it to his 146,000 followers; the post got 815,000 views. (Due to the traumatizing nature of the burnerverse’s campaigns against these women, WIRED is withholding their names and altering details to protect their anonymity, unless they’ve gone public with their experiences, like Cornett and Kowalski.)
From there, the burnerverse started systemically seeking out young, attractive college women to shame on a national stage. These women attend colleges across the country, ranging from the Big 10 to the Atlantic Coast Conference; some have had pornographic images and videos of them posted without their consent, while others have gone viral simply for unverifiable rumors about their sex lives. Whoever the victim, whatever the details of the campaign, the treatment is relentless, and unsparing.
The burnerverse efforts are often highly organized, says Adam Ludwin, Kowalski’s attorney, who specializes in cyberharassment. “When you look at some of these cases, things escalate so much more rapidly than the other types of cases that I’ve dealt with,” he says. “The volume of views and reposts and comments—it’s not the kind of thing that would happen in such a short time without some level of coordination.”
In Kowalski’s case, coordination appears to have taken place on X Spaces, the platform’s live audio-based conversation feature. One of the earliest X posts about her, for instance, features a screengrab from one such Space: “Kowalski Analysis” (a reference to a character from the 2014 film Penguins of Madagascar). Though no public recordings exist, a screengrab shows that at one point, more than 220 X users were participating in a discussion of Kowalski’s nonconsensual intimate images (NCII) under the veil of anonymity.
It doesn’t help that X, the burnerverse’s platform of choice, is famously subject to little moderation. Since Elon Musk acquired the social network in 2022, its algorithm has regularly boosted racist, misogynistic, and antisemitic content, making it the ideal petri dish for a coordinated harassment campaign. On X, it’s extremely easy for defamatory or outright illegal content, such as Kowalski’s NCII, to spread far and wide before someone can issue a complaint or file a takedown request. “The platforms tend to be pretty hands-off,” says Ludwin. “They’re also financially incentivized by followers, by views, by clicks … they’re making money off this.” (X did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)
Most burnerverse victims remain silent following their harassment, hoping for the uproar to blow over. The majority did not respond to requests for an interview, or declined to go on the record. They’ve spent thousands of dollars, if not hundreds of thousands, on legal fees, therapy, and reputation management firms. “We are unfortunately navigating something that I wouldn’t wish on my worst enemy,” one father of a victim tells me anonymously. “I just don’t think she’s ready at this time.”
Even months or years after they go viral, the victim’s NCII are still widely available on leaked amateur porn sites; their names, linked to graphic and defamatory rumors, are eminently googleable, their faces edited over those of dead presidents to make memes with names like “Mount Rushwhore.” Cornett says the burnerverse continues to post about her on a near-daily basis, taking screenshots of her Instagram posts and making memes. Now 20 and in her junior year, she’s still hounded whenever she goes out on campus, and she lives in fear of someone taking a photo of her and posting it online. “It’s a terrible feeling to never not feel like you’re being watched or observed or talked about,” she says. “I read every single post, every single comment, every hashtag. It consumes my whole life.”
Maddie Kowalski has always felt like an outsider. She was adopted at birth and her family moved around a lot; when she was 7, her father was diagnosed with stage-four cancer, which caused her to act out in school. “There was a lot going on at home, and I didn’t have a lot of friends,” she says. “I would play alone during recess. I was definitely a weird kid.”
At the start of middle school, Kowalski’s family relocated to an affluent Floridian suburb. She disliked it almost immediately: “All the kids are beach kids whose parents are old money,” she says. “And they think you’re poor if you don’t live in a $20 million house.”
After Covid, she became heavily involved with theater, appearing in her high school’s productions of Kiss Me, Kate and High School Musical. But she struggled to adjust socially. “She was definitely sheltered,” Blake says. “She didn’t drink or go out very much, and she’d get grounded if she had a drink. She was very straight-laced, and that was probably seen as a little weird or awkward at the time.”
Kowalski worshipped the cool older girls at her school with their “little Pinteresty Instagrams,” most of whom ended up in Greek life at UF. When it came time to apply to college, UF was one of her top choices. “I was like, ‘I wanna join a sorority and wear a cute blue and orange outfit.’”
Like most SEC schools, UF has a strong focus on Greek life: Frats and sororities are the hubs of campus culture, with approximately 21 percent of the 41,000 undergraduate student population rushing. Kowalski loathed rush: She hated traipsing from house to house in high heels, her makeup sweating off in the Florida humidity. But she didn’t want to be like the “weird” kids who hunkered down in their dorm rooms or the library all day. She accepted a bid from the sorority Delta Zeta, which has a reputation for being “proper,” one student tells me; it’s a stereotypical SEC sorority, where members attend tailgates in cowboy boots and flouncy minidresses.
At first, Kowalski’s college experience was typical. She majored in theater, worked part-time as a server and bottle girl, and volunteered at a camp for kids whose parents had cancer. But Blake says Kowalski had a “strong need to fit in” and seemingly wanted to prove she wasn’t still a sheltered theater kid. “I think it was probably a little intimidating for her to go to college with so many people who’d gone to our high school and already had a preconceived notion of her,” she says.
Kowalski became deeply immersed in the party scene, going out to bars every night and sometimes drinking heavily. The bar-hopping took a tremendous toll on her mental health; her grades started plummeting, prompting her to temporarily withdraw from classes in late October, shortly before the burnerverse targeted her. “I was so inebriated I had absolutely no idea what was going on. I barely remembered my own birthday,” she says. Of that particular period of her life: “I was making bad decisions. And I trusted the wrong people.”
For Kowalski, the weeks following the leak were hell. Students shouted slurs as she walked to class; one even threw an egg at her. Kowalski says many of her Delta Zeta sisters blocked or unfollowed her on social media. She alleges that the sorority held a chapter meeting where they discussed how the incident would reflect on the organization—rather than talking about her welfare. (Delta Zeta did not respond to a request for comment.)
“A lot of people were sad for what happened, because it shouldn’t have been filmed and posted,” one UF student tells me. “But there’s obviously people who are blaming her and saying she was doing these things for drugs or that she was crazy.”
Almost immediately after the video leaked, Kowalski reported the harassment to campus police. They assured her they would launch an investigation, then handed it off to the Gainesville Police Department. She says UF administrators also promised to launch an investigation into how the content spread. According to Kowalski, though, they told her that unless the police filed charges, the administration couldn’t take any action against students.
A Title IX investigation was dropped after about a month because, she says UF told her, the video had technically been filmed off campus. UF assistant director of public affairs Blake Trauschke declined to comment on the Title IX investigation, except to say, “UF is committed to creating a sense of belonging and safety by fostering an environment that is safe, secure, and free from all forms of harassment.”
The Kowalskis say they have spent tens of thousands on reputation management and legal fees, hiring a lawyer almost immediately after the video was posted as well as a company to help scrub the illegal content from the internet. Kowalski’s mother, Mandy, says it was surprisingly difficult to find a lawyer to take on the case. “I think people assumed it was just a simple revenge porn case,” she says. “They didn’t understand the scope of it.” Over and over, she says, the family was told that going after the men behind the video’s spread would cost more time and money than it was worth.
There were also multiple accusations at hand, making it hard to focus. Should the family go after the men who had sex with a clearly intoxicated woman? Whoever shot the video? The people who’d shared it in private group chats? Or the burner accounts who made Kowalski’s humiliation a national news story? Real harm had been done to Kowalski, and her family, but identifying who was most culpable was nearly impossible.
Kowalski wasn’t thinking about legal ramifications at the time. To her, the implied message—from the burners, some school administrators, her sorority sisters—was clear: What happened to her was her problem, and her problem alone. The harassing phone calls to her parents, the on-campus bullying, the fact that she had been filmed having sex without her consent in the first place: No one was going to face the consequences but her.
“Nobody fucking cares,” she says, summarizing the past 10 months. “You can do literally whatever you want [even] if it’s illegal, except for literally kill someone. No one gives a fuck.”
By last December, Kowalski had officially withdrawn from the semester’s classes at the University of Florida and moved back in with her parents. Soon after, her hair started falling out. Mysterious rashes showed up all over her face. She started doing intensive outpatient therapy and was eventually diagnosed with PTSD. “There’s only so much therapy can help,” she says. “Maybe it will, long-term. But not now.”
Nonetheless, Kowalski felt compelled to say something, against the advice of some in her family, who worried that a public statement would reinvigorate the harassment. “I just didn’t think it was fair,” she tells me. “Everyone else was making videos about me, and I couldn’t make one or say anything for myself.”
On December 19, she tied her newly dyed blonde hair back into a ponytail, took a deep breath, and decided to introduce herself on Instagram: “Hi, my name is Maddie Kowalski, and you may or may not know me personally, but you may have heard a little bit about me over the past month,” she said, staring directly into the camera.
Wearing a simple gray tee, small hoops, and a gold-plated bow-tie necklace, Kowalski explained what happened, how “several videos from two nights that I could barely remember had been posted on the internet for everyone to see.” She described in detail how she had not consented to the acts in the video, nor to them being filmed; how she and her parents had been relentlessly harassed; how she, in the span of just a few weeks, had felt her “whole world collapse.”
“These last few weeks have been the darkest and hardest moments of my life,” she said in the video, before directing fellow victims of NCII toward a website for legal resources. “But I’m still here, and that’s something that I’m really learning to be proud of.”
The video got tens of millions of views, as well as many positive comments from people expressing support and applauding Maddie for her courage. But her parents’ fears were also well founded: For every encouraging comment, there was one from a burner making crude jokes or propositioning her for sex. The backlash surprised Kowalski. “I’d said everything I wanted to say, and I thought I said it in a way that was appropriate,” she says. “But I still got so much hate.”
Who would want to ruin my life?
It was the main question Kowalski asked herself as she began to process what had happened to her. She had a vague understanding of how the video had circulated on campus among group texts and fraternity DMs. But she didn’t know who @SteveCumfull was, how they got the video, or why they would have publicly posted it on X.
Working with Ludwin, her attorney, Kowalski decided not to pursue charges against the men in the video. Relitigating the events would be retraumatizing. Instead, they wanted to identify the burners. The Gainesville police would eventually file a legal request to X for the subscriber information, IP records, and account information of not just @SteveCumfull but also a few other accounts that were early sharers of the video. (A representative for the Gainesville Police Department declined to comment, saying the case was still “open and active.”) For the burners, “there is a false sense of security when it comes to anonymity,” Ludwin tells me. “And one thing I want to do is reassure victims that just because [the burners] are hidden doesn’t mean we can’t find them.”
Kowalski had assumed that the burner accounts sharing her video were UF students—people she knew personally. From what she learned through police charging documents, she was half right. According to affidavits obtained by WIRED, the @SteveCumfull account was allegedly linked to a 19-year-old named Kamran Ahmed, a first-year UF student from Tampa who was a member of Theta Chi. Kowalski says she had never met Ahmed and had no idea who he was.
Per the police affidavits, the same went for another burner that had been among the first to post the video on X:
@arnie_grape16 was linked to UF freshman Brendan Pitfield, a former star high school soccer player from Atlanta and fellow Theta Chi. Police also identified a third person behind a burner: Jacob Gomberg, a junior from nearby Coral Springs. Gomberg was a relief pitcher for the UF Gators, a Division I baseball team, before transferring to UNLV and later Indiana University. Kowalski didn’t know them either.
It’s not clear how these men allegedly obtained the sexually explicit content, but there is evidence to suggest that two may have known each other. Kowalski’s father, who has been tirelessly collecting evidence, shares a screenshot of an interaction between two Instagram accounts that appear to be linked to both Pitfield and Ahmed, respectively. One commented “SC” (which Kowalski believes is short for Steve Cumfull”) on a November 3 post by the other. (In early September, Ahmed’s Instagram was briefly deleted; it has since been reinstated but is private.) Kowalski says she saw both Pitfield and Ahmed at a bar in the spring. Ahmed looked at her and laughed, Kowalski says, while Pitfield approached her and said: I’m a huge fan, can I get a picture with you?
In December, Kowalski emailed UF’s Office of Sorority and Fraternity Life to make sure they were aware that she was a victim in an ongoing criminal investigation and that it allegedly involved fraternity members. Their response referred her to the Office of Student Conduct, saying it did not “oversee the organizational or individual conduct processes” regarding fraternity members. The Offices of Student Conduct and Sorority and Fraternity Life did not respond to requests for comment.
Kowalski says most of the people involved in the video are still on campus. The spokesperson for Phi Delta Theta could not confirm if this includes any of its members, saying that due to university confidentiality policies surrounding Title IX investigations, it had “not been made aware of the names of any individuals ever affiliated with our organization who are accused of these heinous acts.”
Around the time that Kowalski’s video went viral, Phi Delta Theta was suspended until at least 2030 following the culmination of the hazing investigation. The UF chapter is being reconstituted with a new advisory board and will continue to operate independently of the university. According to one UF student, a huge sign in front of Fort reads “Rush Phi Delt.” On August 13, the frat posted on Instagram to promote Fall 2026 rush: “We’re back.”
When I first began talking to Kowalski in June 2026, she told me the Gainesville police investigation into the burnerverse accounts was on hiatus, as the officer assigned to the case was on leave. She had amassed theories about the identities behind @SteveCumfull and some of the other burners, but no charges had been filed. As such, Kowalski could not publicly comment on the status of the investigation.
“The people who did this to her are living a normal college life—they’re going out and posting and doing whatever they want,” Mandy tells me. “She’s having a really hard time with the idea that they are able to live their lives with no repercussions, while she’s judged for literally everything she does.”
In early August, however, I received a text from Kowalski: After nine months, the Gainesville police had charged Gomberg, Ahmed, and Pitfield with sexual cyber-harassment, a first-degree misdemeanor punishable by up to one year in prison and a $1,000 fine. Additionally, Ahmed has been charged with a third-degree felony: sexually cyber-harassing for financial gain. Per a sworn complaint from the Gainesville Police Department, Ahmed and Pitfield used university IP addresses to access their burner accounts—an allegation that was maddening to Kowalski, as UF had told her they dropped the Title IX investigation because the video was shot off campus.
Kowalski has also brought civil lawsuits in the Northern District of Florida against all three men, alleging sexual cyber-harassment and asking for financial damages.
According to LinkedIn, as of September 3, both Ahmed and Pitfield were still students at the University of Florida. When asked whether they were in good standing despite the charges against them, Trauschke, the assistant director of public affairs for the University of Florida, declined to comment. “Any details regarding a student’s complaint or a student’s disciplinary process or record is protected information under the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA),” she wrote.
Both Gomberg and Ahmed declined to comment through an attorney. Pitfield did not respond to repeated requests, but he filed a plea of not guilty to the misdemeanor charge last week. The LinkedIns of both Ahmed and Pitfield were deleted or edited after being contacted by WIRED. Before their accounts were altered, they listed themselves as current members of Theta Chi. And according to the Gainesville PD’s sworn complaint, as of last summer, Ahmed’s address was listed as that of the Theta Chi fraternity house.
When reached for comment, Theta Chi CEO Michael Mayer told WIRED that “the allegations made within the complaints describe abhorrent actions that run completely contrary to Theta Chi’s ideals,” referring to the charges as “reprehensible.” He added that Ahmed and Pitfield had been placed on “interim suspension” pending the results of an internal investigation.
Still, Kowalski says she’s terrified of seeing Ahmed and Pitfield on campus now that she’s back in Gainesville. “My parents are worried I’m just going to stay in my room all day and not leave,” she says. “But I like to be alone. I like lying down with a face mask on with the lights off, in my own space with the blinds closed. A lot of times in public, people come up to me, and it doesn’t really feel safe.”
But Kowalski is determined to make it work at UF and find a way to move on. She has “an ability to be sunshine in a room of thunderstorms and clouds and shitty people,” Blake says. “And every single person that said something, DM’d something, emailed something, participated in the video, shared the video, talked about the video, watched the video—every single one of them took advantage of her kindness and her ability to forgive.”
In the weeks leading up to her return to school, Kowalski mostly slept or scrolled on TikTok, posting the occasional video of herself unboxing Squishy Dumplings or belting “Total Eclipse of the Heart” in a friend’s car; she trained her new puppy, a mini goldendoodle named Rosie. She doesn’t have a job, because she quit her part-time gig as a bottle girl and server after the burnerverse harassed her employer. “It’s hard enough for my friends who don’t have this on their record to get a job,” she says. “None of them can get hired at all right now. So how am I supposed to get one?”
Her primary source of income is TikTok Live, where she “battles”—essentially, competes for tips—with creators, including livestreams with Clavicular. (They have mutual acquaintances, but she says she only started hanging out with him because she had a crush on his cameraman.) She has around 42,000 followers. Prior to getting doxed, Kowalski harbored ambitions of moving to New York or LA to become an actor; she fantasized about graduating and landing a role on a show, or even winning an Oscar. “It would be cool if I had 2,000 followers as a result of doing TikTok dances or something like that,” she says. “But being known for this? This is not fun.”
She recently took a trip to Dublin with her family, and then went to London to celebrate her friend Blake’s birthday. While there, she saw Moulin Rouge and posted cute TikToks dancing in front of the Saltburn mansion. In London, Blake says she and Kowalski went to dinner at a restaurant with panoramic views of the city, and someone even recognized her there, interrupting them to take a photo. Another night, they met a cute guy at a bar who asked for her number and social media handle. She just gave him her first name, terrified he’d find out who she was and leak it.
“She has so much trauma that she can’t even have these normal experiences,” Blake says. “She can’t meet someone and not have her guard up.” Kowalski is plagued with panic attacks, and worries that she’s never going to have a partner or a family or a semblance of a normal existence. The burners “stole her life,” Blake says. “They stole her girlhood.”
VIII
In March, another girl was doxed by the burnerverse. We’ll call her Addison King. Like Kowalski, King was a student at a large university with a Division 1 football team; her name and identity went viral on X after a video purportedly showing her having sex in a bar bathroom started circulating.
The moment the video hit X, the burner accounts swung into action, reposting it, unearthing her old Instagram posts, commenting on her body, spreading rumors that she had cheated on a boyfriend back home. Kowalski saw it on X at 4 am. Her guts roiled as she lay in bed, scrolling through tweet after tweet. She found King’s Instagram and, even though it was private, DM’d her offering support. King DM’d her back, giving thanks.
Kowalski knew from her own experience what would come next: The men who’d doxed her had taken a victory lap on X Spaces, and she suspected they were doing the same thing to King. She logged on to X, joining an X Space where members of the burnerverse were plotting further ways to embarrass the young woman.
The 19-year-old sat in bed with her phone, listening to the disembodied voices casually discussing frat gossip and the Texas Rangers. “I was like, seriously? Get a life,” she says. Then the burners moved on to King. “Tell that bitch to hang from a tree,” one of them said. “Hang and dangle!”
Irate, Kowalski left the Space and turned on her camera—no makeup, her hair unbrushed. “This network of men that posted me … are doing this to more girls, just as they did to girls before me,” she says in the clip posted in late March, which now has over 271,000 likes. “And nobody seems to care.” Her fury at the people and institutions that had failed her—social media platforms, “old-ass men up at 4 in the morning talking about women’s bodies” on the internet—unfurled in torrents. “Genuinely this could happen to anyone,” she concluded. “And it’s gonna continue to happen … [unless] we stop it.”
As expected, burners descended on Kowalski’s comments section, salivating at the opportunity to continue their harassment campaign. “Bro where is the videoo [sic],” one said. “Everytime i see u speak i am always reminded of that one glorious day,” commented another.
But she was also flooded with thousands of comments of support; the burners’ insults were pushed down to the bottom of the pile, becoming a small minority. “Sometimes life takes an unexpected turn, and you find yourself with a voice you didn’t know you had,” wrote a supporter. “You have a chance [to] push for change and I’m so proud of you for taking it.” People told her they cared, that it was not her fault, that she should stay strong. The empathy from strangers wouldn’t make everything OK again; not yet, at least. But it would be a reminder that just as the burnerverse would keep going, so would she.

In late July, one of the world’s most famous mathematicians issued a warning to his field. Math is entering a “turbulent period,” the UCLA professor Terence Tao said in front of a packed lecture hall at the International Congress of Mathematicians. AI is getting so good at math, he said, that it’s causing a “crisis in our mathematical values and practices.”
Earlier in the same week that Tao gave his talk at math’s most prestigious conference, a researcher at Anthropic had used Claude to disprove an 87-year-old math conjecture. Still, when I asked mathematicians at the conference about their experiences with AI, most hadn’t thought deeply about the topic. Many seemed a little surprised that a journalist was asking them about it at all.
Now mathematicians are paying attention. Last week, OpenAI announced that its bots had cracked the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems regarded as among the grandest challenges in the field. Navier-Stokes has stumped mathematicians since the 1930s: “It’s a career-killing problem—you can spend all your career doing it and never get the solution,” David Dritschel, a mathematician at the University of St. Andrews, told me. OpenAI said its swarm of 10,000 AI agents solved the problem in less than four days.
In the math world, the initial shock over OpenAI’s result has morphed into something of an existential reckoning for the discipline. Although OpenAI was able to solve the Navier-Stokes problem only by pulling from nearly a century’s worth of human efforts, academics are realizing just how much power the AI industry now has over math. “We’re seeing how swiftly an entire field can be ravaged by AI,” Max Weinreich, a math professor at CUNY Baruch, told me.
OpenAI’s breakthrough is as notable as how it was achieved. The night before OpenAI announced its solution, the NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster released a statement alleging that he had been scooped by OpenAI. With the heavy assistance of AI tools, Buckmaster and his collaborator, Levent Alpöge (who works at Anthropic), had made major progress toward solving the Navier-Stokes problem. Buckmaster implied that OpenAI might have copied their approach by accessing his messages with OpenAI’s agents. “Almost nobody else I know of was working on it,” he wrote.
In an announcement the next day, OpenAI said that it had tasked its AI systems to work on all of the Millennium Problems after hearing rumors that Anthropic had solved two of them. OpenAI claims that it focused on the Navier-Stokes problem only after finding promising partial results, and that it never looked at Buckmaster’s inputs. In any case, OpenAI poured incredible resources into solving this problem—expending millions of dollars in tokens—all because it heard an unfounded rumor of a solution. (OpenAI declined to comment.)
This drama has underlined concerns many mathematicians have about AI developments within the field. AI companies are encouraged to solve problems in a way that generates good headlines for their bots—marshaling resources that academics never could—but those solutions won’t necessarily aid further discoveries or help humans understand mathematics. On Friday, 25 winners of the Fields Medal (sometimes called the Nobel Prize of mathematics) released a statement called “A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics.” “The push by AI companies to solve mathematical problems as a benchmark is detrimental to the science of mathematics, and to the mathematical community,” they wrote.
All of this can seem obtuse. Isn’t the point of mathematics to solve problems? But there’s more to a problem than just knowing whether it’s true. Solving a major problem in pure mathematics is often like getting a man on the moon: symbolically meaningful but with little direct value. Even though the Navier-Stokes problem deals with one of the most important models in fluid dynamics—a topic of great interest to airplane designers, climate modelers, and many other scientists—knowing the actual result is basically useless.
However, with both a math problem and the moon landing, the process of reaching that goal can indirectly develop all sorts of useful tools applicable to other problems. As part of the Apollo missions, NASA engineers and contractors had to solve subproblems that ultimately proved useful elsewhere. The need for an onboard computer, for example, helped spark the nascent computer-chip industry. Perhaps more surprising, to ensure that astronauts did not get sick while in space, the Apollo program helped set food-safety standards that have since become standard in the industry.
Mathematicians hope that OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes proof will end up containing ideas that make it easier to study all sorts of other problems, inside and outside of pure mathematics. This has happened before. For instance, efforts to prove Fermat’s Last Theorem produced mathematical tools that now underpin the newest online encryption methods.
It’s still too early to tell what humans might be able to learn from OpenAI’s proof. The paper is 166 pages and “almost incomprehensible,” Dritschel said. Yet over the coming months and years, mathematicians will exert substantial effort to dissect and distill OpenAI’s proof until its central ideas are understood enough to (hopefully) be applied elsewhere.
Humans won’t be able to do that for most AI-generated math results, however. Already, there are AI proofs that no human understands, not because the ideas are impossible to grasp, but because no one has had the time to look through the solution carefully. It’s easy to imagine a future in which mathematicians use AI to prove ever more impressive results ever more quickly—but they don’t understand what they’re proving in much detail. AI systems can speed the rate of problem-solving, but they can’t make it that much easier for human mathematicians to grasp a proof.
So if the field as we know it is to survive, mathematicians need to figure out how to adapt. One idea is to give less credit for solving a problem and more credit for work that communicates the ideas behind a solution in a way that can benefit the broader mathematical community. Yet it’s hard to say exactly how that works in practice. Unlike solving problems, evaluating how well a mathematician has communicated with their peers has no clear metrics.
It will take time for mathematicians to figure out the best response. All the while, AI is continuing to develop incredibly quickly. In less than the time that it takes to complete a Ph.D., systems such as ChatGPT have gone from struggling with basic arithmetic to solving some of the most famous problems in the world. Math’s turbulent period, as Tao deemed it, isn’t ending anytime soon.

Cop used his foot to nudge man lying in street before driving off and leaving him to be hit by another car
The Philadelphia police officer who failed to help before the fatal hit-and-run will be fired, officials said
A Philadelphia police officer used his foot to nudge a man lying in the street — and then left him there and drove off — just before a car fatally hit the man.
Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel said Monday that the officer has been suspended for 30 days, and that they plan to fire him after, WPVI reported.
“All of us, whether you’re a Philadelphia police officer, or you can be an officer on the other side of the country, have a duty to follow an officer’s code of ethics,” Bethel said.
“In those ethics, we specifically describe, ‘My fundamental duty is to serve the community and safeguard the lives and property.’ He did not do that on that day and as a result of that, he has been given 30 days to dismissal from the police department.”
Authorities have not named the officer, but said he has been with the department for two years.
The officer approached Eugene Beauford, 48, around 1:40 a.m. of August 27, driving up alongside him as he walked unsteadily along the bike lane of a road. Video showed Bueaford staggering along the road.
As the two talked, Beauford fell, prompting the officer to exit his vehicle.
Video obtained by NBC 10 showed the officer coming up to the prone Beauford and standing over him. The officer then used his foot to nudge the man. The cop returned to his vehicle and drove away from Beauford, who remained on the ground.
Another person later walked over and spoke with Beauford, who was lying between the street and bike lane. That bystander eventually walked away, as Beauford was still on the ground.
Less than five minutes later, a green Kia entered the bike lane to pass another vehicle and hit Beauford, the video showed. The car quickly drove off.
Both the initial bystander and another person later moved Beauford to the curb and called 911. Emergency responders — including the cop who initially approached Beauford — arrived at the scene.
That same officer failed to provide Beauford with aid once again. Authorities also said he failed to file a police report after the horrifying incident.
Beauford was taken to a nearby hospital, where he later died. Police officials said they only learned of the fatality after the department was contacted by the medical examiner’s office.
“We live by a code of ethics, and we have to be driven by that each and every day if we want to do this job properly,” Bethel said. “I felt disgusted.”
The green Kia involved in the hit-and-run and its driver have been located, authorities said. No arrest or charges have been announced.

Pro Ref chief Howard Webb admits VAR had 'tunnel vision' on Erling Haaland leading to Enzo Fernandez error
Pro Ref chief Howard Webb says VAR had tunnel vision on Erling Haaland which led to them missing Enzo Fernandez's offside in the Manchester derby; Haaland's goal was given offside but VAR overturned the decision, despite Fernandez interfering with play from an offside position
Tuesday 15 September 2026 17:04, UK
Pro Ref chief Howard Webb says VAR missed Enzo Fernandez being offside for Erling Haaland's winning goal in the Manchester derby due to "tunnel vision".
Webb says he is "really disappointed" by the decision to award the goal, which was initially ruled out on the field due to Haaland being flagged offside.
VAR then checked the incident and determined the striker was onside but failed to account for Enzo Fernandez impacting play from an offside position.
Fernandez dived for the ball before it was steered home by Haaland, and despite severely hindering Lisandro Martinez and Senne Lammens, Fernandez's offside position was overlooked once the VAR officials had confirmed he had not touched the ball - even though a player can be offside without touching the ball.

Webb: VAR had 'tunnel vision' on Haaland and missed Enzo offside
Pro Ref chief operating officer Howard Webb:
"We felt it was important that we acknowledged an error in the situation. We know that Erling Haaland was penalised for offside and wasn't in an offside position.
"We also know that Enzo Fernandez, who was in an offside position, almost certainly interfered with the Manchester United defence and probably the goalkeeper.

In this case, let’s create a to-do list app because that is a very good starting point, even for beginners. Remember to select “app” as an option while creating, because Google Stitch supports both app and website designs.
Step 2: Now, enter a prompt to generate the UI of the app. Then tap on Enter
Step 3: Now wait until Google Stitch provides a full UI design of the app.
Step 4: You can tap on any element or use AI to describe the changes you want, or you can just use the built-in basic tools to edit sections, text, and much more.
Step 5: If you dont like the design, you can click on the plus icon and tap on upload files, and then you can upload the reference files.
Step 6: To preview how the app works, you can tap on the prototype option to preview how the full app works
Step 7: And once you have the design, tap on Export, and you can export directly to Google Antigravity or save it as a ZIP file.
I recommend downloading it as a ZIP file because sharing to Google Antigravity doesn’t work in most cases.
Step 3: Open Google Antigravity
Now open Antigravity and set it up as a CLI. You can also use it as an agent for UI; Antigravity supports both, but I prefer the CLI experience. Now tap on Open Folder and create a new app, or you can select an existing folder. For those who are unaware, all app files will be stored in this folder.
Now open the CLI, and on the right, you can see the chat interface. Now, in the chat, you can tap on the model’s name and select Google 3.8 Flash High. For your information, Google 3.8 Flash is better than the Pro series. It is the latest model and very good at AI generation, especially if you have reference images.
Step 4: Add your UI reference images
Now, click on the plus icon and attach the images. You can attach up to five images at a time.
Now enter this prompt to ask Google Antigravity to create an app.
Please build an Expo React Native app in TypeScript based on the attached UI designs.
Requirements:
Replicate the layout, typography, colors, and components from the attached screenshots as closely as possible.
Use standard Expo packages (@expo/vector-icons, @react-native-async-storage/async-storage, expo-linear-gradient, react-native-safe-area-context).
Implement full client-side state with local persistence using AsyncStorage so added tasks and items persist across app reloads.
Keep the code modular with clean components in a src/ folder.
Ensure there are zero TypeScript compile errors.
Step 5: Create the app using Gemini
Once you are done, wait for some time until Google Gemini 3.8 Flash creates an app.
Since it runs on Expo, you can preview the build on your Android phone. Simply enter this prompt, and it will generate your QR code in the terminal. If you want to make any changes, you can ask Google Gemini to do that for you.
Step 6: Preview the app on your Android phone
Now, open your Android phone and install the Expo app. Open the Expo app on your Android phone and tap on “Scan QR code,” and the app will be installed on your device. Now you can preview all the changes that you have made.
If you want to make any changes, you can enter the prompt with the required changes. Maybe also include better UI references to help the Google Gemini model understand better. In my experience, Google models hallucinate a lot. Once everything is finished and you are happy with the output.
Step 7: Create an Expo account
Now, before that, you need to go to Expo.io and create a free account. If you have already created one, you can just sign in. Now, Expo EAS will use your Expo account to create the build.
Now, once the account is created, there are two ways to connect Expo Go with your Google Antigravity. First is using a local authentication session, which is stored in your home folder. You can run login in Terminal at any time to connect.
To do that, open Terminal in Antigravity and then run this command
Command: npx eas-cli login
Now enter the username and password you created for your Expo account. Google Antigravity will remember these credentials for all future builds. So this is a one-time process; you don’t need to do this for every new app build.
If you don’t want to submit your credentials, you can create an Expo access token (perhaps for one-time use, or if you are sharing with a friend). You don’t need this if you are using it personally on your device.
However, if you want to connect your Expo account through an access token:
- Go to expo.dev/settings/access-tokens.
- Create a token, name it “Antigravity”, and generate the new token.
- Open the terminal and run this command:
Commad: export EXPO_TOKEN="your_copied_token_here"
Step 8: Build the Android app
You can simply enter the prompt and wait for some time until Google Antigravity starts an Expo build in the Expo build app. Once it finishes, it will give you a direct download link for the app.
Prompt:
Since you are using a free version, Expo offers some free rate limits, and then later it uses buffer time to build the app, which averages between 1 and 7 hours, depending on the traffic. If you are lucky enough, the app should be ready in less than 5 minutes. Once it’s ready, Google Antigravity will offer a direct download link.
Step 9: Download the app
You can copy the download link and paste it into any app on your Android, tap on it, and install the app. Alternatively, you can just download the app on your PC and share it to your Android.
Once the build process is completed. you can see the app download link. You can directly share the download link to an Android device.
Step 10: Scan the app before installing
Even though the app is built by you, I highly recommend scanning it before installing it on your Android phone. You can use any free online scanners to scan the app and confirm there are no security issues or malware within your app. Once you are done, you can install the app.
Step 11: Install the app on your Android phone
If this is your first time installing a third-party app, Google Chrome will block the app download from unknown sources. When prompted, you can enable unknown sources; once enabled, you can use the package installer to install the app on your Android phone.
Connect your Android app to Supabase (Optional)
Now that the basic Android phone app has been set up and will successfully run on your device, if you want to back up data in the cloud, you can connect it to Supabase.
Supabase is a free database hoster that lets you host small files in the cloud so that your app can use this data, allowing you to use the same app on other devices with sync enabled.
Step 12: Enable Supabase Integration
To connect it to Supabase: Go back to Google Antigravity and enable Supabase MCP. Next, open this URL and create a new account in Supabase. Now, in Supabase, create a new project. Example: my-to-do-app.
Once a project is created, go to your project settings and then API, and copy the following details:
- Project URL – You can go to Project Settings > General
- Publishable key (Go to Supabase project settings > API and find the key here: Publishable key
Step 13: Connect the app to Supabase
And now, once you have connected your Supabase account to Google Antigravity, open Google Antigravity and enter the following prompt: Next, ask Google Antigravity to create a new Supabase database to use for storing the data.
Prompt:
“I want to sync this app’s data with Supabase.
Here are my Supabase project details:
Supabase URL: https://your-project-id.supabase.co
Supabase Anon Key: your-anon-key-here
Please do the following:
Install @supabase/supabase-js.
Create a Supabase client configuration file in src/services/supabase.ts.
Provide the SQL table definition script I need to run in the Supabase SQL Editor for our tasks and projects.
Update our data context so that it fetches from and syncs with Supabase when online, while falling back gracefully to offline local storage.
Now wait for some time until your app is connected to the Supabase free plan. Once done, your application successfully uses and stores data in the cloud, and it fetches it to your app in real time.
Step 14: Test the Expo build again
To confirm again, you can ask Google Antigravity to use this prompt to access the Expo build on your Android device, so that you can check everything. And once you’re done, you need to rebuild the app.
Step 15: Rebuild the app
Enter this prompt, and Google 3.8 Flash will start the build on Expo Application Services (EAS). Wait for some time until it provides a direct app download link. Once it does, you can download it on your PC and share the app directly to your Android, or share the link directly to your Android.
This time, you will see an update prompt instead of an install prompt, since you have already installed the app on your Android phone.
That’s it. On a high level, this is how easily you can create an Expo Android app on your Android phone using Google Gemini. Except for getting access to the Google Gemini models, every other process is free to use.
Since you are using Expo, in the future, if you want to build an iOS version from the same app, you can just open Google Antigravity and start the iOS app build. In the future, we will learn a detailed way to create iOS apps for Siri.
But for now, I hope you find this guide helpful. If you are facing any issues while installing the app, you can comment below, and I am happy to help you.

Why cash continues to thrive even as India's digital payments grow
- Published
Every year, more Indians tap, scan and swipe. Every year they also hoard more paper.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) - the country's central bank - now has 176 billion banknotes in circulation. It's printing 28-30 billion fresh ones across six denominations annually and retiring roughly 21 billion. It is a vast logistics operation.
And yet, as Unified Payments Interface (UPI) digital transactions surge towards a billion a day, cash sloshing around the economy keeps climbing at a brisk pace.
"Currency in circulation continues to grow at double-digit rates even as cash's share of individual transactions declines, thanks to growing digital payment adoption. That combination makes future demand harder to predict, which complicates our planning for production and distribution capacity," Shirish Chandra Murmu, RBI deputy governor, said in a speech to central bankers in Jakarta last month.
He called it the "cash paradox". But what exactly do we mean by currency in circulation?
It is the total value of physical banknotes and coins held by the public and businesses, whether spent or simply held. In India, cash reaches them through four main channels: the RBI's 19 regional offices; bank branches; more than 250,000 ATMs and cash dispensers; and millions of "business correspondents", local agents who provide basic banking services in rural areas and smaller towns.
That is a huge stock of cash by any measure. For context, about 56 billion US dollar bills and 30 billion euro banknotes were in circulation at the end of last year, according to Murmu.
The comparison comes with a caveat: the RBI's count is partly driven by a higher share of lower-value notes, meaning more notes are needed to handle the same value of transactions.
The puzzle is not that Indians still use cash - 94% of transactions were cash-based as recently as 2019, according to new research, external by Anirudh Tagat, Mehmet Ozmen and Pushpa Trivedi. It is that cash is growing even as its share of everyday payments shrinks.
"The cash paradox has been examined globally, and India is a unique and novel case study of the same given the scale of both cash and non-cash payments," Tagat, an economist who studies Indian payment behaviour, told the BBC.
He notes that the phenomenon of cash growing alongside digital payments has been especially prominent since the 2007-08 global financial crisis, with Bank for International Settlements research showing a similar pattern worldwide.
In Tagat's framing, currency still serves three purposes - as a means of payment, a store of value and a hedge against calamity. Apps are replacing only the first. That helps explain why digital payments alone cannot tell the whole story of cash demand.
David Humphrey of Florida State University, who has studied cash use across 14 economies with co-author Tanai Khiaonarong, says digital payment adoption is just one of several factors that can influence how much cash people hold.
That raises another question: are households holding more cash outside the banking system - for emergencies, safekeeping or to buy assets such as gold in India?
He also points to a factor that is especially important for major reserve currencies: a lot of the growth comes from notes held or used abroad, rather than in the country that issued them.
The US is a case in point: large-denomination $50 and $100 notes are widely held and used overseas but are "rarely seen in normal domestic legal cash transactions", Humphrey says.
He add that the Federal Reserve regularly receives unfit US currency from abroad, replaces it with fit notes and returns them to the sender. Most of the value of these unfit notes is in $50 and $100 bills.
This helps explain, he says, why the Fed reports that the total value of US currency in circulation continues to rise even as the value of cash withdrawn from domestic ATMs - a proxy for everyday spending, mostly in $20 notes, along with $5 and $10 bills - has recently fallen.
Then there is the less visible side of the cash economy. Humphrey's research identifies the rising value of domestic illegal activity, which often relies on unrecorded cash transactions, as one structural reason currency growth can outpace recorded spending - a factor particularly relevant to India.
Property deals in India routinely involve cash payments, partly because stamp duty and government-set "circle rates" can lag market prices, giving buyers and sellers an incentive to under-declare the transaction and settle the difference in cash.
Demonetisation, which overnight invalidated 86% of the country's cash by value in 2016, attacked the stock of "black" cash but left this flow largely untouched, say economists. That helps explain why decades of estimates of "black money" sunk into real estate have never produced a reliable figure.
Then there is what might be called the psychology of frictionlessness. Tagat points to research, including work published recently in the Journal of Consumer Research, showing digital payments are increasingly engineered to strip out the "pain" of paying - the wince of handing over notes - and replace it with a satisfying beep.
That should, in theory, hollow out cash demand further. That it has not suggests something else is propping currency up: fear - not just the fear of spending, but the fear of what happens when digital systems fail.
Here the Indian story rhymes with Europe's.
The European Central Bank (ECB) has watched euro banknotes in circulation rise from about €1 trillion in 2016 to €1.6 trillion, external this year, even as cash's share of point-of-sale transactions has fallen towards half.
Philip Lane, the ECB's chief economist, told a summer conference in Ireland this year that while the number of notes used in transactions is falling, the stock held by households keeps growing - something identical to what Murmu alluded to in Jakarta.
Olive McCarthy, a professor at University College Cork, traces this to the ECB's own 2021 research, external on what it dubbed the "paradox of banknotes", driven by households hoarding cash as savings and by demand for euros outside the currency zone itself.
Governments in Austria, Finland, external, Germany, external, Sweden, external and the Netherlands, external have responded by formally advising citizens to keep a minimum amount of cash at home, insurance against blackouts, cyberattacks or war. Clearly, cash, in rich democracies as much as in India, is being repositioned as critical infrastructure for bad days rather than good ones.
McCarthy lists who depends on it most bluntly: the elderly, the rural poor, domestic-violence victims hiding transactions from an abuser, and children learning what money is. "Some consumers," she told me, "prefer the privacy and convenience of cash."
For India's RBI, this creates an awkward budgeting problem.
It runs its own paper mills, four currency printing presses and ink plants - an entire supply chain built for self-reliance - while promoting the world's most successful instant-payments network.
Tagat says this creates a difficult choice for the RBI: how much to invest in managing cash and how much in promoting digital payments, especially as trials of 10 and 20 rupee polymer notes - first proposed a decade ago - finally get under way. (Polymer notes are more durable than paper ones, potentially reducing the cost and frequency of replacing worn-out cash.)
Murmu framed reliable cash as part of "monetary sovereignty". Tagat says the rupee's informal use across South Asia gives India another reason to keep its currency machinery running, as a shock-absorber for the whole region.
"The RBI," Tagat says, "has a strong case for keeping cash going despite new digital payments alternatives."
If UPI, as reported, starts attracting transaction charges on smaller payments, cash may claw back share even in the payments column, not just the savings one, he adds.
The lesson for policymakers is clear, and mildly humbling: digital payments have not made cash obsolete. Cash is less a technology being replaced than an insurance policy nobody wants to give up.

Rahul Gandhi meets Congress secretaries ahead of reshuffle buzz
The meeting comes weeks after Rahul Gandhi interviewed possible candidates last month to appoint new secretaries as part of an organisational overhaul.
Leader of the Opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Tuesday met Congress secretaries to learn about their work and the issues they face ahead of an organisational reshuffle that could bring more responsibilities to these leaders, people familiar with the matter said.
According to some of the secretaries, who are mid-rung leaders in organisation, the former party chief was keen to assess their performance and commitment.
The meeting comes weeks after Rahul Gandhi interviewed possible candidates last month to appoint new secretaries as part of an organisational overhaul. Congress general secretaries KC Venugopal and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra were also present.
While some general secretaries and in-charges have been changed, the next phase of the reshuffle would involve the 56 secretaries working under general secretaries, the people said.
Last week, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge shifted general secretary Bhupesh Baghel from poll-bound Punjab to Assam and had given Karnataka general secretary Randeep Surjewala additional charge of Gujarat, which goes to polls next year. The party dropped three in-charges and handed over the responsibility of Punjab to Sachin Pilot, the former Rajasthan deputy chief minister.
Rahul and Priyanka asked the mid-rank leaders about their visits to states. Rahul told them to spend at least 15 days in their states, emphasising touring and meeting people rather than operating from Delhi.
“There was an indication that Rahul, Priyanka and Venugopal are keen to define roles and responsibilities. They asked a number of questions related to this topic,” said a secretary involved in a north Indian state.
According to leaders, several secretaries highlighted the lack of opportunities. “At least four leaders mentioned the need to define roles in poll-bound states and in states where elections are not due in the near term,” a second secretary said.
In another meeting, the leaders argued that during Sangathan Srijan (an organisational overhaul), the state observers along with in-charges had set up the district committees but secretaries had no role in the process. “The Congress has an in-charge-centric system. Secretaries are not required to give feedback and we are not a part of the decision-making system,” said the first leader quoted above.
A leader considered close to Rahul Gandhi, however, refuted these charges. Calling the meeting a “regular affair”, he said such interactions aim to strengthen the organisation.
“These charges of not getting defined roles or little opportunities are baseless. Opportunity also depends on the person’s calibre. I was appointed a secretary after working in the organisation for 17 years. Some people might have come from other backgrounds. They cannot expect to do heavy lifting from day one,” said the leader.
He added that the party high command, especially Rahul Gandhi and Venugopal “know every worker’s tasks. How many days they have spent in the states and the areas a secretary had covered. They know what is going on.”

Bestiality takes over Kash Patel’s testimony as Senators zero in on new rules for applicants
FBI director defends loosening hiring practices amid purge of agents and apparent staffing crisis at the law enforcement agency
FBI Director Kash Patel was repeatedly forced to clarify during a Senate hearing whether the nation’s top law enforcement agency was employing people who committed acts of bestiality, quickly derailing hotly anticipated testimony under an avalanche of criticism and controversy.
Patel faced pointed questions from both Democratic and Republican members on the Senate Judiciary Committee Tuesday about the apparent staffing crisis at the bureau, including from GOP Senator John Kennedy, who explicitly asked, “You’re not telling us today that if a human being had sex with an animal, that they can still be an FBI agent?”
No, Patel said. He argued that newly loosened hiring standards are meant to protect survivors of human trafficking and people who were forced into acts of bestiality, not open the agency to offenders.
The agency quietly amended its hiring practices earlier this year and will reportedly consider applicants for special agent positions and other bureau roles even if they have paid for sex, though FBI officials have repeatedly stressed that people who committed sex crimes would still be ineligible.
“Applicants who have engaged in bestiality,” said Patel, referencing the hiring language, “means they were victims of bestiality because they were forced to do so.”
Patel grilled over ‘bestiality’
Kennedy, frustrated, repeatedly asked Patel why the FBI would even need to specifically clarify hiring language when it comes to bestiality while the bureau faces intense scrutiny over a mass exodus of agents.
“All of this stuff has really hurt the FBI. It’s really hurt the FBI,” Kennedy said. “Why would you, in light of the context, and what we’re going through — we’re having a hard time attracting agents, good quality agents we all can trust, because so many people, fairly or unfairly, think in order you have to be an FBI agent now, your political point of view matters. Why would you even get into bestiality?”
Patel then tried to answer before the senator offered an example.
“If Joe participated in bestiality, not as the animal but as the human, don’t you think he oughta be disqualified?” Kennedy said.
Patel said that person would be disqualified from the bureau if they “voluntarily” engaged in bestiality, but not if they were trafficked.
“How do you involuntarily do it?” asked Kennedy, who suggested that the hiring language was recommended to Patel by other FBI employees.
“I say this with respect,” Kennedy said. “The person who recommended it, why didn’t you just say, ‘What planet did you parachute from?’”
Applicants also will not be automatically disqualified from the bureau if they stole from an employee, as long as the incident occurred more than three years ago.
It remains unclear what prompted changes to the application process and hiring language, but retired FBI agent Daniel Brunner told the Associated Press that likely indicates a staffing problem at the bureau, which lost more than 1,000 special agents in 2025, according to an analysis of federal personnel data from Justice Connection.
“If they’re moving the bar for sexual encounters to include prostitution, what is that saying about the applicant pool? They’re trying to bring in more people, which to me indicates that the applicant pool is extremely shallow right now,” Brunner told the outlet.
The FBI director defended the mass purge of agents from the bureau, claiming they were “weaponizing” the agency under President Joe Biden.
Agents were removed “for reasons that they basically failed to meet the standards of the FBI,” then claimed that they “were terminated for weaponizing the Federal Bureau of Investigation.”
Patel refuses to say FBI won’t ‘interfere’ with elections
Democratic members of the panel repeatedly asked Patel whether he intends to deploy FBI agents to the polls on Election Day after several officials from Donald Trump’s administration refuse to dismiss the idea of federal agents or federalized National Guard troops stationed at polling stations.
“We have election crisis coordinators manned at all 56 field offices,” he told Senator Peter Welch. “The FBI will not shy away from that effort.”
But he refused to answer whether the FBI will “in any way interfere in the will of the American people” when they cast their ballots.
“I pledge unequivocally that I will not participate in your charade of lies,” Patel told Welch.
Patel says he’s the victim of ‘smear campaign’ over questions on spending and drinking
Patel filed a $250 million defamation lawsuit earlier this year against The Atlantic, which is standing by a journalist’s reporting that characterized the FBI director as a deeply paranoid figure prone to drinking to excess. His lawsuit accuses the outlet of publishing a “sweeping, malicious and defamatory hit piece.”
“As a U.S. citizen, I have every right to claim the truth,” Patel told the committee Tuesday. “She printed false material. I am taking her to court.”
He then shot back at Democratic Senator Peter Welch, who was questioning Patel, for “participating” in a “smear campaign” against him.
“You cannot stand the fact that President Trump and this FBI have made America more secure than it’s ever been,” he said. “Your time’s up.”
Asked whether the FBI is investigating the journalist, Patel told Welch: “You hard of hearing? I just said no.”
Patel is also the subject of several investigations from Democratic members of Congress over his alleged “misuse” of taxpayer funds for “luxury” expenses, including a fleet of BMW vehicles, while jet setting on “official” business that includes jet ski trips and helicopter tours.
The investigation, launched by top Democrats on the House and Senate Judiciary Committees, follows a letter to Patel from Republican Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley, who demanded that the FBI director answer questions about luxury cars, his use of government aircraft and whether he reimbursed taxpayers for personal travel.
In their letter, dated July 8, Rep. Jamie Raskin and Sen. Dick Durbin said Patel has been accused of demanding special “perks” during international travel, including “VIP snorkeling” trips in Hawaii and jet skiing, helicopter tours and other recreational activities while on FBI business.
Grassley — a top Trump ally in the Senate — asked Patel in May to “please explain why you decided to purchase BMW vehicles instead of Chevy Suburbans.”
Pressed by Democratic Senator Cory Booker on whether he enlisted a SWAT detail to protect and drive his girlfriend, Patel accused him of “attacking me and my loved ones.”

Death toll from Philippines ferry fire climbs to 35, with dozens still missing
- Published
The Philippine Coast Guard says it has recovered 30 bodies from the wreckage of a ferry that caught fire this week, bringing the total death toll to 35.
More than 130 people were on board the MV June Aster when the blaze erupted on Wednesday as it neared its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron, after departing from Manila.
Forty-three people were rescued, with many receiving treatment in hospital, and searches continue for more than 50 people who remain unaccounted for.
The country's coast guard says more bodies remain on the boat, which they were unable to board until Friday due to toxic fumes and lingering heat.
In a press conference, coast guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said most bodies had been retrieved from the sleeping area of the boat, which had been making a 22-hour journey.
"Agencies are currently undertaking the proper recovery and identification of the remains in accordance with established procedures," Cayabyab said.
"We recognise the grief of the families affected by this tragic incident."
Earlier, the coast guard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest that the fire started in the cargo hold. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted.
A survivor who was hauled to safety on a rescue boat told the BBC he had heard frantic cries onboard when the fire erupted, and was trampled by panicked people as he tried to escape.
The Philippines' maritime authority is investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.
The ferry, built in 2002, held valid safety certificates and passed an enforcement inspection in March, but investigators are looking into potential manifest discrepancies, cargo loading integrity, and crew emergency response protocols, the Palawan Daily reported.
The vessel was carrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members.
Atienza Interisland Ferries, the vessel's operator, has pledged full cooperation with the inquiry.
"Our hearts remain with the affected families, and we will not rest until all individuals are accounted for," the company said in a statement on Thursday.
