On Monday evening, the Supreme Court handed down its long-awaited decision in United States Postal Service v. California — the case involving President Donald Trump’s attempt to sabotage voting by mail in the United States.
The Supreme Court has finally had it with Trump’s plan to steal the midterms
The Republican justices often put a thumb on the scale to benefit the GOP, but not all of them will put a boulder on it.
If Trump’s attack on mailed ballots had succeeded, it would have given a significant advantage to Republicans in the upcoming midterms because Democrats were much more likely to vote by mail than Republicans in the last several US election cycles.
The decision is a rout. Trump didn’t just lose; the Court’s brief order slips in a line indicating that Trump exceeded his authority and cannot implement such an attack on voting by mail under any circumstances. Not one member of the Court, including the dissenting justices, argues that Trump had the power to shut down voting by mail in the way he attempted to. Trump, in other words, found a line that even this Supreme Court would not let him cross.
The decision in USPS is also the second Supreme Court decision in less than a week that shuts down a Republican Party effort to skew the 2026 midterms in its favor. Last week, the Court ruled that the state of Missouri must use the same congressional maps it used in 2024 (which elected two Democrats), instead of new maps that were expected to elect seven Republicans and only one Democrat.
All of this, from a Court where Republicans hold six of nine seats, and where that Republican majority is often unafraid to go out on a limb to benefit the GOP and its leaders. This is, after all, the same Court that held that Trump is allowed to use the powers of the presidency to commit crimes.
So what’s going on?
The short answer is that, as the Court moves rightward, the mix of cases that reaches the Supreme Court also changes. Liberals and Democrats — or, at least, savvy liberals and Democrats — stop bringing lawsuits that rest on legal theories that right-leaning judges are unlikely to accept. Republicans, meanwhile, grow more brazen and start bringing cases that would be summarily rejected by a less friendly bench. And red-state lawmakers decide to roll the dice on laws that would be immediately declared unconstitutional if the federal courts were less Republican.
As Dartmouth political scientist Brendan Nyhan wrote after the Court (despite its Republican majority) had an unusually liberal term in 2015, “the court’s recent decisions may reflect a change in the cases being considered by the court rather than a shift in the preferences of the justices.”
Eventually, however, lawyers and policymakers who raise dubious legal theories or who enact clearly illegal policies will do something that is so beyond the pale that the justices will start to push back, and that’s what happened in USPS. Republican lawyers and policymakers will undoubtedly make more attempts to skew the midterms in the coming weeks. At the very least, the USPS decision shows that there are some limits to what this Court will tolerate.
Trump lost, badly
Trump’s attack on voting by mail wasn’t just illegal; it also imposed such heavy burdens on state election officials so close to the 2026 election that it likely would have been impossible for many states to comply with Trump’s new policy.
USPS concerned a wide range of new restrictions on mailed ballots that the Trump administration announced in late August, just weeks before states needed to start mailing those ballots to voters. Among other things, the new rules required states to mail ballots in envelopes that include several federally mandated design features. These envelopes were to be preapproved by a federal official, and the Postal Service would refuse to deliver ballots that do not comply.
The new rules also required state officials to enter certain voter data into an online platform that doesn’t actually exist yet, but that the Trump administration has insisted will be available anytime now.
Many of the new rules appeared designed to make it impossible for states to distribute ballots by mail. One new requirement, for example, was that mail ballot envelopes must be individually scanned in a process that the Trump administration claimed will take “less than a minute per mailpiece.”
But, as several states that sued to block the rules pointed out in their complaint, the state of California alone needs to mail 23 million ballots to voters. So that adds up to as much as “23 million minutes…or more than 43 years” that state officials would need to spend just to comply with one small part of the new regulations.
Trump had claimed that vague statutes that permit the Postal Service to adopt rules governing the “collection, handling, transportation, delivery, forwarding, returning, and holding of mail” or to make rules “as may be necessary in the execution of its functions” allow him to effectively shut down voting by mail throughout the United States.
Broadly speaking, the Court could have blocked these new requirements in two ways. They could have either concluded, as several lower courts already have, that the Trump administration lacks the legal authority to issue the new rules. Alternatively, the Court could have concluded that it would not be “equitable” to allow the new rules to go into effect during the 2026 election, given the high likelihood that states could not comply with them.
A majority of the justices, however, decided to go with both options. Though the Court’s order is brief — only three sentences long — it states both that Trump is “unlikely to succeed on the merits” of his claim that the new rules are legal, and also that “the equitable factors applicable for obtaining emergency relief from this Court do not favor” Trump.
Translated from the legalese, that means that most of the justices concluded both that the new rules cannot be implemented in 2026, but also that they most likely cannot be used in any election because the Trump administration lacks the authority to implement them.
Justice Samuel Alito is the Court’s most reliable Republican Party partisan, and so he did write a dissent, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, that would allow Trump’s attack on mailed ballots to take effect. But it’s notable that even Alito doesn’t try to argue that Trump’s rule is legal. Instead, Alito makes a convoluted procedural argument that, he claims, allows Trump to dodge judicial review of his new rules — at least for now.
Briefly, Alito argues that federal law makes it relatively easy for plaintiffs to challenge Postal Service rules governing “the mailability of matter,” but much harder to challenge rules that do not concern what can be mailed. He also claims that Trump’s new rules do not count as restrictions on “mailability,” even though those rules would forbid the Postal Service from delivering ballots that do not comply with a labyrinth of new restrictions.
Alito, in other words, is clearly much more willing to excuse weak arguments from the leader of his own political party than are many of his colleagues. But the biggest takeaway from the USPS decision is that not all of the Court’s Republicans are incapable of shame.
The Court’s Republican majority is extraordinarily tolerant of Trump’s antics. They gave him the right to commit crimes. They ruled that Trump may order the Justice Department to bring “sham” investigations and prosecutions against his perceived enemies. They’ve largely immunized ICE officers from the law, and blessed “Kavanaugh stops” that target suspected immigrants because of their race.
But there is apparently still a line that most of the Republican justices will not allow Trump to cross. And shutting down voting by mail a couple of months before an election crosses that line.

Jammu, Sep 15: Inspector General of Police (IGP) Jammu Tejinder Singh on Tuesday visited Reasi and reviewed the overall security and policing arrangements.
Reasi district is home to Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine and vital railway infrastructure, including the iconic Chenab Bridge and the cable-stayed Anji Khud Bridge, an official said.
The arrangements came up for review during a high-level security meeting chaired by the IGP at the District Police Lines, Reasi, a police spokesman said.
He said the meeting was attended, among others, by Deputy Inspector General of Police, Udhampur-Reasi Range, Shiv Kumar Sharma, and Senior Superintendent of Police, Reasi, Mukund Tibrewal.
He said the IGP reviewed key security and policing measures, including operational preparedness, intelligence gathering, preventive action and surveillance.
Security arrangements at critical installations were also reviewed, with directions to further strengthen security and ensure close coordination among all stakeholders, the spokesman said.

Tech giant Google has picked four Indian startups as part of its debut AI focused accelerator ‘Google DeepMind Accelerator: AI for the Planet (APAC)’, which aims to address urgent environmental challenges using artificial intelligence (AI). The four startups — Terrastack, Varaha Climate, Farmers for Forests and Climitra Carbon — will join a cohort of 16 startups operating across the Asia Pacific (APAC) region. Over the next three months, these startups will receive access to the latest Google AI stack, tailored technical support and expert mentorship to scale their sustainability-focused AI solutions, the company said. "Kicking off this week with a hands-on bootcamp in Singapore, the program, which supports startups, nonprofits, and research teams, will help them advance their ideas using frontier AI models — like AnthroKrishi, ForestCast, AlphaEarth Foundations, SpeciesNet, and Perch — to tackle urgent environmental challenges," Google APAC regional sustainability head Spencer Low and APAC developer ecosystems head Sami Kizibash said in a blog post on September 7. Google is expanding its climate initiatives in India across solar, clean energy, agriculture and research. It is scaling its AI-powered Solar API across 300 Mn Indian rooftops to help automate roof surveys and solar layouts. Besides, it has signed a four-year agreement with climate tech startup Mitti Labs to supply 1 Mn carbon credits through 2030, with financial terms undisclosed. The fixed offtake will cover credits generated from rice farming projects across Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka, where Mitti Labs currently covers more than 1 Lakh hectares. The startup uses alternate wetting and drying (AWD) to reduce methane emissions and water use in rice cultivation, while sharing carbon-credit revenue with farmers. Its AI-powered platform uses satellite data, remote sensing, field measurements and biogeochemical models to track emissions and water savings. The company also signed a 150 MW long-term solar power agreement with ReNew Power in Rajasthan to address supply chain emissions, taking its announced Scope 3 solar projects in India to 300 MW. With that, let’s take a closer look at the four startups selected for the Google DeepMind Accelerator: AI for the Planet (APAC) initiative. Climitra Carbon Founded In - 2025 Founders - Shubhankar Mihir Seth, Shaurya Sharma and Aryaman Mihir Seth Headquarters - Delhi NCR Climitra focusses on converting waste biomass into industrial-grade bio-coal and biochar. Its bio-coal is designed as a 1:1 replacement for fossil coal in steelmaking, while it focuses on permanent carbon dioxide removal under its biochar business. Farmers for Forests (F4F) Founded In - 2019 Founders - Krutika Ravishankar, Aditya Avinashe, Arti Dhar Headquarters - Pune F4F uses a payment for ecosystem services (PES) approach to incentivise farmers and communities to convert degraded land into biodiverse forests. Its programmes cover agroforestry, forest protection and restoration, urban biodiversity, human-elephant conflict prevention and climate/ecology education. Terrastack Founded In - 2024 Founders - Aaryan Dangi, Milind Sohoni Headquarters - Mumbai Terrastack is building a geospatial data platform for rural land intelligence and transactions, combining satellite imagery, mapping tools and digital land records to structure land information. Its platform focuses on digitising land boundaries and ownership, enabling data analysis for governments and enterprises, and simplifying land verification, transactions and governance. Varaha Climate Founded In - 2022 Founders - Madhur Jain, Ankita Garg and Vishal Kuchanur Headquarters - Delhi NCR The WestBridge-backed startup operates carbon dioxide removal projects across India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan and Ivory Coast. It works with smallholder farmers to promote regenerative agriculture and agroforestry, generating carbon credits that businesses can use to offset emissions. It also plans to partner with industrial companies, offering digital monitoring, reporting and verification and carbon-credit origination services.

Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, is investigating potential ties between the White House and a Russian oligarch who paid for a portion of Donald Trump Jr’s wedding.
In a letter sent to Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, on Monday, Garcia expressed concern about “any possible foreign entanglement” between the president’s son and the oligarch, Umar Kremlev. Garcia asked Wiles to provide documents, records and communications between the White House and Trump Jr about Kremlev, among other requests.
“As the son of President Donald Trump and the part-owner and major investor of multiple companies with extensive Department of Defense contracts, any apparent ties to members of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s inner circle raises serious questions about pay-to-play schemes and foreign intelligence infiltration of the President’s family,” Garcia wrote in the letter.
In a separate letter addressed to Trump Jr, Garcia expressed similar worries and asked the president’s son to provide more details about his wedding events bankrolled by Kremlev, including: all dates of communication between Trump Jr and Kremlev, any communications Trump Jr may have had with the White House about Kremlev, financial records of purchases made by foreign nationals and a complete list of wedding gifts from foreign nationals.
It came just hours after ProPublica revealed that the Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on wedding celebrations for Trump Jr and his wife, Bettina, earlier this year. The couple also confirmed Kremlev’s financial involvement on Monday.
“I have no idea who Umar is, never heard of him, and he didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day from the wedding. It was an ‘afterparty’ given in their honor. Not a big deal! I was not present at the party,” the US president said in a statement in response to the report.
“Why did a Russian oligarch close to Putin fund Trump Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas?” Garcia wrote on X after the ProPublica report was published.
Garcia added: “Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers.”
Axios was the first to report on Garcia’s letter.
The investigation into Trump Jr’s wedding is part of the House Oversight Committee Democrats’ larger investigation into the ways the Trump family has allegedly enriched themselves since President Donald Trump took office last year.
The Guardian reached out to Garcia’s office and the White House for further comment.

In 2006, Donald Trump was firing people on The Apprentice and Dr. Phil was daytime television's reigning tough-love therapist.
Twenty years later, the former is president of the United States, the latter, his informal UFO ambassador—recently trusted with unreleased government files on unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) to gauge how the public might handle what's inside.
"Here's what comes in stages. First they acknowledge it, then they confirm it's real, then they tell you where it's from," Dr. Phil said in an August 7 Instagram video discussing UAP disclosure. "And somewhere down that road, maybe, is the big one—the government of the United States standing at a podium and saying out loud, we are not alone."
For most of 2026, a rumor has consumed the world of UFOlogy: President Trump is sitting on a finished speech confirming humanity isn't alone. Whether the “disclosure speech” actually exists is a topic of rabid discussion on X, the r/UFO subreddit, and dozens of extraterrestrial-curious podcasts, but the reasons so many people believe in it are very real. Humans are arguably experiencing the most consequential era for the UFO scene since the ’40s and ’50s, when a mysterious crash outside Roswell, New Mexico, and unexplained radar blips over Washington, DC, birthed decades of legends of little green men and flying-saucers.
There's no doubt that the government has been engaging with the topic. Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently confirmed that Stephen Miller, one of the most powerful figures in the White House, has been handed the UAP portfolio.
Tim Gallaudet, a retired Navy rear admiral who helped run the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration during Trump's first term, testified before Congress about UAP in 2024, and now sits on a UAP Science Advisory Council reporting to the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. He called the increased government interest “a total change in executive-branch transparency from the last 80 years."
But he’s unsure if that would ever culminate in a speech from a sitting president, because they would “have to acknowledge that we're not in control, that we're not the highest level of intelligence on the planet, and that's going to be a very hard thing for any government to admit."
A White House spokesperson tells WIRED via email that “No such speech is planned—rather, the administration continues to release files as they become available, and the public to make up their own minds about the information uncovered.”
For believers, the modern UAP disclosure began in 2017, when a New York Times article revealed a secret Pentagon program quietly investigating UAPs. The Pentagon went on to confirm in 2020 that leaked videos of Navy pilots tracking seemingly impossible objects were real. A 2021 intelligence report conceded the phenomena existed and remained unexplained, and in 2022 the government established an official investigation office. Then, from 2022 to 2025, Congress held yearly public hearings where pilots, military officers, and intelligence veterans (including Gallaudet) testified under oath.
What’s also novel is that UAP disclosure has bipartisan support. Both the House task force on declassifying federal secrets and the House UAP Caucus are made up of legislators from across the aisle.
This year, the drumbeat of government interest turned into a drumroll about a potential Trump speech. In January, filmmaker Mark Christopher Lee claimed a disclosure speech was imminent, pegged to the 79th anniversary of the alleged Roswell crash on July 8. Few took him seriously.
But in February, the president's daughter-in-law, Lara Trump, gave the idea new legs, saying on the Pod Force One podcast she'd heard Trump had a speech ready touching on "some sort of extraterrestrial life." Around the same time, Barack Obama mused in a podcast interview with Brian Tyler Cohen that aliens are “real” before conceding “I haven’t seen them.” Trump then accused his predecessor of disclosing classified information, and announced that he was directing agencies to release their files on "alien and extraterrestrial life."
What followed was bizarre even by this administration's standards. In May, Trump posted an AI-generated image of himself escorting a handcuffed gray alien, and a mysterious loading page appeared on the domain aliens.gov, leading to rampant speculation within the UFO community that the big reveal was coming. But when the White House finally launched aliens.gov late in the month, it ended up being a Star Wars–style website that functioned as an ICE tip line—with aliens being a reference to undocumented people.
The machinery of disclosure kept grinding forward. Since May, the government has released five batches of declassified videos and documents onto the Department of War's website. Detractors say the files lack context and the videos prove little.
Even after the Roswell date passed, rumors about a disclosure speech intensified. In late July, Liberation Times—an independent news website with a record of breaking UAP stories—reported that a speech confirming some UFOs are of non-human origin had been prepared for Trump.
The site’s founder, Christopher Sharp, tells WIRED the story began with a call from a source he deeply trusts.
"They basically said, ‘Look, I'm quite shaken, because it looks like Trump may make some kind of announcement on UAP disclosure’." Another source described the speech itself, he says, alleging it basically reads, “we're not alone, we have captured some of these or retrieved some of these things, they're of non-human origin, and that there is a reverse engineering effort."
Sharp was also told Trump wouldn't deliver it unless unspecified conditions were met.
"If you're the president, you have to be sure that there's firm evidence," he says. "The worst thing you can do is come out with this speech and then whatever you put out could be debunked straight away ... You'll go down in history as a laughingstock."
In August, the rumor hit a fever pitch. Robert Bigelow, the billionaire aerospace mogul who has bankrolled UFO research for decades and once owned Utah's infamous Skinwalker Ranch (a 500-acre plot of land renowned for alleged alien and paranormal activity and later the namesake of a popular History Channel series), told veteran Las Vegas journalist George Knapp that he'd met Trump in the Oval Office months earlier and personally handed him a speech containing a single sentence: "A non-human, intelligent presence has been on Earth for a very long time, using spacecraft and with performances completely beyond our capabilities and our human physics.”
Bigelow said he advised the president to deliver the line casually, on his way to boarding Air Force One—no evidence, no press conference, just confirmation. Trump hasn't said it. Yet.
If the cycle of presidents and UFO disclosure feels familiar, that's because it is. For nearly 80 years, someone has always supposedly been on the verge of revealing the truth, but no president has ever delivered.
"Politicians overpromise," says Greg Eghigian, a professor of history and bioethics at Penn State and author of After the Flying Saucers Came. "The reality is that even presidents are not privy to a lot of classified information that lies within the bowels of the military and intelligence community bureaucracy."
Still, for the believers, the stakes justify the hope.
“Often in the mainstream, when this topic gets brought up, there's a giggle factor. I can tell you who is not giggling about this: senior members of the administration, senior intelligence officials, senior members of the military, senior members of Congress,” says Jordan Flowers, executive director of the Disclosure Foundation, a nonprofit that advocates for UAP transparency. “When the door closes, no one ever says, ‘Oh, this is all made up, isn't it?’ No. The door closes and they say, ‘We know there's something happening here, we know this is serious, what do we do about it?’"
But that discourse still hasn’t been confirmed, at least in a meaningful way to the general public.
"A speech from the President of the United States confirming the existence of things in our airspace that we do not understand would unequivocally contribute to the public taking this issue seriously," says Flowers.
Eghigian, however, isn't so sure a Trump pronouncement would settle anything, particularly from "this president, who has a long history of not telling the truth."
If the past is any indicator, this could be another nothingburger.
“Unless something radically different happens, which I know a lot of people are counting on, what we could probably expect is that this will eventually die down,” he says, citing an 80-year history of “intense moments where societies are really focused on the subject, and then all of a sudden interest wanes, and then all of a sudden it appears again."
Right now, interest is arguably at anall-timee high. Few politicians enjoy a public spectacle as much as Trump, and what spectacle could be bigger than news that transcends our planet, and potentially our galaxy. Maybe the rumor just becomes another footnote on presidents and UFO lore. Or maybe it becomes the most important proclamation in human history, delivered by a reality TV star, with a talk show shrink by his side.

WNBA's influence felt as Women's World Cup vows schedule changes
NEW YORK, Sept 15 : The WNBA season resumes on Thursday after the league’s growing influence was felt at the FIBA Women’s World Cup, where a punishing schedule underlined the difficulty of staging major international tournaments without accommodating the world’s leading women’s league.
The WNBA paused its season for the tournament, frustrating some fans, while FIBA has already said the 2030 World Cup will be staged later in the year, another sign that the league’s growing power is reshaping the global basketball calendar.
"We are pleased that the collaboration between global women’s basketball stakeholders, and adjustments we are seeing in the global women’s basketball calendar, more easily allow players to fulfill both WNBA and international team commitments," a WNBA spokesperson told Reuters.
The season restarts only four days after Sunday’s final, in which the United States beat France 97-79. Many players had rushed from their WNBA teams to join their national squads in Berlin, leaving little time to prepare and adding to fatigue as the tournament progressed.
FIBA Secretary General Andreas Zagklis acknowledged concerns over the compressed schedule.
"We had to have a schedule here that will not be repeated, I can confirm that," Zagklis told reporters on Sunday, promising there would be no back-to-back games at the 2030 tournament in Tokyo.
"I'm still convinced we did the best we could in the circumstances we had... while admitting that it was not perfect."
Seventy current and former WNBA players went to compete in Berlin, compared with about 30 active players at the tournament four years ago, illustrating the league’s increasingly central role in the international game.
'THE MOST TALENTED LEAGUE IN THE WORLD'
The WNBA season, which runs from spring to early autumn, does not align with the traditional international basketball calendar. But amid an increasingly congested schedule, the league has found itself at the head of the table with increasing power and influence.
"To perform well in FIBA, (teams) need the WNBA players,” said Jerica Williams, a WNBA scout who has consulted for multiple front offices around the league. “It is without a doubt the most talented league in the world."
The WNBA said FIBA’s calendar change would reduce disruption for players balancing club and international commitments.
"The FIBA Women’s World Cup, like the Summer Olympics, is important for the growth of women’s basketball both in the US and globally given the global stage it offers," the spokesperson added.
The schedule shift marks the latest development in an ongoing push by the league to ensure their leading players prioritise the WNBA.
Players have long supplemented their income by competing overseas during the off-season, often enduring gruelling year-round schedules with little opportunity to rest. Some overseas competitions also overlapped with the start of WNBA training camps.
Prioritization rules that came into effect three years ago required veteran players to report to their WNBA teams before training camp or by May 1, even if they had to depart from their overseas obligations early.
NEW OFF-SEASON ENTERPRISES
The rules were an early demonstration of the WNBA’s growing clout during a period of rapid expansion, with new teams joining amid viewership growth and the popularity of bankable stars such as Indiana Fever's sharpshooter Caitlin Clark.
International sales of WNBA merchandise have exploded - up by 200 per cent over the past three years with merchandise shipped to more than 50 countries outside the U.S. in 2026 alone.
Improved salaries in the league's latest CBA, plus the addition of appealing new off-season enterprises like Unrivaled, a three-on-three off-season league that launched in North America in 2025 to extraordinary interest from the top talent in the WNBA, have further tipped the scales in the WNBA's favour.
"Over time you're going to see less of the superstars playing in every single qualifier, every single tournament," said Alex Bazzell, the president and CEO of Unrivaled.
Unrivaled lured players with its supersized paychecks and a lighter workload - teams play just 14 games apiece - fitting more comfortably into the WNBA offseason. After its latest funding round, the league was valued at $650 million in August.
"We had to see which way the schedule was trending when we started out in this," said Bazzell.
"Certainly, there were a lot more months of the offseason when we first started, but I think we positioned ourselves and that's why you see these players who are now kind of all flocking to us, those that hadn't played in the offseason before and then those who have obviously traditionally played overseas."

A probe has been ordered by Bhopal Police Commissioner Sanjay Kumar, a day after at least four MBBS intern doctors suffered injuries due to water cannons that were used against them during their protest in the campus of government-run Gandhi Medical College (GMC) to demand a hike in their stipend.
On Monday (September 7, 2026), hundreds of interns of the GMC, Bhopal, protested at their campus over their longstanding demand that their stipend be increased from the current ₹14,437 to ₹30,000. However, as they planned a march to the Chief Minister’s residence, the police used water cannons on the protestors, visuals of which appeared on the internet.
The protestors also alleged that as they continued their march later in the day, the police also resorted to baton charge on them near the campus. The march was stopped less than 2 kilometres from the CM house, prompting them to launch a sit-in at the site.
The sit-in in Bhopal’s Kamla Park area continued through the night and on Tuesday (September 8) even as they boycotted the OPD and routine operation theatre (OT) services, while emergency services remained operational. Services were also interrupted at Gwalior’s Gajra Raja Medical College in support of the protest.
Four interns injured in the police action
Speaking to The Hindu, Siddhartha Kumar Rai, undergraduate student wing president of the Junior Doctors’ Association (JDA), Madhya Pradesh, said that at least four interns got seriously injured in the police action, including one person suffering a broken arm and another an eye injury.
“It was a completely peaceful protest inside the campus but still the interns who perform 36-hour-long duties and contribute the most in handling the heavy patient load at government hospitals were treated like goons by the police. They even targeted the girl interns who were standing on the side,” he said.
Meanwhile, various other doctors’ bodies in the State have also come out in support of the interns’ protest while condemning the police action.
Mr. Rai said that if a written assurance was not given by Tuesday night, the JDA and various other bodies will boycott medical services across the State from Wednesday (September 9).
Dr. Kavita N. Singh, Dean and CEO, GMC, Bhopal, also slammed the use of force in a letter to Commissioner Kumar while seeking an inquiry into the matter and action against responsible officers.
“Water cannon was used and lathicharge was done on the intern students at the emergency gate in which two students were injured.
Taking such action against intern students on the hospital campus without prior notice is completely inappropriate,” she wrote.
In an order, Mr. Kumar said that the matter was brought to attention by Deputy Chief Minister and Health Minister Rajendra Shukla and that Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP), Zone 2, Vikas Sahwal has been appointed to conduct an “impartial investigation of the whole incident”.
“It has been brought to the notice by Shri Rajendra Shukla, Deputy Chief Minister, that during the protest of intern doctors in Bhopal on September 7, 2026, the police sprayed water using water cannon near the gate of Hamidia Hospital, due to which some doctors were injured,” the order read.
Mr. Rai also claimed that Madhya Pradesh ranked 28th in the country in the amount of stipend given to MBBS interns, after the Uttar Pradesh increasing the amount from ₹12,000 to ₹25,000 in August.
“But in terms of MBBS fee at government colleges, we are at the third position with about ₹1.15 lakh. How is this fair,” he asked.
Meanwhile, Mr. Shukla also held a meeting with senior officials and the management of the GMC to discuss the issue and interns’ demand and said that a resolution will be reached soon.
“I am aware of the issue raised by intern doctors in Bhopal regarding an increase in stipends. The expectations and problems of young doctors in the state are being taken seriously. I am in constant touch with representatives of the intern doctors on this matter,” he wrote on X.
“Our effort is to engage in positive discussions with all parties and arrive at an appropriate and practical solution to this issue. Young doctors play a vital role in strengthening the health services of the state, and the government is sensitive to their rightful expectations. Following discussions and necessary deliberations, appropriate and necessary decisions will be taken in this regard,” he added.

Indonesian rescuers were searching on Sunday for 140 people from a passenger ship that was earlier reported missing in the Java Sea after 103 others were evacuated, one of whom died, a search and rescue agency official said.
A passenger ship carrying more than 240 people was reported missing after losing contact during bad weather in the Java Sea early on Sunday, the country’s search and rescue agency said.
The Virgo Transport 8 ship set sail on Saturday from the East Java city of Surabaya to the South Kalimantan city of Banjarmasin before losing contact.
I Putu Sudayana, the head of the agency’s Banjarmasin office, said in a video statement that 103 people had been evacuated using different ships and some of them would be taken to an East Java port.
Rescuers launched a search, deploying a team, ships and a helicopter toward the passenger vessel’s last known position, he said, without stating what happened to the ship.
The search and rescue office in the city of Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan, which is located on Borneo island, said it received a report two hours after contact was lost with the Virgo Transport 8 at about 2am on Sunday.
“The ship’s operator reported the incident to authorities after receiving information that the vessel had encountered bad weather,” Sudayana, who heads the search and rescue office, said in a video briefing.
Indonesia, an archipelago of 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries as a key mode of transportation, with sea routes more affordable and readily available than air travel.
However, safety standards are not always rigorously enforced, resulting in a relatively high accident rate.

Last week, the Atlantic hurricane season blew through its traditional peak—which comes around September 10—with nary a tropical wave in sight, let alone a storm or hurricane.
This is remarkable. Usually this is the time of year when sea surface temperatures reach their warmest in the tropics, and with a favorable atmosphere it should be smooth skating for tropical systems. But this year, the main region where most tropical systems develop is choked with Saharan dust and wind shear.
No one is complaining. Landfalling hurricanes are incredibly destructive for coastal areas and have the potential for considerable inland rainfall. Even storms at sea, in the Gulf of Mexico, can send energy prices skyrocketing—the last thing needed this year.
This has never happened
Nevertheless the quietude is historic.
Beginning in 1944 the United States began monitoring the Atlantic basin, which includes the Gulf, Caribbean Sea, and northern Atlantic Ocean, with aircraft to detect hurricanes. Dating back to 1944, a hurricane had formed every year by September 11. The latest “first” Atlantic hurricanes came in 2002, with Gustav; and in 2013, with Humberto on this date.
Atlantic hurricane records officially go back to 1851, although older records are less reliable because observations of storms developing at sea were reliant on reports from shipping vessels. So some storms were missed. If we extend the hurricane record all the way back to 1851, every year still records at least one Atlantic hurricane. But in 1941, the first hurricane did not form until September 17. This is the date of the latest first Atlantic hurricane on record.
I’m here to tell you that the Atlantic will not produce a hurricane by the end of Thursday. The National Hurricane Center is presently monitoring a single disturbance in the Atlantic, but it gives this system a “near zero” percent chance of becoming a tropical depression or storm during the next two days. The likelihood of it ever becoming a hurricane is low.

NATO fighter jet shoots down drone over Lithuania
Russia and Ukraine ignore Trump's plea to not attack energy infrastructure amid ongoing war
An Italian NATO fighter jet shot down a drone over Lithuania shortly after midnight on Tuesday morning, the Lithuanian National Crisis Management Centre said.
The drone, which was likely to have entered from Belarus, was shot down near Pratkunai village in southern Lithuania, near Kaunas, the second-largest city, the centre's spokesperson said. Its origin had yet to be determined, he said.
Military drones straying into the airspace of Russia's neighbours have stoked concerns that Russia's war in Ukraine is spilling over NATO's borders.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said that strikes close to the alliance's territory would drive the trans-Atlantic organization to increase its support for Kyiv. Rutte also pledged to bolster the 32-nation alliance's own defences along its long eastern border with Russia.
Officials did not say whether the drone was believed to be Ukrainian or Russian. In recent months, Ukrainian drones have repeatedly entered NATO airspace in the Baltic region. Kyiv says they were steered off course by Russian signal jamming.
A drone alert was issued earlier in the capital Vilnius and surrounding region.
The Lithuanian army shared video from the site of the crash, showing debris scattered in grass. Some of the parts appeared to be made from wood and some appeared charred.
Fighters with the NATO Baltic Air Defence mission have patrolled the skies of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia since the Baltic countries joined the alliance in 2004. The mission's jets shot down stray Ukrainian drones over Estonia in May, and over Latvia in June and August.
Denmark reports encounter with Russian ship
Separately, Denmark said a Russian frigate fired two flares towards a Danish military helicopter on Monday. Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen called the incident "unacceptable" and said it could have endangered human lives.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the incident was serious but not surprising, calling it part of a pattern in which an increasingly aggressive Russia has intensified its hybrid warfare against Europe and is testing NATO.
The Baltic Sea region is on high alert after incidents involving gas pipeline outages, airspace violations and drone sightings.
Russia has dismissed accusations over such incidents and repeatedly denied carrying out hybrid attacks in Europe.
Russia accused Danish military helicopters of making dangerous manoeuvres near its warships in the Baltic Sea and handed an official note to Copenhagen complaining about such incidents, Russia's ambassador to Denmark said Tuesday, according to Russia's RIA state news agency.
RIA cited Ambassador Vladimir Barbin as blaming Denmark for the episode.
Ukraine reports deaths
Meanwhile, Russia hit petrol stations in Kyiv on Tuesday and Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery, as the warring sides carried on with strikes on each other's energy targets despite an announcement on social media by U.S. President Donald Trump the previous day that they had agreed to stop.
Russia launched 200 drones at Ukraine's capital and other cities in overnight attacks, killing two people. In addition to the petrol stations in Kyiv, it struck energy and port infrastructure in other regions, Ukrainian officials said.

Trump on Sunday had called on Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian diesel infrastructure, saying the attacks were causing a shortage of the fuel that is "hurting the world."
Trump didn't offer further details on the purported agreement between the two sides.
Zelenskyy said late Monday that Kyiv was "ready to support de-escalation," but expressed doubts Russia would adhere to such a demand.
On Tuesday, the Kremlin said it welcomed what it termed a U.S. proposal, while adding that "illegal" sanctions on Russian energy supplies should be lifted.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Trump's suggestion was a "very good idea," but it would take more than that to bring down global fuel prices. He said Russia would stay in touch with the Americans about Trump's proposal.
In additional fighting on Tuesday, the regional governor of Odesa, Oleh Kiper, said that Russia hit port infrastructure in Ukraine's southern Black Sea region overnight, with residential buildings, logistics facilities and transport infrastructure coming under attack.
Russian forces hit a cargo ship and a ferry carrying military supplies in Ukraine's port of Chornomorsk, the Russian Defence Ministry said on Tuesday.

A Medicare experiment in paying for technology to help people manage chronic conditions has just barely gotten underway, and already, officials are moving to expand it.
Announced last year, the ACCESS model will pay approved companies to manage the chronic conditions, including diabetes, high blood pressure, chronic musculoskeletal pain, depression, and diabetes. The model introduces outcome-aligned payments, in which providers are paid more if their patients’ conditions improve.
Regulators on Tuesday announced that they would expand the number of chronic conditions that will be eligible for the ACCESS model to include substance use disorder, heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease tobacco use, and longer-terms support for musculoskeletal conditions. The new condition tracks will start in spring 2027.

A fourth person in Pennsylvania has died of measles, the state health department confirmed Tuesday. The latest death was in an unvaccinated 18-year-old resident of Mifflin County.
In the announcement, the state health department also confirmed a county coroner’s report over the weekend of the death of an unvaccinated 40-year-old woman in Jefferson County. The state had previously reported two deaths in Lancaster County; both were infants—a newborn boy and a 6-week-old girl, both too young to be vaccinated.
According to the Mifflin County coroner, Andrea L. Alcalde, the 18-year-old’s cause of death was determined to be acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM), which is a rare but known severe complication of measles. The condition is characterized by a rapidly progressing autoimmune disorder in which aberrant inflammation from an infection strips away the protective coverings of nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord. Before measles vaccines were widely used, ADEM was commonly associated with measles, though other viral infections can also spur its development.
In a new release posted to the coroner’s Facebook page Tuesday, Alcalde said the death determination was made after a review of medical records and all available information. Alcalde said no other information would be released about the deceased.
The state health department released a statement confirming the measles death of the 18-year-old, as well as the death of the 40-year-old. The two deaths will be added to the state’s outbreak data dashboard Wednesday as part of the regular update, the department noted.
Death reporting
So far, the state has reported 693 measles cases in 38 counties this year. There have been 99 cases reported in the last seven days. In all, 133 people have been hospitalized.
“My thoughts are with the two families who lost loved ones to this highly contagious virus, as Pennsylvania faces the worst measles outbreak in more than three decades,” Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Debra Bogen said in a statement, referring to the two latest deaths. “We remain committed to working with our partners across Pennsylvania to stem this outbreak and prevent more deaths. That means ensuring people have the facts about measles and access to the MMR [measles, mumps, and rubella] vaccine—which kept measles outbreaks at bay for decades.”

- The claim that attendees of the 2026 Republican National Convention in Dallas, Texas, caused an outage of popular gay dating app Grindr circulated online in September 2026.
- The rumor stems from incident reports shared on social media, taken from a third-party service called Downdetector during the time of the event. However, the incidents were not isolated to Dallas, and Grindr itself did not report any major outages connected to the event.

With high-stakes midterms looming in November 2026, the Republican National Convention took place in Dallas, Texas, on Sept. 9 and 10, 2026. Rumors spread that the convention's attendees were causing an outage of the popular gay dating app Grindr.
People on social media sites shared a purported screenshot that showed a map depicting hotspots of Grindr outages across the country, with the brightest spot focused on Dallas.
The popularity of the rumor led many Snopes readers to reach out via email and social media, asking if the claim was true.
We weren't able to independently verify claims of Grindr outages in Dallas, so we've left this claim unrated. The screenshots appeared to be taken from Downdetector, a third-party service that tracks outages of popular services, and did not show signs of fabrication or misleading editing.
According to Downdetector, users did report incidents at the time and location in question, but the incidents reported on Sept. 9 and 10 were not limited to Dallas or even Texas. There was also no way to confirm that the reports reflected real issues with the app, as Downdetector does not require users to submit any proof.
Grindr itself did not report any outages during that time.
A spokesperson for Grindr told Snopes via email: "Grindr has not experienced recent outages. Third party sources that often make these claims rely on unreliable data such as self-reporting, while Grindr reports outages directly on its status page."
The company's status page showed no outages or incidents in August or September 2026.
Downdetector tracks data for the prior 24 hours and does not archive its history.
Snopes first checked Downdetector's page for Grindr on Sept. 10, 2026. It showed a spike of reported outages on Sept. 9 around 8:49 p.m., with the highest number of reports clocked at 460.
Grindr outage report on Sept. 10, 2026. (Downdetector)
When we checked Downdetector on Sept. 11, the past 24 hours showed a peak of only 73 reports around 3:18 p.m. on Sept. 10.
Grindr outage report on Sept. 11, 2026. (Downdetector)
The incident heat map provided by Downdetector, which we first checked on Sept. 10, showed the highest concentration of outages in Dallas and Austin, Texas, but also indicated reports were being submitted in other major cities like New York, Boston and Chicago.
Grindr outage map on Sept. 10, 2026. (Downdetector)
A look at the same map one day later showed lower concentrations of reports of problems in the same cities.
(Grindr outage map on Sept. 11, 2026. (Downdetector))
The page explains that Downdetector "calculates a baseline volume of typical problem reports for each service monitored" based on an average over six months, and "only reports an incident when the number of problem reports is significantly higher than the baseline."
Further, Downdetector allows users reporting the issues to comment on the page. During the period of Snopes' review for this claim, multiple comments on Grindr's Downdetector page referenced the RNC with comments like, "Convention in Dallas, as always." There was no indication those comments came from people genuinely experiencing connection issues in Dallas.
So while it appeared that some users may have had trouble with the service on Sept. 9 and 10, 2026, including in and around the area where the RNC was being held, there was not enough evidence to conclude without a doubt that the reported errors were entirely authentic or that they were indeed caused specifically by attendees at the RNC.
We reached out to Ookla, the parent company of Downdetector, for further comment and will update this article if we hear back.
For further reading, we've investigated similar claims about Grindr, such as rumors of alleged Grindr outages near Charlie Kirk's memorial in September 2025.

Around 200 SpiceJet passengers protested at Delhi airport after flights to Dubai were rescheduled multiple times and faced delays since Monday, PTI reported.
Two SpiceJet flights -- SG 5111 and SG 5105 -- were scheduled to depart from Delhi for Dubai on Monday morning (8.30 am) and evening (10.10 pm), respectively. However, both flights were rescheduled, leaving several passengers stranded at the airport, a source told PTI.
The passengers protested at various locations at Terminal 3 (T3) of the Delhi airport from late Monday evening. Airport officials have taken up the matter with SpiceJet executives.
Visuals shared on social media showed passengers sitting on the floor in protest against the airline. Some users claimed that the passengers also raised slogans against SpiceJet. Mint could not independently verify these claims or the authenticity of the videos.
SpiceJet cites aircraft grounding
Responding to the disruption, a SpiceJet spokesperson on Tuesday apologised for the inconvenience caused to passengers and said alternate flights were being arranged.
"SpiceJet flights SG 5111 and SG 5105, operating from Delhi to Dubai, have been delayed due to operational reasons following the grounding of an aircraft," the spokesperson told PTI.
"Alternate flights are being arranged to accommodate the affected passengers, and the airline is making every effort to minimise the inconvenience caused," the spokesperson added.
According to an Indian Express report, the alternative flights had not departed for Dubai till 2 pm on Tuesday.
SpiceJet faces multiple challenges
The budget carrier has been facing multiple headwinds in recent times. In July, the airline's domestic market share dropped to 1.6 per cent from 1.9 per cent in June.
The airline is reportedly facing financial issues and there has been a delay in payment of salaries to the staff. Salaries have not been paid to many employees since May.
The domestic share of the airline has declined since February. It had finalised lease agreements with three aircraft operators earlier this month for the induction of 20 planes.
"The aircraft are scheduled to join the fleet in phases between mid-October and mid-November, ahead of the winter travel peak beginning with the Durga Puja period. The induction will strengthen capacity across SpiceJet's domestic and international network and provide additional capacity through the winter and the following peak summer travel season," the airline had said.
Last week, Civil Aviation Minister K Rammohan Naidu told PTI that the civil aviation ministry and aviation regulator DGCA were closely monitoring the airline's financials and operations.
"Every month, we engage with all the airlines regarding whatever difficulties or issues or challenges they have. SpiceJet also, in the same regard, we have been meeting," Naidu said.

The US government launched at least three previously unreported investigations into trading on the prediction market Polymarket, according to documents obtained by WIRED through a Freedom of Information Act request.
Voting records from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that regulates prediction markets, shed new light on how the government approaches these investigations. In early May, CFTC chairman Michael Selig approved an order allowing the agency’s enforcement division to launch a private investigation into potential insider trading on Polymarket event contracts related to pardons issued by former president Joseph Biden. The order granted permission to take testimony, obtain subpoenas, administer oaths, and require the production of documents in the course of the investigation.
The documents obtained by WIRED did not specify which trades were under suspicion, but the order came several weeks after an NPR report on a suspicious Polymarket trader who netted over $300,000 on pardon-related markets in the final days of the Biden administration. The trader correctly wagered that the former president would issue preemptive pardons to a number of prominent MAGA critics, including former US representatives Liz Cheney and Adam Kinzinger, and US senator Adam Schiff.
At the end of May, Selig approved another investigation order. This time, the topic was “Iran event contracts” on Polymarket. As with the Biden pardon documents, the investigation order did not provide details, but it came two weeks after 60 Minutes aired a report on a network of suspicious Polymarket accounts that made $2.4 million on Iran-related trades, with a 98 percent win rate.
“If these investigations are being prompted solely by press reports of potential violations of the Commodities Exchange Act, that’s a significant sign of weakness in this regulatory scheme,” says Joseph Konizeski, a former chief trial attorney in the CFTC’s division of enforcement. The agency has come under fire in the second Trump era for its perceived friendliness to the prediction market industry.
In July, Selig greenlit a third investigation, this time focused on suspected insider trading on Google-themed Polymarket event contracts. In an email exchange included in the documents obtained by WIRED, Paul Hayeck, the acting director of the CFTC’s department of enforcement, noted that the investigation would focus on “additional individuals who may have engaged in insider trading related to Google’s 2025 Year in Search Ranking.” Hayeck wrote that the Southern District of New York is conducting a “parallel investigation.” He specified that the CFTC's investigation would be separate from the ongoing case against Michele Spagnuolo, a Google engineer accused of insider trading.
SDNY declined to comment. Google declined to comment. It pointed WIRED to a statement it released in June noting that Spagnuolo was no longer with the company. The CFTC did not respond to requests for comment and questions about the status of the investigations.
“While we do not comment on specific investigations, we regularly refer matters to law enforcement and support ongoing investigations as part of our commitment to protecting the integrity of our markets,” Olivia Chalos, deputy chief legal officer at Polymarket, told WIRED in an email.
The CFTC is also reportedly investigating Polymarket itself. The company, which had its flagship platform banned from the United States in 2022, was permitted to launch a US-regulated version with a narrower set of markets in late 2025. It recently underwent a fundraising round led by Donald Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm, 1789 Capital, which valued the company at $21 billion.
The CFTC has also launched investigations into potential insider trading on Kalshi, Polymarket’s archrival, in the past. According to The New York Times, Kalshi has referred at least 32 cases to the agency. The CFTC fined former US representative George Santos $35,000 for his behavior related to a Kalshi contract about whether he would attend Trump’s 2026 State of the Union address.
Kalshi issued its first-ever lifetime ban to Santos for violating its rules on market manipulation for the same behavior, and also fined him just over $71,000. Santos was not criminally charged.
So far, two arrests have been made stemming from Polymarket insider trading investigations. In April, federal authorities arrested a US special forces officer who prosecutors say used classified information to make more than $400,000 in profits on event contracts related to the capture of former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro. And in May, Spagnuolo, who allegedly made over $1.2 million on insider trades, was arrested while traveling to New York. In both cases, the CFTC filed civil charges, and the Department of Justice filed criminal fraud charges. Both men are fighting back by arguing that Polymarket trades are a form of betting and not subject to commodities law.
It’s unclear if the Department of Justice has launched parallel investigations into the Iran War or Biden pardon contracts. The DOJ did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
A former CFTC staffer tells WIRED that parallel criminal investigations are likely, “given the significance of the matters.”
Additional reporting by Maddy Varner.

Courtney McAnuff was out of a year-long relationship in the summer of 2024 and starting to date again when she agreed to grab drinks with a potential suitor.
They met at a bar in midtown Manhattan. He arrived wearing a baseball cap pulled low and sported a pair of black-framed glasses, she says. As conversation flowed, from discussions about navigating life in New York to past relationships, he mentioned that his glasses were Meta Ray-Bans.
“I wasn’t familiar with them,” McAnuff, a 28-year-old project manager who now lives in Toronto, tells WIRED. It was her first time seeing the smart glasses up close, which can record images and video from the wearer’s viewpoint. He let her try them on and even showed her a couple of videos that he’d taken previously, she says. “That was it. We stopped talking about it after that. I figured that was the end of the use.”
The next day, checking her Instagram, McAnuff noticed she’d been tagged in one of his story posts. To her surprise, it was footage of them at the bar and on the subway together, en route to a basketball game uptown. In the video, McAnuff is captured from an above angle, sitting across from her date who is holding a drinking glass; WIRED has seen screenshots of the footage. “I felt super violated,” McAnuff says. “Like, what if I don’t want everyone knowing what I’m up to? He felt so free to film me and post it. There was no conversation about it.”
Meta sold more than 7 million pairs of the Ray-Bans in 2025, as its smart glasses have infiltrated public spaces thanks to pranksters with dreams of viral fame, some of whom even film people while they’re at work. The phenomenon, which has also spread to pickup artists hitting on women, has earned the hardware the nickname “creep glasses.”
Among singles, and particularly women, Meta’s AI-powered eyewear has become a recurring nuisance, as people share a spreading unease about being covertly filmed on dates.
“Ban those glasses completely,” posted a young woman on Bluesky in August, writing that her date “leaned over to show me pictures he took of me I had no idea he was taking.” One TikToker claimed in a video after a date that she “immediately felt uncomfortable,” questioning why people are “so comfortable videoing everything. It’s a terrible way to portray yourself, wearing a fucking camera on your face and you’re sitting in my face.”
In a Reddit post from August, users debated the ethics of the trend, wondering if it was OK to continue a date when someone showed up wearing them; in a separate thread, one person said they had ghosted a guy after realizing he’d worn the glasses on their date. “I didn’t notice until toward the end of the night. I kissed him while he was wearing the glasses,” they said. In July, a man was put under investigation in Seoul, South Korea, for allegedly filming four women he had gone out with and later uploading clips to social media, according to The Korea Herald.
In many regards, dating has been reframed by our dependency on technology. Apps connect people. Chatbots are used for all sorts of things these days: as wingmen and for role-play. Smartphone cameras capture important moments together. But while a phone being held up to someone’s face gives them a clear opportunity to object, smart glasses largely erase that opportunity. (Meta’s glasses do have a front-facing LED that switches on when the glasses are recording, but the light is the only warning, and it can be disabled by hacking the hardware.)
For McAnuff, the trend is about more than privacy instructions. She was worried about what would happen with the footage afterward. “He didn’t ask if I wanted to be recorded or if I wanted my face uploaded. And now he has this video file of me forever. It’s definitely a big trust issue,” she says.
In a 2025 YouGov survey of US adults focused on factors contributing to successful relationships, trust ranked the highest, with 94 percent of respondents categorizing it as “very important.”
Gary Lewandowski, a psychology professor at Monmouth University whose research focuses on the science of romantic connection, says adding covert cameras to the mix will only make building trust harder. He says beyond posting for the ’gram, a number of factors could be driving men to do this. The most logical, non-creepy reason may be tied to post-date analysis, in that the glasses can help men identify blind spots around their own behavior.
“A lot of men out there are eternal optimizers. They want better, more efficient ways of doing things, so reviewing game tape allows them to learn from mistakes,” Lewandowski says. “But I do wonder if some are doing it to build a case instead of a connection—why they’re right and the other person is wrong—or to help better identify red flags.” That type of surveillance “makes the date less about getting to know each other and more about fact gathering,” he adds.
The trend has also reanimated discussions around consent when it comes to dating. Yue Xu, cohost of the Dateable podcast, believes new social norms are needed to keep up with our evolving tech. “It’s bringing in a third party, which is disturbing. It just shows that this person lacks respect for the integrity and privacy of the date,” Xu says, adding that she fears that the glasses are triggering a future “where people have no more anonymity.”
Concerns have intensified as issues about the device have continued to make headlines. Meta and EssilorLuxottica, which owns Ray-Ban, are facing a class action lawsuit alleging that they captured and stored users’ private data without consent. This month, Semafor reported that Meta disabled the recording function for thousands of users who tampered with the light that notifies people that the Meta Ray-Bans are filming. Following the addition of an unreleased face-recognition feature called NameTag to its eyewear earlier this year, revealed by a WIRED investigation, Meta scrubbed the code from its app in June and is facing another proposed class action over allegedly breaching Illinois and California privacy laws by collecting biometric information from users’ photographs without their knowledge.
“This lawsuit is without merit and misrepresents our work,” a Meta spokesperson tells WIRED in reference to the NameTag lawsuit. “We've been transparent about how we use people's information to build and improve our AI products. As for NameTags, nothing has shipped to consumers, and no final decision has been made on what to do here, if anything. If we do decide to roll something out, we will take a thoughtful approach and do so with full transparency. One decision we can be clear about—we are not building a universal face database.”
EssilorLuxottica did not respond to a request for comment.
According to Meta, if people tamper with the recording light, including placing blockers over it, the camera will not turn on. Additionally, the company says it removes accounts and content that violate its policies when it becomes aware of them, including content meant to degrade or shame others. In August, Meta expanded its public awareness efforts through a social media campaign focused on helping people identify when someone is recording with the glasses.
“We don't want people to be surreptitiously taking videos of other people and harassing them and then posting them on our platform. So we're trying to fight that every way we can,” Meta's head of Instagram Adam Mosseri said in July.
That hasn’t stopped regulators around the world from pushing to enact harsher privacy laws for consumers. A California bill just passed both chambers that mandates visible recording indicators on recording devices and bans users from turning them off. Likewise, Australia’s eSafety Commissioner is asking tech companies to automatically blur people’s faces recorded with their smart glasses, writing that “as smart glasses evolve and become more common, they may become increasingly interconnected with and create new ways to perpetrate different types of harms, such as image-based abuse, adult cyber abuse, cyberbullying of children, or the livestreaming of violent or other harmful content.”
When McAnuff realized footage of her had been uploaded without her approval, she confronted her date over text. He apologized for his actions but she says that “he didn’t think it was that serious.” She hasn’t seen him since.
For McAnuff and many others, Meta’s smart glasses have simply become the latest privacy issue hiding in plain sight.
“Being in each other’s physical space is such a beautiful experience in itself. We don’t need to have gadgets around,” McAnuff says. “I don’t think that every moment needs to be captured.”

At least 21 dead after multi-vehicle crash in South Africa
The crash started with the two minibus taxis colliding head-on, after which an SUV crashed into them, the Western Cape Mobility department said
At least 21 people have been killed and several others severely injured following a head-on collision between two minibus taxis and a third vehicle on a major highway in South Africa, authorities said on Monday.
The incident occurred on Sunday night in the Western Cape Province between Prince Albert and Leeu-Gamka, roughly 380 kilometres (236 miles) east of Cape Town, according to the Road Traffic Management Corporation.
The agency noted that the death toll "may change as emergency services and authorities in the Western Cape continue their assessment of the scene."
Three of the casualties were rushed to hospital but were pronounced dead upon arrival, police said.
The Western Cape Mobility department stated that the crash is believed to have started when the two minibus taxis collided head-on, after which an SUV crashed into them.
The N1 highway was closed at the site as the Road Traffic Management Corporation launched an official investigation.
Minibus taxis are the main mode of public transport for millions of people in South Africa and are often involved in fatal collisions. Two separate crashes involving minibus taxis in January left at least 25 people dead, including 14 children.
Earlier this month, at least 25 people, including many teenagers, were killed after a bus plunged into a ravine on the Cape Verdean island of Fogo.
The fatal crash occurred late on September 5 along the mountainous Campanas de Cima route, where the passenger vehicle left the road and fell around 30 metres down a steep incline.
Cape Verde’s government has announced two days of mourning following the disaster, which the president José Maria Pereira Neves branded "a great catastrophe".
A mass funeral for the victims took place on Sunday at Sao Lourenco Church in the town of Sao Lourenco.
Local media reported that many of the passengers were primary and secondary school students.
Relatives and local residents carried the coffins, with 18 displayed together inside the church during the service.

Carney's European address will find an eager audience in a continent rattled by Trump
PM to speak at European Parliament as Canada, EU appear poised to move closer
One of the drawbacks of giving a historic speech like the one that Prime Minister Mark Carney gave in Davos, Switzerland, in January is that people expect an encore every time you speak.
The Carney government has been at pains to lower expectations for anyone who's hoping for another worldwide viral moment when Carney addresses the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday morning.
There will be nothing that will really surprise those who've been following the prime minister's publicly expressed thinking, or the progress of the growing rapprochement between Canada and the European Union, one senior government official told CBC News.
And yet neither the Canadians nor the Europeans are downplaying the large expectations they have for an expanded EU-Canada alliance that goes far beyond the current Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA).
Carney 'nailed it' at Davos: EU committee chair
"Europeans looked very positively on him and on that speech in Davos," said Sven Simon, chair of the European Parliament's committee on constitutional affairs. "He nailed it. He put it really in the right direction. I think in those uncertain times, we, both the Europeans and Canadians, have a huge interest in closer co-operation."
Carney himself, while stressing that this trip is not the grand finale of a grand bargain, told Bloomberg News that he expects great things in the future.
"It's an exciting time. Look, it's not going to be solved this week in Strasbourg. This, to be clear, it's the start of a process, but it's the start of a high-ambition process."
All indications are that both sides are heavily focused on the Canada-EU Summit scheduled for Oct. 29-30.
"I think that there is a significant step to be done in October because both parties would like to enhance or to elevate their relationship," EU Ambassador to Canada Geneviève Tuts told CBC's Power and Politics.
"We want to reimagine the relationship between the EU and Canada."
Rattled Europeans
Hans-Gert Pöttering, a former president of the European Parliament who visited Canada last week, told CBC News that the Trump administration's treatment of Canada had shocked Europeans.
"There is somebody who wants to make Canada the 51st state of the United States. And all these crazy ideas, I think are the basis that we see how important Canada is for us," he said.
Both Canadian and European officials often say they want to work with "like-minded" allies, and for the Canadians, "like-minded" has increasingly come to mean "European," while for Europeans, it increasingly means "Canadian."
Both sides have poured cold water on any talk of Canada joining the EU. The Canadians say they aren't interested in the basic formula of EU membership under which countries give up some sovereignty in return for access.
Canada is engaging with Europe in order to strengthen its sovereignty, not to dilute it, a senior official told CBC News.
The same official said that reporting in the Wall Street Journal that suggested Canada was looking to reproduce arrangements that non-EU members such as Norway have with the union — which do involve some concessions on sovereignty — are false.
No name yet to define the relationship
European officials also say they envision an alliance between the EU and Canada, rather than an amalgamation. But the partnership they envision would go further than the current relationship with the United Kingdom.
Germany's David McAllister, who chairs the foreign affairs committee of the European Parliament, told CBC News that neither side had yet paid much attention to labels — but stressed the EU is not trying to get Canada to surrender sovereignty
On the contrary, McAllister, who trained in Manitoba at CFB Shiloh as a young soldier in the German Army, said Europe was willing to collaborate with Canada to protect itself from U.S. threats.
- What we know about Carney's push for a 'unique alliance' with the EU
- AnalysisZelenskyy's comparison of Canada to Ukraine is imperfect — but it matters
"We in Europe understand that threats and economic pressure against an ally simply damaged the trust which we need among transatlantic allies," he said. "That's why the U.S.-Canadian dispute, which President Trump is responsible for, has received such wide media coverage all over Europe."
On the trade front, 99 per cent of commerce between Canada and the European Union is already tariff-free. Both sides speak about the importance of getting 10 holdout countries, including France and Italy, to ratify CETA, but that's mostly symbolic.
Canada is also already integrated into two vital pan-European projects: the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program that provides low-interest loans for joint military procurement and the Horizon program that funds scientific research.
Untapped possibilities
But both sides say there are areas of co-operation that remain under-exploited or even unexplored.
There have been signs of openness to increased labour mobility, although it's very unlikely that would go as far as the full freedom of movement that exists in the EU.
Two areas appear to be of greatest interest. The first is to use the free trade framework that already exists to build a genuine synergy between Canada's natural resource and energy wealth, and Europe's large market and manufacturing capacity, to the benefit of both economies.
CETA "is actually a fantastic framework, but we are not fully using it either in Europe or in Canada," said Tobias Cremer, who sits on the foreign affairs and defence committees of the European Parliament.
"A lot of our especially medium- and small-sized companies don't even know the potential we have. Canada has all this potential, but the infrastructure for instance isn't actually set up yet to go across the Atlantic."
- Mark Carney to meet with Emmanuel Macron in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon
- European Parliament to open Ottawa office as Carney seeks 'unique alliance' with EU
Both Carney and the Europeans often point out that Europe — large and rich but resource poor — and Canada — lightly populated but resource and energy-rich — complement one another naturally. That is not always as evident in the U.S.-Canada relationship where, in any case, the current U.S. administration views Canada more as a rival than a partner.
A second avenue is to combine forces in sovereignty-protecting projects that would be difficult for Canada to do on its own.
In his interview with Bloomberg, Carney said that "sovereignty is determined by where you stand in a series of strategic capabilities in space, obviously in AI, in sovereign computing, in critical minerals, in energy."
Carney also mentioned financial payments as a potential vulnerability, one of "those interconnections, that integration [that] can be used as leverage against you."
China has long viewed dependence on the U.S. dollar and the U.S.-based SWIFT system for international payments as a weakness, and sought to "de-dollarize" not only its bond holdings but also its trade with other countries. India, Brazil, Saudi Arabia and the U.A.E. have all set up new facilities for trading payments to avoid the dollar and go around U.S. banks, and increasingly, traditional U.S. allies are thinking along the same lines.
The U.S. would likely perceive any move by Canada and Europe to cut SWIFT out of their trading arrangements as another threat to a U.S. dollar that is already losing ground as the world's go-to currency for trading and saving.
Planning and stockpiling together
Building sovereign resilience could also involve holding shared stockpiles of essentials. The pandemic, as well as transportation bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz and Suez Canal, and the trade disruptions of the Trump era have moved governments away from the just-in-time delivery mentality of a decade ago to one of planning and hoarding.
"We're hearing talk in Canada about stockpiling raw materials," said Mark Camilleri, Brussels-based president of the Canada EU Trade and Investment Association. "Maybe there's a way that we can work together in a trusted manner, in a more efficient way, in what's becoming a very inefficient world."
Canada is sending a message to the Trump administration, says Brian Clow, former prime minister Justin Trudeau's chief adviser on the Canada-U.S. relationship: "We can sell elsewhere. We can have security partnerships elsewhere."
"Both Europe and Canada are under attack, frankly, by the United States on our economy, on our sovereignty, and that is pushing us closer together," said Clow.
For the Carney government, Europe is not only a place to trade, but also a potential replacement partner with which to integrate sovereign networks, launch satellites, stockpile critical minerals and build a strong defence manufacturing base, or as Carney put it to Bloomberg, a place to "deepen co-operation with like-minded partners so you have sovereignty, so you have resilience, so you have independence.
"No country can do that alone."

'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'
- Published
A Nigerian man has shared the story of how he rose up out of "abject poverty" as a child, to become one of the leading UK academics in his field.
David Etor, 43, who grew up in Nigeria, only learned to read and write aged 12 and was told as a child that "nothing good will come out of you", but is now a lecturer in electrical and mechanical engineering at the University of Bristol.
He told the BBC how his family was so poor growing up that his mum would pretend to cook food in a kitchen they shared with others, "to protect our integrity" in front of neighbours.
"I didn't see a way out," he said.
'The poor called us poor'
Speaking to John Darvall on BBC Radio Bristol about the publication of his first book, Etor described growing up in a "compound" with several other families, all sharing a single kitchen, toilet and bathroom.
"It was a very poor neighbourhood. We were particularly very poor that the poor neighbours would refer to us as poor," he said.
"I do remember that there was a time where my mum would boil water.
"[She would] go back in and out, lift the lid, stir the water, go back into the room [and] come back as though she was preparing food...
"She would come back in with that pot of water after a couple of hours and it will be as though she's just finished cooking a meal, but it was just water.
"She was trying to protect our integrity."
