Can merchants pass UPI charges to buyers? Key questions on MDR, its implementation answered
The finalized MDR framework and threshold structure will take effect from October 15, 2026, for the updating for software and billing systems.
The announcement of a 0.4% Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on UPI payments above ₹2,000 made to merchants has raised several questions on how the charges will work, who will bear them and can these be shifted on to consumers in any way.
The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) on Tuesday issued a clarification on the MDR – from the ₹2,000 threshold for merchant payments and fee caps. It further addressed queries on fuel purchases, utility bills, platform fees and person-to-person transactions.
Key questions on MDR and its implementation
Why the introduction of MDR now?
On the introduction of 0.4% MDR above transactions of ₹2,000, the NPCI said that UPI processes billions of transactions every month.
Deep Dive
“The MDR is distributed only amongst the UPI ecosystem, to further invest into infrastructure resiliency, innovation, cybersecurity (protecting the UPI Infrastructure with banks and non-banks) and customer service,” the NPCI stated.
Also Read | What is Merchant Discount Rate and how MDR will be calculated after revised UPI charges
However, it said the annual government incentive/ subsidy for UPI was designed as a “short-term bridge funding” rather than a permanent measure to compensate the cost incurred by the payment industry.
According to industry estimates, maintaining UPI payment operations, server bandwidth, fraud prevention systems, and bank technical support costs around ~ ₹20,000 crore annually. Relying solely on fiscal budget allocations creates funding uncertainty and limits long-term technology investments by banks and fintech, NPCI said.
When will the MDR charges take effect?
The finalised MDR framework and threshold structure will take effect from October 15, 2026, giving acquiring banks, payment aggregators, fintech applications, and corporate accounting platforms adequate lead time to update their software engines and billing systems.
Can merchants pass the MDR to the consumers?
While the charges are now being applied to merchants, there have been concerns about these being passed on the buyers.
However, the NPCI clarified that merchants on-boarded cannot pass on MDR charges to customers while accepting payments through UPI. It said the framework ensures that consumers pay “only the posted price.”
How will MDR be calculated for transactions?
The charging of MDR will follow a clear, predictable formula based on transaction value thresholds. For example, for a purchase of ₹3,000, applying the 0.4% rate results in an MDR fee of ₹12 paid by the merchant to its acquiring bank.
Similarly, for a ₹50,000 purchase, a 0.4% fee equals ₹200. However, for a a high-value purchase of ₹1,00,000, the 0.4% calculation (which equals ₹400) is superseded by the fixed maximum cap of ₹300 ( ₹300 is the fixed maximum cap per transaction for payments of ₹75,000 and above. Any transaction under ₹2,000 incurs no MDR.
How does the MDR charge in UPI compare to debit and credit cards?
UPI MDR is structured to be much lower than all traditional card-based transaction fees, according to NPCI. Standard credit card MDRs typically range from 1.5% to 2.5% per transaction, while debit card MDRs are capped up to 0.90%. However UPI MDR sets the baseline at 0.4% on transaction above ₹ 2,000 and caps it at ₹300 for high-value purchases.
The cost difference will help merchants lower their payment processing expenses while accepting digital transactions, NPCI said.
Who decides on the implementation and enforcement of UPI caps?
The final decision on the operational parameters, fee distribution models, and category caps is made by the UPI and Services Steering Committee, headed by NPCI.
Will consumers be charged platform fees or for person-to-person transactions?
P2P transactions will continue to be free-of-cost for both the payer and the beneficiary, and there will be no charges for any person transferring or receiving any amount to or from any other person using UPI.
Further, UPI app providers cannot charge Platform Fee or any other charge for any payment made through UPI.
What happens when small merchants receive payment above ₹2000?
Small merchants operating under the P2PM framework will continue with zero MDR, NPCI said. R. These are small vendors receiving up to ₹1 lac per month through UPI QR directly into their accounts.
Also Read | Govt says no UPI charges up to ₹2,000, Congress scoffs: Inside the digital wallet row
The Person-to-Person-Merchant (P2PM) framework is a specialized account category created by NPCI to support small vendors receiving payments directly into their own personal bank accounts. Under P2PM guidelines, small merchants receiving up to ₹1 lakh per month through UPI QR codes enjoy a mandatory zero-MDR.
Therefore, receiving a payment above ₹2,000 does not impose a charge on a small merchant operating under exempted tiers like P2PM. MDR applicability is determined by overall merchant account categorisation.
Which categories will qualify for a flat MDR instead of percentage rate?
For specific merchant categories such as railways, telecom services, insurance, and fuel among others, a flat MDR of ₹5 per transaction will be applicable for transaction above ₹2,000.
These will not be charged a 0.4% variable rate. These specific sectors pay a fixed fee of ₹5 regardless of the transaction amount, NPCI said.
Fuel purchases made at petrol stations via UPI qualify for the flat concessional rate of ₹5 for payments over ₹2,000. The flat ₹5 fee protects petrol pump operators from high processing fees on tank refills. For all fuel payments under ₹2,000, the MDR remains at 0%,

Foodtech unicorn Rebel Foods managed to cut its net loss for the fiscal year FY26 by 16.3% to ₹281.8 Cr from ₹336.6 Cr in the previous fiscal. Operating revenue rose 20.7% to ₹1,951.6 Cr compared to ₹1,617.4 Cr in FY25. The rise in revenue was led by product sales. Revenue from the sale of food items rose 20.9% to ₹1,891.9 Cr in the year under review from ₹1,565.3 Cr in FY25, while service revenue — commission, storage and franchise income — stayed broadly flat at ₹32.7 Cr. Other operating revenues, which includes delivery services income, rose 38.5% to ₹27 Cr from ₹19.5 Cr last year. Meanwhile, international revenue jumped 38.8% YoY to ₹283.81 Cr, while revenue from India grew 18% to ₹1,667.75 Cr. Revenue from overseas contributed 14.5% to the startup’s top line in FY26, a slight improvement from 12.6% in FY25. Rebel Foods currently operates 45+ brands across India, the United Arab Emirates and the United Kingdom. Including other income of ₹43.4 Cr, the total income stood at ₹1,995 Cr in FY26, up 20.3% from ₹1,658 Cr in the previous fiscal. EBITDA loss also narrowed about 50% to ₹62.4 Cr from ₹123.7 Cr in the previous fiscal. The startup said that a stronger consumer engagement and continued improvements across store operations, tech and supply chain contributed to higher productivity and margin expansion in the fiscal year. “FY26 marks an important step forward for Rebel Foods, with growth and profitability increasingly coming together. As our platform scales, we are seeing the benefits of stronger consumer engagement, higher store productivity and operating leverage flow through to the business. Our focus remains on building a predictable, sustainable and highly scalable food platform for the long term,” cofounder and global CEO Ankush Grover said. Founded in 2011 by Kallol Banerjee and Jaydeep Barman, Rebel Foods started as a delivery-only brand with ‘Faasos’. Over the years it has expanded the number of labels it operates. Its portfolio of quick service restaurant (QSR) brands includes names like Behrouz Biryani, Mandarin Oak, Oven Story Pizza, Sweet Truth, LunchBox, The Good Bowl, Firangi Bake, the Biryani Life and Wendy’s, serving across 120+ cities. The startup has raised $773 Mn in funding to date from the likes of KKR, Temasek, Lightbox, Evolvence, among others. The startup entered the unicorn club in 2021 after raising $175 Mn in its Series F round from investors Qatar Investment Authority, Coatue and Evolvence. Rebel Foods has been recalibrating its financial and operational strategy as it reportedly eyes a public listing in India. Earlier, it had launched QuickiES, a 15-minute food delivery service, and planned to expand its offline footprint through physical restaurants and food courts. However, the startup had to shut down the vertical earlier this year amid high cash burn. It has also been seeking to leverage its global presence and multi-brand portfolio, while improving unit economics and moving towards EBITDA breakeven. A leadership reshuffle, with Ankush Grover elevated to global CEO and Jaydeep Barman moving to chairman and group CEO, further aligned the organisation for its next phase ahead of a possible public listing. Magnifying Rebel Foods’ Spending The startup’s total expenses for the fiscal rose 14.1% to ₹2,265.9 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,986.6 Cr in the previous year. Here is a breakdown of where Rebel Foods spent the most: Cost of Raw Materials Consumed: Comprising 34.6% of the total expenses, the spend on raw materials, components and packing materials rose 15.6% to ₹784.4 Cr during the year under review from ₹678.5 Cr in FY25. Employee Benefit Expenses: Employee costs, which includes salaries, wages, gratuity fund and provident fund, rose 6.3% to ₹412.3 Cr from ₹387.8 Cr in FY25. Brokerage And Commission: The biggest expense growth in FY26 was from this head, where it rose 30.6% to ₹317.7 Cr from ₹243.3 Cr in the previous fiscal.

Rockstar Games’ best-selling Grand Theft Auto series wasn’t often accused of political sensitivity during its legendary run from the late 1990s through the early 2010s.
In fact, parents and activists denounced the franchise for exposing children to a seedy world of sex, violence, crude humor, and wanton crime. Elon Musk even claimed that he couldn’t get into the last installment, GTA V, because he was mortified to play as a character who shoots police officers.
But times (and moral panics) change. In the 13 years that fans have waited for Grand Theft Auto VI—finally out on November 19—the American right-wing grievance machine has drifted from fears of impressionable kids turning to a life of larceny to concerns that they will grow up “woke.” And despite knowing very little about the forthcoming game, the agitators of the latter movement have decided it must amount to a stealth campaign to poison the youth with depictions of gender equality, LGBTQ acceptance, and racial diversity. (Rockstar did not immediately return a request for comment.)
Since the height of Gamergate in 2014, an angst-ridden subset of male gamers have maintained a paranoid vigil against what they see as the creeping influence of women and LGBTQ developers in the gaming world. Between the feverish anticipation for GTA VI and the various delays of its release date, they’ve had ample opportunity to foment a preemptive backlash to what is sure to be a massive hit, not unlike the failed furor over supposedly “woke” elements of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey.
“GTA 6 is a humiliation ritual for all male gamers,” an X user with the handle @Wokenessisevil complained on Tuesday, sharing a clip of the game’s two lead characters, Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, who are in a relationship that evolves based on the player’s choices. In the scene, Lucia, the series’ first mandatory female protagonist, asks Jason to pick an outfit for her and expresses mild annoyance when he seems more or less indifferent to the options she presents.
It’s an exchange that could have been lifted from any sitcom of the past 50 years, yet it seems to have fueled a reactionary narrative about the game’s male protagonist being subjugated to a nefarious feminist agenda. Another X user recently claimed, contrary to the clip’s bog-standard depiction of a heterosexual couple, that Jason has a “gay vibe,” since no straight man would know what sequins are or use the word “cocktails,” as he does in the clip.
“The script is definitely written by a woman who has no clue what a man thinks or how he talks,” they wrote. “Jason is written as a caricature, much like what a delusional woman thinks a ‘man’ should be.”
Similarly, a gaming YouTuber seethed that Rockstar was appealing to women and gay men by showing Jason shirtless in another scene. “Gone are the days of edgy based masculine GTA games,” he wrote on X. “I could be wrong but right now it’s looking like it will be a woke fest.”
While multiple leaks and a 27-minute “extended look” preview on Netflix have revealed key details of the game, and Rockstar creatives declared their intent to realistically portray the diversity of the Miami-inspired setting and bring a fleshed-out female character into the spotlight, would-be detractors are still straining a bit for reasons to pronounce it dead on arrival. One YouTuber has convinced himself that it will subliminally brainwash players with “bisexual lighting.”
Other men have simply defaulted to rank sexism, griping that Lucia’s breasts are too small because of “they/thems” working at Rockstar or posting jokes such as: “female lead in GTA 6? i thought the whole point of GTA was to be able to drive.” An AI enthusiast used an image generator to replace a woman of color in a crop top on the game’s cover with a white blonde in a bikini.
While each new snippet of content has become grist for more manufactured outrage, the tantrums over the ideological trajectory of GTA began long ago. In 2022, for its remastered version of GTA V, Rockstar removed a number of gags and non-playable characters that critics had described as transphobic, leading to complaints from some fans.
The following year, after the game publisher released a trailer for GTA VI, trolls floated the groundless theory that the Lucia character was a transgender woman. Last month, when former video game executive Mark Kern, known for his crusades against “woke” content, deemed Lucia attractive, his followers disagreed in openly racist and misogynistic replies.
Much of this ire is aimed directly at the Rockstar team, who have been blasted for allegedly embracing “identity politics,” reportedly making efforts to avoid punching down against marginalized groups in the game’s storyline, and allowing women to contribute in any way to the franchise. A photo of female staff at the company’s studio in Scotland, shared on social media in 2019 to commemorate International Women’s Day, has circulated widely with sneering comments about how they likely ruined GTA VI.
Yet a few prominent streamers on the right, including Zack Hoyt (better known as Asmongold) and white nationalist Nick Fuentes, have taken a wait-and-see approach, declining to bash the game before checking it out for themselves. Fuentes went so far as to mock those bemoaning its creative direction. “Just go outside, touch grass,” he told one viewer who brought up the topic in his live chat.
If any of these gamers entertain fantasies of an actual boycott or commercial failure, they are bound to be disappointed. According to one estimate of preorders from a third-party data analytics firm, Rockstar has already sold 5.28 million copies of GTA VI, taking in more than $500 million in revenue. Though it is likely the most expensive game ever made, with a budget somewhere north of a billion dollars, the studio stands to easily recoup that cost, possibly by the day it comes out.
That might call for a moment of reflection from the culture warriors—or so you’d think. It’s awfully difficult, it seems, to admit that you’re so out of touch with the mainstream and have no control over the popularity of various media. They will no doubt have their objections to other aspects of the game, but once GTA VI starts breaking records, there won’t be any point in continuing the crusade. By then, the next fake controversy will be on the horizon.

Harleen Deol is raring to go for the newest opportunity in her career: Women’s Caribbean Premier League (WCPL).
The India international became the fifth Indian to join the ongoing edition after a last-minute move saw her sign for defending champion Barbados Tridents.
She’ll share the dressing room with pace-bowling all-rounder Pooja Vastrakar and big-hitter Kiran Navgire. Meanwhile, wicketkeeper-batter Yastika Bhatia and pace ace Shikha Pandey have been drafted by the Trinbago Knight Riders.
“It’s been amazing. I’ve just attended one practice session, and then we went on a cruise for a team bonding activity. That was a really nice experience,” Harleen, for whom this is a maiden international franchise stint, told reporters on Friday.
The 28-year-old has been part of the Women’s Premier League since its inaugural edition in 2023, representing Gujarat Giants for three seasons. Most recently, she played for the UP Warriorz. She has amassed 653 runs in 28 innings overall, striking at 116.19.
“Shashank Shekhar Tapikar (Cricket Operations, Barbados Tridents) sir had approached me and asked whether I wanted to play in WCPL. I said ‘why not’. It’d be a different experience, different wickets, and different people. Franchise cricket is a bit different but it’s good for learning,” the 28-year-old batter revealed.
Harleen was part of India’s 2025 ODI World Cup-winning squad and travelled to England for the historic first-ever women’s Test at Lord’s, although she didn’t feature in the four-day fixture.
However, the Punjab player did not make the T20 World Cup 2026, Asia Cup, and the Asian Games squads. The last time she played a T20I for India was last December. Moreover, she was also left out of the India A squads for the ongoing multi-format home series against the visiting Australians after captaining One-Day A squad during the England tour in May. India won the 50-over leg 2-1, with Harleen registering a half century in the opening fixture too.
Missing out on action with the Indian setup, at A or senior level, doesn’t bother her.
“I don’t think a lot about these things. Wherever I am, it’s the same cricket that is to be played. I just want to play and enjoy, and give my best wherever I’m playing,” she explained.
“I don’t think as a player you change a lot in your technique. Yes, you can watch someone and learn something from them. But I don’t think you can change your technique through this method. I have not changed too much,” she said when asked whether she would use this WCPL stint to better her T20 game.
“If we talk about internationals, it’s not that I haven’t done well in T20Is. It’s about the combinations that fit in.”
For now, Harleen wants to bank on a tried and tested mantra during her stay in the Caribbean: going with the flow.
“ Ye sab plan karte karte banda fass jata hai (You get stuck as soon as you start planning what you want to achieve). I’m someone who takes it one day at a time. If you think too much ahead, it can disappoint you. In T20 cricket, I’m focussing on my process and not the result.”

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Charlotte Mandrier. It has been edited for length and clarity.
On Monday, September 14, I was cleaning up my inbox and deleting emails when I saw that Starbucks was collaborating with the Peanuts brand to sell merchandise inspired by "The Great Pumpkin."
I remembered last year when Starbucks released a small number of bear cups. My daughter, who is 9, had wanted one but hadn't managed to get hold of one. She was so disappointed.
She clearly hadn't known about the Snoopy cups that were going on sale, or I would have heard about it from her. She is obsessed with Peanuts, Snoopy, and "The Great Pumpkin."
She watches the movie all year long
As an autistic person, she has a special interest in Peanuts, specifically "The Great Pumpkin." She watches it all year long, even though it is a very fall movie. She listens to the music from the film's soundtrack. She was born in Santa Rosa, where the museum commemorating Charles Schulz — the cartoonist who created the Peanuts comic — is located. When she was little, she went to a camp at the museum and learned to ice skate at Snoopy's Home Ice next door. She even looks like Linus. She loves everything about this brand.
As it happened, her birthday is in two days. So when I saw that these limited-edition Snoopy cups and other merchandise celebrating the movie would be on sale, I told my husband I was going to try to get one for her.
I woke up in the middle of the night
I set my alarm for Tuesday morning at 3:30 a.m., quietly sneaking out of the house to arrive at our closest Starbucks in downtown Chevy Chase at 4 a.m., when it opens.
Walking six blocks to get there, I only saw one other woman on the street. It turned out she was going to the same Starbucks to wait in line, too.
When I got there, no one was in line yet, and I felt so relieved. I had imagined that there would already be a huge line, with people hoping to take all the stock to resell it later.
I suppose that since it was a fairly commercial area, rather than a residential area, people didn't think to go there to get the merchandise.
Slowly, others arrived. There were three of us waiting for the merchandise, and three regulars who were just there to get their coffee.
Although they were meant to open the doors at 4 a.m., apparently, there was a staffing issue, and they didn't open until 5 a.m. The regulars said that it wasn't normal for the shop to open late.
The lights were on, but we couldn't see anyone inside. We tried knocking because we weren't sure if someone was there, and just didn't know we were waiting. We were desperate to get the good stuff.
There were about 10 Snoopy cups
While we waited, I used my phone to take photos of the merchandise and count how many cups were available. I could see about 10.
Then someone finally unlocked and opened the doors for us. Once I got in, I bought a Snoopy cup, a tote bag, a keychain, a mug, and some pins. It came to about $200.
One of the regulars who was there got swept up in the hype and got a cup, even though it wasn't why she'd come.
It was incredibly exciting that I had managed to get the stuff. I was so excited, imagining my daughter's face in two days when she opens her birthday presents.
Sneaking back into the house at 5:30 a.m. and hiding it all away, I pretended I had just woken up.
As soon as she sees on YouTube that these cups were for sale, I know she'll be disappointed, thinking that, like last year, she missed out. I'll give an Oscar-winning performance, telling her I wish we could have gotten there sooner, and maybe we can look for Snoopy cups that people are selling online.
And then, in two days, I'll give her all the Peanuts presents. I really cannot wait.

Center for Countering Digital Hate founder Imran Ahmed sued to challenge an immigration policy targeting researchers monitoring the biggest US platforms.
Credit:
via CCDH
Center for Countering Digital Hate founder Imran Ahmed sued to challenge an immigration policy targeting researchers monitoring the biggest US platforms.
Credit:
via CCDH
In July, a judge blocked as unconstitutional an immigration policy that the US relied on to weigh whether to detain and deport people who flag illegal or harmful online content as national security risks. In his announcement of the policy, Secretary of State Marco Rubio explained that by targeting a list of researchers—which he stood “ready and willing” to expand—the policy supposedly served to prevent foreign nationals from manipulating digital town squares and censoring Americans.
However, in his order siding with the Coalition for Independent Technology Research (CITR) and staying the policy, US District Judge James Boasberg said the US showed no evidence linking any targeted researchers to a foreign power that might be attempting to censor Americans or manipulate US public debate. Deemed too broad, the policy could sweep in seemingly any noncitizen working in content moderation, the judge said.
Last week, the US appealed that ruling, a move that CITR expected. It notably came two days after another court found that it had no jurisdiction to decide a case raised by a hate speech researcher and lawful permanent resident fighting to strike down the policy permanently.
In that case, US District Judge Loretta Preska called out Rubio for determining that the founder of a United Kingdom group called the Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH), Imran Ahmed, was a threat due to his lobbying and advocacy.
“Without any hint of irony,” the secretary decided it was “necessary” to deport Ahmed in order to protect American “freedom of expression” and to “reject encroachments” that “undermine the exercise of our fundamental right to free speech,” Preska wrote.
Ultimately, however, she ruled that Congress had removed courts’ authority to block the US government from initiating removal proceedings, so she could not grant Ahmed’s request for a permanent injunction. Even though “Ahmed may very well have valid causes of action,” Preska wrote that his lawsuit was “premature.” Technology researchers are alarmed that the decision seems to suggest that federal courts can never review the legal basis for an immigration policy connected to removal proceedings, even if it’s unconstitutional.
For Ahmed, Preska’s ruling came with high personal stakes. Although the Trump administration has not initiated removal proceedings, Preska’s order allowed it to start that process after only five days. Acting quickly, Ahmed appealed, then asked both Preska and the appeals court to extend a temporary restraining order blocking his detention or deportation. Since she expressed sympathy in her order, it’s not surprising that Preska quickly granted that request, blocking the US from taking any action until the appeals court rules on Ahmed’s request.
But now his fate depends on the appeals court agreeing that a federal court should have the “power to prevent the illegal arrest, detention, and transfer of a green card holder based on the Administration’s policy of retaliating against speech criticizing the practices at the major technology companies,” his appeal said.
Ahmed told Ars that he remains optimistic that the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit will see through the government’s seeming plan to use the policy to “broadly chill protected speech.”
“As a plurality of the active judges of the Second Circuit has already held,” the State Department’s cited authorities “do not permit the Executive to arrest, detain, or transfer noncitizens without judicial review,” Ahmed argued.
Boasberg apparently agreed. He held in the CITR case that it matters that “the prospect that [a] policy may later contribute to some noncitizen’s removal does not transform a challenge to the policy into the review of an order of removal.”
US lacks evidence of censorship
Ahmed noted that the US never opposed the restraining order, even though his research with CCDH has continued. Last week when the US started more aggressively defending the policy, CCDH contributed research to a major New York Times investigation. In that report, spot checks showed that some of the “most egregious examples” of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) continue to go undetected on Elon Musk’s social media platform X.
CCDH “gave access to more than four million links to Grok-generated images compiled for researchers” at the Canadian Center for Children Protection for that review, the NYT reported. In total, 65 AI-generated CSAM images were found, as well as 75 known CSAM images. Some images were viewed hundreds of times. (Asked for comment, X linked to an X Safety post saying, “X has zero tolerance for CSAM.)
Ahmed told Ars that officials specifically cited his group’s support for the European Union fining X a record $1 billion as cause for his national-security designation. However, so far, no evidence has shown that he might pose “serious adverse foreign policy consequences.” Instead, officials rely on “shifting, contradictory, and unsupported rationales” to justify what Ahmed alleged is retaliation for being a thorn in Musk’s side.
Meanwhile, Ahmed “faces the imminent prospect of unconstitutional arrest, punitive detention, and expulsion” from his home country, where he lives with his American wife and daughters.
“I may be British, but even I know that transparency isn’t censorship and that speaking truth to the most powerful person on the planet is precisely the intention of the First Amendment,” Ahmed said.
Reached for comment on what risk Ahmed’s ongoing research might pose to American tech firms or online discourse, a spokesperson told Ars that the State Department does not comment on ongoing litigation. However, the spokesperson reiterated that the department has authority to recommend removal proceedings for any noncitizen whose US activities could have “serious adverse foreign policy consequences.”
Appeals court may favor content mods
In his appeal, Ahmed argued that the immigration policy violates several laws, including the First Amendment and the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment.
Preska agreed that those claims may be valid, but she nevertheless found that the relief he was supposedly seeking—a permanent injunction blocking the US from using the policy to detain or deport him—stripped the federal court of jurisdiction.
Although Ahmed disclaimed seeking that relief and sought other relief, including vacating the policy and declaring the government’s actions unconstitutional, his “single most important reason for filing this case is to be able to remain here with his wife and daughters,” Preska wrote. To her, it seemed the relief he sought was “inextricably linked” to “any potential removal order he might face because it is ‘a necessary prerequisite’ to stop his deportation.”
Preska was further bound to deny Ahmed’s petition because of a recent ruling that found the government’s authority over removal proceedings can extend to “questions of law and fact” arising in challenges to removal, “not just removal orders,” she wrote.
But that recent ruling is currently being challenged, Ahmed’s appeal noted. “The full Court took the unusual step of granting rehearing en banc before a petition for rehearing was filed,” due to the belief by six judges that federal courts do “have jurisdiction to provide relief in these circumstances,” his appeal said.
“That history strongly suggests that the Court will soon hold that federal courts possess jurisdiction,” Ahmed argued. “At the very least, it raises a strong showing” that he “will prevail on the merits with respect to jurisdiction.”
He also argued that courts have distinguished claims of retaliatory detention as independent of claims tied to removal proceedings.
To keep his fight alive, Ahmed reiterated to the appeals court that he does not want an injunction that “would prevent the Government from commencing removal proceedings against him.” Instead, he wants to resolve his challenges regarding the “government’s use of arrest and detention to punish protected speech,” which he argued “can be resolved without reviewing a removal order or preventing an immigration court from adjudicating his removability.” That’s necessary to prevent widespread harms across the content-moderation sector, he alleged.
“It would be deeply concerning if people could be detained at the whim of any government official,” Ahmed told Ars.
“We will not be silenced”
Ahmed is hoping the appeals court will approve his request to stay the restraining order while weighing these questions that could impact technology research across the US.
In his appeal, he confirmed that he “does not intend to leave the United States or voluntarily submit to immigration detention while he seeks appellate review. He will remain with his American wife and children and continue to advocate for transparency and accountability for social media companies. Without a stay, he will do so under the immediate threat that the government may arrest and detain him at any time.”
Ahmed told Ars that he’s willing to risk temporary detention to protect technology researchers’ speech rights. But he thinks that “anyone with a passing familiarity with the US Constitution will be able to see this for what it is, which is the use of the awe-inspiring power of the US government to silence someone who has annoyed a friend of the administration, Mr. Musk.”
He said that he founded CCDH with the goal of making platforms safer for everyone after losing a colleague to a gunman radicalized online. About 90 percent of that work is simply testing if promised safeguards actually work, Ahmed told Ars. Despite the pressure from Trump officials, CCDH continues to flag defective safeguards. This fall, they’re preparing a report on safety on AI platforms that he confirmed will show that safeguards from firms, including OpenAI, aren’t working as they should.
“If the aim of the State Department or the tech overlords who’ve been celebrating this and no doubt urging them on from the beginning was to silence us, they failed,” Ahmed told Ars. “We will not back down,” he continued. “We will not be silenced.”
At home, his daughters are too young to understand how his work now threatens to break up their family. Seven years into CCDH’s monitoring of social media for harmful content, Ahmed told Ars that he remains dedicated to protecting Americans online and still hopes to become an American citizen one day. If necessary, he’ll take his fight to the Supreme Court.
“We have to show that we will not be cowed from this vital work, and it is vital,” he told Ars.
And while the focus isn’t completely on Musk, when it comes to X—which has come under fire globally after its chatbot Grok generated CSAM—Ahmed questioned why the Department of Justice hasn’t sparked their own probes based on his group’s and others’ reporting.
“I do think that DOJ should be focusing on a platform that is now proliferating and creating child sex abuse material rather than trying to punish the person who’s identifying the problem,” Ahmed told Ars.
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

It was a battle cry that was heard on the sands of the Marina on Tuesday (September 15, 2026) when representatives of fishermen panchayats issued an ultimatum for the Tamil Nadu government to give up the proposal for building the Secretariat-cum-Assembly complex at Foreshore Estate.

On food labelling and misleading claims, weight loss drugs, climate change, rabies, cancer care, and more
(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Ramya Kannan writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
This past week, as with the previous week, the nation continues to be concerned with food labelling. With the Supreme Court bringing up the packaged food labelling issue up again, a couple of weeks ago, it has been surely and firmly dragged into the public platform. There has been a great deal of interest in the Food Safety and Standards Association of India’s recommendations on front-of-pack labels, and debate about the merits of the case.
What are these standards that FSSAI promises to hold the packaged food in India up to? We took a long,hard look.
For an idea of what the whole FSSAI submission on labelling was, initially, check out this conversation between Zubeda Hamid and I; we also indicate trends worldwide, in Sunday’s Health Wrap video. While appreciable that some standards have come to play in this entirely unregulated sector, there are questions about the caveats in the proposed recommendations. FSSAI has proposed that the warning initially apply to products high in two or more of the three “nutrients of concern” — added sugar, added saturated fat and salt — as well as specified highly sweetened beverages. Activists find the “two or more” classification problematic.
For a more detailed explanation on what the Red hexagon on your snack pack means, read what Bindu Shajan Perappadan wrote. FSSAI has proposed a two-phase rollout. In the first phase, products high in at least two of the three nutrients would carry the red hexagon, along with specified highly sweetened beverages. In the second phase, the warning would extend to products high in any one of the three nutrients. However, FSSAI has not specified a firm timeline for moving to the second phase. The FSSAI proposal refers to added sugar and added saturated fat, rather than total sugar and total fat. The plan is to exempt single-ingredient foods and products inherently rich in these nutrients, including ghee, edible oil, jaggery and honey.
Meanwhile, Soibam Rocky Singh explains why the Central Consumer Protection Authority is cracking down on ‘100%’ claims on food products. Such claims can give consumers an impression of absolute purity or completeness that may not match what is actually inside the packet. The FSSAI has also asked food businesses to stop using “100%” claims on food labels, packaging and promotional material.
Here, Prabalika M. Borah examines the hype behind Proffee: protien+coffee, and here are the highlights of an ICMR-NIN study which shows that Vitamin D3 outperforms D2 in supporting muscles and heart.
Close on the nutrition topic is weight loss drugs. A recent study showed that GLP-1 weight loss drugs are effective even at low starter doses, with lower side effects. Yet another study in the United States showed that more children under 12 in U.S. are being prescribed weight-loss drugs. Prescriptions for GLP-1 weight-loss drugs among children under 12 in the U.S. have risen more than 300-fold since 2019.
Here is a supervised experiment of a fitness coaching putting himself through a GLP 1 course, recording minute observations through the course. Arvind Ashok writes: ‘I’m a fitness coach. I tried a GLP-1 drug for three weeks’, issuing a statutory warning to readers not to attempt the same at home without a prescription.
Climate change will also never be further than a beck and call away. It has dominated headlines periodically, and likely will be even more frequent in future. Jacob Koshy writes: Global warming will exceed limit, UN says in a report that maps path to get back below danger zone. UNEP’s detailed ‘overshoot, peak and decline’ pathway seeks to hold the peak as low as possible and then bring temperatures back down below the 1.5°C limit; report terms it ‘best remaining option’.
Yet another new study highlights the life-saving role of air conditioning, but indicates that it comes at a cost. Do check this story out, for the details: Keeping cool saves thousands of lives yearly, but at a cost of worsening global warming, experts say.
On the rabies front, there was some exciting news in the region. I record how Bhutan leads South-East Asia in eliminating rabies as public health problem. The WHO also validated Bhutan’s claim and explained that this was achieved through conscious of deployment of the One Health approach, affording some key lessons for neighbour India too.
Meanwhile, Authorities are probing ‘counterfeit’ rabies vaccine, and the counterfeit ‘Abhayrab’ rabies vaccine batch remains under investigation. Why is this important? With rabies, the margin for error is exceptionally small. A genuine, potent vaccine administered promptly can prevent a fatal disease; a counterfeit product can create the dangerous illusion that protection has been provided.
On dogs, segueing into cancer, we had an interesting article this week on whether dogs can sniff cancer? Bengaluru-based startup Dognosis is using AI to analyse dogs’ brain activity, respiration and body language, turning their reaction to scent into data. Click on the link to learn more.
Dr. Jayanth Reddy meanwhile wrote on how transplant oncology is rewriting the story of liver cancer, and why surgeons, instead of trying to cut the cancer out of the liver, remove the entire diseased liver and replace it with a healthy one.
In the In Focus podcast, there’s a discussion with Dr. Narayana Subramanian about cancer ‘vaccines’ and if will they revolutionise treatment. What are these new therapies and what cancer do they treat? Why are they called vaccines when they don’t actually prevent cancer? How does mRNA tech work and how is AI helpful in this? Will these personalised treatments be available in India any time soon and how expensive will they be?

The Supreme Court on Thursday (September 10, 2026) refused to entertain a PIL raising concerns over the government-run nationwide human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination campaign for adolescent girls to prevent cervical cancer.
A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana said whenever there is a case of incorrect vaccination, ordinary rules of compensation will apply.
"Would you like to withdraw? Do you want us to comment something?" the Bench observed.
"Don't ask us to make harsh observations. If petitioner members are doctors, it's a very very serious issue. It's a question of health of millions of our daughters. And you want to derail this," it said.
The top court orally said that the PIL was filed with an ulterior motive and lacked bonafide.
The lawyer appearing for the petitioner said that he was only pressing on adverse events and compensation, nothing on HPV.
"I am not at all anti-vaccine. My first contention is the way it is being implemented. Second, there is no adverse event mechanism. Whenever there is an adverse event, it must be monitored. There should also be a compensation scheme," the lawyer said.
When the apex court refused to entertain the plea, the counsel withdrew the plea and the matter was dismissed as withdrawn.
The top court was hearing a plea filed by the Universal Health Organisation challenging the manner in which the government-backed HPV vaccination programme is being implemented.
The plea alleged that it violates constitutional guarantees of informed consent, bodily autonomy, transparency and accountability.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched the nationwide HPV vaccination campaign for 14-year-old girls from Ajmer in Rajasthan on February 28.
A single-dose Gardasil 4 vaccine, a quadrivalent HPV vaccine, is being used under the campaign. The injection provides protection against HPV types 16 and 18, which are responsible for cervical cancer, as well as types 6 and 11.

Quick Answer
Apple’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, could give the stagnant foldable market a much-needed push. It may not reinvent the category, but Apple’s reach, software focus, and mainstream appeal could make foldables far more popular.
September is here and so are the new iPhones. This year at Apple’s Surprise and Shine event, the Cupertino tech giant came with a number of changes, not just in terms of devices but in terms of management too. There was a new CEO – it was John Ternus’ first event as CEO – as well as new Apple Watches, AirPods and, of course, new iPhones too.
The Duo dominates the new iPhones
Even though Apple showcases a number of products during its September event, it is mainly the iPhones that the world waits for. And even in iPhones, it is usually the Pro and Pro Max iPhones that make the headlines (barring the odd occasion when the Air popped up). The plain iPhones are usually pushed to the sidelines and launched as the more “economical”, “affordable” iPhones whose price tags and generally minor upgrades in specs and design are the only things that get them any attention.
For the longest time, we have been feeling for the plain iPhones because they are quite capable and bring in big sales numbers (especially in markets like India, where they are bestsellers) and yet do not get the hype they deserve. Well, this time around, the iPhone Pro and the Pro Max got the taste of this bitter medicine. The two smartphones had to fold (pun intended) and give up all their headline space for the more expensive, exclusive, and most different iPhone since the inception of the original iPhone: the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable iPhone.
With the iPhone Duo, Apple has finally marked its official entry in the world of foldables. It comes with a starting price of Rs. 299,900 in India ($1,999 in the US), which has naturally inspired a tsunami of reinvented kidney jokes and all sorts of comparisons about all that you can buy for that price. It has also got many competing brands scoffing at Apple’s very late attempt at foldables, calling the Duo a “copy”. While some of the criticism and cynicism around the Duo is valid, we think a foldable phone from Apple is just what the foldable market needed to make foldables mainstream. Not because the Duo is an out-of-the-tech-world, never-seen-before, and extraordinary folding smartphone (hey, we haven’t reviewed it yet), but for much simpler reasons.
Ghost of foldables past: A story mainly of Samsung
Samsung is considered by many to be the modern foldable phone pioneer. It was the trailblazer that was responsible for actually bringing in foldable phones that not only landed on the tech moon but also managed to stick around for seven2 years – Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold arrived in 2019, followed by the Galaxy Z Flip in 2020. The brand did not really have a working blueprint that they could have used back then to have perfected their foldables and technology around it, but it enjoyed an early mover’s advantage in the segment and managed to create a very strong reputation for itself. They built a strong rapport with the consumers that none of the other brands could develop, even after launching just as good, just as powerful foldable smartphones.
Following Samsung’s start, many leading tech brands have been surfing the foldable wave for a while now. The OG flip phone master, Motorola; the Android originator Google; the flagship killer OnePlus; the Chinese Apple, Xiaomi; Vivo, Oppo, and others have created foldables with their own touches and twists. Huawei has gone one step further and has launched a tri-fold – a smartphone that folds twice. But even after all this effort, none of them could really be a standout foldable smartphone brand. Only Samsung did.
But in spite of Samsung’s consistency and the efforts of other brands, foldable smartphones have not become mainstream. They have never really made impressive numbers or become popular/common devices. Yes, most of them come with premium price tags, but even those that are relatively affordable – mostly flips or budget foldables (yes, there are some) – have not gained the kind of traction that had been expected. The foldable revolution that many had predicted seemed to have stalled, and apart from a few devices (mainly from Samsung), growth was largely limited.
Apple and the tech snowball effect… could it come to foldables?
Now Apple has stepped into the foldable ring, and while there are many contenders in it already, we think the Cupertino tech giant might get the buzz around foldables going. It has been quite a trend setter in the tech world, and is identified with premium innovation. Features, functions, and devices that existed long before Apple “reinvented” them suddenly became popular once they started shipping with an Apple logo and Apple’s own unique take on them. They not only became mainstream but also often became a common sight on products from other brands as well. Touchscreen phones, apps and app stores, music stores, portrait mode, notches (Dynamic Island), are just some of the products that Apple did not invent, but made a part of
everyday technology.
Of course, every time this happens, the Internet is flooded with techies pointing out how the particular feature or product has been around for years and how Apple is not really innovating or, rather, thinking differently (Apple’s very tagline). Despite all the chatter and gossip around this topic, somehow the feature picks up momentum, and soon enough the world gets interested in knowing how it works and then owning a device that lets them use it. This initiates a snowball effect of sorts, which leads to that feature or device becoming extremely popular.
We will keep it simple: quite often, it basically takes an Apple device or feature to grab mainstream attention. It happened with GUI, MP3 players, ultra-portable notebooks, touchscreen phones, tablets, TWS, smartwatches, and we think it could happen with foldables too. The Duo has the potential to put the seemingly jammed foldable wheels in motion.
It is important to remember that it is not like whatever Apple does just becomes a hit automatically. The brand has a loyal following, but it has released many features, devices, and functions that did not strike a chord with consumers and have faded away. The Apple Vision Pro, HomePod, iPhone Mini and iPhone Plus, the Touch Bar on the Mac…Apple’s failure list is quite long. It may be one of the most successful tech brands in history, but Apple is no tech Midas – there is no real guarantee that the iPhone Duo would be an absolute hit. The stakes are quite high for the Duo, especially given its price tag (which is even higher in India).
It has got the hype, but what would make the Duo click?
Unlike Samsung, Apple has not had to reinvent the foldable wheel. It has had time to read, research, develop, try, and make mistakes, and fix them all, even while observing the efforts of other tech brands. And while the Duo’s design and specs, and indeed, many of its features, are nothing we have not seen before, these are not areas where Apple differentiates itself from the regular crowd. The iPhone Duo needs to bring Apple’s attention to detail when it comes to user experience, and software tuned exactly to suit the needs and capabilities of the device it supports.
We have not yet had the pleasure (or pain) to experience the device but so far, from the looks and the videos on the Internet, we can tell you there are a few things we love about the iPhone Duo – the TouchID on the side (yes, we actually love it), the vertical tool bar for easy access, the matte display layer which makes the crease largely invisible, and yes, of course, the animation that blurs out the side/front screen when the phone is being opened or folded. But it’s not all pink skies and red roses. We are not very convinced by the asymmetrical shape of the device, the insanely high price tag, and, well, even the name. Duo? Really, Apple? We are also really curious about how Apple has worked on apps for the cover display as well as the inner ones.
But these are early days. The iPhone Duo is more than a month away, and we are sure Apple will fine-tune it even further before releasing it. In the meantime, we expect the kidney jokes to continue and even gather momentum, but on the flip side, curiosity will also grow, as we are sure more will be revealed about the device and its features and functions.
The iPhone Duo has generated more buzz about the foldables in a few months than other players in the field got in years, but it is all going to boil down to how well and how differently it works from other foldables. Given the interest levels around it, it might just prove to be the elixir that foldables need.

During a June 2026 congressional hearing, Steiner said a proposed rule would mean the Postal Service would not mail out ballots in states that failed to hand their absentee voter lists to the federal government. The service created the rule to comply with an executive order President Donald Trump signed in March, supposedly to ensure "citizenship verification and integrity in federal elections." Stipulations in the order included the use of secure envelopes with barcodes and a demand that states send their voter rolls to the service for eligibility verification purposes. However …
… The Postal Service confirmed the new rule pertained only to determining voter eligibility in the mailing out of blank ballots, not returning completed ballots. Also, Steiner didn't appear to provide multiple "ways" (plural) to block the delivery of mail-in ballots, as users alleged.
Snopes readers emailed us to ask about this rumor, with some of them attaching a screenshot of a Threads post. The screenshot, showing a partial profile image, read:
Postmaster General has already said there are ways he WILL block mail-in ballots, so… The minute you get your ballot, fill it our and take it to the nearest drop box, usually near libraries. Do NOT mail your ballot through USPS!
Find a BALLOT DROP BOX only !!!!
Please copy this and share on your feed.
(Received via Snopes reader email)
A reverse image search for the same screenshot located users sharing the same image on Facebook, Threads and X.
A Threads search found the original post (archived) matching the partial profile image from the above screenshot. That user presented the claim and the advice to avoid mailing completed ballots on Sept. 2:
(@kirkanthonyb2020 via Threads)
A search on X for similar text located a popular post (archived) from June 25 that contained a version of the claim about the postmaster general, without the advice to use designated drop boxes. That post read, "JUST IN: U.S. Postmaster General CONFIRMS he'll BLOCK mail-in ballots to states refusing to share citizenship and voter data with the Trump administration":
(@jackunheard via X)
On June 24, one day before that X post, Steiner was a witness in a televised hearing before the Senate Homeland Security Committee. During the hearing, Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., asked Steiner, "Yes or no: If a state refuses to turn their absentee voter list over to the federal government, will the Postal Service still mail their ballots under this proposed rule?"
Steiner answered, in part, "Under our proposed regulation, no." (The full hearing is available on YouTube, with pertinent remarks beginning at the 30:37 mark.)
In sum, this rumor about the postmaster general's alleged statements and guidance on voters delivering their completed ballots mixed truth and falsehood.
It's true that, during the June hearing, Steiner confirmed one way the Postal Service might block, or decline, the delivery of mail-in ballots. At the time, Steiner was referencing a proposed rule. The rule
That rule, which may restrict mail-in voting, stemmed from an executive order President Donald Trump — who has repeatedly promoted false claims of massive voter fraud — signed in March. Part of that order mentions of the use of secure envelopes with barcodes. It also stipulates that states that intend to use the Postal Service to deliver mail-in or absentee ballots should send their voter rolls to the service so that it can verify voters' citizenship and eligibility to vote in federal elections.
However, the claim that voters should avoid mailing their completed ballots through the Postal Service and instead directly deposit them into designated ballot drop boxes doesn't accurately reflect what the new rule means in practice. The Postal Service confirmed the new rule pertained only to determining voter eligibility before mailing out blank ballots — not when completed ballots are mailed back in — meaning that while there's nothing wrong with using drop boxes to ensure delivery of completed ballots, the reason some users recommended them was not reflected in the rule.
Additionally, Steiner didn't appear to provide multiple "ways" (plural) to block delivery of ballots, as users alleged.
On Sept. 14,
Snopes contacted the Postal Service to request comment about the rumor, and spokesperson Nikolaj Hagen shared the following statement in an email:
The Postal Service is committed to fulfilling our role in the electoral process when public policy makers choose to utilize us as a part of their election system. We rely on longstanding, robust and tested policies and procedures, which have proven successful in the secure and timely delivery of Election Mail. Through August 28, the Postal Service has delivered 233.3 million pieces of Election Mail nationwide during Fiscal Year 2026, with an on-time score of 97.94%.
White House spokesperson 
'Misinformation and speculation'
In a Sept. 4 news release, Steiner addressed what he called "misinformation and speculation" about the issuance of the Postal Service rule and defended the service's duty to comply with Trump's executive order.
The release also featured a recent whistleblower complaint that warned of "potentially catastrophic problems in the development of the United States Postal Service's new system for handling federal election ballot mail." The complaint specifically referenced the service's new rule establishing a voter verification system that officials would use to determine which voters receive blank ballots via mail.
One part of the complaint alleged that if one barcode on a single ballot in a bulk mailing of 10,000 blank ballots failed to properly scan during the verification process, the entire batch would be rejected and sent back to the state, meaning none of those voters would receive their ballots.
Steiner said the Postal Service "takes these concerns seriously," as well as that, "Regardless of political party or perspective, we share a common goal: ensuring that Americans can have confidence that their election mail will be handled securely and delivered reliably should their election officials choose to use the mail for ballot delivery."
For further reading, we previously reported about the many details of the new Postal Service rule, Trump's executive order and the beginning of the many legal challenges associated with the matter.

In the quest for a seam-bowling all-rounder, particularly when Hardik Pandya’s battle with injuries has resembled a long-running soap opera, India has backed Nitish Kumar for the best part of two years. The 23-year-old from Visakhapatnam has himself had his tryst with injuries of late, but evenings like the one at the Arun Jaitley Stadium on Tuesday will go a long way towards boosting the youngster’s confidence.
Nitish, who has ramped up his speed in recent months, scalped three for 24 in his three overs as Shreyas Iyer & Co. restricted Afghanistan to 159 for eight and clinched a seven-wicket win in 14.5 overs. With it, India took an unassailable 2-0 lead in the three-match T20I series.
After conceding 30 runs in two overs in Sunday’s (September 13, 2026) opener, Nitish needed a productive outing with the ball, especially as he was returning from a quadriceps injury.
If Nitish stepped up, so did Sanju Samson. With 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi watching from the dugout in the first two games, the pressure on the 31-year-old to hold his own as opener is unmistakable in every outing. In the circumstances, Samson responded ably with a belligerent 22-ball 57.
Once again, Jasprit Bumrah set the foundation by starting with a maiden over. Arshdeep Singh reaped the rewards in the next over. Off the left-armer’s third delivery, Rahmanullah Gurbaz’s desperation to get Afghanistan off the mark manifested in a hasty pull. The miscue was pouched by Ravi Bishnoi at mid-on.
After the second-wicket stand between Ibrahim Zadran and Sediqullah Atal accrued 51 runs, Nitish delivered the breakthrough as the Afghan skipper’s heave across the line found deep midwicket.
Bishnoi, who replaced the injured Varun Chakaravarthy, struck shortly after when Sediquulah holed out to Tilak Varma at long-off. More joy came India’s way as Gulbadin Naib skied Nitish to Samson.
A brisk 29-run stand between Azmatullah Omarzai and Darwish Rasooli was laced with lusty blows. Omarzai even had that tincture of luck that every batter needs when Bishnoi spilled an easy chance off Axar Patel’s left-arm spin with the Afghan all-rounder on five. But when both batters departed in quick succession, the Afghans were back in a blind alley at 100 for six in 14.1 overs.
In getting to the total that Zadran & Co. ultimately did, Mohammad Nabi and Rashid Khan displayed their secondary skills. The spin duo, more than capable of chipping in with the willow, put together 48 runs for the seventh wicket.
Will such cameos suffice, however, against this Indian unit? Not on Tuesday’s (September 15) evidence.

Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.
Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.
Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.
The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.
The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.
Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.
The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.
The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.
Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”
The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.
Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”
Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.
Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.
Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.
Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.
“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.
Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

Months after a fractured wrist had healed, a 42-year-old homemaker from Mysuru was still unable to cook or even tolerate the touch of clothing on her hand. Despite repeated investigations confirming that the fracture had healed, she continued to have severe burning pain, swelling, stiffness and changes in skin colour.
She was eventually referred to pain specialists and diagnosed with Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS), in which the nervous system continues to generate pain long after the original injury has healed. With specialised pain management, she gradually regained function and independence.
Pain specialists say such cases highlight the need to recognise chronic pain as a condition that may require specialised care.
At Victoria Hospital, attached to the Bangalore Medical College and Research Institute (BMCRI), more than 1,200 patients have undergone specialised pain-relieving procedures since its pain clinic was established in June 2023. The clinic, run by the Department of Anaesthesia, Critical Care and Pain Medicine, has also provided outpatient consultation to over 4,000 patients.
Public awareness campaign
As September is observed as Pain Awareness month, the Karnataka Chapter of the Indian Society for Study of Pain (ISSP) has launched a public awareness campaign urging people not to accept chronic pain as an unavoidable part of life, but to seek specialised care when it persists beyond the normal healing period.
“Our team led by our head of the department Nethra S.S. has performed over 1,200 advanced pain intervention procedures and has seen over 4,000 patients in the outpatient department,” said Satish Kumar M.N., associate professor, Department of Anaesthesia and Pain Medicine, BMCRI, and treasurer of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP.
The clinical team, comprising associate professor Nethra H.N., assistant professor Harshavardhan H.S., Satish Kumar and Dr. Nethra, treats patients with cancer pain, neuropathic pain, musculoskeletal disorders, spine-related pain, knee and shoulder pain, trigeminal neuralgia and other chronic pain conditions.
Besides image-guided nerve blocks and joint injections, the clinic performs advanced procedures such as radiofrequency ablation, which interrupts pain signals from affected nerves.
Dr. Kumar said the acquisition of a radiofrequency ablation machine had enabled the BMCRI to offer procedures that were previously available largely in corporate hospitals.
Pain is more than a symptom
Sadasivan S. Iyer, consultant and lead, Pain Medicine, Manipal Hospital, Old Airport Road, and vice-president of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP, said a common misconception was that patients should simply learn to live with chronic pain.
“Many patients are told to simply live with pain because investigations do not reveal an obvious cause. But persistent pain can itself be a medical condition requiring specialised evaluation and treatment,” he said.
While acute pain serves as the body’s warning signal after an injury or illness, pain lasting beyond three months can become a condition in itself, he said. The nervous system can continue to transmit pain signals even after tissues have healed. Therefore, normal scans do not necessarily mean that the pain is imaginary, while abnormalities on imaging do not always explain the severity of symptoms.
Beyond painkillers
Pain medicine is not limited to prescribing stronger painkillers. Depending on the condition, treatment may include medication optimisation, physical rehabilitation, psychological support, lifestyle modification and minimally invasive, image-guided procedures such as nerve blocks, epidural injections and radiofrequency ablation.
“The goal is not simply to reduce a patient’s pain score. It is to help them sleep better, return to work, perform daily activities and regain independence. Pain relief is ultimately about restoring quality of life,” said Murali T.S., consultant and lead, Pain Medicine, Apollo Hospitals, Bengaluru, and president of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP.
When should patients seek help?
According to the ISSP, millions of Indians live with persistent back and neck pain, sciatica, diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia, trigeminal neuralgia, cancer pain and pain that continues after surgery.
Specialists advise people to seek evaluation if pain lasts for more than three months, repeatedly returns, interferes with sleep or daily activities, persists despite treatment of the original illness, or is accompanied by burning, shooting or electric shock-like sensations.

In Summary
- Apple’s new CEO John Ternus is expected to take centrestage on 9 September in Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event. This will be
- Ternus’ first appearance in an Apple event since he took over from Tim Cook.
- Apple is expected to launch new iPhones at the event, including the much-talked-about iPhone Ultra, its first foldable phone.
- As the event draws near, we write an open letter to Apple’s new CEO, requesting something that was once very much Apple – being different.
Dear John,
You will shortly be making your first public appearance as CEO at a major Apple event. Over the years, the iPhone launch pretty much sets out the tech agenda for the rest of the year. For the iPhone is not just a tech launch but a trend setter of sorts – it influences which colors, shapes, features, and functions matter in the industry in the coming days. About a decade ago, we would have laughed at the notion of a notch in any device. Until last year, orange was associated more with juice than tech. You get the idea.
Indeed, very few names have influenced our lives in the way in which Apple has over the past few decades. The brand made computers and touchscreen smartphones that were effortlessly easy to use, put thousands of songs in our pockets, created notebooks that could be carried in stationery envelopes, showed us that Bluetooth earbuds could exist without wires, added a third screen to many of our lives in the form of a tablet, got us looking at our watches for more than just the time, made us realize that there was “an app for that…”, and much more. It was seldom the first to come out with a particular product, but it often put a different spin on products, making them easier to use. It was the brand that thrived on its legendary motto, ‘Think Different’. Other brands could match Apple’s features and spec sheet, perhaps, but never the ‘feel’ or ‘vibe’ of an Apple product.
In recent times, however, this Apple feel or vibe has been getting increasingly diminished. Some would say that perhaps an “inspired” (read “copycat”) competition is closing the gap on the market leader. Perhaps. But then, it is not as if competition and “copy and paste” mode did not exist in the past. Remember how Steve Jobs went ballistic at Google for Android, claiming that it had been copied from Apple? “I’m going to destroy Android, because it’s a stolen product. I’m willing to go thermonuclear war on this,” Jobs raged when speaking of the topic, in Walter Isaacson’s biography. But even then, Apple’s products continued to be strikingly different. The competition could offer a similar appearance (camera units, straight sides, similar colors), but beneath that familiar surface, it was clear that they were just knockoffs.
That is no longer the case. Somewhere in its pursuit of market share over the past decade, Apple started losing its mystique, going from Hogwarts to Harvard. The brand’s sales volumes and capital value have shot up exponentially, but all this has come at a creative cost. Apple now seems more a part of the crowd rather than apart from it. Don’t get me wrong. Apple’s products are still very good, but while their pricing is more premium than ever, the products themselves are not as different as they used to be. In fact, in many cases, they do not even seem to be too different from their own predecessors.
The brand that championed “Think DIfferent” has been increasingly thinking similarly of late. From being among the first to popularise graphical UIs, capacitive touchscreens, app screens and face unlock systems, it has graduated to being last in line in the foldables and AI race. It might end up winning both of those contests even now, such is its market domination, but that would be a victory of volumes rather than delivered value, similar to how IBM ended up bossing the PC market in the early eighties even though it was a latecomer. IBM’s motto was incidentally “Think,” and is believed to have inspired Apple’s “Think Different.” Oh, the irony.
There has always been a large section of people who believed that most people who bought Apple products did so just to “show off the logo,” as products from other brands were just as good. For a while, this was a very unfair accusation, as in spite of their premium price tags (even more so in India, because of customs duties, we are told), Apple’s products seemed to be in a totally different league. Today, Apple still has the high ground in privacy and security and its face unlock remains unmatched, but in many other regards (yes, even in apps and interface), the brand seems content to swim in the mainstream, rather than walloping the competition from within its famous “walled garden.”
We are coming to the stage when a lot of people are actually buying Apple products for the logo on them rather than what they do. At one level, it tells us that the Apple brand has such equity that people are willing to invest large amounts in a product because it has an apple engraved on it. At another, it tells us that the products are now being defined by the brand rather than the other way around – a foldable phone is special because it comes from Apple, rather than Apple being special because it made a foldable phone.
Today, Apple is arguably the world’s greatest tech brand, but it has more money than mojo. For other brands, that would be just perfect. But since when was Apple just another brand? Mind you, money is a wonderful thing. After all, it enables one to do things and invest in ideas that don’t have a short-term payback. We did not say that; Steve Jobs did. Well, Apple has the money. Perhaps it is time for it to do things. Differently.
All this is easier said than done, of course. My colleague Akriti Rana recently wrote eloquently of how you now hold not just the reins of arguably the most high-profile tech company in the world, but also bear the burden of two massive, yet contrasting legacies. How you decide to honor them is your choice. You could choose to sail in a sea of successful sameness. Or maybe just spend more time in that walled garden.
Still, as someone whose first ever story in tech was about an Apple product (the iBook in 1999) and who confidently predicted that the first iPhone would fail (and was delighted to be proved wrong) in 2007, I have a request.
I am not asking for slimmer portfolios. Or lower price tags. I am asking for something much more basic – the experience of going to an event without having any idea of what will happen.
Of seeing a product without having seen it being leaked more often than a local municipal pipeline.
Of feeling a sense of wonder while using a product, because there is nothing else quite like it.
Of looking at the Apple logo and thinking of wizardry rather than wealth.
The universe is waiting, John Ternus. Go put a ding in it.
Regards,
Nimish Dubey

Pulley, a software that startups rely on to track their funding, is shutting down after seven years.
The company said in a statement published on its website on Tuesday that it will cease operations after December 8.
Pulley had raised more than $50 million from investors, including Founders Fund, General Catalyst, Stripe, and 8VC. It previously tried to challenge its much larger rival, Carta, in the cap table management business — software that helps companies track who owns shares and issue new equity as they raise money.
As part of the wind-down, Carta has agreed to help move customers and is offering them a limited-time promotion, according to Pulley's statement.
Yin Wu started Pulley after she sold an Android app called Echo to Microsoft in 2015.
"Though this is the closing of one chapter I, along with many of our strongest team members, have no intention of riding off quietly into the night," Wu wrote in a LinkedIn post on Tuesday. "There has never been a better time to solve big problems. For the immediate future, we are focused on working with Carta's team to take care of our customers."
On Tuesday, founders posted screenshots of the email they received from Pulley.
"We have worked diligently to develop a transition plan that ensures you won't experience any disruptions as we cease operations," the company wrote in the email. Customers who move to Carta will be able to keep their current Pulley pricing for the first year, and Carta will credit any unused portion of their Pulley subscription.

National Park Service warns visitors to stay away from elk and black bears - or face the consequences
It’s illegal for parkgoers to get closer than 25 yard from an elk or 50 yards from a black bear
America’s national park lovers should get outside to view majestic wildlife this fall - as long as it’s from a safe distance, officials warned Monday.
There will be increased elk and black bear activity this season, officials at Tennessee’s Great Smoky National Park cautioned.
Wild animals are unpredictable and getting too close can lead to harmful human-wildlife encounters.
Deaths are extremely rare but a handful of park goers have been mauled by protective mama bears and gored by bison in the past few years.
“Enjoy wildlife responsibly by remaining at least 25 yards away from elk and 50 yards away from black bears,” the agency cautioned in a statement.
Part of the risk to humans is related to the time of year. Black bears are feeding on fall food sources ahead of hibernation, consuming up to 20,000 calories a day to build fat reserves that sustain them through the winter months.
That’s why they can be highly active during the autumn months, moving across the park as corns and other fall foods become abundant.
It’s also the annual elk breeding season, known as the rut. During this period, male elk experience elevated levels of the male hormone testosterone, which can lead to heightened aggression toward any perceived threats, including people, vehicles and pets.
Both elk and black bears are seen at parks across the U.S., including Wyoming, Montana and Idaho’s Yellowstone National Park, Washington state’s Olympic National Park and Wyoming’s Grand Teton National Park.
It’s illegal for park goers to get closer than 25 yard from an elk or 50 yards from a black bear, as well as any distance that causes an animal to change its behavior.
“Violations may result in fines or arrest,” the park noted. Fines can range from hundreds to several thousand dollars.
However, many people get too close to park wildlife each year, whether it’s their intent or not.
In July, a grandfather was hurled eight feet into the air by a male bison in Yellowstone, shattering the man’s femur. There have been multiple bear attacks in Glacier National Park including one which led to the death of a Florida man.
People who accidentally find themselves too close to an approaching elk or black bear should slowly back away, the park said.
“If a black bear continues to follow, stand your ground, be loud, throw rocks and continue to back away slowly. If an animal approaches you, it is your responsibility to safely and calmly maintain the legal distance,” officials advise.
Fight back if a black bear is attacking, but find shelter or a strong protective barrier if an elk attacks.
“If nearby shelter is not available, run away,” the park service says.
